Ḥreno mas sowayḏan omar, omar... u goran, hano m be xori Ṣamuyel, Šamʕən əmmiwayle, mḥase hani kmo əšne, omar: "Ḥəkəm d tre mətrowat ʕulyo w ḥəkəm d arbʕo mətrowat pəṯwo, hawxa kšalle ʕal i qalto dag galloye a kṯowe d Mar Doḏo w du gabo di tare dag galloye w hanək kulle marfalle i nuro appe w u mede, d lo yaqiḏi, as sowe ḥrene d maḥkalle, əmmi maḥtənwanne bu mqabəl laltaḥ mi qaraqole w mi qalto dag galloye, me tamo maḥtiwa aʕlayye ba tfənag w bu šəklawo mparpsənne w mtawlfənne."
contents.versio: 007. Ein anderer unserer Alten sagte, nach ..., - dieser stammte aus der Familie des Xori Samuel, Šamən nannte man ihn, er starb vor ein paar Jahren (in Deutschland) - er sagte: Auf rund zwei Metern Höhe und vier Metern in der Breite stapelten sie die Bücher der Mar-Dodo-Kirche und die der anderen Seite des Galloye- _ Dortfviertels auf dem Misthaufen des Galloye-Viertels. Alle diese (Bücher) fackelten sie ab. Und alles, was nicht abbrannte - dies erzählten andere Alte - brachten sie hinunter auf die gegenüberliegende Seite und von der Gendarmerie-Station und vom Misthaufen des Galloye-Viertels, von dort schossen sie auf sie mit den Gewehren. Auf diese Weise zerfledderten und zerstörten sie sie (alle).

contents.textus: 008. W lu goran muqsiye, sawto kətwaylan m be Gawro, haṯe ste maḥkela əmmo, i mḏara du mḥasyo du Eliko be Pəyyoke mliṯo wa hul lu femo, hayo stene kṯowe. Nafili bayne raġle daq qanyonaṯṯe daḥ ḥanfe w dišənne w qṭiʕənne w mḥalqənne, hani kulle msakri w azzehən.
contents.versio: 008. Nach ..., wir hatten eine alte Jerusalempilgerin aus der Gawro-Familie, auch diese hat erzählt und gesagt: Das Gästezimmer des seligen Eliko be Pəyyoke, auch dieses war voll bis zum Anschlag (lit.: voll bis zur Öffnung) mit Büchern. Sie fielen unter die Füße ihrer Rinder, der Ungläubigen. Sie zertrampelten sie, zerrissen sie und warfen sie weg. Alle diese (Bücher) sind verloren gegangen, sie sind (unwiederbringlich) weg. .

contents.textus: 009. ʕAm aṯe kətwaylan lfuṯ di sohduṯo das sobe traḥsar ngalyune ra, kṯiwe bi ḥəbro du dahwo, mede, d kətwalle qime, d qime rab me dəṯṯe, d latwa, maḥtənne, səmwalle bi umonuṯo d meqəm, xəzna bayn lu šuro du maḏbḥo d Mar Doḏo w lu šuro di maʕmodiṯo, šuro faṯyo, kibe mətro w falge zəd, mede hawxa yo, ftəḥwalle gawe du šuro, m ayna gabo lo koḏaʕno w b umonuṯo ġalabe ḥəssas maḥatte a traḥsar kṯowani w ġalabe sefoqe mqadše di ʕito stene tamo w tə nošo lo koḏaʕ, tarʕo yo.
contents.versio: 009. Zudem hatten wir, nach dem Zeugnis der Alten, zwölf Evangeliare aus Pergament, geschrieben mit goldener Tinte, so dass es nichts Wertvolleres gab als sie. Sie. (d.h. die Dorfbewohner) legten sie ... Sie hatten nach der damaligen Handwerkskunst eine Schatzkammer in die Mauer gebaut - zwischen die Mauer des Altars des Mar-Dodo und die Mauer des Baptisteriums. Die Mauer war breit, sie maß anderthalb Meter oder mehr, etwa so breit. Die Dorfbewohner hatten die Mauer ausgehöhlt, ich weiß nicht von welcher Seite, und legten dort diese zwölf Evangeliare dit.: Bücher) und auch viele geweihte Gefäße der Kirche, mit größter Sorgfalt (lit.: in einer sehr empfindlichen Art), hinein. Niemand konnte erkennen, dass (dahinter) eine Tür steckte.

contents.textus: 010. Šamošo me diḏan ewangeloyo, aloho, aloho ʕofele, hawi ṭayo w hano, bətr me d hawi ṭayo, maqəlle ʕal i xəznaṯe w məlle: "Kito xəzna d kṯowe, e, kito xəzna harke, mak koḏaʕ, mək kito eba." Yaʕni d maḥle ruḥe baṭ ṭaye.
contents.versio: 010. Einer unserer Erzdiakone, Gott, Gott möge ihm vergeben, konvertierte zum "Islam. Nachdem er Muslim geworden war, hat dieser dieses Versteck (lit.: Schatz) verraten. Er sagte: Es gibt einen Bücherschatz, nein, es gibt hier einen Schatz, wer weiß, was sich darin befindet! Dies tat er, um sich bei den Muslimen beliebt zu machen.

contents.textus: 011. Qam, ftəḥhe u šuro w mofaqqe a kṯowani w hanək ste, mə ǧarəlle, lo kəḏʕina, bas u mede, d koḏaʕno, haṯe bi sohduṯo d babi, i naqqa u Šamʕən be Ḥaydo, d kətwa b Mor Aḥo, hiye w tre gabre ḥrene azzehən laf ele, mḥalaqla li ʕaskar ʕal u quṣro d Sarḥano b Bemanʕəm, Saroxano zbəṭwayle tre ngalyune mani, məlle: "Komwahadno ʕam Aloho, i naqqa d ʕərmo Bsorino, a ngalyunani d Bsorino gmalḥaqnanne l Bsorino.
contents.versio: 011. Dann öffneten sie (d.h. die Muslime) die Mauer und holten diese Bücher heraus. Auch vom Schicksal dieser (Bücher) wissen wir nichts. Was ich aber weiß, dies nach der Aussage meines Vaters, als Šamən be Haydo" in Mor Aho lebte, waren er (d.h. mein Vater) und zwei weitere Männer ihm zur Hilfe gekommen. (Sie sahen, dass) das Militär das Schloss des Sarohano, bzw. Saroxano, in Beman'am?*, angegriffen hat. Saroxano hatte zwei von diesen Evangeliaren an sich gerissen und gesagt: Ich schwöre vor Gott, sobald Bsorino wieder aufgebaut ist, werde ich diese Evangliare Bsorinos nach Bsorino zurückbringen (lit.: gelangen lassen).

contents.textus: 012. Hiye stene bi xayəntiye qṭəlwalle, aydarbo hawi, yaʕni latwa ḥaḏiro, mḥalaqla li ʕaskar ʕal u quṣro, ḥzalle, a tre ngalyunani tamo, qayimi, mḥalaqqe ḥa manne li nuro, ṭabʕan ġalabe b maḥisuṯo simiwa w ḥiṣiwa, xayifo i nuro l azza aʕle, mkawzar əšmo, ap palkatayḏe me larwal.
contents.versio: 012. Auch ihn (d.h. den Saroxano) hatten sie hinterlistig umgebracht, wie es auch war, er war nicht anwesend. Die Soldaten griffen das Schloss an und fanden die zwei Evangeliare dort. Sie warfen eines von ihnen ins Feuer. Nun, die Evangeliare aren in hoher Qualität hergestellt und festgebunden, so konnte das Feuer es nicht schnell verbrennen. Seine Blätter wurden ein wenig von außen versengt.

contents.textus: 013. U yuzbaši, d koḥoyar ʕal i ʕaskar, ḥzele, d li ʕaskar mḥalaqla li nuro, mazʕaqle aʕlayye, mofaqle mi nuro w mədle hawo. W u ḥreno ste, a tre midile w məblile r ruḥe.
contents.versio: 013. Der Kommandant (lit.: Hauptmann) beobachtete die Soldaten und sah, dass sie (das Evangeliar) ins Feuer warfen. Er schrie sie an und nahm es aus dem Feuer, und auch das andere, beide nahm er und brachte sie zu sich.

contents.textus: 014. W i naqqa d kətwayno bi dayro d Zaḥfaran, ṣluṯayye ʕaman, ḥasyo Yuḥanən Dolabani baḥ ḥaye w ḥasyo Išəʕ d ʕAmariqa aṯi l tamo.
contents.versio: 014. Als ich im Zafarän-Kloster lernte, lebte Bischof Yuhanan Dolabani noch und der Bischof Isho‘ von Amerika - ihre Gebete mögen uns begleiten — war dorthin gekommen.

contents.textus: 015. Mšayeli sayyədna, hano d ʕAmariqa, omanno hiye, d... xud uʕdo d Shabo mbaḥaswayle ʕal a kṯowe, omanno: "Ngalyun me diḏan yaqə..., mḥalaqqe lu nuro, lo yaqəḏ b Bemanʕəm, mərre, lu yuzbaši, rabo d mo di ʕaskar, mbele hiye w ngalyun ḥreno, d lo mawqaḏ, w msakri, azzən, traḥsar ngalyune kətwaylan, l aḏiʕina, mən ǧarəlle, hani žġayn ma kṯowe ḥrene."
contents.versio: 015. Ich habe seine Exzellenz, diesen aus Amerika, gefragt ... wie jetzt der Shabo, hatte auch er von Büchern gesprochen, ich sagte: eines unserer Evangelien ist verbrannt worden, nein, man hatte es in Bemanəam ins Feuer geworfen, es verbrannte aber nicht ganz. Der Hauptmann, das heißt der Befehlshaber einer Hundertschaft beim Militär, hat dieses und ein anderes, das nicht verbrannt wurde, mitgenommen. Beide sind verloren. Wir hatten zwölf Evangeliare und wir wissen nicht, was aus ihnen geworden ist, ganz zu schweigen von den anderen Büchern.

contents.textus: 016. Hedi u ḥasyo Išəʕ, ṣluṯe ʕaman, omar: "Həngi b ṭimo yo u ngalyunawo, d kəmmat, u mkawzro", — omar, — "b šrolo ba palkat komizaban b ʕAmariqa."
contents.versio: 016. Da sagte Bischof Isho, möge sein Gebet uns begleiten, weil jenes versengte Evangeliar, von dem du sprichst, weil es so wertvoll ist, - so sagte er, wahrlich, - wird es in Amerika blattweise verkauft.

contents.textus: 017. Haṯe ste i sohduṯo d feme du qadišawo d aloho, šaməʕna me feme. U mede, d kətli iḏiʕuṯo ʕal a kṯowe d Bsorino, haṯe yo.
contents.versio: 017. Dies ist die Aussage jenes Heiligen Gottes, ich habe sie aus seinem Mund gehört. Das war es, was ich an Kenntnis über die Bücher in Bsorino habe. .

contents.textus: 018. W kətwaylan stene fanqiṯo rabṯo d kule ḥuḏro šatonoyo, kəpwayla ʕal u mamro, mətro w falgi, balki mede hawxa yarəxto, w kəpwayla ḥuḏre, mətro pṯiṯo w ap palkat ḥlime du kaġat d meqəm, lu goran dak kaṯowe mhire, kṯiwowalle, kule ḥuḏro šatonoyo, me qudoš ʕito, w u ṣawmo w u qayṭo w ab bəṭlone hani kulle eba wayne.
contents.versio: 018. Wir hatten auch eine große Fangito mit den Stundenbüchern für den ganzen Jahreszyklus. Sie war, so heißt es, ca. 1,5 Meter lang und etwa einen halben Meter breit.” Die Blätter waren dick aus Papier von früher. Sie war in der Art der begnadeten Schreibmeister geschrieben. (Sie enthielt) das ganze Jahresbrevier, von der Kirchweih bis zum (Brevier) der Fasten(zeit), des Sommers und der Feiertage, sie alle waren darin.

contents.textus: 019. Səhḏiwa as sowayḏan, əmmi, i naqqa d me qadišo l qadišo mitawblowa, ya maṭaʕniwayla ʕal ḥaṣe d ḥaywan, d ḥmoro mede, ya arbʕo stene maydiwayla bi darbaste kəmminala, baq qayse, maḥtiwayla ʕal aq qayse ṭəʕniwayla me qadišo l qadišo. Hayo stene midalle, simalle hadaf la tfəngaṯṯe, hayo ste ba tfənag mparpəsalle laḥ ḥanfe.
contents.versio: 019. Unsere Alten bezeugten und sagten: Wenn die Fangito von einer zur anderen Kirche gebrachte wurde, wurde sie entweder auf den Rücken eines Lasttieres, eines Esels oder so, geladen, oder vier (Männer) trugen sie auf einer Holzkonstruktion von einer zur anderen Kirche. Auch diese Fangito nahmen sie (d.h. die Muslime) und stellten sie zur Zielscheibe für ihre Gewehr(schüsse). Die je Ungläubigen zerstörten auch diese mit den Gewehren.

contents.textus: 020. Palləke mena, i naqqa d qəṭʕiwayla, lu ʕalʕolo ayko məblole, ḥoli, u Gallo d be Giragos əmmiwayle, oṯewa mu čol, omar: "B šrolo mu ʕalʕolo naḥət palləke manək qumi, ono aṯoyo l Bsorino mu čol, midowayle, məsqowayle lu qriṯo, annaqqa mən ǧəralle, lo kəḏʕina.
contents.versio: 020. Als sie sie zerrissen wirbelte ein Staubteufel einen Papierfetzen daraus (in _ der Luft), wohin brachte er ihn? Mein Onkel mütterlicherseits, Gallo d-be Giragös nannte man ihn, er kam gerade aus der Ebene”. Er sagte: Wahrlich, als ich auf dem Weg von der syrischen Ebene nach Bsorino war, fiel vom Staubteufel einer dieser Papierfetzen vor mir. Diesen (Fetzen) hatte er (d.h. mein Onkel) aufgegriffen und ins Dorf gebracht. Wir wissen also.nicht, was aus (diesen Büchern) geworden ist.

contents.textus: 021. (ST: fayšowa i pallayo?) He? (ST: i palle, d ḥəzyowayle, u warqo, d ḥzele!) i warqo, d ḥəzyowayle (ST: mu ʕalʕolo, d nafilo) mi, mi hnayo, mi fanqiṯo rabṯayo wa, (ST: yani mamṭole li qriṯo w kofayšo) lo, lo kofayšo, ma mə gfayšo, Aloho mhawan!
contents.versio: 021. (ST: War jener Papierfetzen noch da?) Was? (ST: Der Papierfetzen, den er gefunden hatte, das Blatt, das er gefunden hat!) Das Blatt, das er gefunden hatte (ST: welcher vom Staubteufel gefallen war) war aus Dingsda, ... von jener großen Fangito. (ST: Heißt das, dass er es ins Dorf gebracht hat, existiert es noch?) Nein, es existiert nicht mehr, wie soll es noch existieren, Gott möge sich unser erbarmen!

contents.textus: 022. (ST: w abuna, hani, u mede, d maḥkelux, kulle bu zabno du sayfo, du fərman hawən?) Kulle bu zabno du fərman hawən, e, ašər.
contents.versio: 022. (ST: Hochwürden, hat sich das, was du erzählt hast, alles in der Zeit des Sayfo, des Fərman ereignet?) Alles hat sich in der Zeit des Fərman ereignet, ja, glaube mir!

contents.textus: 023. Annaqqa u šamošano, d komannux, ftəḥle (ST: yani u šamošo hiye, meqəm mu fərman hawi ṭayo, wəlla bəṯr?) bu fərman hawi ṭayo! (ST: hiye bu fərman hawi ṭayo, laǧan d lo məqṭəl), bu fərman hawi ṭayo, əmmiwayle u Yaḥqo be Ḥablo, laǧan d mbasam ruḥe baṭ ṭaye, maqəlle ʕal i xəznaṯe, mafatḥole.
contents.versio: 023. Nun dieser Diakon, von dem ich dir berichtet habe, dass er geöffnet hat ... (ST: Nun, ist der Diakon vor dem Fərman oder danach zum Muslim geworden?) Während des Fərman ist er Muslim geworden! (ST: Er ist im Fərman zum Islam konvertiert, um nicht getötet zu werden!) In der Zeit des Fərman ist er Muslim geworden, er hieß Yahgo be Hablo. Um die Gunst der Muslime für sich zu gewinnen, hat er diese Schatzkammer verraten und sie öffnen lassen.

contents.textus: 024. W bəṯr me d lo ḥazi dahwo mede eba, kṯowe, a kṯowe wayne, məlle: "Balki bu qawro du mafaryono kito."
contents.versio: 024. Nachdem darin kein Gold oder so gefunden wurde, Bücher, nur die Bücher waren es, da sagte er: Vielleicht gibt es (Gold) im Grab des Maphrians.”

contents.textus: 025. Hano, u qawro du mafaryono, babi ste shəḏle w as sowe du dawrayḏe stene shəḏḏe, əmmi, mi naqqa d qṭil u mafaryono w d mamṭe l Bsorino, kətwa šəbbak, čučəko wa hawxa, ṭrewalle bu qawra..., bu qabrayḏe w aq qandele d meqəm du... latwayno zayto, ganak... ganak wayne, xud da šroġe, maqəṯṯe qandelo mani w mʕalaqto wa, yaʕni iḏe d ənsanat lo komoṭele, hawxa šəbbak čučəko komadiqi, ḥayri eba, fayišo i qandelaṯe mu ṣlowo du mafaryono, mu qaṭlayḏe w hul lu waxtawo nahərto.
contents.versio: 025. Bezüglich des Grabes des Maphrians, hat mein Vater erzählt und auch die Alten seiner Generation bezeugten und sagten: Seit der Zeit als der Maphrian ermordet und (sein Leichnam) nach Bsorino gebracht wurde, gab es eine Öffnung (lit.: Fenster), sie war so klein, die man in seinem Grab zurückgelassen hatte. —- Die Lampen von früher wurden nicht mit Olivenöl gefüllt, sondern mit Ganak-Öl ..., sie brannten mit Ganak-Öl, wie die Handöllampen. - Man hatte eine dieser Öllampen angezündet, und sie hing (in der Gruft), niemand gelangte dahin, es war eine kleine Öffnung, man konnte nur hineinschauen. Diese Lampe brannte seit der Kreuzigung des Maphrians, seit seiner Ermordung bis zu jener Zeit.

contents.textus: 026. I naqqa di qandelaṯe ṭafyo, kətwaylan tre kohne, i naqqayo xori Gawrie d be ʕAṭoro w qašo Danḥo d be Goge. A trani i naqqa, me d ḥzalle, ṭafyo i qandelo, əmmi: "Swirinoye, ḥaḏeru ruḥayxu, fərman yo. I qandelo du mafaryono ṭafyo, fərman yo aʕlayxu."
contents.versio: 026. Als diese Lampe verlosch, hatten wir zwei Priester, es waren damals Erzpriester Gawriye d-be Atoro und Pfarrer Danho d-be Goge. Als diese zwei sahen, dass die Lampe ausgegangen war, sagten sie: O, Leute von Bsorino, macht euch bereit, es ist ein Krieg. Die Lampe des Maphrians ist ausgegangen, das bedeutet, ‚esist ein Krieg gegen euch im Gange!

contents.textus: 027. Xəd məllan bi qamayto, a swirinoye w di sare, i sare ḥəkmowa ʕal i xaṣra taḥtayto yo, ʕal i ṭayuṯo w ʕal i mšiḥoyuṯo, xəd malko hol lu ḥudud du xatt, w be Gawro ste ḥəkmiwa ʕal u gabo ʕeloyano, hul d moṭe lam maye rabe.
contents.versio: 027. Wie wir bereits zu Beginn über die Leute von Bsorino und von Sare gesagt haben, Sare herrschte über jene südliche Seite, über Muslime und Christen, wie ein König bis an die (heutige) Staatsgrenze, und die Familie Gawro herrschte über dieses obere Gebiet bis zum Tigris.

contents.textus: 028. Yaʕni taḥt iḏe da tre gabe alfowat qəryawoṯe kətwa, i naqqa hanək zəbṭiwa ḥḏoḏe, d makarxiwa dawro, i ṭayuṯo xwa b xwa gqəšʕowa ḥḏoḏe, hənnək gfayšiwa yatiwe. Annaqqa u mḥasyo du Šamʕən zbiṭ, mawbal lu ḥabs w a ḥrene l aḏiʕi, mdabri u šuġlo, ḥariwo baynaṯṯe w mtasalmi a tarte qəryawoṯe laṭ ṭaye.
contents.versio: 028. Das heißt, unter der Macht .der beiden Parteien gab es tausende Dörfer, wenn sie zueinander gestanden und ihre Rolle gespielt hätten, hätten sich die Muslime gegenseitig vernichtet. Nun war aber der selige Šamən gefangengenommen und ins Gefängnis gebracht worden und die anderen haben es nicht verstanden, die Geschäfte zu führen. Sie haben nicht zusammengehalten, und beide Dörfer wurden von den Muslimen eingenommen.

contents.textus: 029. W ʕal d Bsorino kətwa riše du dino me ġalabe qəryawoṯe stene noše aṯila w mə, d lo səmme mede, hedi mayiṯi mu kafno w i qolera w i ḥabo, raḥəq me foṯayxu, čiko baynaṯṯe, u yawmo bam mowat moyaṯwa žġay m du qaṭlo.
contents.versio: 029. Und weil Bsorino als "Haupt des Glaubens" galt, waren auch Menschen aus vielen anderen Dörfern zu ihm gekommen. Nachdem (die Führer) nun nichts (für sie) gemacht hatten, starben (die Menschen) vor Hunger. Die Cholera und die Pest - entschuldigt mich (lit.: möge es eurem Gesicht fern sein) - sind bei ihnen ausgebrochen, und täglich starben Hunderte, zusätzlich zu denen, die (durch Feinde) getötet wurden.

contents.textus: 1. I+qriṯo d̥kəmmina B̥sorino, bu+suryoyo d̥kətyo dəmmina d̥koṯe... əšma ‘Beṯ Sabro’. Yani dukṯo ḥa dmaḥme ruḥe, d̥ṣotar bdukṯo.
contents.versio: 1. The village that we call Bsorino, which in Syriac there are, let’s say, places ... its name is ‘House of Hope’. Like, a place where someone defends himself (lit. ‘a place one that he defends himself’), where he shelters himself.

contents.textus: 2. B̥sorino qriṯo ġắlăbe ráb̥ṯowa. Me zabno ʕatiqo, dəmmina. Aḥna kəmmina, meqəm me Mšiḥo dóṯeste, kətwa aq+qəryawoṯani harke. I+Sare d̥kəmmínala, aḥna kəmmina ‘Gawayto’. A+d̥koṯe kəmmila ‘Sare’, Gawayto, mede ʕmumi.
contents.versio: 2. Bsorino was a very big village. From ancient times, let’s say. We say that even before the coming of Christ (lit. ‘before Christ, that he also came’), these villages were here. The one we call Sare (lit. ‘Sare, the one we call it’), we call ‘Gawayto’. People (lit. ‘places’) call it ‘Sare’, Gawayto, something ‘common’.

contents.textus: 3. Hiya walaye zatan ʕatə́qtowa. Háṯeste dukṯo dәšḳafte, dəmmina, a+šḳaftat di+Sàrewayne.
contents.versio: 3. Anyway, it was an ancient city. This one is also a place of caves, let’s say, the caves were Sare’s.

contents.textus: 4. B̥sorino kə́tlawa qaroye ŭ kaṯowe ġắlăbe. Bwaxt, dəmmina, me ʕatiqo, kə́tlawa qaroye ŭ kaṯowe. Madrašto rab̥ṯo, d̥kə́tlawa kṯóweste ġắlăbe.
contents.versio: 4. As for Bsorino, it used to have many educated people and authors. At the time, let’s say, from antiquity, it used to have educated people and authors. There was also a big school, which used to have many books as well.

contents.textus: 5. Hani a+kṯowayḏan, ínaqqa du+Fərmā̀n, mṣakrilan. Yani, mblənne, ŭ qṭiʕənne, ŭ gniwənne, ŭ muqḏənne, hawxa.
contents.versio: 5. These books of ours, when the Firman (happened), we lost them. Like, they took them away, and they cut them up, and they stole them, and they burned them, like so.

contents.textus: 6. Kətlan, xəd‿məḷḷan, ḥamšo+ŭ+ʕəsri+qadiše bә B̥sorino. Aḥ+ḥamšo+ŭ+ʕə́sriste hēš kopayši.
contents.versio: 6. We have, as we said, twenty-five shrines in Bsorino. The twenty-five still survive.

contents.textus: 7. Ŭ i+ʕito, d̥kəmṣalina uʕdo eba, d̥kul yawmo d̥koṯina, i+ʕito d Mor+Dodo. Dəmmina, ham d̥kətyo u+faġràyḏeste, yani u+qabrayḏe gabáynayo.
contents.versio: 7. The church, in which we now pray, to which we come every day (lit. ‘which every day which we come’), is the Church of Mor Dodo. Let’s say, there is also his remains too, meaning, his grave is at our place.

contents.textus: 8. Hano u+ʕaslayḏe d̥kətwa me Muš, kəmmina Malazgírt, qăza me diḏa. Əšma di+qriṯayḏe Síduswa.
contents.versio: 8. This one, who was originally from Muş (lit. ‘his origin that was from Muş’), we call it Malazgirt, one of its districts. The name of his village was Sidus.

contents.textus: 9. Hiye bəṯr me Mor Barṣawmo, bu+doro dann+ə̀štowa. Qrélewa aḥ+ḥaye d Mor Barṣawmo l Mor+Dodo. ʕAyni aḥ+ḥaye d Mor Barṣawmo abəʕ ʕoyašše.
contents.versio: 9. He lived after Mor Barṣawmo, in the sixth century. He had studied the life of Mor Barṣawmo, Mor Dodo. He wanted to live the same life as Mor Barṣawmo.

contents.textus: 10. ʕAl... dəmmina, i+emo ŭ u+babo Šemʕun ŭ Heleni, sowe ... naʕime dláttewayne. Hánəkste, bi+səbba ddayroyo dhawəlle ḏayfo, əšme du+dayròyoste Dáwiḏwa.
contents.versio: 10. Because... let’s say, his mother and father, Šemʕun and Heleni (were) old ones ... they didn’t have children. Those ones also, because the monk was their guest (lit. ‘because the monk who was their guest’), the monk’s name was also David.

contents.textus: 11. Mšayele, ḥəḷḷe, naʕime latte, ʕəmrayye dmaṭi, dəmmina, bəṯr maḥ+ḥamši, ŭ gəzzewa, azólowa lu+Qudəs.
contents.versio: 11. He inquired, he saw, they didn’t have children, that their age had reached (lit. ‘their age, that it had reached’), let’s say, over fifty, and he would go, he was going to Jerusalem.

contents.textus: 12. Mərre, ‘Kəbʕina ddoʕatlan, dәmṣalat’. Mṣalele ʕal rišayye ŭ azzé lu+Qùdəsste; tamo dʕélalle. Bəṯr tarte+əšne daṯi, kawle naʕimo. Ele ršəmle ŭ maʕmaḏle, maḥatle bəšme Dawiḏ.
contents.versio: 12. They said, ‘We want you to petition for us and pray’. He prayed over their heads, and went to Jerusalem too; he petitioned for them there. Two years later, he came back (lit. ‘after two years that he came back’), and they had just had a child. He signed the cross over him and baptized him, he gave him the name (lit. ‘he put him in the name’) David.

contents.textus: 13. Bəṯərṫə́r ʕəmre d Mor+Dodo, dəmmina, dmaṭi la+traḥṣar, la+tloṯaḥṣar əšne, u+babo māṯ, ŭ bəṯr mayiṯo i+emo.
contents.versio: 13. And after Mor Dodo’s life, let’s say, reached (lit. ‘let’s say, that it reached’) twelve, thirteen years, his father died, and then his mother died.

contents.textus: 14. Hiye qām ṭrele ab+bote, i+zanganayḏe, kulle mpalġile laf+faqire. Azzeyo gab Dawiḏ u+dayroyo. Howewa b̥ Tabriz i+walaye, uʕdo d̥kətyo bu+Irā̀n. Kətwa dayro tamo, pāš tarte+əšne qm‿iḏe.
contents.versio: 14. He up and left the houses, his wealth, he distributed everything (lit. ‘all of these’) to the poor. He went to Brother David. He was in the city Tabriz, which is now in Iran (lit. Tabriz, the city now that is in Iran today). There was a monastery there, he spent two years as his apprentice (lit. ‘at his hand’).

contents.textus: 15. Bəṯr mat+tarte+əšne, komar, u+dayroyo mšanele. Hiye Mor+Dodo, nafəq me tamo, saləq lṭurone, ʕelóyene, tamo du+talgo. Pāš tmone+əšne b̥qarʕe du+ṭurawo.
contents.versio: 15. After two years, it says, the monk departed. He, Mor Dodo left there, he went up to some mountains, they are high, where there’s snow (lit. ‘there, of the snow’). He stayed eight years on top of that mountain.

contents.textus: 16. Bəṯr mәd̥‿pāš tmone+əšne, komar, ad+dayroye di+dayro lə+ḥzalle, laḏiʕi, lo+mšayalle aʕle. Ŭ laḏiʕi dnáfəqste.
contents.versio: 16. After he stayed there eight years, it says, the monks of the monastery did not see him, did not know, did not ask about him. And they didn’t know that he had left as well.

contents.textus: 17. Komar, naqqa, bəṯr me tmone+əšne, rišdayro, u+rišo di+dayro, ḥzele bu+ḥəlmo: kanné am+malaxe d̥kamṭan ṣəfro du+muklo, kamṭalla ldayroyo.
contents.versio: 17. It says, once, after eight years, the abbot, the head of the monastery, saw in a dream: here’s the angels bringing a tray of food, bringing it to a monk.

contents.textus: 18. Mšayele, məḷḷe, ‘I+ṣəfraṯe, lman kəmblútulla?’ Mərre, ‘Hano dayroyo Dawiḏ, meqəm tmone+əšne nafəq me gabayxu. Noše lo+mšayele aʕle, lăǧane kəmblínala’.
contents.versio: 18. He asked, he said, ‘This tray, to whom are you bringing it?’ They said, ‘This monk David, eight years ago, he left your company. Nobody asked about him, we are bringing it for him’.

contents.textus: 19. Xud məḷḷan, ʕabada ʕayni xəd Mor Barṣawmo, d̥fōšwa dayəm bu+qayṭo bi+šəmšo, ŭ boramwa lu+gorā̀n di+šəmšo. Yani, matʕabwa ruḥe bu+saṯwo taḥta tálgewa dăwamli.
contents.versio: 19. Like we said, divine service the same as Mor Barṣawmo, who always stayed in the sun in the summer, he would turn following (lit. ‘according to’) the sun. Like, he would wear himself out in the winter, he was under the snow continuously.

contents.textus: 20. Bəṯr edi qām lu+rišdayro mḥele lu+noqušo, maltamle ad+dayroye, mšayele aʕle, mərre, ‘Ašə́r mínaqqa dmāṯ u+rabayḏe hedi haw ḥzelan’. Qām nafiqi azzə́n lgabe, azzə́n lgabe, ṭləbbe dnoḥat li+dayro.
contents.versio: 20. After that, the abbot up and rang the church bell, he gathered the monks, he asked about him, they said, ‘Really, since his master died, we haven’t seen him any longer’. They up and went out to go to him, they went to him, they requested that he come down to the monastery.

contents.textus: 21. Aṯi li+dayro, ḥəlle kəmyaqrile ġắlăbe. Lo+rḥəmle dәmyaqrile. Qām nafəq me tamo, aṯi harke Roġulo d Gihano, d̥kəmminala, laltaḥ me Midən.
contents.versio: 21. He came back to the monastery, he looked – they revere him a lot. He didn’t like that they revere him. He up and went out of there, he came here, Hell’s Creek, as we call it, below Midən.

contents.textus: 22. Ḥzélele šaqfo tamo, ʕbədle tamo, si+qriṯo d Aspəs. Bəṯr mәd‿әḥzalle lu+ʕamo d Aspəs, d̥kətyo qadišo, myaqarre. Ŭ kalé komanəḥ kayiwe, medone.
contents.versio: 22. He found himself a crag there, he served (God) there, by the village of Aspəs. After the people of Aspəs saw him, that he was a saint, they revered him. And here he is, healing sick people, such things.

contents.textus: 23. Mərre ... ašə́r, əzzé ŭ oṯewa noše ġắlăbe gabe. Dukṯo ʕeláytowa, mərre, ‘Lappe an+noše əzzə́n ŭ oṯən әmbli ak+kayiwaṯte’.
contents.versio: 23. They said ... really, many people went and they would come to him. It was a high place, they said, ‘People cannot go and come to bring their sick people’.

contents.textus: 24. Qām maʕmárralle dayro bi+qriṯo. Ínaqqa dmaʕmárralle dayro, komar, u+waxt dәftəḥḥe u+tămal di+dayro, komar, kurfo pise ġắlăbe dwə́ṣlawa tre+mah... mah+hostawataṯṯe, mayiṯi.
contents.versio: 24. They up and built a monastery for him in the village. When they built a monastery, it says, the time they excavated the monastery’s foundation, it says, a very bad snake bit two of ... two of their craftsmen, they died.

contents.textus: 25. Bəṯr mәd mayiṯi, komar, mərre l Mor Dawiḏ (ínaqqayo hēš Dáwiḏwa, dəmmina, latwa hēš Dodo). Mərre, ‘Ašə́r i+măsale háwxayo’. Məḷḷe, ‘Mṭáwune gabi, ŭ hatu zoxu lu+šuġlaṯxu’.
contents.versio: 25. After they died, it says, they said to Mor David (at that time, he was still David, let’s say, he wasn’t Dodo yet). They said, ‘Really, the problem is such-and-such’. He said, ‘Bring them to me and you go back to your work’.

contents.textus: 26. Qām mamṭanne gabe, ŭ dʕele ŭ mṣalele, baš+šubḥe d Aloho maqimile.
contents.versio: 26. They up and brought them to him, and he petitioned and prayed, through the glory of God, he raised them.

contents.textus: 27. Hedi me tamo ṭləble d̥owe əšme Dodo. Yani, məḷḷe, ‘Lә+košoweno towe xŭd əšmi Dawiḏ u+nbiyo, d̥kətwa lebe d Aloho’. Me tamo maqlable əšme Dodo.
contents.versio: 27. Then from thereon, he asked that his name be Dodo (i.e., ‘Uncle’). That is, he said, ‘I am not worthy to be like my namesake, the Prophet David, who was God’s favourite (lit. ‘heart’)’. From thereon, he changed his name to Dodo.

contents.textus: 28. Pāš tamo ʕəmre hul d̥awi əšti. Bəṯr mann+əšti, komar, Tagrit i+walaye bu+ʕƏraq, mšanélewa lu+ḥasyaṯte, azzə́nwa gab u+faṭəryarxo. Mor Feṭre u+faṭəryàrxowa u+waxtawo.
contents.versio: 28. He stayed there until he was sixty years old (lit. ‘his age, until it became 60’). After [his] sixties, it says, the city Tikrit in Iraq, their bishop departed, they went to the patriarch. Mor Feṭre was the patriarch at that time.

contents.textus: 29. Mərre, ‘Kolozamlan ḥasyo’. E, baš+šubḥe d Aloho dʕele híyeste, mṣalele, ḥzele bu+ḥəlmo d̥kito kalé, dəmmina, dayroyo Dawiḏ, kalé d̥košowe lu+darġawo.
contents.versio: 29. They said, ‘We need a bishop’. Yes, through the glory of God, he too petitioned, he prayed, he saw in a dream that there’s a monk, Brother David, here’s someone who is worthy of that grade.

contents.textus: 30. Qām mšayele me tamo larke, məḷḷe, ‘Zoxu mbálunxuyo. Hawo ksaymínanxu ḥasyo’. Qamayto lábəʕste. Bi+zorik̇a masraḥḥe, səmme ḥasyo.
contents.versio: 30. He up and asked from there to here, he said, ‘Go, bring him for yourselves. We will make that one a bishop for you’. At first, he didn’t want it either. But they ordained him by force, they made him a bishop.

contents.textus: 31. Pāš ʕəsri+əšne b̥ Tagrit, ġắlăbe kayiwe manəḥle. Omar, məd mašəġwa iḏe, marəswa am+maye ʕal ak+kayiwe, ʕal am+medone, noyáḥḥewa.
contents.versio: 31. He spent twenty years in Tikrit, he healed a lot of sick people. It says, when he would wash his hands, he would sprinkle water on the sick people, on things, they would become healed.

contents.textus: 32. Tamo mšanele, ʕəmre, dəmmina, tmoni+əšne. Pāš tamo. Bəṯr mə tmonaʕ̥ṣar+əšne u+abro du+ḥolayḏe, dayroyo Isḥoq, ḥzele bu+ḥəlmo, məḷḷe, ‘Mbayli marke’.
contents.versio: 32. There he departed, his age, let’s say, eighty years. He stayed there. After eighteen years, his uncle’s son, Brother Isḥoq, saw him in a dream, he said, ‘Take me away from here’.

contents.textus: 33. Qām azzé, amṭele me tamo u+faġrayde bgawe d̥sanduqo. Mṭele li+dayrayḏe d Aspəs. Pāš tarte+əšne tamo, bəṯr mat+tarte+əšne ṭləble mene, məḷḷe, ‘Mbayli marke disa, mbayli l Ṭur ʕAbdī́n’.
contents.versio: 33. He up and went, he brought his remains from there inside a chest. He brought him to his monastery in Aspəs. He stayed there two years, after two years he made a request of him, he said, ‘Take me away from here once again, bring me back to Tur Abdin’.

contents.textus: 34. Komar, ínaqqa daṯi, amṭele m Aspəs, d̥xaləṣ ʕal B̥sorino, māṯwa naʕimo... u+rabo di+qriṯo. Ab+botani di+dərto di+ʕito díḏewayne. Əšme du+naʕimo Šémʕunwa.
contents.versio: 34. It says, when he came back, when he brought him from Aspəs, as he passed through Bsorino, a child had died ... the head of the village. These houses in the yard of the church belonged to him. The name of the child was Shemʕun.

contents.textus: 35. Komar mballe li+mәqbăra, ŭ hə́nnəkste mṭalle u+faġro du+qadišo. U+waxtawo, komar, kətwa kohne ġắlăbe bә B̥sorino. Ḥa manne ḥzélewa bu+ḥəlmo, məḷḷe, ‘Gdoṯelan hadiye rabṯo’.
contents.versio: 35. It says they took it to the cemetery, and they also brought the remains of the saint. At that time, it says, there were many priests in Bsorino. One of them had seen in a dream, he said, ‘A great gift will come to us’.

contents.textus: 36. Edi ínaqqa dәḥzalle u+faġro du+qadišo, mšayalle, mərre, ‘Ašə́r u+faġro d̥qadíšoyo. Gәmblínale l Mor+Gabriyèl’.
contents.versio: 36. Then, when they saw the saint’s remains, they asked, they said, ‘Really, it’s a saint’s remains. We will take them to Mor Gabriel’.

contents.textus: 37. Komar qām maḥatte i+laše du+naʕimo ʕal u+faġro d Mor+Gabriyèl. Tamo mṣalalle ŭ dʕalle, maqəmle baš+šubḥe d Aloho. Mərre, ‘Demekki haṯe i+hadiye élanwa, háṯewa gdəṯyowa’.
contents.versio: 37. It says they put the boy’s corpse on the remains of Mor Gabriel. There they prayed and petitioned, he raised him up through the glory of God. They said, ‘So that means this was the gift to us, it is this one that was going to come’.

contents.textus: 38. Afrem: Mor+Gabriyèl, Mor+Dodo?
contents.versio: 38. Afrem: Mor Gabriel, Mor Dodo?

contents.textus: 39. Besim: L Mor+Gabriyèl gәmblílewa hәnnək. Hənnək u+faġro du+qadišo, du+qadišo mṭalle, gәmblílewa ltamo. Edi laqən bә B̥sorino lәḥḏoḏe. I+mәqbărayḏan tamo, láltaḥyo.
contents.versio: 39. Besim: They were taking him to Mor Gabriel. They brought (here) the remains of the saint, of the saint, they were taking him there. Then they (i.e., the funeral procession and the monks with Mor Dodo’s remains) met each other in Bsorino. Our cemetery is there, down below.

contents.textus: 40. Hedi qām mamṭalle, maʕmarre. Maš+šeṯmo, ŭ čaʕ+ŭ+ʕəsrì u+qadišano hul u+waxtano.
contents.versio: 40. Then they up and brought him, they built it. Since 629, this shrine until this time.

contents.textus: 41. Xud məḷḷan, ḥamšo+ŭ+ʕəsrì qadiše kətlan d̥kopayši. U+qamoyaṯṯe d̥kəmmínale Mor Ešaʕyo, Osyo, Mor Osyo. Kanné bi+dərto, hiya i+ʕito+ʕatəqto dә B̥sorino háyoyo.
contents.versio: 41. As we said, we have twenty-five shrines which still remain. The first of them is the one we call Mor Ešaʕyo, Osyo, Mor Osyo. There they are in the yard, that one is the oldest church of Bsorino.

contents.textus: 42. Ŭ qāmlan bә B̥sorino tloṯo+faṭəryarxe, ŭ tloṯo+mafəryone, təšʕo+ŭ+tleṯi+ḥasye, dayroye ḥušwo láttewa.
contents.versio: 42. And there arose for us in Bsorino three patriarchs, three maphrians, and thirty-three bishops, countless monks (lit. ‘monks, there was no counting them’).

contents.textus: 43. Háṯeste, xəd məḷḷan, bann+alfo+ŭ+mo ŭ šwaʕ+ŭ+əštì kətwa komar maṯe+bote mšiḥoye bә B̥sorino ŭ mo+ṭàyewayne.
contents.versio: 43. As for this, as we said, in 1167 there were, it says, two hundred Christian houses in Bsorino and there were one hundred Muslim ones.

contents.textus: 44. Hawə́lle probleme, ʕayiši bayn ḥḏoḏe, haw aṯən lәḥḏoḏe. Mərre la+mšiḥoye, mərre laṭ+ṭaye, ‘Ya hatu šqalu sahmayna, gnəfqina mi+qriṯo, ya hatu hawu sahmayxu, aḥna g̊šuqlínale ŭ hatu nfaqu mi+qriṯo’.
contents.versio: 44. They had problems, they lived amongst one another, they were no longer in agreement with each other (lit. ‘they no longer came together’). The Christians said, the Muslims said, ‘Either take our part, (then) we’ll leave the village, or you give away your part, we’ll take it and you leave the village!’

contents.textus: 45. Komar aṭ+ṭaye b̥ḥila mətfakarre, mərre, ‘Uʕdo gəmzabnina sahmayna, gəzzano ldukṯo mani, bəṯr šato disa gduʕrina bi+zorik̇a lә B̥sorino’.
contents.versio: 45. It says the Muslims thought duplicitously, they said, ‘We’ll sell our part now, we’ll go to one of these places, after a year we’ll return again to Bsorino by force’.

contents.textus: 46. Komar, aṯənwa u+waxtawo bәtraḥṣar+reṭle du+dahwo. Reṭle ánnaqqa mə́qqawayne, kilówatwayne, sə́ṭlewayne du+dahwo, mə́nwayne. Aṯən lәḥḏoḏe.
contents.versio: 46. It says, they came that time with twelve pounds of gold. Now then, pounds, how much were they: they were kilos, they were buckets of gold, whatever they were. They came to an agreement (lit. ‘they came to each other’).

contents.textus: 47. Komar, maltamme ldә B̥sorino u+dahwaṯṯe, komar, naqəṣ əšmo mene, lawi tēr dəṯṯe. Azzə́n l Mor+Gabriyèl, ṭləbbe me Mor+Gabriyèl dahwo. Mkamalle u+dayno, húwanne ŭ mofaqqe aṭ+ṭaye mi+qriṯo.
contents.versio: 47. It says, those of Bsorino gathered their gold, it says, it was a little less than it, it was not enough. They went to Mor Gabriel, they requested gold from Mor Gabriel. They fulfilled the debt, they gave it to them and drove the Muslims from the village.

contents.textus: 48. Payiši, kətlan... hēš kəmmínale u+diyā̀r daṭ+ṭaye, i+dukṯo d̥payiši, yani. Mǧarabbe ġắlăbe waxtən dʕəbri li+qriṯo. Mḥarabbe diḏan, lə+ṭralle ʕəbri. Aq+qadìšeste, dəmmina, ṣə́trawayne.
contents.versio: 48. They stayed, we’ve got... we still call it the abode of the Muslims, the place where they stayed, that is. They tried many times to (re-)enter the village. Ours fought back, they did not let them (re-)enter. Also, the saints, let’s say, were the defense.

contents.textus: 49. Edi aṭ+ṭayanək nafiqi, qām naḥiti baq+qəryawoṯe das+suryoye ŭ maḥrawwe. Ŭ uʕdo kanné b̥ Súriya, hēš kəmmənne as+Saləhiye. I+ʕašərtàyḏanyo, čunku kətlan ṭáyeste ŭ čalkoye harke, kəmmənne as+Saləhiye. Hēš kopayši hanək tamo.
contents.versio: 49. Then those Muslims left, they up and went down to the Christian villages and destroyed them. And now they are in Syria, they still call them the Salihan. It is our tribe, because we’ve also got Muslims and Yazidi here, they call them the Salihan. These ones still remain there.

contents.textus: 50. Hedi ʕal hawxa B̥sorino kul ʕayla ʕal u+daynawo d Mor+Gabriyèl. Hēš kobina, dəmmina, mak+karme nabišóṯene, ŭ mu+săwā̀l gweto ŭ ḥalwo, am+medonani. U+daynawo maqbelan ʕal ruḥayna hul l ʕolam.
contents.versio: 50. Then, for this reason, Bsorino, every family is in that debt to Mor Gabriel. We are still giving, let’s say, they’re raisins from our vineyards, and from our cattle cheese and milk, these things. That debt we have taken upon ourselves in perpetuum.

contents.textus: 51. Yani kul Swirinoyo lazəm kul šato obe u+daynawo d Mor+Gabriyèl. Yani hēš kəmdawmina hayo. Ŭ kul ʕáylaste obowa u+naʕimayḏa, u+bəkkər, l Mor+Gabriyèl, tamo d̥qore, dyolaf ŭ d̥owe dayroyo. Nuḏrólewa ltamo. ʕAl haṯe qṓmlanwa dayroye ŭ ḥasye, medone ġắlăbe.
contents.versio: 51. Like, every Bsorinian has to pay this debt to Mor Gabriel every year. Like, we still continue this. And every family would give their child, their firstborn, to Mor Gabriel so that he could study there (lit. there so that he study), learn there and become a monk. It dedicated him to there. Therefore, monks and bishops would arise for us, many things.

contents.textus: 52. Ŭ B̥sorino ínaqqa du+Fərmā̀n kə́tlawa, Mor+Dodo tabi rab maṯe, rab mu+šəklànowa. Dəmmina, ġắlăbe rab̥ṫərwa. Hawiwa dáyroste, d̥payšiwa ad+dayroyoṯo eba bwaxt, u+ḥasyo eba, kul mede.
contents.versio: 52. And Bsorino, in the time of the Firman… Mor Dodo was, of course, bigger than this one, bigger than this form. Let’s say, it was much bigger. It used to be like a monastery, where the nuns would stay at the time, the bishop in it, everything.

contents.textus: 53. Ínaqqa du+Fərmā̀n, kə́tlanwa ḥa+šamošo+swiʕo. Qaləb híyeste; hawi ṭayo. Yani hak̇a maz+zuʕ̥ṯe, ŭ hak̇a mu+hno qaləb̥.
contents.versio: 53. At the time of the Firman, we had one full deacon here. He converted, too; he became a Muslim. Like, either out of fear or out of whatsit he converted.

contents.textus: 54. Mərle, ‘Toxu, kətte tarte+xə̀znat, ḥḏo manne u+qawro du+mafəryono Šemʕun’, dməḷḷan i+qəṣṣayḏe. Bəṯr, hiye baḥ+ḥayàyḏeste, səmle ġắlăbe ʕəǧubát. Bəṯr məd maḥat bu+qawràyḏeste, səmle ʕəǧubát ġắlăbe, dəmmina.
contents.versio: 54. He said, ‘Come, they have two caches, one of them is Maphrian Šemʕun’s grave’, whose story we told. Then, when he was still alive, he performed a lot of miracles. And even after he was put in his grave, he did many miracles, let’s say.

contents.textus: 55. Madʕalle… naqqa u+naḥlo di+‘qadišat Aloho’, aš+šamoše d̥ṭaʕan, hiye mu+qawro dmadʕalle.
contents.versio: 55. He responded…when the melody of the Trisagion, when the deacons forgot (lit. ‘the deacons that forgot’), then he responded from the grave (lit. ‘he from the grave that he responded’).

contents.textus: 56. Ŭ d̥kətwa bahro ebe, dəmmina, maḥatte mann+alfo ŭ šwaʕmo ŭ arbʕi hul lann+alfo ŭ čaʕmo ŭ arbaʕ̥ṣar, kəmmi, pāš qayiṯo ebe.
contents.versio: 56. And that there was a light in it, let’s say, they put him (there) in 1740 until 1914, they say, it stayed burning in it.

contents.textus: 57. Məṛṛe, ‘Kətte tarte+xə̀znat’. Ḥḏo u+qawro du+mafəryono. Ḥḏo kə́tlanwa dukṯo da+kṯowe, bayn lu+maḏәbḥo ŭ li+ʕito. Komar hani ak+kohne ŭ aš+šamoše+swiʕe tăne əḏʕə́newa.
contents.versio: 57. They said, ‘They have two treasuries’. One is the maphrian’s grave. Another one, we had a place for books, between the altar and the church (i.e., the nave). It says, these, only priests and full deacons knew about them.

contents.textus: 58. Kə́tlanwa traʕ̥ṣar+mgalyune, du+dahwo i+kṯawtaṯṯe. Ŭ fanqyoṯe, ŭ ḥusoye, ŭ medone, ḥəšwo láttewa. Komar ínaqqa zatan qṭə́llewa bam+mo+təšʕi, yani qṭə́llewa man+noše di+qriṯo. Edi aṯən mofaqqe a+kṯowe.
contents.versio: 58. We had twelve biblical manuscripts, their writing is golden. The hymnals, prayers, and things, they were countless. It says, by then they had killed ninety percent anyway, that is, they had killed some of the people of the village. Then they came and took out the books.

contents.textus: 59. Komaḥkən diḏan as+sowe yani, dәḥzállewa qṭiʕə́newa, muqḏə́newa. Ab+bašqòqone, am+medonani, kulle, kәmmi, malənwa palək̇at, medone mani.
contents.versio: 59. Our elders tell, like, that they had seen they had tore them apart, they had burned them. The streets, these things, all of them, they say, they filled with pages, those sorts of things.

contents.textus: 60. Ŭ ftəḥḥe u+qawro du+mafəryònoste, mofaqqe. Hēš, komar, i+badlayḏe, kul+mede aʕle, tə+mede lo+ǧarila. Ŭ maḥatte harke, šməṭṭe i+badlayḏe, pliġalle baynә‿ḥḏoḏe.
contents.versio: 60. And they opened the grave of the maphrian as well, they took him out. Still, it says, his suit, everything on him, nothing happened to it. And they put him here, took his suit off, and divided them among themselves.

contents.textus: 61. Bəṯr edi waxt, daṯən, dəmmina, as+sowe, disa. Naqqa ḥreto d̥pāšwa manne, maḥatte disa u+faġrayḏe bdukṯe. Xud məḷḷan, a+kṯowe, am+medone azzehən.
contents.versio: 61. A bit after then, when they came, let’s say, the elders, again. Once more, whatever had survived from them (i.e., from the pillagers), they again put his remains in his place. As we said, the books, the things were gone.

contents.textus: 62. Haṯe, d̥kəmmina, bann+arbaʕ̥ṣar, dhawi u+Fərmā̀n. B̥sorino lo+ṣafyo. Mḥarabla tlaṯ+əšne, noše lo+qadər aʕla.
contents.versio: 62. This, as we say, is in ’14, when the Firman happened. Bsorino was not cleansed. It fought for three years, nobody could prevail against it.

contents.textus: 63. Bəṯr me tlaṯ+əšne hənnək ḥariwi lәḥḏoḏe, d̥kəmmínanne be Ḥaydo ŭ be Gawro. Be Gawro zatan dә B̥sorínone, be Ḥaydo di+Sàrene. Šamʕune Ḥaydo, u+waxtawo Šamʕune Ḥanna Ḥaydo bu+ḥàbbəswa, d̥kətwa… u+rabo di+dukṯaṯe u+aḥuno u+Màlkewa.
contents.versio: 63. After three years, they soured on each other, the ones whom we call the Ḥaydos and the Gawros. Anyway, the Gawros are from Bsorino and the Ḥaydos are from Sare. Shamoun Ḥaydo, at that time, Shamoun Ḥanne Ḥaydo was in prison at that time, so there was ... the leader of this place was his brother Malke.

contents.textus: 64. Híyeste, u+Malke, zatan harke b̚ Mor+Dodo qṭəlwa. Ŭ am+mədhoye ŭ Tamárz, kəmmina, ad+Derà, aq+qəryawoṯani kulle latimiwa harke.
contents.versio: 64. As for him, Malke, anyway, he was killed here in Mor Dodo. The Midənites and Tamarz, we call it, the Derans, all the villages had gathered here.

contents.textus: 65. Ba+šwaʕ̥ṣar edi xalyo, yani pāšwa kmo. Hániste dmidə́nnewa greʕe lruḥayye, medone. Hul laš+šeṯ ŭ ʕəsri B̥sorino payišo ḥaruto. Čikiwa ṭaye. Bəṯr maš+šet ŭ ʕəsri edi disa məṛṛe, ‘Kul+ḥa doʕar li+dukṯayde’.
contents.versio: 65. Then in ’17 it was empty, that is, a few had remained. These ones too, they took them as servants for themselves, things (e.g., shepherds, cowherds, ploughmen, farmers). Until ’26, Bsorino stayed ruined. Some Muslims had sneaked into it. After ’26, then they said again, ‘Let everyone return home (lit. ‘to his place’).

contents.textus: 66. Daʕiri a+Swirinoye. Aġlab diḏan azzənwa l Súriya ŭ lu+ʕƏràq. Howənwa ʕaskar, bu+ʕƏràq du+Ingilə̀zwayne, b̥ Súriya d̥ Fránṣawayne.
contents.versio: 66. The Bsorinians returned. Most of us had gone to Syria and Iraq. They would become soldiers, they were in British Iraq, they were in French Syria.

contents.textus: 67. Bəṯr baš+šeṯ ŭ ʕəsri daʕiri, naqqa+ḥreto dʕamiro, hul la+tmone+ŭ+ʕəsri. Ba+tmone+ŭ+ʕəsri, d̥kəmmina, u+taḥqibàt d̥ Ḥáǧowa, gĕrek tmone+ŭ+ʕəsri aw šeṯ+ŭ+tleṯi? Komaṇṇo, ba+tmone...
contents.versio: 67. After ’26, they returned, so it got built up again, until ’28. In ’28, as we say, Ḥaǧo’s pursuit, it must have been ’28 or ’36? I would say in ’8…

contents.textus: 68. [AA: Šeṯ+ŭ+ʕəsri d̥ Ḥáǧowa] ... tmone+ŭ+ʕəsri, tmanyo+ŭ+ʕəsri. Hano qāmwa mqabəl di+dawla, ḥa rabo dak+kurdən, xd‿uʕdo di+PKK, d̥kəmmina.
contents.versio: 68. [AA: ’26 was Ḥaǧo’s deal] ... ’28, ’28. He had rebelled against the government, a leader of the Kurds, like now one of the PKK, as we say.

contents.textus: 69. Amma ánnaqqa sə́mmewa, məṛṛe, ‘Hano kosotar baʕ+ʕitawoṯo ŭ bad+dayre, bam+medone’. ʕAl‿awxa i+dawla dəryowa aʕ+ʕitawoṯo, am+medone.’ Háṯeste d Mor+Dodo dəryállewa bad+dĭnamitat i+ʕito.
contents.versio: 69. But at that time, they had done it, they said, ‘This one shelters in the churches and the monasteries, in the things’. That’s why the government would blow up the churches, the things. They had blown up this one of Mor Dodo too with dynamite, the church.

contents.textus: 70. Payišowa lann+alfo+ŭ+čaʕmo+ŭ+ḥḏo+ŭ+ḥamši ḥaruto. Naqqa+ḥreto d̥səmme Qašo Gallo, ínaqqayo Ḥasyo Ḥanna Dolabániwa.
contents.versio: 70. It had stayed ruined until 1951. Once more, they made Father Gallo (i.e., they ordained him), at the time it was Bishop Ḥanna Dolabani.

contents.textus: 71. Bi+mʕawanayḏe maʕamralle. U+maḏəbḥo rabṫə́r mánowa, ʕayni xud u+ʕulyo di+ʕìtowa. Ŭ čik̇e mdagašṫərwa i+ʕito. Naqqa+ḥreto ftiḥalle li+ṣluṯo.
contents.versio: 71. With his help, they (re-)built it. The altar was bigger than this one, it was the same height as the church (i.e., the nave). It was a bit more changed, the church. They opened it once again for prayer.

contents.textus: 1. Hiye, xәd dməḷḷan, Mor Baséliyos šemʕun u+Manǝʕmoyo. Aḥna .. kito aḥ+Ḥabsoye, kṯuwwe kṯowo aʕle. Kəmmi me Ḥábsəsyo. Aḥna, u+mede d̥kuḏʕina Manəʕmoyo kəmmínale.
contents.versio: 1. He, as we said, is Mor Basil Simon the Manʕamite. We… there are Ḥabsәseans, they wrote a book about him. They say he is from Ḥabsәs. As for us, the thing we do know is that they call him a Manʕamite.

contents.textus: 2. Kalá i+dayrayḏe harke, qaruto lә Bsorino. I+qriṯo dbe Manʕam, kito i+dayro d Mor Abḥay eba. Haṯe i+dayraṯe, komar, kito tlaṯmo ŭ ḥammǝ́š+ŭ+əštì qeloyoṯo, xud ay+yawme di+šato, eba.
contents.versio: 2. Here’s his monastery over here, near Bsorino. The village of Be Manʕam, there’s the Monastery of Mor Abḥay in it. This monastery, it (i.e., the book) says, there’s three hundred and sixty-five cells, like the days of the year, in it.

contents.textus: 3. Hiye támowa, i+... i+mafәryonuṯayḏe. Bu+waxtàwoste, komar, kətwa ṭáyeste ŭ kətwa ṣuróyeste bbe Manʕam.
contents.versio: 3. He was there, his... his maphrianate. At that time, too, it says, there were both Muslims and there were Christians alike in Be Manʕam.

contents.textus: 4. U+rabo di+dukṯo, di+qriṯo, dəmmina, ḥa ṭáyowa. Əmmíwaynale ʕAvdál Aġá, əšme. Hano kə́tlewa greʕo ṣuroyo, u+greʕano diḏe, u+ṣuroyo, abǝʕ i+qaritayḏe.
contents.versio: 4. The chief of the place, of the village, let’s say, was a certain Muslim. We called him Abdallah Agha, his name. This one had a Christian servant, this servant of his, the Christian, desired his (own) godsister.

contents.textus: 5. Kətwa, dəmmina, ʕlaymṯo mšiḥayto, i+qaritàyḏewa. Abəʕla ṭolabla lruḥe. E, aḥna bu+hno di+ʕito, yani čara layto, zatan lu+hno di+qarito, lu+šroyo di+qarito du+hno. ṭləble mu+Mafәryono. Məḷḷe, ‘Ašə́r čara layto’.
contents.versio: 5. There was, let’s say, a Christian girl, she was his godsister. He wanted to request her (hand in marriage) for himself. Right, we, in the church’s whatsit, like, there is no way, anyhow, according to the godsister’s whatsit, the godsister’s release from the whatsit. He requested (permission) from the maphrian. He said, ‘Really, there is no way’.

contents.textus: 6. Ánnaqqa hano u+mšiḥoyo, u+greʕo du+ṭàyowa. Laṭ+ṭaye kə́ttewa ʕade. Dəmmina kəmmina i+dargəšto, yani u+naʕimk̇o du+ṭayo, ḥa dәmḥalaq ruḥe brax diḏe, mən d̥ṭolab mu+ăġayḏe, komaqbal i+ṭằlăbayḏe.
contents.versio: 6. Now then, this Christian was the servant of the Muslim. The Muslims had a tradition. Let’s say, we call it the cradle, like, the Muslim baby, anyone who stretches out beside him, whatever he requests from his agha, he accepts his request.

contents.textus: 7. Hánoste azzeyo, mḥalaqle ruḥe gab i+dargəšto dəmmina du+ăġà. ṭlǝble, məḷḷe, ‘Ašə́r i+masalayḏi háwxayo: ono kobaʕno, kito k̇ačk̇e ʕlaymṯo, i+qaritàyḏiyo, u+Mafәryono lo+kəmbaraxla’.
contents.versio: 7. This one went and stretched out beside the cradle, let’s say, of the agha. He requested, he said, ‘Really, my problem is like so: for me, I want, there is a young girl, she is my godsister, the maphrian isn’t marrying her off’.

contents.textus: 8. Qām lu+ăġà dəmmina, qrele lu+Mafәryono. Ašə́r lu+Mafәryono məḷḷe, ‘Yani, hīč dasṫər bi+ʕito lu+medano lə+kowe!’ ḥatta məḷḷe, ‘Yani, d̥owe hnoste, u+aḥuno ŭ i+ḥoṯo komibarxi, elo u+qariwo ŭ i+qarito, d̥kətne qariwone, dasṫər bu+medano layto’.
contents.versio: 8. The agha, let’s say, up and summoned the maphrian. Really, the maphrian said, ‘That is, by no means is there ever permission in the church for this thing!’ He even said, ‘That is, even if it were a whatsit, the brother and the sister get married, but a godbrother and a godsister, who are godsiblings, there isn’t any permission for this thing’.

contents.textus: 9. Mən d̥səmme ebe lo+mbarxile. Qām komar, hano mšāʕle u+ăġà... dәmmina kətwa u+ʕmiro dab+Boṭa dәmmina, d̥ḥokamwa ʕal i+bolga dәmmina di+ṭayuṯo kula.
contents.versio: 9. Whatever they did for him, he wouldn’t marry them. Then it says, the agha sent him, let’s say, there was the Emir of Bohtan, let’s say, who ruled over the region, let’s say, of all of Islam.

contents.textus: 10. Hano howewa bә Gziro, qām komar, kṯulele maktū́b̥ lu+ʕmiro daṭ+ṭaye. Lu+ăġano mǝḷḷe, ‘Hano kəmḥaram u+muklayḏan, ŭ komoḥe bi+ṭayuṯo, kul+mede di+ṭayuṯo kəmbahdela. Yani, lǝ+komaqbal mede mdi+ṭayuṯo’.
contents.versio: 10. This one was in Cizre, then it says, he wrote a letter to the Emir of Muslims. This agha said, ‘This one prohibits our food and he strikes at Islam, he dishonours everything about Islam. That is, he doesn’t accept anything from Islam’.

contents.textus: 11. Qām mšāʕle u+Mafәryono lgab u+ʕmiro dab+Boṭa. Mšāʕle u+maktūb̥ste. Komar, ínaqqa lu+ʕmiro dәqrele u+maktub, məḷḷe, ‘Hano demekki mqabəl di+ṭayùṯoyo’. Ŭ mə́ḷḷele, ḥatta məḷḷe, ‘Mən muklo dmaḥtat qume, u+baṣro ŭ am+medonani, gəmḥaramme, lǝ+g̊oxalle’.
contents.versio: 11. Then he sent the maphrian to the Emir of Bohtan. He also sent the letter. It says, as soon as the Emir read it, he said, ‘This one, it means, he is against Islam’. And he said to him, he even said, ‘Whatever food you put in front of him, the meat and these things, he prohibits them, he won’t eat them’.

contents.textus: 12. U+waxtàwoste, komar ṣawmo+ràbowa. U+Mafəryono zatan... dəmmina ak+kohne, ṣayómene. Komar, qām sə́mlele muklo. Kul+šəkl dab+baṣrone maḥatle qume.
contents.versio: 12. And that time too, it says, it was Lent. And the maphrian, anyway... let’s say the priests, they are fasting. It says, he up and made him some food. All kinds of meat he put in front of him.

contents.textus: 13. U+Mafәryono kətwa mnoṯo du+qayso du+Ṣlibo, kəmmi, bәqḏole mʕálqowa. Komar ínaqqa dyatu ʕal u+muklo, məḷḷe lu+ʕmirayḏe, məḷḷe bu+šəkl du+ṣlibo ma məḷḷe, ‘Ma marke oxanno? Ma marke? Ya marke? Ya marke?’
contents.versio: 13. The maphrian had a piece of the wood of the Cross, they say, it was hanging from his neck. It says, when he sat down to eat, he told his emir, he said (making a gesture) in the shape of the cross, didn’t he say, ‘Shouldn’t I eat from here? Here, no? Or from here? Or from here?’

contents.textus: 14. Baš+šubḥe d Aloho, komar, u+muklawo qaləb gelo. Axile komar ṫə+mede, bəṯr komar, húwalle qaḥwe msamamto, štele i+qaḥwe msamamto xud kito bu+Mgalyùn. Komar, ‘Ínaqqa d̥owutu ṭowe ʕam Aloho, mən dobənxu, yani ak+kurfe bila, lo+gmaḏirənxu’.
contents.versio: 14. Thanks to God, it says, that food turned into herbs. He ate, it says, nothing, then it says, they gave him a poisoned coffee, he drank the poisoned coffee as it is in the Gospel. It says, ‘If you are good with God, whatever they give to you, even snakes, they won’t harm you’.

contents.textus: 15. štele i+qaḥwe, lo+ǧarile. Mqatele ʕam a+greʕayḏe, məḷḷe, ‘Áydarbo? Məḷḷi, “Maḥetu samo bi+qaḥwe!”’ Bi+ḥarayto, hiye azzé maḥatle samo ġắlăbe bi+qaḥwayḏe. Mǧarable naqqa+ḥrètoste, lo+ǧarile mede.
contents.versio: 15. He drank the coffee, it didn’t happen to him. He struck his servant, he said, ‘How? I said, “Put poison into the coffee!”’ Finally, he himself went to put lots of poison into his coffee. He also tried once more, nothing happened to him.

contents.textus: 16. Komar ṭləble mene, mǝḷḷe, ‘Gdəmmatli uʕdo zmīrto, yani gdəmmatli qolo ʕal ... yani ... mede hawxa ... ʕal i+ṗire lə+kowe d̥owe mede eba’.
contents.versio: 16. It says, he demanded from him, he said, ‘You’ll sing me a ballad now, like, you’ll sing me a hymn about… like... such a thing... about women, it can’t be that there’s anything in it’.

contents.textus: 17. Uʕdo kətle i+lavìž, dǝmmina kṯawto dmirole haṯe bu+kurdoyo, dəmmina bu+k̇urmanǧì, ġắlăbe basə́mtoyo, ʕal u+Mawto, ŭ ʕal i+Gihano, ŭ ʕal aḥ+Ḥaye, mirole hawxa b̥k̇elik̇e meqəm ruḥe.
contents.versio: 17. Now, he has the Lavij, let’s say, a text that he said in Kurdish, let’s say, in Kurmanji, it’s very nice, about Death, about Hell, about Life, he said it like so in a moment on his own.

contents.textus: 18. U+ʕmiro məḷḷe, ‘Ašə́r, hano zlām qadíšoyo, yani ġắlăbe ṭáwwoyo’. Qām marfele, marfele məḷḷe, ‘Zuxyo’.
contents.versio: 18. The Emir said, ‘Really, this man is a saint, like, he is very good’. Then he released him, he released him, he said, ‘Go!’

contents.textus: 19. Qām aṯən, hiye, ŭ kə́tlewa ḥásyoste lu+mafәryono qəm iḏe. Kəmmina maṭən larke li+Sare, kətwa Be Manʕam, mi+Sare kiba tlaṯ+saʕayat raḥəqto. Komar, ‘Ṭawəʕ u+yawmo, ʕatəm’.
contents.versio: 19. Then they came, he, and the maphrian had a bishop too at his service (lit. ‘hand’). We say they arrived here at Sare, Be Manʕam was there, it’s (lit. ‘it contains’) three hours from Sare. It says, ‘The sun set, it got dark’.

contents.textus: 20. Komar məḷḷe, ‘Ašə́r záḥmeyo dmoṭina, yani, əzzano bu+ʕətmano bu+darbano’. Komar, lu+Mafәryono mṣalele, dʕele, məḷḷe lu+yawmo, ‘Ya Yawmo mbarxo, kobaʕno d̥kolat hul dmoṭina li+dukṯayḏan’. Komar kali u+yawmo tamo, ŭ malaxxe hul dmaṭən li+dukṯaṯṯe.
contents.versio: 20. It says he said, ‘Really, it is difficult for us to reach, like, to go in this darkness on this road’. It says the maphrian prayed, he petitioned, he said to the sun, ‘Oh, blessed Sun, I want you to stop until we reach our place’. It says, the sun stopped there, and they walked until they reached their place.

contents.textus: 21. Komar bəṯr məd maṭən, hano ánnaqa u+ʕAvdál Aġá, dəmmina d̥kətwa harke b Be Manʕam, komar ḥzele ddaʕər, ʕaǧəz ġắlăbe. Komar bəṯr hiye naḥət li+qamaytayḏe.
contents.versio: 21. It says, after they arrived, this one then Abdallah Agha, let’s say, who was here in Be Manʕam, it says he saw that he returned, he got very angry. It says, then he went out to meet him.

contents.textus: 22. Qām qṭile u+Mafәryono, ṣlule bu+šəkl... dəmmina, ʕal qayso, bu+šəkl dә Mšiḥo ṣlule, u+mafәryònoste ŭ u+ḥasyàyḏeste aʕme.
contents.versio: 22. He up and killed the maphrian, he crucifed him like (lit. ‘in the way of’)... let’s say, on a piece of wood, he crucified him like the Messiah, not only the maphrian but also his bishop with him.

contents.textus: 23. Komar, bəṯr mәd̥‿šamiʕi a+mšiḥoye, komar, a+swirinoye azzehǝn damṭən u+faġrayḏe, dәmmina. Hənnək, ann+arboye, kalá i+qriṯo d Árboste tamo, qayiṯi b̥qarʕe dәḥḏoḏe. Mqatalle ʕal u+faġro du+mafәryono.
contents.versio: 23. It says, after the Christians heard, it says, Bsorinians went to fetch his remains, let’s say. They, the Arbans, there’s also the village Arbo there, they went head-to-head (lit. ‘they touched each other’s heads’). They fought over the remains of the maphrian.

contents.textus: 24. Bəṯrṫə́r komar kətwa dayroye tamo. Mərre, ‘Toxu mḥalqina pəšk̇ layna d̥qoyaṯ’. Mḥalaqqe pəšk̇, qāṯ u+mafәryono u+faġrayḏe elan. Ŭ u+ḥasyo qāṯ lann+arboye, ŭ amṭalle larke xud məḷḷan.
contents.versio: 24. Even later it says there were monks there. They said, ‘Let’s cast lots for whichever one it falls (lit. ‘it touches’)’. They cast the lots, the maphrian, his remains fell to us (lit. ‘touched us’). And the bishop fell to the Arbans, and they brought him here as we said.

contents.textus: 25. Bəṯr mәd maḥatte bu+qàwroste, dәṭralle bahro, dəmmina, dә... šroġo qaṯto bu+hnayḏe, hul ínaqqa du+Fərmā̀n, kəmmi fayišo qaṯto. Naqqa ṭaʕən u+naḥlo di+‘qadišat Aloho’, komar, lu+mafәryono mu+qawrayḏe madʕaḷḷe.
contents.versio: 25. After they had put him into the grave, left a light of, let’s say, a lit lamp in his whatsit, until the moment of the Firman, they say it remained lit. When they forgot the melody of the Trisagion, it says, the maphrian responded to them from his grave.

contents.textus: 26. U+faġràyḏeste, ínaqqa dmofaqqe, kǝmmi hēš yani lo+ḥaruwa u+faġrayḏe, u+hnayḏe. Edi mu+waxtawo kalé gabayna. Kətle kṯowe ele biḏe dәkṯiwile, kanné hēš b̰ Mor Awgín, diḏe di+kṯawtayḏe.
contents.versio: 26. As for his remains, when they took them out, they say his remains, his whatsit, still hadn’t decayed. Since that time, it’s there with us. He has books that he wrote with his own hand, they’re still in Mor Awgin, his autographs (lit. ‘his from his writing’).

contents.textus: 27. ǧġeni mi+mafәryonuṯayḏe, hiye ʕobádwaste, xud ad+dayroye dmeqəm, waxt mālwa ruḥe, dǝmmina li+ʕabada, lam+medone lrúḥeste, ǧġeni mi+mafәryonuṯayḏe. Qadišo mšamho dәkṯule ġắlăbe kṯowe di+tewoloġiya, d̥kətwa qaroyo ġắlăbe.
contents.versio: 27. Apart from his maphrianate, he would also worship, as the monks of yesteryear, when he withdrew himself, let’s say, for divine service, for things for himself too, apart from his maphrianate. A famous saint who wrote many books on theology, who was very much a scholar.

contents.textus: 001. G. Ayko hawət? Ŭ ayko kofayšat aġlab?
contents.versio: 001. Gule. Where were you born? And where do you stay mostly?

contents.textus: 002. ḤD. Bә Kfarze. Uʕdo b Mə́ḏyaḏno. Hani, aṯino, hawi čaʕ+ŭ+arbʕi+əšne daṯino l Məḏyaḏ.
contents.versio: 002. HD. In Kfarze. Now I am in Midyat. Already, I came, it has become 49 years that I came to Midyad.

contents.textus: 003. ḤD. Uʕdo hárkena hūl d Aloho mkamal aʕmayna, dəzzano li+briṯayo, hárkena, aḏiʕat? Yani, layt blebayna mazlo dəzzano, d̚ṭorina ab+botayḏan ŭ hani.  Lo+kəzzano.
contents.versio: 003. HD. For now we are here until God is done with us, until we go to that creation, we are here, you know? Like, we have no intention of going, of leaving our houses and so on. We aren’t going.

contents.textus: 004. G. I+ṣənʕayḏux mənyo?
contents.versio: 004. G. What is your profession?

contents.textus: 005. ḤD. I+ṣənʕayḏi qamayto ono mbayḏónowayno, qalayǧí ŭ sṓmwayno ṣobat. Bəṯr manək səmli tăǧara. Sṓmwayno, šoqálwayno ṭlawḥe, ḥəmṣe, ḥeṭe, hawxa. Bəṯr manək səmli tăǧara dag+galde. Galde. Šeṯ+əšnè səmli ṣobat, ŭ bəṯr mədli lag+galde. Səmli tăǧara dag+galde, TdĕrĭǧĭlikT bu+tərki.  Ono, uʕdo ʕwodo laytli, taqawətno. Ono, uʕdo latli ʕwodo. An+naʕimayḏi, ġắlăbe mənne b Áwrúpane, kətli arbʕo hárkestene. A+ḥrene b Áwrupane.
contents.versio: 005. ḤD. My profession, initially I was a tinsmith, tinner, and I used to make stoves. After those I traded. I used to do, I used to buy lentils, chickpeas, wheat, and such. After those I traded leather. Some leather goods. Six years I made stoves, and afterwards I took leather. I traded leather, dericilik in Turkish. I, now there is no work for me, I am retired. I, I have no work now. My children, many of them are in Europe, I have four children here as well. The others are in Europe.

contents.textus: 006. ḤD. Sṓmwayno bote, hani dak+kefe. Ab+botani uʕdo diḏan eli simili, mʕawnili ah+hōstawin, kətli tre+tloṯo+bote ḥrene xwano, e.
contents.versio: 006. I used to build houses, these ones out of stone. These here houses of ours, I built them, I helped the builders, I have two or three other houses like this one, right.

contents.textus: 007. ḤD. Yani, domannax, aḥna mequm kurxíwayna, mbayḏónewayna, ṣənʕa saymíwayna. Bar+raġle kurxíwayna, lo baʕ+ʕàrabat. ʕÁrabat latwa u+zamanawo. Azzino li+Bəšeriye, azzí las+Səliva, azzí … As+Səliva ḥeḏər Diyarbákərne, ḥeḏər Bə́sməlne. Azzino lad+Deravariye, azzí lab+Báhrava, támoda barimina lar+Rašk̇ota. (Kogoraš, latyo hawxa?). Mar+Rašk̇ota qalibina laġ+Ġarzà. Aġ+Ġarzà dukṯe du+ʕamayḏan dann+armnòyewa. E, hani aġlab ann+armnoye, u+Armenistàn mənne nafəq. Kulle manək, ann+armnoye me tamo nqili azzə́n lu+Armenistàn, aḏiʕat?
contents.versio: 007. HD. Like, let me tell you, back then we used to go around, we were tinsmiths, we used to work. We went around by foot, not by car. There were no cars at that time. I went to Beşiri, I went to the Silivans, I went … The Silivans are around Diyarbakir, they are around Bismil. I went to the Deravari, I went by the Bahrava, over there we turned back to the Reşkotan. (It’s recording, isn’t it?) From the Reşkotan we turned to Garzan. Garzan was a place of our people, of Armenians. Yes, these (were) mostly Armenians, Armenia came out of them. All of those, the Armenians moved from there, they went to Armenia, you know?

contents.textus: 008. ḤD. Azzí: Awrupa. Azzino ḥamməš+šeṯ+šwaʕ̥+kore l Awrupa. Xud mə́ḷḷilax, naʕímene b Awrupa. Azzino l Almanya, azzino l Swičra, azzí l Bálčiqa, azzí l Hollanda, azzino l Făransa. E, yani azzino l šwaʕ̥+tmone+dawwal me d Awrupa, e.
contents.versio: 008. I went: Europe. I went to Europe five, six, seven times. As I told you, there are some children in Europe. I went to Germany, I went to Switzerland, I went to Belgium, I went to Holland, I went to France. Yes, like, I went to seven-eight countries of Europe, right.

contents.textus: 009. G. Azzúx li+ʕaskariye?
contents.versio: 009. G. Did you go to military service?

contents.textus: 010. ḤD. Li+ʕaskariye? Azzino. Azzino li+ʕaskariye, ono bi+ʕaskariye mbayḏónowayno, qalayǧí b Adərna. B Adərna mbayḏónowayno, lo+makuwa noše mini riše ắbadan. Ono mbayáḏwayno as+sefoqe. Oṯənwa, ínaqqa doṯənwa ar+rabe, šuqliwa puwane ġắlăbe mu+ṣənʕa d̥sṓmwayno, e.
contents.versio: 010. HD. Military service? I went. I went to military service, I was a tinsmith for military service, tinsmith in Edirne. In Edirne I was a tinsmith, nobody ever cared about me.  I would mend pots and pans. They would come, when the officers would come, they would take a lot of kudos on account of the work that I did, right.

contents.textus: 011. G. Azzúx li+màdrăse?
contents.versio: 011. G. Did you go to school?

contents.textus: 012. ḤD. Lo! Lo+màdrăse du+tərki azzí ŭ lo du+suryoyo. U+mede dyaləfno, hawxa qafadán yaləfne. E, qafadán yaləfne.
contents.versio: 012. HD. No, I did not go to either Turkish or Syriac school. Whatever I learned, I learned so off the cuff. Yes, I learned off the cuff.

contents.textus: 013. Əšme dǧəddi Málkeyo. Babi – Sawme, muqsi Sawme. Emi – Maqsiye Farida. B Kfarze hawən. Lešono dbabi – səryoyo, émiste səryóyoyo.
contents.versio: 013. My grandfather’s name is Malke. My father – Sawme, Sawme the pilgrim. My mother – Farida the pilgrim. They were born in Kfarze. My father’s language – Syriac, my mother too, it’s Syriac.

contents.textus: 014. GD. Ayna lešone oḏaʕwa babux?
contents.versio: 014. Which languages did your father know?

contents.textus: 015. Babi səryoyo ŭ kurmanji. Ŭ tərkoyo əšmo, ġắlăbe əšmo, Émistene, səryoyo ŭ kurdoyo. Lešono dǧəddi səryóyowa, e. Ǧəddi, əšme Málkewa, u+babo dbabi u+Sawme. U+Sawme bábiwa, ŭ ǧəddi, əšme Málkewa, ŭ u+babo dǧəddi əšme Ḥánnawa, əšmiyo, e.
contents.versio: 015. My father, Syriac and Kurmanji. And Turkish, a little, very little. My mother as well, Syriac and Kurdish. My grandfather’s language was Syriac, right. My grandfather, his name was Malke, the father of my father, Sawme. Sawme was my father, and my grandfather, his name was Malke, and the father of my grandfather, his name was Hanna, it is my name, right.

contents.textus: 016. i+dukṯo dhawən emux ŭ babux?
contents.versio: 016. The place where your father and mother were born?

contents.textus: 017. B Kfarze, ǧə́ddiste.
contents.versio: 017. In Kfarze, my grandfather too.

contents.textus: 018. əšma di+barṯayḏux?
contents.versio: 018. Your daughter’s name?

contents.textus: 019. Maryam, b Kfarze hawyo.
contents.versio: 019. Maryam, she was born in Kfarze.

contents.textus: 020. Ayna lešone koməǧġolat ǧġeni mu+səryoyo?
contents.versio: 020. What languages do you speak apart from Syriac?

contents.textus: 021. Ǧġeni mu+turkoyo kibi koṯawno. ʕárabi  ki… koḏaʕno, hăma kṯawto lo. Komofaqno nofaqno me ḥaq diḏi, yani kibi məǧġəlno ʕarabi, ʕam aš+šaġole, dəmmina, dab+botani d̥simi kulle ʕarabóyene yani mḥalmóyene, ʕarabi məǧġəlwayno aʕmayye. Bas kṯawto lo ʕarabi ŭ lo səryoyo latli.
contents.versio: 021. Other than Turkish; that I can write. Arabic I can … I know it, but writing – no. I produce it, I can handle myself, meaning I can speak Arabic, with the workers, let’s say, of those houses that were built, all are Arabs, meaning Mhallami, I used to speak Arabic with them. But writing, I have neither Arabic nor Syriac.

contents.textus: 022. G. kuḏʕat suryoyo kṯobonoyo?
contents.versio: 022. Do you know literary Syriac?

contents.textus: 023. HD. Ono, u+lišonayḏi səryoyo ṭuróyoyo. Uʕdo aḥna, u+səryoyayḏan d Kfarze ṭuróyoyo. E, ṭuroyo. Dəmmat, Ăḷa, kṯobonoyo flān, bele, kofəhmina, bas lə+gməǧġolina, hno. Ono komaṇṇo, ṭro u+lišonayḏan, u+ṭuroyo, lo+mivayaʕ, aḏiʕat? Lo+mivayaʕ! Ánnaqqa diḏan am+məlfone komaqlbile kṯobonoyo, fawdo ráboyo. Ġắlăbe fáwdoyo. Ínaqqa‿dhawxa maqlbi u+lišono kṯobonoyo, gəmvayʕina u+səryoyayḏan, u+ṭuroyo. U+səryoyayḏan, u+ṭuroyo, ádyawma latyo du+terfiyayḏe. Latyo yani d̥ḥa mtarakle, e.
contents.versio: 023. HD. As for me, my language is Ṭuroyo Syriac. Now then, we, our Syriac in Kfarze is Ṭuroyo. Yes, Ṭuroyo. You might say, gosh, the written type, well, we understand it but do not speak it, sort of. I say, let our language, Ṭuroyo, not get lost, you know? It should not get lost! Now then, the teachers of ours swap it for the written language, it’s a big mistake. It’s very much a mistake. If they swap it for the written language like so, we will let our Syriac, Ṭuroyo, get lost. Our Syriac, Ṭuroyo, ought not be abandoned now. Like, one ought not cast it aside, right.

contents.textus: 024. G. Hat naʕimo, emux aw qaštux maḥkówaylux ḥəkkoyat?
contents.versio: 024. G. Did your mother or your grandmother tell you stories when you were a child?

contents.textus: 025. ḤD. Áydarbo? Xud mən? Xud əmmat, du+Fərman, du+hno…
contents.versio: 025. How? Like what? Like you might say, about the Firman, about the whatsit…

contents.textus: 026. I. Čirok̇at, ḥəkkoyat.
contents.versio: 026. Fables, stories.

contents.textus: 027. ḤD. Čirok̇at, ḥəkkowat hawxa maḥkənwa, qăna ddəmxina blalyo. Gdəmmiwa, ‘Hedi gdəmmanxu čirok̇e, u+dewo aṯi, hawxa səmle, u+taʕlo hawxa səmle…’ Medone flān, hul dəmxíwayna. Madəmxíwaylan, e.
contents.versio: 027. Fables, such stories they used to tell so we would fall asleep at night. They would say, ‘I will quietly tell you a fable. The wolf came, did so and so, the fox did so and so…’ Such things, until we would fall asleep. They would put us to sleep, right.

contents.textus: 028. G. Kibux maḥkat? ḤD. Áydarbo? G. Uʕdo. ḤD. Uʕdo, ḥzelax, konofaq u+hnawo, i+Šange ŭ Pange’. Hawxa medone əmmiwa, medone baṭile.
contents.versio: 028. G. Can you tell one? ḤD. How? G. Now. ḤD. Now, you know, that thing comes out, ‘Shange & Pange’. They would tell such things, useless things.

contents.textus: 029. I. Bas kowe măsálatste. Gule, latyo illakí towe dəmmina čirok̇e. Kibe maḥke taríx, kibe maḥke ḥəkkoyat ḥrene, kibe maḥke, dəmmina, me medone tašәʕyoṯo, medone dǧari briše, dəmmina baq+qәryawoṯe, dazzé lu+šuġlo.
contents.versio: 029. IL. But accounts are also possible. Gule, it doesn’t necessarily have to be what we call fables. He can tell history, he can tell other stories, he can tell, let’s say, some chronicle things, things that ‘came upon his head’, as we say in the villages, as he went to work.

contents.textus: 030. ḤD. Uʕdo, aḥna əzzáwayna dawamli, kurxíwayna baq+qәryawoṯe… M. Ínaqqayo fayšiwa tloṯo+yarḥe.
contents.versio: 030. HD. Now then, we would repeatedly go, we would go around in the villages. M. At that time he would stay three months.

contents.textus: 031. ḤD. Ḥur, kə́twaylan aḥna mədū́r di+banqa. Xalq Banqasí. Aṯi, azzino, mə́ḷḷile, ‘B̥xer aṯat!’ Yatiwina, ǧġilina ono ŭ hiye tarte+saʕayat, lo+marfèleli. Mṭele qaḥwe, ŭ mṭele čaye, ŭ mṭele wasayra. Ŭ mšayele šeyole ġắlăbe mini! Ínaqqa dәmšayele šeyole ġắlăbe, mə́ḷḷile ġắlăbe medone, ġắlăbeste basәmle! Uʕdo, omar... Lo, omaṇṇo, ‘Mədū́r, ono qraye lə+qreli! Me TʕAli Oqul mezunuT no’. Bi+ʕaskariye azzí lu+maktab d ʕAli oqulú əmmíwayle. Tamo yaləfno u+turkoyo, e.
contents.versio: 031. See, we had a bank manager. Halkbank. He came, I went, I told him, ‘Welcome!’ We sat down, he and I spoke two hours, he did not let me go. He brought coffee, and he brought tea, and he brought so and so. And he asked me many questions! When he asked many questions, I told him many things, it pleased him a lot too! Now then, he says… No, I say, ‘Manager, I have not studied a word! I am from Tan Ali School graduateT’. During military service, I went to the school they used to call the Ali School. There I learned Turkish, right.

contents.textus: 032. Ínaqqa dmə́ḷḷile hawxa, qḥīr. ‘Áydarbo’, omar, ‘hawxa kəmmat? Kosaymat ḥănák̇ diḏux ebi?’ ‘Qay’, omaṇṇo, ‘Tmədurum?T’ ‘Yawo’,  omar, ‘ono Tkoskocaman fakulteden mezunum,T ŭ i+mŭdurtiye di... d Xalq Banqasí latyo mede qoláy!’
contents.versio: 032. When I said so to him, he became angry. ‘How’, he says, ‘do you say such a thing? You are pulling a prank on me!’ ‘Why’, I say, T‘my manager?’T ‘For goodness’ sake’, he says, T‘I am a graduate of an immense college,T and the management of Halkbank is not a minor thing’.

contents.textus: 033. Hawxa ele mə́ḷḷeli, ‘Lo+nafəqno rišo aʕmux. Zəd mini … yani am+medone dәmšayeli minux, hulux u+funoyaṯṯe!’ Ḥur, u+funoyo yani kṯobonóyoyo, yani ‘hulux u+ǧŭwabaṯṯe’. Aḏiʕat, bu+ṭuroyo hulan u+ǧŭwabaṯṯe. Ŭ mṭeli i+qănaʕayḏe dloḏáʕwayno turkoyo. Azzino, bi+ʕaskariye yaləfno u+turkoyo, ínaqqa hawxa aṯyo i+qănaʕayḏe, omar, ‘Ġamo layt! Ġắlăbe šafiro!’
contents.versio: 033. So, he told me, ‘I can’t compete with you. More than me … that is the things that I asked you, you gave their response’. Look, ‘response’ is literary, that is, ‘you gave their answer’. You know, we gave their answer in Ṭuroyo. I persuaded him that I did not know Turkish. I went, I learned Turkish during military service, when he became persuaded so, he says, ‘Never mind! Very nice!’

contents.textus: 034. Kito kṯowo, komaydínale, komar, ‘Ma u+ḥa d̥korax ġắlăbe koḏaʕ dobe ǧŭwabat? Yaxut u+ḥa d̥qore ġắlăbe?’ Hiye ánnaqqa məḷḷe. E, omaṇṇo, ‘Ono koḏaʕno mənyo’. Omaṇṇo, ‘Păki’, omaṇṇo,  ‘Ayna u+naʕimo mən məḷḷe hanək?’ Omar, ‘Hat kibux dəmmat?’ Omaṇṇo, ‘Hawo d̥korax ġắlăbe! TGezan bilir!’T Omar, ‘Brawo!’ Ínaqqa dməḷḷe ‘gezan bilir’, šqile puwane lu+zlām, u+qaroyo. Šqile puwane. Yani, u+karoxo, d̥korax bayn u+ʕamo, zəd mu+qaroyo koyolaf.
contents.versio: 034. There is a book, we take it, it says, ‘Does the one who travels a lot know the answers to give? Or the one who studies a lot?’ Now then, he said it. Yes, I say, ‘I know what it is’. I say, ‘Alright’, I say, ‘Which of these did the boy say?’ He says, ‘Can you tell?’ I say, ‘The one who travels a lot. TThe one who travels knows’.T He says, ‘Bravo!’ When he said, T‘The one who travels knows’,T the guy, the student, scored points. He scored points. That is, the traveller, the one who travels among the people, learns more than the student.

contents.textus: 035. E, aḥna hawxa kurxíwayna ġắlăbe. ʕƏmri šwaʕ̥, tmone+əšne hani (hawi u+mede d̥komaṇṇo) ḥamməš+ŭ+əšti, šeṯ+ŭ+əšti, kuzzino bayn… yani, koṯe lboli am+medone d̥saymíwayna, dəzzáwayna bayn i+k̇urmanǧiye, kulle, e.
contents.versio: 035. Yes, we travelled a lot like so. Age seven-eight years, these (what I am speaking about has been happening) sixty-five, sixty-six, I have been going among… like, I remember the things we used to do, (the places) we used to go among the Kurds, all of them, right.

contents.textus: 036. ḤD. Aḥ+ḥaye di+qriṯo, ono koṯe lboli, me šwaʕ+əšne ʕəmri hul uʕdo koṯe lboli. Aḥ+ḥaye di+qriṯo,  əzzáwayna lu+šuġlo ʕam u+ʕamo.  U+yawmayḏan bwáraqa ŭ rúʕowa, aḏiʕat? Bwáraqa ŭ ruʕo ono azzino lu+šuġlo, li+fəʕlayiye. Bas aḥ+ḥaye di+qriṯo, ínaqqayo latwa muklo ġắlăbe, latwa laḥmo d̥ḥeṭe, u+laḥmo dәsʕórewa, Kē ǧayī būna, ṫa fehm k̇ər?K  U+laḥmo da+sʕòrewa.  U+ḥa d̥saymíwayle bu+ṣawmo, čik̇e dlaḥmo dobə́nwanne, haqqa ʕaṣriye uxlíwayna, hawo ʕmírowa, e, hawxa.
contents.versio: 036. HD. The village life, I remember it, from age seven until now I remember it. The village life, we went to work with the people. Our day was at the rate of one and a quarter liras, you know? For one and a quarter liras I went to work, for day labour. But the village life, at that time there was not much food, there wasn’t any wheat bread, the bread was made of barley, Kit had been one made of barley, do you understand?K The bread was made of barley. The one for whom they made it during the fast, a little bit of bread they would give them, we would eat such an amount in the evening, that one was a prince, right, like so.

contents.textus: 037. Ánnaqqa, ma+šwaʕ̥+əšne koṯe lboli, mắsala, ṭlawḥéwayne, gársowa, aḥ+ḥaye di+qriṯo. Ŭ əzzáwayna laq+qayse, kibi domaṇṇo, ham ba+ḥmore əzzáwayna ŭ ham molíwayna ak+karrək̇at, karrək̇at kəmmínanne, hawxa qayse, čuqliyat, ŭ molíwaynanne. Maḥtíwaynanne ʕal kaṯpayna, mṭíwaynanne. Hawxa, yani, aḥ+ḥaye di+qriṯo. Ḥṣódowa, ḥṣódowa. Gera, dyoqo di+gèrawa.
contents.versio: 037. Now then, from age seven I remember, for example, it was lentils, it was cracked wheat, the village life. We would go for twigs, I might say, either we went on donkeys, or we filled bundles, we call them bundles, so twigs, branches, and we filled them. We would put them on our shoulders, we would bring them back. So, like, village life. It was harvesting, it was harvesting. Animal threshing, it was crushing by animal threshing.

contents.textus: 038. ḤD. Ŭ ḥuṣdíwayna, e, əzzáwayna laq+qayse lu+ṭuro, əmṭíwayna ṭaʕne ŭ oṯíwayna qmu+tarʕoste, tawríwaynanne. E, e, emi əmmowa, ‘De, abri, twárene! ʕAl baṭlux, e, yani, hat taʕóbohat… hăma twárene ŭ mbálene lawġul!’ Hul dobíwayli haqqa dlaḥmo. E, háwxawa. E, bašqa, áydarbo dəbʕat, amár! Gdomaṇṇax. E, hani uʕdo u+Alyàs ŭ u+Fahmi hani lə+ḥzalle u+kafnano.
contents.versio: 038. HD. We harvested, yes, we went to the forest for twigs, we brought back loads and came to the door too, we broke them.  Yes, yes, my mother would say, ‘Come on, my son, break them! In spite of your exhaustion, yes, like, you are tired…  break them right away and bring them inside!’ Until they would give me such an amount of bread. Yes, it was like so.  Yes, anything else, however you like, tell me! I will tell you. Yes, these here now, Ilyas and Fahmi, these haven’t seen this kind of hunger.

contents.textus: 039. IL. Ḥolo Ḥanna, ʕal i+šato di+Ġala, koṯe lbolux i+šatayo, lukṯe lbolux?
contents.versio: 039. IL. Uncle Hanna, about the year of the Famine, do you or don’t you remember that year?

contents.textus: 040. ḤD. Lo, lo. Ono bi+Ġala, bi+Ġala ... bat+tarte+ŭ+arbʕi bdela, bann+arbaʕ+ŭ+arbʕi hawino.
contents.versio: 040. HD. No, no. I, during the Famine, during the Famine … It started in ’42 and I was born in in ’44.

contents.textus: 041. IL. Mən mede šamiʕat ʕal u+mede dhawi bi+Ġala, mắsala?
contents.versio: 041. IL. What thing have you heard about the thing that happened during the Famine, for example?

contents.textus: 042. ḤD. Bi+Ġala, domaṇṇux mede, ḥamməš+əšne i+Ġala madəmla. Bat+tarte+ŭ+arbʕì bdela, hăma hăman hul laš+šeṯ+ŭ+arbʕì, aḏiʕat? Ono, ʕəmri arbaʕ+ŭ+arbʕiyo, bann+arbaʕ+ŭ+arbʕì hawino.
contents.versio: 042. HD. During the Famine, let me tell you something, the Famine lasted five years. It started in ’42, approximately until ’46, you know? I am age ’44, I was born in ’44.

contents.textus: 043. IL. Yani, xud əmmat, u+ʕamo məqqa maḏərla li+Ġala, məqqa …
contents.versio: 043. IL. Like, as you say, how much did the Famine damage the people, how much …

contents.textus: 044. ḤD. Maḏərla li+Ġala ġắlăbe. I+Ġala, kibi domaṇṇo, zəd mu+Fərman hne ʕal u+ʕamo səmla, Tetkilema,T ha, məlfono?
contents.versio: 044. HD. The Famine caused much damage. The Famine, I can say, did more whatsits against the people than the Firman, impact, right, teacher?

contents.textus: 045. IL. Mu+kafno?
contents.versio: 045. IL. From hunger?

contents.textus: 046. ḤD. Mu+kafno, mu+hno hawxa. E, hawxa. Yani, səmla, li+Ġala makula u+ʕamo.
contents.versio: 046. HD. From hunger, from the whatsit, like so. Yes, like so. Like, it did, the Famine harmed the people.

contents.textus: 047. IL. Baz+zabnanək ǧġeni mi+Ġala howewa maḥṭašíyatste?
contents.versio: 047. IL. In those times other than the Famine it was also droughts?

contents.textus: 048. ḤD. Əmmiwa i+maḥtašiye. Domaṇṇux, naqqa əzzáwayna li+Babeše lam+maye. Kofəhmat ma mənyo? Me Kfarze əzzáwayna lam+maye. Kə́twaylan ḥa. ‘Yawo’, omar, ‘uʕdo kuzzano lam+mayani, hul lalye du+ʕEḏo… d ʕEḏo+Naʕimo’. Am+maye mi+Babeše, mṭíwaynanne mi+Babeše. ʕÁynoyo si+Yardo. Hăma omar, ‘Uʕdo kalkomṭina am+mayani, hăma ramḥəl ktowe maṭro ŭ talgo… áydarbo gəzzano?’ ‘Yawo, mәd hawi maṭro ŭ talgo, haw … lukṯina, edi  ktowelan maye’. Fahimat mə‿məḷḷi? ‘Ktowelan maye ínaqqayo, ma qay gdoṯina lam+maye?’ Yani, hawxa kətwa.
contents.versio: 048. HD. They called it drought. Let me tell you, once we were going to Babeše for water. Do you understand what it is? From Kfarze we used to go for water. We had a certain man. ‘For goodness’ sake’, he says, ‘Now we are going for this water [every day] until the eve of the holiday, of Christmas’. The water from Babeše, we would bring it back from Babeše.  It’s a spring by Yardo. Now he says, ‘Right now we are bringing back this water, but tomorrow there will be rain and snow… how shall we go?’ ‘For goodness’ sake, when rain and snow have come, no longer … we shall not come, we’ll have water then’. Did you understand what I said? ‘That time we shall have water, why should we come for water?’ Like, it was like so.

contents.textus: 049. ḤD. Am+maye, domaṇṇux, məlfono, saymiwa, am+maye, aǧ+ǧule, latwa. Dəmmat, Ăḷa, xud ádyawma u+yawmo tarte+kore ksoḥən. Kul ḥamšaḥṣar+yawme náqqawa. Kul ḥamšaḥṣar+yawme naqqa soḥənwa. Aǧ+ǧùleste hawxa, aǧ+ǧule ḥewore, ksaymə́nwanne bam+maye, ŭ bəṯr ksaymiwa ak+kome, b̥šun dəṯṯe, bam+mayanək daḥ+ḥewore. Məd sə́mwalle ak+kome, edi maxlənwa ar+rəsnanək, obə́nwanne laq+qanyone. Latwa maye! Maye latwa. Šamiʕat aʕli! Obə́nwanne laq+qanyone, obə́nwanne laq+qanyone. Hawxa, hawxa.
contents.versio: 049. HD. The water, let me tell you, teacher, they did, the water, the clothes, there wasn’t. So to speak, gosh, like today they bathe twice a day. It was once every fifteen days.They used to bathe once every fifteen days. Also clothes like so, the white clothes, they would do them in the water, and then do the black ones in their place, in that water from the white ones. When they had done the black ones, then they would empty that greywater, they would give it to cattle. There wasn’t any water. As for water, there wasn’t any. Did you hear me? We would give it to cattle, we would give it to cattle. Like so, like so.

contents.textus: 050. ḤD. Bas hawxa hawina, dəmmina, me ḥṣar+əšne ŭ afarke da. Bi+qriṯo ʕənwe kətwa, žabaš kətwa, hanək bu+waxtaṯṯe.  Laybux dəmmat … uʕdo ann+arbʕo waxtat di+šato kúlmede kito su+manawǧi, latyo hawxa?  Uʕdo latyo … latwa hawxa sidan. Domaṇṇux, hul dlo+nəfqiwa ab+baǧanat d Eše, da+d̥koṯanək, aḥ+ḥabuše, mṭə́nwanne, mqayḏíwaynanne bəsʕore, aḏiʕat?
contents.versio: 050. HD. But we became so, let’s say, from ten years ago until now. In the village there were grapes, there were watermelons, those in their season. You cannot say … now four seasons of the year there is everything at the greengrocer’s,  isn’t it so? Now it isn’t … it wasn’t so by us. Let me tell you, until the tomatoes of Eshe, of those places, would ripen, the apples, they would bring them back, we would exchange them for barley, you know?

contents.textus: 051. IL. Mḥalfū́twanne.
contents.versio: 051. IL. You exchanged them.

contents.textus: 052. ḤD. E, mḥalfíwaynanne. Štay i+qaḥwayḏux! Man kə́pwayle … kətle qaḥwa? Man kə́twayle čaye? I+čaye, latwa šakar, saymiwa, əmmiwa, ‘Sumu čaye!’ Maḥtiwa dibəs eba! KDəms žber dela šekər danīya čay.K
contents.versio: 052. HD. Yes, we exchanged them… Drink your coffee! Who could…  has coffee? Who had tea? The tea, there was no sugar, they made it, they would say, ‘Make some tea!’ They would put molasses in it. KThey had put molasses instead of, in place of, sugar in tea.K

contents.textus: 053. Fahmi. Qădáḥeste latwa?
contents.versio: 053. F. Were there no glasses as well?

contents.textus: 054. ḤD. E, qădaḥe. Domaṇṇux, lotamwa, glotamwa ʕəsri+tleṯi+ḥamši+šaqṣat bi+ǧәvate, bi+odaye. Uʕdo kətlan odaye, dəmmina, rabṯo, kuzzela ḥamši+šaqṣat, zəd.
