Ánnaqqa, ínaqqa dyətwiwa, amṭənwa ṭaṣe hawxa rabṯo, molə́nwayla maye ŭ gdobewa ḥa biḏe du+ḥreno. Kul ḥa g̥̥̊šotewa pašk̇e, hul d̥taymowa. Latwa xud uʕdo. Uʕdo d̥šoteno ono bu+qădaḥano ŭ k̇elik̇e ḥreto d̥šoteno ebe, an+naʕime gdəmmi, ‘Qayyo?’ ‘Yawo, ma lo u+qadaḥàyḏiyo?’ E, hawxa. Fahimat aʕli?
contents.versio: 054. HD. Yes, glasses. I tell you, some twenty-thirty-fifty persons used to get together, they would get together for an assembly, in a room. Now we have a room, let’s say, a big one, fifty people, more, go to it.   Now then, once they were sitting, they would bring a cup so big, they would fill it with water and one would pass it to the other’s hand. Each one would drink a little bit until it finished. It wasn’t like now. Now, if I drink from this glass, and some other moment I drink from it, the children will say, ‘Why?’  ‘For goodness’ sake, isn’t it my cup?’ Yes, like so. Do you understand me?

contents.textus: 055. SL. Kibux maḥkatlan ʕal an+naʕimayḏux?
contents.versio: 055. SL. Can you tell us about your children?

contents.textus: 056. ḤD. ʕAl an+naʕimayḏi? An+naʕimayḏi, domaṇṇux, kətlan naʕime. Naʕime dan+naʕìmeste kətlan ġắlăbe, ŭ b Awrúpane. Kətlan tarte+k̇ačk̇at harke ŭ tre+abnèwayne. U+məlfono azzeyo, mvayaʕlan, ŭ kətle arbaʕ+k̇ačk̇at sidan. Ha hawo u+abràyḏiyo.
contents.versio: 056. HD. About my children? My children, let me tell you, we have children. Grandchildren, too, we have many, and they are in Europe. We have two daughters here and there were two sons. The teacher is gone, we lost him, and he has four daughters at our place. This is my son.

contents.textus: 057. An+naʕimayḏan ṭawwe, yani problám latlan man+naʕime. Me lebi komaṇṇo, ġắlăbe ṭawwe nafiqi an+naʕime. Komaškrina u+Moryo u+Alohayḏan, tabi uʕdo hano dazzé, twərle lebayna bnaqqa ḥḏo. Kətle arbaʕ+k̇ačk̇at ele, arbaʕ+k̇ačk̇at kətle. Tarte mənne kuzzehən, aḥna kəmmínala ‘fan lisasí’, yani u+maktab ʕeloyo d̥kətyo harke, dəmmina, b Məḏyaḏ, e. Dlowən ap+puwanaṯṯe ʕeloye, lo+kәblәnne lu+maktabawo.
contents.versio: 057. Our children are good, like, we have no problems with the children. I say from my heart, the children turned out to be very good. We thank the Lord our God, naturally now this one that went away, he broke our heart at once. He has four of his daughters, he has four daughters.  Two of them go, we call it a T‘science high school’,T that is the top school there is here, let’s say, in Midyat, right. If their scores are not high, they do not accept them to that school.

contents.textus: 058. Ap+puwane ʕeloye, Fahmi, gəblənne l fan lisasí. Gmatimi u+lisaṯṯe tamo. I+rabṯo da+tloṯo koquryo uʕdo, ŭ i+naʕəmto du+ḥa, yani dnaʕəm mina. At+tarte ḥrene harke kuzzə́n. An+naʕimayḏan a+ḥrene b Awrúpane. A+ḥrene an+naʕimayḏan mašallá ṭáwwene, ŭ kətte naʕime, gawiri an+naʕimàṯṯeste. E, škur mine d Aloho.  Hə́nnəkste, twīr lebayye ʕal u+aḥunaṯṯe, yani ġắlăbe, e, hawxa. Šewole dhowelux mede ḥreno, ksaymina hedi hedi.
contents.versio: 058. The top scores, Fahmi, they accept them to a science high school. They will finish their high school there. The eldest is studying in the third year now, and the youngest in the first, that is, the one younger than her. The other two go here.  Our other children are in Europe. Our other children, thank God, are good, and they have children, their children got married too. Yes, thank God for it. They too, their heart broke on account of their brother, like, very much, yes, like so. The other questions that you have, we will deal with them little by little.

contents.textus: 059. ḤD. Ono məḷḷi bu+šàwṭoste, ʕəmri me tmone+əšne əzzíwayno ʕam a+mbayḏone. ʕƏmri ḥamšaḥṣar+əšne, hawino mbayḏono.  Čaləšqánwayno ono, yani šaġólowayno ġắlăbe, ġắlăbe šaġólowayno. ʕƏmri ḥamšaḥṣar+əšne, azzino li+byaḏa šan ruḥi, e. Ŭ bəṯr azzino li+ʕaskariye. Bi+ʕaskarìyeste mbayḏónowayno. B Adərna mbayáḏwayno, e. Ǧġer mi+byaḏa tə+šuġlo lo+səmli bi+ʕaskariye. Yani, dəmmat, Ăḷa. Mən domaṇṇo, dars, yatim, flān behvān lə+ḥzeli, lo? .
contents.versio: 059. HD. I said a while ago as well, from age eight, I used to go with the tinsmiths. Age fifteen, I became a tinsmith. I was diligent, like, I was a workaholic a lot, I was very much a workaholic. Age fifteen, I went tinsmithing for myself, yes. And then I went for military service. During military service as well I was a tinsmith. I used to tinsmith in Edirne, yes. Other than tinsmithing I didn’t do any other work during military service. Like, so to speak, gosh. What should I say, studies, basic training, such-and-such things, I didn’t see any of it, right?

contents.textus: 060. Mə‿saymina? Mede … Škur mine d Aloho, disa u+amro d Alóhoyo. Ŭ Ăḷḷah u+zʕurayḏi dləzzewa, briṯo kula díḏiwa. E, u+zʕurayḏan dazzeyo, twirina čik̇e… ġắlăbe, ġắlăbe twirina ebe, yoqsa ma ono... U+māl ġắlăbe, ġắlăbe koqoṭal u+moro. Towe normál, dayne, dlowe ʕal ḥa… ŭ bote ... u+baytayḏe dowe ṭawwo flān, komakfe, komakfe!
contents.versio: 060. What can do we do? Anything … Thank God, once again this is God’s will. And, by God, had not my son passed away, the world would be my oyster. Yes, our boy who passed away, we were broken a little, a lot, we were broken a lot because of him, or else wouldn’t I have… Wealth really, really takes away the life of its owner. If it is normal, debts, if it doesn’t fall upon someone … and houses… if one’s house is good, and so on, it’s enough, it’s enough!  (01.42)

contents.textus: 061. ḤD. Kətwa meqəm bi+qriṯayḏan, barbaríyewa. Aṣ+ṣuroye flíġewayne. Yani a+mšiḥoyayḏan flíġewayne. Hən bi+xaṣràyowayne ŭ hən payo, daṭ+ṭaye. Ŭ howewa qalat ġắlăbe. Howewa qaṭle, howewa ġắlăbe medone bu+zamanawo, e,  hul‿ani kmo+əšne, hani kmo+əšne. TḤáqqatanT u+ʕamo čik̇e kali, ġắlăbe ṭáwwoyo, lu+gorā̀n dmeqəm. Lu+gorā̀n dmeqəm, ġắlăbe ṭáwwoyo u+ʕamo. E, ašə́r.
contents.versio: 061. Once in our village there used to be, it was partisanship. Christians used to be divided. Like, our Christians used to be divided. Some were on that side and some on that one, of the Muslims. And it was a lot of quarrels. It was murders, it was many things at that time, right, until these however many years, these however many years. TReally,T the people calmed down a little bit, it is very good, compared to before. Compared to before, the people are very good. Yes, really.

contents.textus: 062. IL. Ma bu+zabnawo, dínaqqa dəzzóxu li+byaḏa, ḥolo Ḥanna, rəšwone, byaḏa, ṣobat…
contents.versio: 062. IL. At that time, when you used to go to tinsmithing, Uncle Ḥanna, packsaddles, tinsmithing, stoves. . .

contents.textus: 063. ḤD. Ono laṣ+ṣobaṭ ŭ li+byaḏa azzí, rəšwone lo+səmli.
contents.versio: 063. HD. I went for stoves and tinsmithing, I did not make packsaddles.

contents.textus: 064. IL. Păki, mən ǧorewa brišayxu? Áydarbo ʕayšútuwa ḥaye tamo?
contents.versio: 064. IL. Alright, what happened to you guys? How did you live your lives there?

contents.textus: 065. ḤD. Yaho naqlawoṯe fayšíwayna kafine, aḏiʕat?
contents.versio: 065. HD. For goodness’ sake, sometimes we remained hungry, you know?

contents.textus: 066. IL. Gab man fayšútuwa? Mən šəkl ʕayšútuwa? Áydarbo šuġlútuwa?
contents.versio: 066. IL. With whom did you stay? In what way did you live? How did you work?

contents.textus: 067. ḤD. Saṭ+ṭaye! Yawo, saymíwayna … hawxa domaṇṇux, əzzáwayna. Aq+qәryawoṯe iḏíʕewayne, əḏʕíwayna, dəmmina, bi+qriṯaṯe noše lə+kḥowe noše. Saymíwayna dăbara aʕlayye, hawxa. Ono ŭ u+Nəʕmowayna ʕam ḥḏoḏe, dbe Qačo. Kuḏʕatle lu+Nəʕmk̇o dbe Qačo?
contents.versio: 067. HD. With Muslims. For goodness’ sake, we would make- … so I’ll tell you, we used to go. The villages were well-known, we knew, let’s say, in this village nobody hosts anybody. We make-believed for them, so. Nəʕmo and I were together, the Qačo family one. Do you know Nəʕmk̇o Qačo?

contents.textus: 068. IL. Šaməʕno əšme, bas lo+koḏaʕne.
contents.versio: 068. IL. I have heard his name, but I don’t know him.

contents.textus: 069. ḤD. ʕAm ḥḏoḏe əzzáwayna laṣ+ṣobat. Ánnaqqa, azzán yawmo l Be Narín. ‘E, Ăḷḷáh, m Be Narín’, əmmi, ‘noše lә+kḥowelan’. Omaṇṇo, ‘Klay! U+muxtā̀r manyo?’ Mšayeli mu+naʕimo dmaṭínale. ‘Flānkasyo, flān’. ‘Áynayo u+baytayḏe?’  ‘Haweník̇eyo!’ Aṯina qmu+tarʕo… ‘Šōš! ‘KBәrazī! Bārḗ xwa dayna!K (ḥat u+ṭaʕno! Šlomo aʕlayxu!) KRožawa b̥xer!K’
contents.versio: 069. HD. We would go together for stoves. Now then, once we went to Be Narín. ‘Yes, by God, from Be Narín’, they say, ‘nobody will host us’. I say, ‘Wait! Who is the headman?’ I asked the boy whom we encountered. ‘It is so and so, etc.’ ‘Which is his house?’ ‘It’s over there’. We came up to the door. ‘Whoa! KNephew! Put down your load!K’ (Put down the load!) ‘Hello! KGood afternoon!K’

contents.textus: 070. Maḥatlan u+ṭaʕno. Oṯewa maṭro. E, kətte hno, bote ha hawxa, i+xaṣraṯe ŭ haṯe odayatne, ŭ u+ṣalòn hawxa bu+falġo, ġắlăbe ... Ŭ maḥatlan bu+ṣalon+rabo as+sefoqayḏan, ŭ azzano li+odaye, ‘KŽxwá žә malēna’.K U+Nəʕmo omar, ‘Hak, Ḥanna, mə‿səmlux?’, omar. ‘Yawo!’, omaṇṇo, ‘e, kəmmat dlowe hawxa, lə+kḥowəllan’. Ḥa drišux, fayišina arbʕo+yawme tamo.
contents.versio: 070. We put down the load. It was raining. Yes, they have a whatsit, such houses, on this side and on this one are rooms and the hall in the middle like so, many… And we put our tools in the big hall, and went to the room. K‘Of course, we are from the house’.K’ Nəʕmo says, ‘Hey, Ḥanna, what have you done?’, he says. ‘For goodness’ sake,’ I say, ‘yes, you might say, if it were not so, they would not host us’. On your life,  we stayed there four days.

contents.textus: 071. IL. Yani, hənnək lo+ḥowənwa, hanək lo+ḥowənwa?
contents.versio: 071. IL. Like, they would not host, those would not host?

contents.textus: 072. ḤD. Yaho, lo+ḥowənwa. Səmlan ruḥayna mu+bayto.
contents.versio: 072. HD. For goodness’ sake, they would not host. We made ourselves at home.

contents.textus: 073. ḤD. U+muklo, u+maštyayḏan, ŭ saymíwayna ṣobat. Yani, ʕawdíwayna, lo+kolìwayna.
contents.versio: 073. HD. The food, our drink, and we made stoves. Like, we worked, we didn’t stop.

contents.textus: 074. IL. Aṣ+ṣobat di+qriṯo kula hatu saymútwanne?
contents.versio: 074. IL. Did you make stoves for the whole village?

contents.textus: 075. ḤD. E, saymíwaynanne. U+ḥa dhowewa aṣ+ṣobatayḏe twire, u+ḥa dobaʕwayle ḥḏo ḥaṯto. Hawxa saymíwayna.
contents.versio: 075. HD. Yes, we made them. The one who was broken stoves, the one who wanted a new one. So we did it.

contents.textus: 076. IL. Me tamo gmatimutu i+qriṯayo, gəzzoxu ánnaqqa ləqriṯo ḥreto?
contents.versio: 076. IL. After you were finished in that village, you would move then to another one?
077. HD. Yes.

contents.textus: 078. IL. E, hawxa hul dəbʕutu.
contents.versio: 078. IL. Yes, so as far as you want.

contents.textus: 079. ḤD. Haṯe, Be Narín, kelayo ʕul mu+Rədwān. U+Rədwān, i+šato du+Fərmān, bări mu+Fərmàn, kətwa ṣuroye bu+Rədwān. Kətwa qašo bu+Rədwàn. U+qašo du+Rədwan, azzeyo ḥa, mḥalaqle ʕal i+qriṯo, mbele hawxa kmo ʕlayme ʕam ruḥe, xorṫín. Məḷḷe, ‘Mbalu u+qašano, mḥāwle, mʔadēble!’ Azzeyo mballe. Mballe u+qašo. Moḥənwa, moḥənwa ʕal gawe. Omarwa, ‘Ay ḥaṣi!’ Ŭ moḥənwa ʕal ḥaṣe. Omarwa, ‘Aloho mozadxu!’ Košəmʕat? Fahimat u+xabrano?
contents.versio: 079. HD. This one, Be Narín, here it is higher than Rədwan. Rədwan, the year of the Firman, before the Firman, there were Syriacs in Rədwan. There was a priest in Rədwan. The priest of Rədwan, someone came, he attacked the village, he brought however so many young men with him, young people. He said, ‘Take this priest, beat him, discipline him!’ He went to take him. They took the priest. They beat him, they beat him on the gut. He said, ‘O, my back!’ And they beat him on his back. He said, ‘May God multiply you!’ Have you heard? Did you understand this word?

contents.textus: 080. ḤD. Aṯən məṛṛalle lu+aġaṯṯe, əmmi, ‘Yawo, lə+ḥzelan hawxa mede. Komoḥina ʕal gawe, komar, ‘ay ḥaṣi!’ Ŭ komoḥina ʕal ḥaṣe, komar, ‘Aloho mozadxu!’ Omar, ‘Lawo, ṭrawu mine! Dhowéwayle, ínaqqa d̥komoḥutu ʕal gawe, dhowéwayle ḥaṣo, lápwalxu moḥutle! Ḥaṣo latle!’ Ŭ ínaqqa d̥komoḥən, ‘moḥutu ʕal ḥaṣe, komar, ‘Aloho mozadxu!’, qăná d̥qayṯutu bәḥḏoḏe!’  Xud uʕdo, ma lo i+ṭayuṯo lo+qayiṯo bәḥḏoḏe?
contents.versio: 080. HD. They came, they told their agha, saying, ‘For goodness’ sake, we haven’t seen any such thing. We beat  him on his belly, he says, ‘Oh, my back!’ We beat him on his back, he says, ‘May God multiply you!’ He says, ‘Guys, don’t mind him! Had he had, when you were beating him on his gut, had he had a backer, you wouldn’t have been able to beat him. He has no backer!’ And when they beat, ‘you beat on his back, he says, “May God multiply you!’, so that you plague one other!’ Like now, have or haven’t the Muslims plagued one another?!

contents.textus: 081. ḤD. E, yani domáṇṇolux, əzzáwayna hawxa laq+qәryawoṯe, ḥozíwayna ʕasqúṯoste. Azzano li+Xanduk̇e, bayn aġ+Ġarzayo, bi+hno, bi… se Xatma, Qarabadrá… hani, Ačk̇a, flān (Ilyas: Bayn ad+Dera, bayn az+Zaxuraniye, as+Saləhiye). U+ḥa+lalyo səmlan (u+bayto d̥kə́twayna ebe), səmlan aṣ+ṣobat, mzabanlan tlaṯ+arbaʕ. U+bayto d̥kənna ebe, húlanle ṣoba. Hule ak+kallawatayḏa, bəṯr omar, ‘Ăḷa, lə+gbaʕna!’  ‘Qay lo+kəbʕatla?’
contents.versio: 081. HD. Yes, let me say to you, we would go like so to the villages, we experienced difficulty. We went to Xanduk̇e, it is among the Garzanians, in the whatsit, in the . . . by Xatma, Qarabadra, these ones, Ačk̇a, etc.  (I. Among the Derans, among the Zaxuranians, the Salehians). One night we made (the house in which we were), we made stoves, we sold three or four. The house in which we stayed, we gave it a stove. He gave its money, afterwards he says, ‘By God, I don’t want it!’ ‘Why don’t you want it?’

contents.textus: 082. Merame. Bu+baytaṯṯe šuqliwa kallawat mənne.
contents.versio: 082. M. In their own home they were taking money from them.

contents.textus: 083. ḤD. Noše lə+ḥzele hawxa!
contents.versio: 083. HD. Nobody thought so!

contents.textus: 084. Yaho, omaṇṇo, aḥna səmlan ṣobat, ay gmaḥtínanne? Law+koʕorən ʕal u+ḥmoro… Ăḷáh, dlo … Mədlan ḥaq diḏa mine… ʕAṣriye, ono ŭ u+Nə́ʕmona, ḥzeli u+zlām. Kəlán yani hawxa bayn i+nvinayḏan, aṯi u+zlām. Kətwa, hawxa saymiwa ay+yanat dmeqəm, layto? Ánnaqqa, tamo saymə́nwanne mu+ṭino, gawayye xalyo, gawayye xalyo.
contents.versio: 084. For goodness’ sake, I say, we made stoves, where shall we put them? They don’t fit on the donkey. By God, unless … We took its value from him.  In the evening, it’s Nəʕmo and I, I saw the man. Here we are, that is in our bed like so, the man came. It used to be, they made the bedsteads of yesteryear like so, wasn’t it? Now then, there they made them from mud, their inside is empty, their inside is empty.

contents.textus: 085. ḤD. Mədle li+sakṯo du+dworo, mḥele tamo, mofaqle tfənge mina. (Merame, ‘Mi+dəkke?’) ḤD. E, mofaqle, omar, ‘Kriv’, omar, ‘lo+zayʕutu! KMa ṭәrsə́nK’ ‘E, ṣabbav, aḥna lə+gzayʕina! Hat qay ksaymat hawxa?’ Naysa, omaṇṇo, ‘Nəʕmo!’ Omar, ‘Mənyo?’ Omaṇṇo, ‘Qәm! I+beǧama áʕluxyo, nfaq larwal. Hul dləḏʕat, mə‿səmle bi+tfəngaṯe, lәkwe dʕəbrat! Dhowat hat larwal, ono lawġul, laybe sōm mede eban!
contents.versio: 085. HD. He took a farming ploughshare, struck there, he pulled a rifle out of it (Merame, ‘From the bench?). HD. Yes, he pulled it out, he says, ‘Mate’, he says, ‘don’t be afraid! KAre you afraid? K’ ‘Yes, son of a bitch, we are not afraid! Why are you doing such a thing?’ Anyway, I say, ‘Nəʕmo!’ He says, ‘What is it?’  I say, ‘Get up! The pyjamas are on you, go outside. Before you know what he did with this rifle, it’s not right for you to come back. If you are outside, me inside, he can’t do anything to us’.

contents.textus: 086. Merame. Laybe qoṭalxu!
contents.versio: 086. He can’t kill both you!

contents.textus: 087. ḤD. Ŭ hiye ánnaqqa mnaḏafle tamo, i+tfənge. Ŭ simole ŭ ftiḥole, ŭ məhnole, walḥásəli, fāš u+Nəʕmo məqṭār! Aṯi u+Nəʕmo, blályoyo.
contents.versio: 087. HD. And he at that time was cleaning it there, the rifle. And he put it together and opened it up, he whatsited it, and, in short, Nəʕmo stayed a little. Nəʕmo came back, it’s night.

contents.textus: 088. ḤD. Hedi aṯi, omar, ‘Ăḷa, mblole, manḥtole tamo, i+xaṣrayo d̥ Qarabadrá, ŭ támoda azzeyo’, flān. Omaṇṇo, ‘De dmax!’ Hawxa, yani, moṭéwaylan zuḥṯo naqqawoṯe, e, Ăḷa!
contents.versio: 088. ḤD. Then he came back, he says, ‘By God, he took it, he brought it down there, that side of Qarabadra, and he went over there’, etc. I say, ‘Go to sleep!’ So, like, sometimes we would get scared, right, by God!

contents.textus: 089. IL. Tahlikat medone hīč lo+ǧari brišayxu? Dəmmina, bălát medone, qeṣe medone lo+ǧari hīč brišayxu?
contents.versio: 089. IL. Have any kind of dangers never happened to you? Let’s say, have any kind of troubles, any kind of accidents never happened to you?

contents.textus: 090. ḤD. E, uʕdo mən komaṇṇux? Ínaqla u+ʕAzo dbe Marre (bu+yawmo mḥase, Ăloho mḥasele) ŭ qašo+Nə́ʕmānste mbayḏónowa. Ono, ŭ u+Šamʕən daḥuni aʕmáyyewayna, lo, naʕle ʕal u+hno, u+Ṣabrik̇o dbe Malok̇e! Aloho mḥase kulle! Yawo, azzano me Hačk̇a l Qarábadrá. Qarábadrá, kətte ab+botaṯṯe hawxa, ṣalibk̇ine. Hawxa i+dərtaṯṯe, ŭ hawxa.
contents.versio: 090. ḤD. Yes, now what shall I tell you? Once ʕAzo Marre (he died recently, God bless him) and Father Nəʕman as well, he was a tinsmith. My brother Šamʕәn and I were with them, no, damn it, Ṣabriko Maloke! God bless all of them! For goodness’ sake, we went from Hačka to Qarabadra. Qarabadra, they have their houses like so, cross-shaped. Such and such a courtyard of theirs.

contents.textus: 091. IL. Áykone, aq+qәryawoṯani áykone?
contents.versio: 091. IL. Where are they, where are these villages?

contents.textus: 092. ḤD. Bayn as+Səliva.
contents.versio: 092. ḤD. Among the Silivans.

contents.textus: 093. IL. Bu+gabo d Diyárbakər yani?
contents.versio: 093. IL. Nearby Diyarbakir, like?

contents.textus: 094. ḤD. Me Diyárbakər ŭ hawxa. E, ʕayəd d Diyárbakərne. Naysa, e, ṭləblan muklo, noše muklo lo+mṭèlelan. Kə́twalle i+aṯto du+šex, ḥzélalan, əmmo, ‘Hosta, qayyo?’ Omaṇṇo, ‘Lә+mṭàllalan muklo, haymǝ́n’, flān. ‘Oooo’, əmmo,  ‘ma‿gəmṭalxu muklo? Noše, med̥‿ṭawәʕ u+yawmo, laybe nofaq mi+qriṯo! Mayko aṯutu?’ Əmmina, ‘ălá, aṯina me Hačk̇a!’ E, naysa, manḥátlalan dawġe. Ṭləblan mina hawxa fako dlaḥmo, axər xilan pašk̇e. E, mə‿saymina?
contents.versio: 094. ḤD. From Diyarbakir and so. Yes, belonging to Diyarbakir. Anyway, yes, we asked for food, nobody brought us food. They had the wife of a sheikh, she saw us, she says, ‘Sir, what’s up?’ I say, ‘They did not bring us food, really,’ and so on. ‘O, she said, ‘who will bring you food? People, when the sun has set, are unable to leave the village. Where have you come from?’ We say, ‘Gosh, we came from Hačka’. Right, anyway, she gave us some ayran. We asked her for such a piece of bread, finally we ate a little bit. Yes, what should we do?

contents.textus: 095. ḤD. Əmmo, ‘Haymǝ́n, doṯutu me tamo, kozayʕono dlo ʔoṯən, a+hne, mḥalqi aʕlayna! Aʕ+ʕašqiya!’ ‘E, ba mə‿saymina?’ Əmmo, ‘Koḥozutu i+dərto? At+tarʕe kulle, ač+čənqalataṯṯe me láwġuldane. Lo+maḥtutu ruḥayxu biḏayye. Ínaqqa dʔoṯən, mahzemu! Tlawu ruḥayxu b̥dәkoṯe!’ Hăḷḷa, Hăḷḷa.
contents.versio: 095. She says, ‘Really, if you come from there, I fear lest they come, the whatsits, they will attack us! Highwaymen!’ ‘Yes, what shall we do? She says, ‘Do you see the courtyard?  All the doors, their hooks are from the inside. Do not surrender yourself to them. The moment they come, flee. Hide yourself anywhere!’ Good grief.

contents.textus: 096. Kətlan ḥmóreste, maḥtilan lawġul. E qay fəlge+dlalyo lə+gnəfqi ab+bexwadiya da+ḥmore, a+tloṯo ḥmore. Hăḷḷa, Hăḷḷa! Nafiqi, ‘Raq, raq, raq, raq’. ‘Hə! B Aloho!’ Omaṇṇo, ‘Tiqo!’  Yawo, áydarbo saymina? U+Šamʕən komar, ‘Klay, moqaḏlux babe dbabayna!’ U+mḥasyo du+ʕAzzo, ‘Dewo, klay! Yawo’. Omar, ‘Klay!’ Naysa, hawxa ġắlăbe hno, ŭ raqqa raq!
contents.versio: 096. We had donkeys too, we put them inside. Right, why don’t those goddamned donkeys go out in the middle of the night, all three donkeys? Good grief! They went out, clop-clop, clop-clop. ‘Hey, by God!’ I say, ‘It blew up!’ For goodness’ sake, how shall we act?’ Šamʕәn says, ‘Wait! You screwed the pooch!’ The late Azzo, ‘Dewo, wait! For goodness’ sake’. He says, ‘Wait!’ Anyway, a lot of such whatsit, and clippity-clop! (HD_4 13.05)

contents.textus: 097. E, lo+kəmmat, ab+bexwădiya da+ḥmore nafiqi, maʕlū́m maʕ̥ṣéwaylan qumayye, hăma nafiqi. Kito hno bi+dərto, tanure sime, Merame. Twəṛṛe a+tre+tloṯo tanuranәk.
contents.versio: 097. Yeah, say nothing, the abandoned donkeys went out, clearly we had locked them in, but they went out. There is a whatsit in the courtyard, finished clay ovens, Merame. They broke two-three of those clay ovens.

contents.textus: 098. IL. Ḥariwo i+măsale wăki!
contents.versio: 098. IL. The situation was bad enough (lit. ruined) then.

contents.textus: 099. ḤD. Hăḷḷa hăḷḷa, e?! Ḥayra!..  U+Šamʕən omar, ‘Ăḷáh ono komaṇṇo, latyo šuġlo d ʔinsanat hano…’ Naqqa, ḥzelan hawxa hno, li+aṯto du+šēx qrela, əmmo, ‘Hosta lo+zayʕutu! A+ḥmoràṯxune, nafiqi. Fahimat? A+ḥmoràṯxune, nafiqi, lo+zayʕutu, layt mede!
contents.versio: 099. HD. Good grief, right?! Buddy! Šamʕən says, ‘God, I think, this isn’t the work of humans...’ Now then, we saw such a whatsit, the sheikh’s wife called, she says, ‘Sir, don’t be afraid (pl.)! They’re your donkeys, they went out. You understand? They’re our donkeys, they went out, don’t be afraid (pl.), it’s nothing!’

contents.textus: 100. Merame. Kəmmono i+aṯto du+šēx ṭáwtowa.
contents.versio: 100. M. I would say that the sheikh’s wife was good.

contents.textus: 101. ḤD. E, háwxawa. Hedi qam nafiqina, maʕəbrilan disa. U+ṣafro fā́šwaylan šmənto dәhnó, mkamelan ŭ mahzamlan, aṯina. Yani, hawxa xošbešín.
contents.versio: 101. HD. Yes, she was like so. Then we went out, we brought them in again. In the morning of a bit of whatsit was left for us, we finished it and ran off, we came back. That is, such pleasantries.

contents.textus: 102. IL. Hawxa medone ǧorewa brišayxu?
contents.versio: 102. This kind of thing used to happen to you guys?

contents.textus: 103. ḤD. E bavo! Eeeeeee komar, ‘Ǧorewa?’ Áydarbo lo+ǧorewa?! Waḷḷahi domaṇṇux, ha hawxa mṭay lboli…
contents.versio: 103. HD. Of course, daddy-o! Yessss, he says, ‘Did it happen?’ How didn’t it happen?! By God, I tell you, remind me about such things!

contents.textus: 104. k̇urro azzano.. bi+Kerxe ʕawdíwayna, bi+Kerxe, b Kerxa k̇ik̇a kəmmila. Hayəste bayn as+Səlivayo, aḏiʕat? Kofəhmat mək‿komaṇṇo? E, yawmo du+sačīmwa. Yani, sačī́m saymiwa xud uʕdo, du+sačimano. Tlaṯ+arbaʕ̥ qәryawoṯe saymiwa tamo u+sačimaṯṯe. Naysa, hul dhuwallan pašk̇e, mṭallallan pašk̇e ddawġe ŭ kətlan laḥmo, xilan fako. Aṯi … I+dukṯo dəmmi, ‘Gmaḥtutu’, e, lo+kəmmat aṯi u+abro. ‘Mənyo?’ Əmmi, ‘Ăḷa a+mbayḏone gmaḥti!’ ‘A+mbayḏone aṯən dəšše harke bu+ʕafrayḏan du+bayto?’ Əmmi, ‘E’.
contents.versio: 104. Boy, we went, we used to work in Kerxe, in Kerxe, in ‘Kerxa k̇ik̇a’ they call it. It (i.e. the name) is also among the Silivans, you know? Do you understand what I am saying? It was Election Day. Like, they used to do an election like now, this kind of election. Three-four villages did their election there. Anyway, until they gave us a sip, they brought us a bit of ayran, and we have some bread, we ate a bit. He came … the place they say ‘you will settle down’, right, say nothing, along came the son (i.e., of the owner, saying), ‘What is this?’ They say, ‘Gosh, the tinsmiths are going to settle down!’ ‘The tinsmiths came, they trampled here on our land of our home?’ They say, ‘Yes’.

contents.textus: 105. M. As+səryoye!
contents.versio: 105. Syriacs!

contents.textus: 106. ḤD. Pak! Omar, ‘Mḥaram u+bayto! Áydarbo g̊sōmno?’ Ḥəḷḷi, kelé bi+qurniṯo, kəmʕašlan. E hano, haw kobə́llanyo. ‘De gdobínanxu,’ komaḥke. Omaṇṇo ‘ǧəǧe!’ Omar ‘Mənyo?’ Omaṇṇo ‘Ḥariwo! ḥuṣ, ḥuṣ a+hne, aṭ+ṭaʕne!’ U+Usəvànoste aʕmáynawa, u+Usəvano dbe Qarrada, aḏiʕat? ‘Ḥayra,’ omaṇṇo, ‘Ḥuṣ … aṭ+ṭaʕne.’ [15:40]
contents.versio: 106. HD. Wow! He says, ‘The house is defiled! What shall I do?’ I looked, there he is in the corner, watching us. Right, this one, they’ll no longer give it to us. ‘Sure we’ll give it to you’, he says. I say, ‘Ǧəǧe!’ He says, ‘What is it?’ I say, ‘It’s all fucked up (lit. ruined)! Tie up, tie up the whatsits, the loads!’ This Yusef was also with us, this Yusef from the Qarada family, you know? ‘Buddy,’ I say ‘Tie up the … loads!’

contents.textus: 107. ḤD. ‘Lo+makiwat rišux, howe dahwo harke, haw kiban fayšina! Lo+mərxinala. Ḥa d riši, lo+diḏux, u+zlām, ʕayne aʕláynayo! U+hno, u+kăya, kăyá əmmə́nwanne lam+muxtarin tamo, aṯi, omar, ‘Tux dobenux dukṯo dmaḥtat’, məḷḷele lu+ǧəǧe. Omar, ‘Gdoṯeno maḥanno. U+ḥa dlobaʕ lébiste, lə+g̊somno as+sefoqayḏe!’ ‘Ha,’ omaṇṇo, ‘ăḷa, ánnaqqa ḥariwo! Hawo u+daywonawo tamo, e ma mede məḷḷe!
contents.versio: 107. HD. ‘You don’t need this headache, even if there were gold here, we can’t stay any longer! Let’s not draw it out. On my one head, not on yours, the man has got his eye on us. The whatsit, the kăyá, they called mayors kăyá there, he came, he says, ‘Come so I can give you a place to settle down’, he told Ǧəǧe.  He says, ‘I shall come and settle down. Also, the one whom I don’t like, I shall not make his utensils’. ‘Oh,’ I say, God, now it is fucked up! That crazy guy is there, and what he said?!’

contents.textus: 108. M. Qay daywono?
contents.versio: 108. M. Why ‘crazy’?

contents.textus: 109. ḤD. Laybi domaṇṇux məs‿səmle! ‘ălah, hawxa, hawxa g̊somno bi+aṯtayo diḏux!’– Yawo, ṣanki dəmmat … Ma mede məḷḷele!  - ‘Abro!’, omaṇṇo, ‘Komaṇṇux ḥuṣu aṭ+ṭaʕne, malexu!’ Naysa, malaxlan! Malaxlan, aṯən zbəṭṭe lu+ʕamo, zbəṭṭe, flān. Ḥəṣlan, malaxlan. Qalibina, tabi, azzano af u+Bašniq. Aq+qəryawoṯani kulle, koḏáʕnanne. ŭ ba u+ḥa dlə+ḥzile, laybe mafhamme.
contents.versio: 109. HD. I cannot tell you what he did. ‘By God, so, I shall do so to that wife of yours!’ For goodness’ sake, as if you were to say … what he said to him?! ‘My son’, I say, ‘I tell you, you guys tie up the loads, get going!’ Anyway, we went away! We went away, the people came and grabbed him, they grabbed him, etc. We tied up, we went away. We set off, naturally, we went to Bašniq. All of these villages, I know them. And someone who hasn’t seen them isn’t able to describe them, right?

contents.textus: 110. Ḥzeli kaṯi u+zlām bəṯrayna, kaṯi u+zlām, omaṇṇo, ‘ǧəǧe, maláx! Dlowat baynoṯayna, balki lə+mtane!’ ʕayn hawxa! ‘ăḷa, lu+gḏaʕno mə‿g̊somno ebe…’ Kodoʕar aʕle. ‘Lawo, layban! Gnəfqo i+qriṯo kula, gdəṯyo bəṯrayna!’ B Aḷḷa wakī́l, nafiqo i+qriṯo kula bəṯrayye, aḏiʕat! Annaqqa u+ǧəǧe madʕaḷḷe … ba ánnaqqa … suʕre bemrḗs … de de de de… u+ǧəǧe maxlaṣle. Azzé, omar, k‘Waḷḷá, azē k̇uṫṫəma diya ṫa da! Ma na ṫə k̇urre wi yi!’k  Lu+Brahim, u+Brahim aʕmáynawa.
contents.versio: 110. I saw the man was coming after us, the man was coming, I say, ‘ǧəǧe, go! If you aren’t among us, maybe he won’t retaliate’. Exactly like so! ‘God, I don’t know what I’m going to do to him!’ He (i.e., ǧəǧe) is going back to him (i.e., the landlord’s son). ‘Boy, we can’t! The whole village will come out, it will come after us!’ As God is my witness, the entire village came out after them, you know? Then ǧəǧe answered him … then, right … filthy insults, hey hey hey hey…. and ǧəǧe ran away. He went, he says, k‘By God, I shall fuck your mother. Are you not his son?!’k to Brahim, Brahim was with us.

contents.textus: 111. M. Loṣewa aʕlayye.
contents.versio: 111. M. He was watching them in order to attack them.

contents.textus: 112. ḤD. Aḷḷáh wakī́l, ʕayn hawxa! ánnaqqa e, ăḷá, čikno bayn ele ŭ ele. ‘Hedi, krīv’, lu+k̬ḏaʕno mune. ‘Mahzám lawo, mahzám!’ Mahzamle háwoste. Fāšno ono. Omar, ‘ăḷá, azē d̥patk̇e bave ṫa gēm, ṫa həšt go bā́zbədən! E, Aḷḷá wakī́l, ṫa həšt go bā́zbədən! .
contents.versio: 112. HD. As God is my witness, exactly like so! Then, right, God, I got between the two of them. ‘Slow down, godfather’, I don’t know what. ‘Run, boy, run!’ That one also ran away. I stayed. He says, k‘By God, I shall fuck your father down his throat. You let them escape! Yes, as God is my witness, you let them escape!’k

contents.textus: 113. ḤD. E, mə́dlelux kefo. Mətyaqnat m Aloho, čikno ažžək̇at əmmə́nwanne, xud a+ṭlàwḥene, xud ak+kùšnene. A+ʔažžək̇at, e yabo. Dəšli, koməġməṭ. Raġli haqqa bu+fəlḥonaṯṯe. [18:14]
contents.versio: 113. He picked you a boulder. By God you can believe me, I got into what they call almonds, they are like lentils, they are like vetch. The almonds, right, daddy-o.  I trampled it, it is sinking. My feet are yea deep in their ploughed soil.

contents.textus: 114. Mḥéleli kefo. B Aḷḷá wakī́l, hēš koḥōm dukṯa, hēš koḥōm dukṯa ha! Ha harke diḏi! Qayimo i+kefo hawxa. Kefe mani du+hno, du … mar aʕmi … du+qum, maš+šahikani. Waḷḷá azzí bu+femo li+arʕo, ŭ qāmno. Ləng, bave mə, ləng! E ălá, aṯina. ġắlăbe medone səmle eban.
contents.versio: 114. He hit me with a boulder. As God is my witness, its spot still burns, its spot here still burns! Over here on me! The stone got back up like so. These kinds of stones are made out of whatsit, of … tell me … made out of sand, these smooth kind of ones. By God, I landed with my mouth to the earth, and I stood up. kA leg, my father, a leg! k Yes, God, we came back. He did many things to us.

contents.textus: 115. ḤD. Hawxa … háwxawa, kurxíwayna. Arbʕo+yawme, ḥamšo+yawme əzzáwayna, lo+fətḥìwayna as+sefòqeste. Hawxa.
contents.versio: 115. So … it was like so, we used to go around. Four days, five days we would go, we would not open the tools too. Like so.

contents.textus: 116. I. Məqqa zabno fayšūtwa?
contents.versio: 116. How long did you used to stay?

contents.textus: 117. ḤD. E domannux, fayšíwayna tre+yarḥe naqqawoṯe, zəd̥. Hawxa yani šuġlíwayna.
contents.versio: 117. Right, I tell you, we used to stay two months sometimes, more. Like so, that is, we would work.

contents.textus: 118. M. Bi+šato tloṯo+yarḥe lo+oṯənwa.
contents.versio: 118. Three months out of the year they wouldn’t come back.

contents.textus: 119. Ḥ. Latwa xud uʕdo, talafone ŭ flā́n ŭ behvā́n. Bə́ba jḗra!’
contents.versio: 119. It wasn’t like today, telephones and so-and-so. kTake it to him! k

contents.textus: 120. M. U+ḥa daṯiwa … u+ḥa dəzzawayle, mamṭewalle.
contents.versio: 120. The one who had come … the one who would go for himself (i.e., for his own purposes), he would bring them.

contents.textus: 121. Fahmi. Malxi, malxi, bəṯr a+ḥmore.
contents.versio: 121. They walk, they walk, after the donkeys.

contents.textus: 122. Susán. Ayko ḥayfūtwa?
contents.versio: 122. Where did you used to bathe?

contents.textus: 123. ḤD. Ohow, ohow, ohow,… Aḷḷáh wakī́l, hedi domannux, haṯe basəmto yo. Ḥədik̇o ŭ u+Ḥano aʕmíwayne. Aloho mḥase a+tre! B Gunde+ʕisò ʕawdiwayna. E ḥáqqatan, ínaqqa d̥ḥozatwa aǧ+ǧulayḏan, mi+daʕ̥ṯo, hăwara Xudé!
contents.versio: 123. Ooh! Ooh! Ooh! As God is my witness, slow down so I can tell you, this one is a nice one. Ḥədik̇o and Ḥano were with me. God bless both of them! We were working in Gunde ʕIsò. Right, truly, if you had seen our clothes, from the sweat, kwatch out!k

contents.textus: 124. M. Ya Səttā́r, məḥ‿ḥāl wa!
contents.versio: 124. Good lord, what a situation it was!

contents.textus: 125. ḤD. Šləḥli tamo aǧ+ǧule, hənnək sḥalle, aṯən ltamo. Ŭ ónoste ánnaqqa šləḥli aǧ+ǧulayḏi dəzzino soḥeno. Hawxa hne yaríxewayne, əmmə́nwanne ṭawlat das+səsye, da+hne, du+săwā̀l. Ŭ mšaḥníwayna maye ʕal u+hno … bad+dəste ʕal u+kuro ŭ soḥiwayna.
contents.versio: 125. I took my clothes off, they washed up, they came there. And me too, now then, I took off my clothes to go wash up. So, the whatsits were long, they called them horse stables, of the whatsits, of the livestock. And we heated the water on the whatsit… with the copper kettles on the forge, and we washed up.

contents.textus: 126. Azzí lugab, aṯi Ḥədik̇o mə́ḷḷele lu+Ḥano, omar, ‘Hani mə́nnani?’ Omar, ‘Aǧ+ǧule dam+mìṯene!’ Lu+Ḥano hawxa məḷḷe, ŭ yabo kalko guḥxi. Haw fahəmno, ‘k̇urro, mənyo hawxa? Mənyo?’ Aṯino ánnaqqa kalkó hawxa maḥtənne ʕal i+dukṯo d koyotawno, lo. Ḥáqqatan dam+mìṯeste lanne hawxa. ‘k̇urro mənyo koguḥxutu?’  Əmmi, ‘Hani aǧ+ǧulani dam+mìṯene!’ Qām ónoste gaḥəkno.
contents.versio: 126. I went over there, Ḥədik̇o came, he said to Ḥano, he says, ‘Whose are these?’ He says, ‘They are dead people’s clothes!’  Ḥano said so, and daddy-o, here they are, laughing. I didn’t understood any longer, ‘Boy, so what is it? What is it?’ I came, now they have put them like so on the place where I sit, no. Really, the dead people’s ones aren’t like so. ‘Boy, why are you laughing?’ They say, ‘These are these dead people’s clothes!’ Then I also laughed.

contents.textus: 127. M. A+kfarzoye ḥzalle taʕbo ġắlăbe.
contents.versio: 127. Kfarzeans had (lit. saw) lots of trouble.

contents.textus: 128. ḤD. E, gaḥəkno, qām sḥeli, hawxa soḥíwayna. E hawxa soḥíwayna, walla domaṇṇax.
contents.versio: 128. Yes, I laughed, then I washed up, we would wash up like so. Right, we washed up like so, by God, I tell you.

contents.textus: 129. B Baṭmán ʕawdíwayna, u+muklayḏan aʕláynawa b Baṭmán. Latwa … lo+ṭulbìwayna mu+ʕamo. Šuqlíwaynalan kilo d … qaṭiro ŭ arbaʕ̥+ḥamməš+ṭalme laḥmo, ŭ fərxíwaynale ebe, ŭ əmmiwa, ‘Yawo bavo xul!’
contents.versio: 129. In Batman we were working, our food was ‘on us’ in Batman. It wasn’t … we wouldn’t ask people (for it). We bought a kilogram of … yogurt and four-five pieces of bread, and we would spread it on it, and they would said, ‘For goodness’ sake, Daddy-o, eat!’

contents.textus: 130. Il. Ŭ kətwa, waláyewa. Məqqa dəmmat, kətwa.
contents.versio: 130. And it was there, it was a city. Whatever you say, it was there.

contents.textus: 131. ḤD. E, e, ḥa drišux, hawxa ... maxrabo, ma ḥāl mafətlan, lo!? Ma ḥāl mafə́twaylan! E, e.
contents.versio: 131. Right, right, on your head, so … tarnation, what a situation we went through, no!? What a situation we have gone through! Right, right.

contents.textus: 132. ʕAmmi howewa, ŭ u+ǧəddayḏe, u+babo di+emo. Azzehən lu+Fīl. Hiye ŭ u+ḥaṯnaṯṯe ḥreno, Málkewa əšme. ḥzalle, zbəṭṭe u+Fīl. ‘Yawo’, əmmi, ‘Kotuqlutu as+sefoqe bu+qapono, ŭ aḥna lo+kuḏʕina bu+qapono! Kosaymutu ḥila aʕlayna. Haymén dlowe bu+qyoso ŭ bi+šehəl, lə+gmaqəblina!’
contents.versio: 132. There once was a uncle of mine, and his maternal grandfather, the mother’s father. They went to Fīl. He and another son-in-law of theirs, his name was Malke. They saw Fīl, they took it. ‘For goodness’ sake,’ they say, ‘you weigh the utensils with a steelyard balance, and we do not understand (lit. ‘know about’) the steelyard balance! You  play a trick on us. I swear if it is not with a weight and a scane, we won’t accept it!’

contents.textus: 133. Hoooow! U+ḥolo ... u+ḥolo, xóriwa. Bi+ḥaraytaṯe, hawi xori. ‘Yawo!’ omar, ‘Bi+šehəl – bi+šehəl! Bu+qyoso, bi+šehəl ksaymínanne!’ E, aṯən … azzehən bəṯr tloṯo+arbʕo+yawme, maḥatte bi+qriṯo, mbayaḏḏe sefoqe ġắlabe.
contents.versio: 133. Oooo... ! The maternal uncle... the maternal uncle, he was a chorbishop. Later, he became a chorbishop. ‘For goodness’ sake!’ he says, ‘With a scane –with a scane! With a weight and a scane, we’ll make them!’ Right, they came [to an agreement], in three-four days they went back, they set up in the village, they repaired lots of utensils.

contents.textus: 134. Lo+məṛṛalle, ‘Aṯina ləḥḏoḏe bu+qyoso ŭ bu+šehəl’. U+ǧəddo du+Alyaswa, aḏiʕat? U+babo di+emo. Howewa ʕámmiste yani, e. Qayəm mbaḏḏe, aṯən a … mora+di+qriṯo, mṭalle šehəl ŭ mṭalle kefe. Ŭ ánnaqqa zbəṭṭe… ḥəḷḷe, ‘Hani mə́nnani?’ omar, ‘Hani mə́nnani?’
contents.versio: 134. They did not tell him (i.e., ʕIse), ‘We agreed (lit. came together) on a weight and a scane’. He was Ilyas’s maternal grandfather, you know? His mother’s father. He was my uncle too, that is, yes. Then they repaired, they came, the … villagers came, they brought a scane and they brought stones. And then they took … he saw it, ‘What are these?’ he says, ‘What are these?’

contents.textus: 135. ‘Yawo’, əmmi, ‘Aḥna, məḷḷan lan+naʕime, aḥna, dlowe bu+qyoso ŭ bi+šehəl, lə+gbìnanxu as+sefoqayḏan dəmbayḏūtne!’
contents.versio: 135. ‘For goodness’ sake’,  they say, ‘We, we told the kids, we, were it not with a weight and a scane, we would not give you our utensils to repair them!’

contents.textus: 136. E, ba áydarbo hnən<ne>… gəd̥tuqli as+sefoqe bu+qyoso bi+šehəl? Taštat hawxa rabe, dəste hawxa, e, ləggə… lappe tuqlənne. Čiki bbăla aʕmayye! Hawi, səmme qarabaləġ lu+ǧəddo ŭ ldi+qriṯo!.. Səmme qarabaləġ. ‘Áydarbo, wah, áydarbo g̊toqálnanne bu+qyoso ŭ bi+šehəl?’ E ḥəḷḷe, hə́nnəkstene hawə́nwa pošmā́n, lappe tuqlənne bu+qyoso ŭ bi+šehəl!
contents.versio: 136. Yes, how are they going to whats… to weigh the utensils with a weight and a scane? Basins so big, such stockpots, right, they won’t… they can’t weigh them. It happened, they made trouble for the grandfather and those of the village! They made trouble (i.e. the ‘kids’).  ‘How, oh, how shall I weigh them with a weight and a scane?’ Right, he looked, they also came to regret it, they can’t weigh them with a weight and a scane.

contents.textus: 137. Aṯi u+ḥolo du+Alyàs, u+xori. Azzeyo omar, ‘Mənyo? Mən qarabaləġ də́ṯxuyo?’ ‘Yaho!’ omar, ‘Hani daywónene, ono áydarbo məḷḷi, “Toqalno as+sefoqe bu+qyoso ŭ bi+šehəl?” Áydarbo g̊toqálnanne?’  E, hiye mə́ḷḷele bu+kurdoyo... e, əšme, u+bàbowa... əšme du+babo ʕÍsewa. Omar, ‘ʕIse!’ omar ‘Či ...’ omar, ‘Mənyo?’ omar, ‘Dlowe ʕaynux ʕal i+ḥila, ha bu+qyoso ŭ bi+šehəl ŭ ha bu+qapono!’ Fahimat uʕdo mə‿məḷḷi?
contents.versio: 137. Along came Ilyas’s maternal uncle, the chorbishop one. He went over saying, ‘What is it? What’s your trouble?’ ‘For goodness’ sake!’ he says, ‘These people are crazy, how could I have said, “I will weigh the utensils with a weight and a scane?” How will I weigh them?’ Right, he (i.e., Yaḥqub̥) told him in Kurdish… yes, his name … he was the father … the father’s name was ʕIse. He says, ‘ʕIse!’  He says, ‘Wha…’, he says, ‘What is it?’ He says, ‘If your heart (lit. eye) wasn’t set on fraud, then this one in the weight and scane and that one in the steelyard!’ Now do you understand what I said?

contents.textus: 138. Omar, ‘Ínaqla dlo+saymat ḥila bu+qapono, ṭrowe ha bu+qyoso bi+šehəl, ha bu+qapono!’ E, di+qriṯo əmmi, ‘Hano mən díḏeyo?’ əmmi, ‘U+abroyo’, əmmi, ‘U+abroyo!!!’ Әmmi ‘Haymén u+kilo saymūtle arbʕo+kilowat, məzdū́təle, bu+qapono tuqlatte, madāmki hawxa məḷḷe!’ E, hənnək kúḏʕistene lappe tuqlənne bu+qyoso ŭ bi+šehəl, ŭ edi tqilənne bu+qapono. Aḏiʕat uʕdo mə‿məḷḷi, lo?
contents.versio: 138. He says, ‘When you aren’t committing fraud with a steelyard, let it be this one with a weight and scane, that one with the steelyard!’ Yes, the ones from the village say, ‘This one, who is he to him?’, they say, ‘He is the son’, they say, ‘He is the son!!!’ They say, ‘I swear you guys make a kilo into four kilos, you guys increase it, when you (i.e., ʕIse specifically) weigh them with a steelyard, since he said so!’ Yes, they also know that they are unable to weigh them with a weight and scane, and so they weighed them with a steelyard. Now do you understand what I said?

contents.textus: 139. I. Taḥḥolo domaṇṇax ḥa+xabro! Kətlax hat xabro, konofaq ḥəs diḏax, bi, bi.. dínaqla daṯina, dəgrəšlan, kəmmo … kəmmat, ‘Hənnən l bandak̇e … hay žə baye falak̇e!’ U+xabrano háwxayo?
contents.versio: 139. Auntie, let me tell you one saying. You have a saying, your voice appears in the …, in the …, when we came, when we recorded, it says… you say, ‘Those in the bandak̇e … that from the baye falake’. Is this saying like so?

contents.textus: 140. Taḥḥolo. E nav bandak̇e, hāž žə baye falak̇e.
contents.versio: 140. Snug as a bug in a rug (lit. the one who is inside the roll, awareness about the winds of fate).’

contents.textus: 141. ḤD. Hiya ‘e nav bandak̇e’ – latyo hənnən! –  ‘e nav bandak̇e’ – ḥzelux? – layfiwa ruḥayye bayn u+batko. Ánnaqqa əmmiwa, ‘hāž nīna … hāž … žə baye falak̇e!’
contents.versio: 141. It’s ‘the one who is inside the roll’ – it isn’t ‘they’! –  the one who is inside the roll – have you seen it? – they used to roll themselves up within the roll. Now then, they used to say, ‘there’s no awareness … awareness… about the winds of fate!’

contents.textus: 142. I. Kito ḥrénoste, šuwolo ḥrénoste. Kəmmat, ‘Dínaqqa dəmbā́ḏwayno, oṯənwa ar+rabe, oṯənwa ar+rabe, šuqliwa puwane.’ Áydarbo? Kobən puwane!
contents.versio: 142. There is another question. You say, ‘When I worked as a tinsmith, officers would come, officers would come, and they would take kudos’. How come? They give kudos!

contents.textus: 143. ḤD. Ínaqqayo bi+ʕaskarìyewayno, ínaqqayo bi+ʕaskarìyewayno, m̩bā́ḏwayno bi+ʕaskariye, qăzanat hawxa mar+rabanək. Ġắlăbe rábewayne! Ánnaqqa qām m̩bā́ḏwayli ḥamšaḥsar+əštaḥsar+qăzanat, hawxa femayye. I+dukṯo dm̩bā́ḏwayno hawxa kulle ma… məhnənwa mačəlṣiwa.
contents.versio: 143. At that time I was in the military, at that time I was in the military, I worked as a tinsmith in the military, such cauldrons of those big ones. They were very big! That time, I up and repaired fifteen-sixteen vats, their mouths like so; every place I repaired like so, it was entirely... it could whatsit... it would shine.

contents.textus: 144. E, aṯi u+… u+hno, Mamdū́ḥ Tamač. Ínaqqayo bərənǧí ordú qomutani wa.
contents.versio: 144. Right, along came the, the whatsit, Memduh Tağmaç.  At that time, he was the Commander of the First Army.

contents.textus: 145. I. U+rabo d̥tamo?
contents.versio: 145. The commander of there?

contents.textus: 146. ḤD. U+rabo du+ordi.  E, azzí, səmlan … grəšli hno … tbu+asás dərúš t, ŭ axər huli u+takmilayḏi,  ə, kelé u+binbašiyàyḏanste aʕme, yuzbašiwa, ŭ kelé aʕme, omar, ‘Hani kulle …’, e, omar, ‘Qomuṭanəm!’ Omar, ‘Hani kulle ele mbayḏile ... dəḥdud tabur, d̥ Silolu, d Babáʔeski, tOnaltənǧə Piyada ʕAlayət … ’, ŭ lə+k̬ḏaʕno mən ŭ mən ŭ mən, ‘Hani kulle, kəmṭənne larke, ŭ hiye kəmbāḏe, hiye kəmbāḏe …’, ŭ ánnaqqa mḥélile tasást, hedi tasás dərúšt ŭ húlile salā́m, ŭ kṫə saġ!k
contents.versio: 146. The chief of the army. Yeah, I went... we did... I pulled whatsit … to tattentiont, and later I gave my oral report, uh, here’s our major too with him, he was a captain, and here he is with him, he says, ‘All of these...’ right, he says, ‘My commander!’ he says, ‘he has repaired all of them … of the border battalion, of Süloğlu, of Babaeski, the tSixteenth Infantry Regimentt …’, and I don’t know what and what and what, ‘all of these things, they bring them here, and he repairs, he repairs …’ and then I sprang to tattentiont for him, then tattentiont,  and I greeted him, and kBob’s your unclek (lit. ‘and you be well’)!

contents.textus: 147. I. Yani, húlelux puwane?
contents.versio: 147. Like, did he give you kudos?

contents.textus: 148. ḤD. E bavooo!
contents.versio: 148. Of course, daddy-o!

contents.textus: 149. I. Húlelux puwane ġắlăbe?
contents.versio: 149. He gave you a lot of kudos?

contents.textus: 150. ḤD. Hule i+hno, lu+ḥreno, lu... i+terfiya! E, yuzbašiwa, səmle binbaší! Aḏiʕat? [...]
contents.versio: 150. He gave the whatsit, to the other one, to the … leave! He was a captain, and he made him a major. You know?

contents.textus: 151. ḤD. Ánnaqqa ínaqla dazzino d̥šoqanno dáskăra, azzino lu+ … ə… lu+tuġày. Azzí lu+tuġày, omar, ‘Layt‿əmbayḏono, kobaʕ̥ fayšat aʕ+ʕaṣro+yawmàniste...’ e waḷḷá omarno, ‘Hat kuḏʕat, qomuṭanəm!’ Naysa fāšno, bəṯr hedi aṯən, mšāʕle bəṯri, azzino, mədle kăġat d̥ḥamši. Kətwa ak+kaweġət daḥ+ḥamši ínaqqayo, əmmíwaynanne Xălaf, Xălaf u+bakči. Lə+ḥzèwaylux?
contents.versio: 151. Once, when I went to get my papers, I went to the … uh … to the brigade. I went to the brigade, and he says, ‘There is no tinsmith, you need to stay these ten days too…’, and, by God I say, ‘You would know, my commander!’ Anyway, I stayed, then after they came, he asked for me, I went, he took a fifty lira banknote. There were fifty lira banknotes back then, we used to call them ‘a Xălaf’, the watchman Xălaf. Haven’t you seen him?

contents.textus: 152. ḤD. Xălaf u+bakči lə+ḥzèwaylux?
contents.versio: 152. Haven’t you seen the watchman Xălaf?

contents.textus: 153. I. Xălaf diḏan?
contents.versio: 153. Our Xalaf?

contents.textus: 155. I. Bele, áydarbo?!
contents.versio: 155. Sure, how come?!

contents.textus: 156. ḤD. Ánnaqqa kə́twayle ṣərṭo lu+bakči ʕal u+ḥamši+noṭat. Húleli ḥamši+noṭat ŭ omar, ‘Zux Ăḷo aʕmux!’
contents.versio: 156. Now then, the watchman had a picture on the fifty lira banknote. He gave me a fifty lira banknote and says, ‘Go with God!’ (8:45)

contents.textus: 157. I. Veǧa komar, komar, ‘Mšayál, mšayál dəmmina lu+ḥolo Ḥanna…’ Komar, ‘As+sefoqe di+byaḏa, mə́nwayne?’
contents.versio: 157. IL. Now then, [Jan dbe Sawoʕe] says, he says, ‘Ask, ask, let’s say, Uncle Ḥanna …’ He says, ‘The tinsmithing utensils, what were they?’

contents.textus: 158. ḤD. Yani u+mede dəmbayḏíwayna appe, ya as+sefòqewayne?
contents.versio: 158. Like, the stuff that we used to repair with them, or were they the utensils?

contents.textus: 159. I. As+sefoqe di+byaḏa... yani b̚mәn mbayḏatwa?
contents.versio: 159. The tinsmithing utensils… like, with what did you repair?

contents.textus: 160. ḤD. Kalpténatwayne. Kalptenat, kə́twaylan kalptenat, femayye hawxa, hən ha hawxa, hən … ḥur, hən ha háwxawayne. Ha, ha, u+femano msawyo ŭ ha hawxa, aḏiʕat? Tlaṯ, tloṯo+šə̀klatwayne.
contents.versio: 160. HD. They were pliers. The pliers, we had pliers, their mouth is like so, some of them just like so, some... look, some of them were like so. Here, here, this mouth is smooth and just like so, you know? Three, there were three types.

contents.textus: 161. Ilyas. ǧġeni mani?
contents.versio: 161. Apart from these?

contents.textus: 162. ḤD. Klay domaṇṇux! hani ak+kalptenat zəbṭíwayna as+sefoqe appe, aḏiʕat?
contents.versio: 162. HD. Wait till I tell you… these pliers, we used to take the vessels with them, you know?

contents.textus: 163. ḤD. ŭ kə́twaylan šəndan, diqo bi+arʕo, ŭ čakučat, ŭ, ŭ msawí … ŭ msawíwayna as+sefoqe appe, msawíwayna as+sefoqe appe.
contents.versio: 163. HD. And we had a hanvil, it was stuck in the ground, and hammers, and, and we smooth … and we used to smooth utensils with them, we used to smooth utensils with them.

contents.textus: 164. I. Msawútuwa as+sefoqe bač+čakučat?
contents.versio: 164. Did you used to smooth utensils with hammers?

contents.textus: 165. ḤD. E, msawíwayna bač+čakučat, bu+doquqo, b̥kul mede. Saymíwaynanne, yani msawíwaynanne, e.
contents.versio: 165. Yes, we used to smooth them out with hammers, with mallets, with everything. We used to make them, that is, we used to smooth them out, right.

contents.textus: 166. I. Ŭ ǧġeni mani, ono ḥzéwayli bzabno, kətwa mákina du+nfoḥo, nəfḥiwa.
contents.versio: 166. And apart from these, I saw a while ago, there was a blowing maching, they would blow.

contents.textus: 167. ḤD. Ha i+màkinayo, ínaqqa, ḥur domaṇṇux, yotawwa u+nafoḥo tamhé, ŭ ono harke. Ŭ ksaymíwayna i+nuro, nofaḥwa hiye, mabramwa u+hno, i+màkina. Mabramwa i+màkina, saymowa i+nuro.
contents.versio: 167. HD. That there instrument, now then, look let me tell you, the blower would sit over there, and over here, me. And we would make fire, he would do the blowing, he would set the whatsit, the machine in motion. He would set the machine in motion, it would make fire.

contents.textus: 168. I. Bele. Mən darmone kə́twayla li+byaḏa?
contents.versio: 168. IL. What ‘remedies’ were there for tinsmithing?

contents.textus: 169. ḤD. Darmone, darmono … ‘qaláy’ əmmíwaynale, ŭ nšadər.
contents.versio: 169. HD. ‘Remedies’, ‘remedy’... we would call it ‘tin’, and sal ammoniac.

contents.textus: 170. I. Qaláy ŭ nšadər.
contents.versio: 170. Tin, and sal ammoniac.

contents.textus: 171. ḤD. E, u+nšadər hawxa hníwaynale, saymíwaynale xəd‿u+qamḥo, aḏiʕat? Ánnaqqa mšaḥníwayna u+sefoqo ŭ mḥalqíwayna u+nšadrawo, u+nšadər yoqaḏwa ʕal u+sefoqo...
contents.versio: 171. ḤD. Right, the sal ammoniac we would whatsit it like so, we would make it like flour, you know? Then we would heat the utensil, and we would throw that sal ammoniac, the sal ammoniac would burn onto the utensil.

contents.textus: 172. I. Məs‿sōmwa u+nšadər yani?
contents.versio: 172. IL. What would the sal ammoniac do, like?

contents.textus: 173. ḤD. U+nšadər, xud dəmmat, mṣafewa u+zəngoro, ŭ aḥna moḥíwayna edi u+darmono ebe. U+nšadər dlo+moḥatle ebe, u+darmono lo+hnewa, lo+fošarwa, aḏiʕat?
contents.versio: 173. HD. The sal ammoniac, so to speak, would cleanse the rust, and we would put the remedy into it. The sal ammoniac, had he not put it into it, the remedy would not have whatsited, would not have melted (i.e., evenly), you know?

contents.textus: 174. I. U+nšadər dlo+moḥatle qamayto, u+darmono dlo+moḥatle, u+qalày lə+gfošar, lə+gzobaṭ ruḥe yani bu+sefoqo?
contents.versio: 174. The sal ammoniac, if you don’t apply it first, the remedy, if you don’t apply it, the tin won’t melt, it won’t stick itself, that is, to the vessel?

contents.textus: 175. ḤD. E. E, ánnaqqa gəmḥalqat hawxa, ŭ bəṯr mədə‿mḥelux u+hno, ŭ hawxa i+kafk̇e biḏux, hawxa haqqa d̥ketono, ŭ moḥatwa hawxa, mbāḏwa, howewa xud u+dahwo.
contents.versio: 175. Yes. Yes, now then you cast it like so, and after you have applied the whatsit, and so the glove is on your hand, so yea amount of cotton, and you would apply it like so, he would repair it, it would become like gold.

contents.textus: 176. I. Sefoqe ḥrene latwa, hániwayne as+sefoqe di+byaḏa?
contents.versio: 176. There weren’t any other utensils, these were tinsmithing utensils?

contents.textus: 177. ḤD. Háwxane as+sefoqe di+byaḏa, háṯewayne. Bi+kalptene zəbṭínala, mәd mkaméwaylan,  maḥtíwayna u+sefoqo tamo.
contents.versio: 177. Such are the tinsmithing utensils, it was like this. With the pliers, we grab it, after we have finished it, we would put the utensil there.

contents.textus: 178. ḤD. Čik̇e dǧomadwa, čik̇e dǧomadwa u+sefoqo, edi maydíwayle. Kə́twaylan hno dəmmina … mani da+… ḥzelux ag+gumoṯe? I+gumṯo, u+hnawo dag+gumoṯe, da+hne, du+abzar, kəmmile xud u+hno, xud dəmmat… Ăḷa... əšme mənyo, mar aʕmi ...
contents.versio: 178. Once it had cooled down a little, once the utensil had cooled down a little, then they would seize it. We had a whatsit that we call … one of those … have you seen looms? The loom, that whatsit of looms, of the whatsits, of the shuttle, they call it like the whatsit, like you say... gosh… what’s its name, remind me (lit. ‘speak with me’)!

contents.textus: 179. M. Ḥuṭe, ḥuṭe...
contents.versio: 179. M. Threads, threads…

contents.textus: 180. ḤD. Lo, ḥuṭe bašqa, hăma ... hno, u+abzar bášqayo, kətwa u+hnawo diḏe, saymíwaynale hawxa, ha hawxa. Ŭ maydíwayna bu+hno, bu+k̇ulav, ŭ məhnənwa, mkafríwayna u+sefoqo.
contents.versio: 180. No, threads are something else, but… a whatsit, the shuttle is something else, there was that whatsit of it, we would do it like so, just like so. And we would hold it with whatsit, with felt, and they got whatsited, we would clean the utensil.

contents.textus: 181. Mən sefoqe mbayḏútuwa?
contents.versio: 181. Which utensils would you repair?

contents.textus: 182. HD. Sefoqe? Oho, oho sefoqe! Dəste, baredəš, ṭaġne, sefoqe, hno … ṣaweni, ṭaṣat rabe naʕime, ṣaweni rabe naʕime, ŭ hawxa.
contents.versio: 182. HD. Utensils? Oooh, utensils! Cauldrons, pots, frying pans, utensils, whatsit … china, drinking bowls big and small, china big and small, and such.

contents.textus: 183. I. Yani, mən sefoqo doṯewa qumayxu mbayḏútuwa?
contents.versio: 183. Like, whatever utensil came to you, you would repair?

contents.textus: 184. ḤD. Ábadan! Baredəš, qošxanat, qulepəġ, hawxa, e.
contents.versio: 184. HD.  Absolutely! Pots, cooking pots, lids, such things, right.

contents.textus: 185. I. As+sefoqe bməqqa kalla mbayḏútuwanne? Yani, u+kalla bu+waxtawo, bmə́qqawa u+kilo?
contents.versio: 185. The utensils, for how much money did you repair them? Like, the money at that time, how much was one kilo?

contents.textus: 186. ḤD. Ḥur domaṇṇux. Ínaqqa, ínaqqa d ʔaḥna … maṭino las+sefoqe, mbayḏíwayna u+kilaṯṯe bəšti+qurùš. Ínaqqa qamayto dnafəqno li+byaḏa, ʕəmri tmone+əšnewa, aḏiʕat. Nafóḥowayno, u+kilo bəšti+qurušwa.
contents.versio: 186. Look, I’ll tell you. When, when we … I got to utensils, we would repair them for 60 kuruş a kilo. When I first went out to tinsmith, I was 8 years old, you know. I was a blower, a kilo was for 60 kuruş.

contents.textus: 187. I. Yani, bəšti+qurùš, mən oṯewa appe, xud əmmat ádyawma?
contents.versio: 187. Like, for 60 kuruş, what would you get for them (lit. ‘what would come with them’), like say today?

contents.textus: 188. ḤD. Әšti+qurùš, oṯewa ġắlăbe medone. Măsala bu+kilo, bann+əšti+qurùš, aḏiʕat. Bəšti+qurùš măsala dəmmina. Tre+kilowat mbayḏíwayna, i+baroše tre+kilowat, mo u+ʕəṣri+qurùš. E, mo u+ʕəṣri+qurùš. Ŭ bəṯr kətwa hən mbayḏíwayna bwáraqa u+kilo, dəkkoṯe. Lo xu‿ḥḏoḏe mbayḏíwayna. Áḥnaste saymíwayna ḥila...
contents.versio: 188. 60 kuruş, you would get (lit. ‘there used to come’) many things. For example, for one kilo for 60 kuruş, you know. For 60 kuruş, for example, so to speak. We used to repair two kilos, a pan was two kilos, 120 kuruş. Yes, 120 kuruş. And moreover, there were some who would repair for one lira a kilo, some places. We wouldn’t repair like each other. We too would cheat.

contents.textus: 189. I. Latwa ḥḏo+fiye?
contents.versio: 189. Was there not one price?

contents.textus: 190. ḤD. Lo yaho! Mbayzríwayna i+fiye dobə́nwaylan.
contents.versio: 190. HD. No, for goodness’ sake! We would negotiate the price that  they would give us.

contents.textus: 191. I. Păki, dínaqqa dəzzóxuwa lәqriṯo, dəmmina gəmbayḏutu as+sefoqaṯṯe. Layko gəzzoxu? Gab man gəzzoxu? Mən šəkəl gəzzoxu?
contents.versio: 191. Alright, when you would go to a village, let’s say, you are going to repair their utensils. Where would you go? Whom would you go to? How would you go?

contents.textus: 192. ḤD. Əzzáwayna su+muxtar, su+rabo di+qriṯo. Ŭ mšaylíwayna aʕle, ‘Ŭ manyo i+qriṯaṯe u+rabayḏa, u+muxtarayḏa? ‘Flānkasyo!’ Gəzzáwayna, ‘Lə+gəmbayḏutu as+sefoqaṯxu?’ ‘Bele! Haymén gəmbayḏínanne!’ Oṯíwayna ləḥḏoḏe. ‘U+kilo bmən? Bməqqa gəmbayḏútulan?’  ‘Šan u+aġà balā́š, kmo+kilowàt?’  Hawxa e.
contents.versio: 192. HD. We would go to the mayor, to the village boss. And we would ask about him, ‘And who is it, this village, its boss, its mayor?’ ‘He is so-and-so!’ We would go, ‘Won’t you repair your utensils?’‘Sure! I swear we shall repair them!’ We would come to an agreement (lit. ‘we would come to each other’). ‘How much is a kilo (lit. ‘the kilo is at what [price]’)? For how much will you repair it for us?’ ‘For the Agha, gratis, how many kilos?’ So, yeah.

contents.textus: 193. I. Bu+šəklano oṯūtwa bi+fiye, ḥḏo fiye, lәḥḏoḏe?
contents.versio: 193. In this way you would come to an agreement about the price, one price.

contents.textus: 194. HD. E, hən mənne bəšti+qurùš, hənna ḥamšo+ŭ+šawʕi+qurùš, hən bwáraqa, hawxa.
contents.versio: 194. Right, some of them for 60 kuruş, some for 75 kuruş, some for a lira, like so.

contents.textus: 195. I. Noše axile ḥaq mənxu bu+medano, bi+ṣənʕaṯe?
contents.versio: 195. Did people stiff you (lit. ‘eat from you the pay’) in this matter, in this profession?

contents.textus: 196. ḤD. Domaṇṇux, i+ṣənʕa, noquṣo, yawo, uxliwa, ṭáyene! Uxliwa hawxa. Mbliwa as+sefoqe, ‘Kallá!’ - k‘Am ē čən parewa ē nə́n’.k Flān. ‘Əmṭina, əzzano.’  Makiwiwa rišayna ġắlăbe, e.
contents.versio: 196. Let me tell you, the profession, a bit, for goodness’s sake, they would stiff, they’re Muslims! They stiffed like so. They would take the utensils, ‘The money!’,  k‘We’re going, we’ll bring your money’,k etc. ‘We’ll bring it, we’re going.’ They would give us a lot of headaches (lit. ‘they would hurt our head a lot’), right.

contents.textus: 197. I. Yani uxliwa?
contents.versio: 197. Like, they would stiff?

contents.textus: 198. ḤD. E, uxliwa, mbayḏíwayna, naqqawoṯe hnoste, yani bdayno!
contents.versio: 198. HD. Yes, they would stiff, we would repair, sometimes a whatsit too, like, on credit.

contents.textus: 199. I. Păki, nošo nafəq bu+darbo hīč lqamuṯayxu, mšalaḥlalxu?
contents.versio: 199. IL. Alright, did anybody ever come out to meet you on the road, to rob you?

contents.textus: 200. ḤD. E, e, e. U+Səlo dbe Rəsqo əḏʕátwayle?
contents.versio: 200. Yes, yes, yes. Were you acquainted with Səlo Rəsqo?

contents.textus: 201. I. Koḏaʕno, u+babo du+hno …
contents.versio: 201. I know him, the father of whosit …

contents.textus: 202. ḤD. Du+Ṣabri ŭ tani, du+Fahmi.
contents.versio: 202. … of Sabri and of these ones, of Fahmi.

contents.textus: 203. I. Du+Fahmi ŭ tani, koḏáʕnanne.
contents.versio: 203. I. …of Fahmi and of these ones, I know them.

contents.textus: 204. ḤD. U+Barṣawmo áʕmewa ŭ u+Yaḥqo dbe Šahin. U+babo du+Šahin ləḏʕátwayle?
contents.versio: 204. HD. Barṣawmo was with him, and Yaḥqo Šahin. Šahin’s father, didn’t you know him?

contents.textus: 205. I. Lo, šaməʕno əšme bas.
contents.versio: 205. No, I just heard his name.

contents.textus: 206. ḤD. U+Yaḥqo, azzehən bayn li+Škastak̇e ŭ li+Mozgalade, tamo mšalḥənne. tṢōnt, dmkamewalle u+hno, i+byaḏa, əbʕiwa doṯən lu+bayto. Tamo čiki b̥qamuṯayye, šqəlle ak+kallawataṯṯe mənne, aḏiʕat.
contents.versio: 206. HD. Yaḥqo, they were travelling between Škastak̇e and Mozgalade, there they robbed them. tFinally,t once they had finished the whatsit, tinsmithing, they wanted to come home. They ambushed them (lit. ‘snuck to meet them’) there, they took their money from them, you know.

contents.textus: 207. I. Bas hatu hawxa mede lo+ḥzalxu, lo+ǧarəlxu?
contents.versio: 207. But you did’t experience such a thing, it did’t happen to you?

contents.textus: 208. ḤD. E, domaṇṇux, aḥna, mən komáṇṇolux, lo+ġằlăbe, lo, zayʕíwayna ġắlăbe, oṯənwa lqamuṯayna.
contents.versio: 208. HD. Right, let me tell you, we, what shall I tell you, not much, no, we were very afraid, they came to meet us.

contents.textus: 209. I. Păki, bu+darbo aʕmayxu kə́twalxu mede ḥmoro, səsyo, baġlo?
contents.versio: 209. Alright, on the way, did you have some sort of donkey, horse, or mule with you?

contents.textus: 210. ḤD. A+ḥmore aʕmayna, kə́twaylan ḥmoro aʕmayna, as+sefoqayḏan di+byaḏa aʕle, ŭ aḥna tloṯo+šàqṣatwayna ŭ qulʕíwayna u+ḥmoro, ŭ malxíwayna bəṯre.
contents.versio: 210. There were donkeys with us, we had a donkey with us, our tinsmithing utensils were on it, and we were three people, and we drove the donkey, and we walked after it.

contents.textus: 211. I. Ḥa+ḥmoro, kul+mede maḥtū́twayle aʕle?
contents.versio: 211. One donkey, you put everything on it?

contents.textus: 212. ḤD. E, as+sefoqayḏan kulle aʕle.
contents.versio: 212. Yes, all our utensils on it.

contents.textus: 213. I. Tloṯo+šaqṣat maǧbúr dəzzoxu, yani?
contents.versio: 213. Is it necessary for you to go as three people, like?

contents.textus: 214. ḤD. E, maǧbúr! Ḥa+mbayḏono, ŭ ḥa+ǧaloyo ŭ ḥa+nafoḥo.
contents.versio: 214. Yes, it’s necessary! One tinsmith, one polisher, and one blower.

contents.textus: 215. I. Baq+qəryawoṯo dazzóxunne, lo+laqutu bhənna armnoye aw suryoye dhawən ṭaye?
contents.versio: 215. In the villages to which you went, didn’t you meet with any Armenians or Syriacs who had become Muslims?

contents.textus: 216. ḤD. Ġắlăbe! Ḥur domaṇṇux, haṯe gorašna, gdəmmutu flān behvān. Laqina ínaqqayo bann+armnoye. Ann+armnoyani d ʔoṯənwa yətwiwa, əmmiwa u+dardaṯṯe. Ṭabi u+zaman d ʔono komaṇṇo, ʕəmre dann+armnoyanək tleṯi+arbʕi+əšnewa, aḏiʕat.
contents.versio: 216. Lots! Look, let me tell you, if I pull that thing out (i.e., the story), you will say such-and-such (i.e., these are tall tales). We met Armenians once. The Armenians that would come would sit down, they would speak about their trouble. Naturally, the time I’m saying, those Armenians were 30 or 40 years old, you know.

contents.textus: 217. Maḥ+ḥamməš ŭ təšʕi, Aḷa, maḥ+ḥamšaḥsar... aḥna əzzáwayna, ʕəmrayna ínaqqayo, ḥsar+əšnewa. Ono dəzzíwayno, tmone+əšnewa. Hani oṯənwa yətwiwa, ʕam u+hosta məǧġoliwa. ‘Qṭəḷḷe babayna, qṭəlle emayna, mballe a+bnoṯayḏan’, hawxa medone ġắlăbe kətwa. Ann+armnoye, e, qayyo u+hnano qayəm?  Uʕdo domaṇṇo, u+Fərmā̀n dann+armnoye, e, əmmi, ‘Li+ḥkume maqəmla!’ I+ḥkume qay maqəmla? Ínaqqayo mərre ‘Kal kaṯi u+hno l K̇avre Qul, Ruṣya!’ Ruṣya l K̇avre Qul, tamo b̥ K̇avre Qul d̥kəmmina, Ruṣya! Čīk xtilaliye, dadí qodí bayn i+ʕaskarayḏe. Me tamo daʕiri.
contents.versio: 217. Since ’95, God, since ’15… we would go, we were ten years old then. When I travelled, it was eight. These ones would come sit down, they would speak with the craftsman, ‘They killed our father, they killed our mother, they took away our daughters’, there were a lot of such things. The Armenians, right, how did this this arise? Now, let me say, the Armenian Genocide, right, they say, ‘The government organized it!’ Why did the government organize it? That time, they said, ‘It has come to K̇avre Qul, whatsit, Russia!’ Russia to K̇avre Qul, there in what we call K̇avre Qul, Russia! Disagreement and gossip crept into its military. From there, they returned.

contents.textus: 218. Hani ann+armnoye əmmíwaylan dáʔima… Yətwiwa an+niše, hən mənne kə́twalle bnoṯe šafire.  ‘Ínaqqa dhowewa noše suryoye, gdobíwaynannenne’. E, ṭabi, əblə́nwanne laṭ+ṭaye, aḏiʕat.
contents.versio: 218. These Armenians would alway tell us … The women would sit down, some of them had pretty daughters. ‘If there had been Syriacs available, we would have given them to them.’ Yes, naturally, they brought them to the Muslims, you know.

contents.textus: 219. ‘E, məḷḷan lar+rabe daq+qәryawoṯe, dəmmina l daʕ+ʕašəryoṯe, “Toxu moḥina bu+ordi b Diyarbakər. Bu+ordi! U+ordi i+dawleyo! Ŭ kfayšo i+dukṯo šanayna!”’
contents.versio: 219. ‘Yes, we told the lords of the villages, so to speak, of the (Kurdish) tribes, ‘Come, let’s strike at the army in Diyarbakır. At the army! The army is the government! And this place will be left for us!’

contents.textus: 220. Hani, kətwa ínaqqayo muxbərčiye, azzə́n am+muxbərčiye hăman mərre li+dawle, aḏiʕat. Mərre, ‘Ann+armnoye hawxa kəmmi lar+rabe daq+qәryawoṯe, daʕ+ʕašəryoṯe, ŭ kəbʕi moḥən bu+ordi, bi+dawle.’ Hăman mšāʕle bəṯr ar+rabe daq+qәryawoṯe, dani daʕ+ʕašəryoṯe, məḷḷe, ‘Toxu! Zoxu mḥawu bann+armnoye, qṭalu a+zlamataṯṯe ŭ mbalu an+nišaṯṯe ŭ a+bnoṯaṯṯe, ŭ g̊fayšo i+dukṯoste alxu! Aḥna lo+šamiʕina! Mḥawu appe!’ Košəmʕat? E, ġbino i+dawla ʕal ruḥa. Ma latyo hawxa?
contents.versio: 220. These ones, there were informers at that time, the informers immediately went and told the government, you know. They said, ‘The Armenians are speaking so to the lords of the villages, of the tribes, and they want to strike at the army, at the government’. He immediately sent to the lords of the villages, of the tribes, he said, ‘Come! Go strike at the Armenians, kill their men, take away their women and daughters, and the place will be left for you! We didn’t hear (a thing)! Strike at them!’ You hear? Right, the government became indignant for its sake. Isn’t it so?

contents.textus: 221. I. Háwxayo!
contents.versio: 221. It is so!

contents.textus: 222. ḤD. Ġbino ʕal ruḥa, ŭ hawxa səmme. Səmme ŭ qṭəlle, edi domaṇṇux, bayn a+Səliva, bayn ar+Rašk̇ota, bayn ab+Bahrava, bayn a ... bi+Bəšeriye, bu+Bàmard, baġ+Ġarza, hani kulle mḥalqənne hawxa lam+maye. Dlo+tfə̀ngestene, mḥalqənne lam+maye, qṭilənne. E, hawxa, bašqa?
contents.versio: 222. It became indignant for its own sake, and they did like so. They did it and they killed them, then I’ll tell you, among the Silivans, among the Reşkotan, among the Bahrava, among the ... in Bəšeriye, in Bamard, among the Garzanians, all these ones, they threw them into the water like so. Without rifles moreover, they threw them into the water, they killed them. Right, like so. Anything else?

contents.textus: 223. I. Balat medone aṯi brišayxu? Qeṣe medone yani ǧari brišayxu?
contents.versio: 223. Did any terrible things come down upon you? Did, like, any misfortunate things happen to you?

contents.textus: 224. ḤD. Áydarbo? Yawo, naqlawoṯe, domaṇṇux mede, fayšíwayna larwal, lo+ḥowə̀nwaylan hən maq+qәryawoṯe. Dəmxíwayna hawxa dəmmina bu+zaboqo.
contents.versio: 224. How? For goodness’ sake, sometimes, let me tell you something, we used to stay outside, some of the villages wouldn’t host us. We would sleep, so to speak, on the street.

contents.textus: 225. I. Howewa háwxaste?
contents.versio: 225. IL. Would this also happen?

contents.textus: 226. ḤD. Howewa hawxa medone, hawi aʕmayna ġắlăbe. Ŭ naqlawóṯestene dukṯayna huyowa basəmto, u+muklo d̥ṭulbíwayna hawo amṭíwayna, aḏiʕat, hawxa, yani…
contents.versio: 226. Such things would happen, many things happened to us. And also sometimes our place would be pleasant, the food we would request, we would get this, you know, so, like…

contents.textus: 227. I. Yani bu+zabnawo káfnowa, áydarbo an+noše ḥowənwa dayfe?
contents.versio: 227. Like, at that time there was a famine, how would people host guests?

contents.textus: 228. ḤD. Lo, saymiwa u+laḥmo, mbayḏíwayna, saymíwayna ṣobat ʕal i+qalto, dəmmina hawxa bu+zaboqo, ŭ saymiwa a+hne ... támowayne at+tanure! Saymiwa u+laḥmano, obə̀nwaylan tarte+ṭalme, tlaṯ+ṭalme. Yīy! I+gavayo luḥkíwaynale, mḥalqíwaynale. E Ăḷa! E, bašqa?
contents.versio: 228. No, they made bread, we did the repairing, we made stoves on the dunghill, so let’s say in the street, and they made the whatsits … the clay ovens were there! They would make this bread, they would give us two loaves, three loaves. Oooh! At that moment we would pounce on it, we tossed ourselves at it. Yes God, anything else?

contents.textus: 229. I. ʕAm u+hno dəmmina, ǧġeni mu ... muklone mḥalfe obənwa yani?
contents.versio: 229. With the whatsit, let’s say, besides the … would they give you any other foods?

contents.textus: 230. ḤD. Kul mede ṭəlbiwayna, naqqawoṯe əmmíwayna ‘Sūmlan baṣro!’ Naqqawoṯe əmmíwayna bərġəl, naqqawoṯe əmmíwayna ‘Sūmlan šamborak ...’
contents.versio: 230. We would ask for everything, sometimes we would say, ‘Make us some meat!’, sometimes we would say bulgur wheat, sometimes we said, ‘Make us some şambörek!’

contents.textus: 231. I. Saymiwa kul mede?
contents.versio: 231. Did they do everything?

contents.textus: 232. ḤD. Eeee, saymiwa naqqawoṯe, əmmíwayna knané ṫoraqk, hawxa hno maḥtiwa baynoṯe… dəmmina, əəə i+hno, i+ǧaǧəq. Maḥtiwa baynoṯa gelo, medone, hno medone, saymíwaylanyo. kNané ṫoraq k əmmíwayle, e, ǧắlăbe basímowa.
contents.versio: 232. HD. Yeeees, sometimes they made, we would call it kcheese breadk, such a whatsit they would put into it … let’s say, uh, the whatsit,  the kashk. They would put into it herbs, things, thingummies, they would make it for us. They would call it kcheese breadk, yeah, it was very good.

contents.textus: 233. I. Maǧrútuwa mhaškrútuwa ruḥayxu, səryóyehatu mšiḥoye?
contents.versio: 233. Would you dare reveal yourselves, you are Syriac Christians?

contents.textus: 234. ḤD. Səryoye, uḏʕiwa səryóyena ma ...
contents.versio: 234. Syriacs, wouldn’t they know we were Syriacs …

contents.textus: 235. I. Yani mhaškrútuwa, noše lápwayle də‿hno, domarxu mede?
contents.versio: 235. IL. Like, you revealed, people were unable to whatsit, to tell you something?

contents.textus: 236. ḤD. Lo, lo+haymèn, lo, lo+səmme mede.
contents.versio: 236. No, not really, they didn’t do anything.

contents.textus: 237. I. Latwa problém dəmmatwa ʕal u+dino, ʕal i+mšiḥoyuṯo?
contents.versio: 237. IL. Wasn’t there any problem you would say about the faith, about Christianity?

contents.textus: 238. ḤD. E, saymiwa naqqawoṯe mǧadala, saymíwayna aḥna, lo+mankrìwayna. Naqqa ʕawdiwayna b Zakko. Zakko qríṯowa. U+Ǧərǧo dbe Malok̇e, əḏʕátwayle lu+Ǧərǧo?
contents.versio: 238. HD. Yes, sometimes would struggle, we would do it, we would not apostatize. Once we would work in Zakko. Zakko was a village.  Jərjo Malok̇e, did you use to know Jərjo?

contents.textus: 239. I. Šaməʕno əšme ṭawwo.
contents.versio: 239. I’ve often (lit. ‘well’) heard his name.

contents.textus: 240. ḤD. U+babo du+Ṣawme. Ono, ŭ u+Ṣawme, ŭ u+Ǧərǧo ʕam u+Galo du+Guldíwayna. U+Galo du+Guldi kuḏʕatle?
contents.versio: 240. Sawme’s father. I, Sawme, and Jərjo, used to be with Guldi’s Galo. Do you know Guldi’s Galo?

contents.textus: 241. I. Šaməʕno əšme.
contents.versio: 241. I’ve heard his name.

contents.textus: 242. ḤD. B Zakko ʕawdíwayna, aṯi u+malla. Yani mərhṓv du+Ǧərǧowa. Yatu omar, ‘Hosta!’ Omar ‘Mənyo?’ Omar, ‘Amaḷḷi uʕdo, hatu b̥ḥaq də‿Mšiḥo mə‿kəmmutu?’ ‘Yawo malla’, omar, ‘Ṭray minan, kdav j‿ma bardak, flān.’ U+Galo hawxa zlām šaḥino ŭ šamóšowaste. ‘E halbat’, omar, ‘Kolozam dəmmatli!’ Omar, ‘Mšiḥo Alóhoyo!’ Komar, a‘ʕIsa nur Ăḷḷá, ʕIsa klam Ăḷḷá, ʕisa ruḥ Ăḷḷá!’a Omar, ‘Mə‿kowe? Kowe Aloho!’
contents.versio: 242. We were working in Zakko, along came the mullah. That is, he was a good friend of Jərjo’s. He sat down, he says, ‘Sir!’ He says, ‘What?’ He says, ‘Tell me now, what do you say about Christ?’ ‘Wow mullah’, he says, ‘Leave us alone, kkeep mouth away from usk’, etc. Galo, was such a hot-tempered man, and a deacon too. ‘Yeah, sure,’ he says, ‘It is critical you tell me!’ He says, ‘Christ is God!’ He says, a‘Jesus is God’s light, Jesus is God’s word, Jesus is God’s spirit!’a He says, ‘What’ll it be? It’ll be God!’

contents.textus: 243. E qām qḥīr, qām azzé nafəq. Nṣəfle ṭize, azzeyo. Yawo, u+hno, u+Ǧərǧo omar, ‘Qay hawxa səmlux, Galo? ‘Əə, gmoqaḏno u+babayḏe, ma gəzzí mankaṇṇo!?’ Ăḷá, ha fayišina yawmo tre, aṯi su+Ǧərǧo, omar ‘Aǧ+ǧule dan+naʕime ʕǧiqi, mṭayene dəmbánnanne dəmbayḏən ... dә‿hnən, dmašiġənne an+naʕime.’ E, haṯe i+šato qamayto heš ʕəmri tmone-čaʕ̥+əšnewa. E Ăḷá, Zakko, Zakko əšma di+qriṯo Zákkowa.
contents.versio: 243. Yes, he up and got angry, he up and went away. He shook off his butt, he went away. Wow, the whatsit, Jərjo says, ‘Why did you do so, Galo?’ ‘Uh, I shall burn his father, am I going to apostatize?!’  God, we stayed here a day or two, he (the mullah) came to Jərjo, he says, ‘The kids’ clothes got dirty, bring them so I can take them away in order to repair… to whatsit, so the kids can wash them’. Right, this first year, I was still eight or nine years old.  Yes, God, Zakko, Zakko, the name of the village was Zakko.

contents.textus: 244. I. Mawxa u+ʕamo kfarzoyo, ono koḥozeno, bi+aġlabiye dhowewa ġắlăbe šaṭər, howewa ġắlăbe bʕaqəl, koraxwa bәbriṯo ġắlăbe.
contents.versio: 244. That’s why the Kfarze people, I see, since they in the majority were very clever, they were very smart, they traveled in Creation a lot.

contents.textus: 245. ḤD. Koraxwa, ḥur domaṇṇux, ono am+medonani, u+mede dhawi aʕmi, ʕəmri+tmone+əšne hul uʕdo, kibi domaṇṇo, kibi maḥkeno mine. Lo+ṭaʕine, aḏiʕat? Kīt hən mu+ʕamo, lo+kuḏʕi mede. E, e Ăḷa háwxayo.
contents.versio: 245. They traveled, look I’ll tell you, I can tell, I can tell everything that happened to me, since I was eight years old till now, I can speak about it. I did not forget it, you know? There are some people, they don’t know anything. Right, God, it’s so.

contents.textus: 1. S. Məǧġə́l ʕal áydarbo yalifat ʕaraboyo ŭ kurdoyo!
contents.versio: 1. Tell us about how you learned Arabic and Kurdish!

contents.textus: 2. I. U+kurdoyo. Aḥna bi+qriṯo me nǝʕmuṯayna, bә Kfarze, me nəʕmuṯayna qayimina bu+lešono, qayimina bu+lešono. Qamayto d̥kəmmínale lešono suryoyo emhoyo. Me emoṯayna, yalifina u+lešono suryoyo. Ŭ d̥ʔaḥna bi+qriṯayḏan, bi+qriṯayḏan dә Kfarze kətwa eba taqriban d... arbʕi+botè suryoye, ŭ kǝtwa šawʕi+tmoni+botè ṭaye.
contents.versio: 2. Kurdish. We in the village since our childhood, in Kfarze, since our childhood, we grew up with the language, we grew up with the language. In the first place, what we call the Syriac mother tongue. From our mothers, we learned Syriac. And so we in our village, in our village Kfarze there were approximately... forty Syriac Orthodox houses, and there were seventy-eighty Muslim houses.

contents.textus: 3. S. Šawʕi+tmoni? Seventy-eighty?
4. I. Šawʕi+tmoni+botè ṭaye.
contents.versio: 4. Seventy-eighty Muslim houses.

contents.textus: 5. S. Ema?
contents.versio: 5. S. When?

contents.textus: 6. I. Bann+alfo ŭ čaʕmo... ŭ ḥamš+ŭ́+tmonì, alfo ŭ čaʕmo ŭ ḥamš+ŭ́+tmonì, alfo ŭ čaʕmo ŭ tǝšʕi, bann+əšnani kətwa qariwo mo, mo+ŭ+ʕәṣrì+ʕaylat.
contents.versio: 6. In 19...85, 1985, 1990, in these years there were nearly one hundred, one hundred twenty families.

contents.textus: 7. S. Hat ema hawat?
contents.versio: 7. When were you born?

contents.textus: 8. I. Ono, alfo ŭ čaʕmo ŭ šwaʕ+ŭ+šawʕì. Šwaʕ+ŭ+šawʕì hawino bә Kfarze. Mәd̥... dínaqqa d̥koyoraw ḥa, d̥koqoyam ʕam ḥḏoḏe, aḥna mšiḥoye ŭ ṭaye, e, məqqa dəmmat u+lešono emhoyo lešono suryóyoyo, koyəlfínale bu+bayto, koyəlfínale ʕam aḥ+ḥawrone. U+lešono kurdoyo, kurdi koyəlfínale bu+šqoqo.
contents.versio: 8. As for me, in 1977. ’77 I was born in Kfarze. When... when someone grows up, gets raised together, we Christians and Muslims, yes, whatever you might say, our mother tongue is Syriac, we learn it at home, we learn it with friends. Kurdish, we learn Kurdish in the streets (lit. ‘street’).

contents.textus: 9. S. Aṭ+ṭaye bi+qriṯo kurdene aw ʕarabóyene?
contents.versio: 9. The Muslims in the village, are they Kurds or Arabs?

contents.textus: 10. I. Kurd̥, ʕarab layt. Kurdne, kulle kurd̥, kurdoyo koməǧġoli, e. Aḥna koyəlfina mənne u+kurdi, bas hənnək lə+gyəlfi minan u+suryoyo. Kīt u+medano, yaʕni. Layt ḥa suryoyo ádyawma bi+qriṯo dlə+k̬ḏaʕ kurdoyo, layt ḥaste. Bas layto tloṯo+šaqṣat dmǝǧġoli lešono suryoyo bi+qriṯo maṭ+ṭaye, mak+kurdoye.
contents.versio: 10. Kurds, there are no Arabs. They are Kurds, all of them are Kurds, they speak Kurdish, right. We learn Kurdish from them, but they won’t learn Syriac from us. There is this thing, like. There isn’t any Syriac Orthodox today in the village who doesn’t know Kurdish, not even one. But there aren’t even three individuals who speak Syriac in the village among the Muslims, among the Kurds.

contents.textus: 11. Mawxa qayimina ʕam ḥḏoḏe bu+maktab, bu+šqoqo, baynә‿ḥḏoḏe ḥawrone, yalifina u+kurdoyo ġắlăbe ṭawwo. ʕAmánoste məqqa dəmmat azzano lu+maktab̥, azzán lu+maktab̥ du+tərki. Bu+tərkiste, ánnaqqa yalifina u+lešono turkoyo, lešono turkoyo d̥kətyo lešono di+dawle bu+maktab̥. E, u+talawәzyòn tə́rkiyo, u+maktab̥ tə́rkiyo. Kǝzzúx li+dàyĭra, lad+dàyĭrat, lar+rasmi, dáyĭrat di+dawle kulle tə́rkine. Bu+šqoqo falge du+ʕamo tərki koməǧġǝl. Mawxa yalifina támoste turkoyo.
contents.versio: 11. Thus (lit. ‘from so’), we got raised together at school, in the streets (lit. ‘street’), friends with each other, we learned Kurdish very well. On top of that (lit. ‘with that too’), whatever you might say, we went to the school, we went to Turkish school. In Turkish, too, now, then, we learned Turkish, which is the language of the state, in school. Yes, the television is Turkish, the school is Turkish. You go to the office, the offices, to official places, the government offices are all Turkish. In the streets (lit. ‘street’), half of the people speak Turkish. Thus, we learned Turkish there too.

contents.textus: 12. Dínaqqa dәmšaylatli, dəmmat, ‘Áydarbo yalifat u+ʕàrabi?’ Ono bann+alfo ŭ čaʕmo ŭ šeṯ ŭ təšʕì azzino... Kito qriṯo qarútoyo l Mərde, əšma Bnebī́l. Tamo, moláfwayno lešono suryoyo. Moláfwayno tamo lan+naʕime di+qriṯo. Yaʕni malfono du+lešono suryoyo.
contents.versio: 12. When you ask me, you say, ‘How did you learn Arabic?’ I, in 1996, I went... there’s a village near Mardin, named Bnebī́l. There, I used to teach Syriac. I used to teach there the village children. Like, a Syriac teacher.

contents.textus: 13. S. Suryoyo kṯobonoyo? Classical Syriac?

14. Kṯobonoyo. Tamo, fayǝšno taqriban lšato. Fayǝšno baynoṯayye dmolafli u+lešono suryoyo. Me tamo, man+noše d̥tamo, man+noše, man+naʕime, mi+ǧămaʕa, me kul+noše, yaləfno tamo ʕárabi. Bas ǧġaliye yalǝfno.
contents.versio: 14. Classical Syriac. There, I stayed approximately a year. I stayed among them to teach me (sic, ‘in order to teach’) Syriac. From there, from the people there, from the people, from the children, from the community, from everybody, I learned Arabic there. I only learned to speak.

contents.textus: 15. S. Ayko i+qrìṯoyo?
contents.versio: 15. Where is the village?

contents.textus: 16. Qaruto l Mәrde, tmanyo+kilomatra. Qriṯo das+suryòyeyo. Mu+yawmo dyawme qriṯo das+suryòyeyo. Bas i+qriṯayo ádyawma fayəš d̥kətne mšiḥoye, bas ádyawma fayəš i+qriṯayo d̥kətne mšiḥoye tamo, bašqa layt.
contents.versio: 16. Near Mardin, eight kilometres. It is a village of the Syriac Orthodox. From ancient times (Lit. ‘from the day of days’), it has been a village of the Syriac Orthodox. Only that village today has remained in which there are Christians, but today that village has stayed so that they are Christians there, there aren’t any others.

contents.textus: 17. S. Ayna lešono komәǧġoli?
contents.versio: 17. What language do they speak?

contents.textus: 18. I. Hani komәǧġoli lešono ʕárabi.
contents.versio: 18. These ones speak Arabic.

contents.textus: 19. S. Suryoyo lo+koməǧġoli?
contents.versio: 19. Don’t they speak Syriac?

contents.textus: 20. I. Lo, lo+kuḏʕi suryoyo, lo+kuḏʕi, ḥa mənne. Me tamo yaləfno mənne u+lešono, u+pratìk d̥koməǧġolínale ádyawma, hawxa ʕárabi. Bas dínaqqa dəmmat, u+ʕàrabi áydarbo ánnaqqa yalifat d̥qoratle? Tamo kətwa ḥoli, qášowa, ḥoli. Qášowa, u+kohno di+qrìṯowa, u+qašo di+qrìṯowa, dә Bnebī́l. Taqriban d̥ḥamši+əšne, tamo səmle kohnuṯo. Foyášwayno tamo gabayye bi+qriṯo, gab̥‿ḥoli, tamo yaləfno mine, moláfleli u+ʕàrabi, i+qraytayḏe. I+qrayto du+ʕàrabi, moláfleliyo, áydarbo g̊ʶqoreno u+ʕàrabi. Ŭ i+štaġaliye... <...>
contents.versio: 20. No, they don’t know Syriac, they don’t know, any of them. From there, I learned from them the language, the functional one that we speak today, such Arabic. But when you say, Arabic, how did you learn to read it? There was my uncle there, he was a priest, my uncle. He was a priest, he was the village parson, he was the priest of the village, of Bnebī́l. For approximately fifty years, he did priest work there. I would stay there with them in the village, at my uncle’s, there I learned from him, he taught me Arabic, reading it. Arabic literacy, he taught it to me, how to read Arabic. And conversation...

contents.textus: 21. S. Mən qrelux b ʕaraboyo?
contents.versio: 21. What did you read in Arabic?

contents.textus: 22. I. B ʕaraboyo qreli u+mgalī̀n, u+mgalī̀n ŭ hani, bi+qamayto u+mgalī̀n, ŭ bəṯr kṯowe ḥrene. Yaʕni, a+kṯowe ḥrene dǝmmina kito, dəmmina, qreli u+qurʔānste.
contents.versio: 22. In Arabic, I read the Gospels, the Gospels and these (sorts of things), at first the Gospels, and then other books. Like, the other books, let’s say, there are, let’s say, I read the Qur’an too.

contents.textus: 23. S. U+qurʔānste?
contents.versio: 23. The Qur’an too?

contents.textus: 24. I. U+qurʔānste qreli, hənna me di+tawra.
contents.versio: 24. I read the Qur’an too, some things from the Torah.

contents.textus: 25. S. ʕAm ḥolux?
contents.versio: 25. With your uncle?

contents.textus: 26. I. Lo, lo, eli lruḥi, eli lruḥi. Uʕdo ono bi+dukkanayḏi kǝtli qurʔā́n.
contents.versio: 26. No, no, I did it by myself, I did it by myself. Now I, in my shop, I have a Qur’an.

contents.textus: 27. S. Qay?
contents.versio: 27. Why?

contents.textus: 28. I. Hawxa. Kobaʕno d̥fohamno mə‿kito tamo. Yaʕni, kobaʕno d̥fohamno bi+ṭayuṯo mə‿kito, yaʕni, i+ṭayuṯo mə‿komaḥko, yaʕni u+kṯowo mə‿komar, u+kṯowaṯṯe. U+kṯowo di+ṭayuṯo, mə‿komar, u+kṯowo du+mgalī̀n mə‿komar.
contents.versio: 28. So. I want to understand what’s there. Like, I want to understand what’s there in Islam, like, Islam, what it says, like, what the book says, their book. The Muslim text, what it says, the Gospel text, what it says.

contents.textus: 29. S. Ŭ qrelux u+qurʔā̀n.
contents.versio: 29. And you read the Qur’an.

contents.textus: 30. E. Kәtli uʕdo kṯowo du+qurʔā̀n bi+dukkanayḏi, ono bi+dukkanayḏi koqoreno u+qurʔā̀n naqqawoṯe. Ham bu+ʔàrabi...<...>
contents.versio: 30. Yes. Now I have a text of the Qur’an in my shop, I’m in my shop, I read the Qur’an sometimes. Either in Arabic...
