contents.textus: 31. Ínaqqa d̥koweli zabno xalyo... <...> ínaqqa d̥koweno xalyo, yatiwo, dlə́kweli šuġlo, komōdno u+kṯowo, koqoreno. Koqoreno u+kṯowo ʕárabi, lăšan dmozadne, lăšan dmozadne hēš, yaʕni, u+ʕàrabi, dmaqwene. E, hani taqriban kibe ʕǝṣri, tarte ŭ ʕǝṣri+əšne, yaʕni, mi+naqlayo yaləfno, əšmo+əšmo koyolafno u+ʕàrabi. Hani ʕǝṣri+əšne yaʕni baynóṯeno, koqoreno.
contents.versio: 31. When I have free (lit. ‘empty’) time... when I am free, sitting down, if I do not have work, I take the book, I read it. I read Arabic writing, in order to improve it, in order to improve it more, that is, the Arabic, to strengthen it. Yes, it’s been (lit. ‘it contains’) approximately these 20–22 years, like, from that time I (first) studied it, little by little I’m learning Arabic. These twenty years, like, I’m in the midst of it, I’ve been reading.

contents.textus: 32. S. Kul+yawmo?
contents.versio: 32. Every day?

contents.textus: 33. I. Lo, lo kul+yawmo. Bi+šabṯo tarte, tlaṯ+kore. <...> ʕAmano, dəmmina, koqoreno ánnaqqa suryóyoste. Koqoreno kṯowe ġắlăbe suryóyeste.
contents.versio: 33. No, not every day. Two or three times a week. On top of that (lit. ‘with that too’), let’s say, I now read Syriac too. I read many Syriac books too.

contents.textus: 34. S. Bas bʕaraboyo qrelux inǧī́l, ŭ qurʔā́n, ŭ bas?
contents.versio: 34. But in Arabic, you have read only the Gospel, the Qur’an, and that’s all?

contents.textus: 35. Bas. Bas hiye... kṯowe du+ʕàrabi, layto harke ġắlăbe, a+kṯowe du+ʕàrabi, harke layt. Lə+k̬miqafən, yaʕni, a+kṯowe du+ʕàrabi. Mawxa, layto kul+kṯowo d̥qorat harke, yaʕni, laybux qorat kul+kṯowo harke, layto. Mawxa, koqorina maǧbū́r... hani a+kṯowànine d̥kətne bu+ʕàrabi, hánine, yaʕni, d̥ḥa kibe qoralle.
contents.versio: 35. That’s all. But it’s... Arabic books, there aren’t many here, Arabic books, there aren’t any here. They aren’t to be found, like, Arabic books. Thus (lit. ‘from so’), every book you read isn’t here, that is, it’s not possible for you to read every book here, they aren’t there. Thus (lit. ‘from so’), (when) we read it’s necessary... these are these books that are in Arabic, they’re these ones, like, which someone could read.

contents.textus: 1.	Ilyas: Qamayto, kə́tlilux šŭwolo qamoyo: kibux maḥkatlan ʕal aḥ+ḥayayḏux? Yani, bări tleṯi+əšne, ŭ ládyawma. Aḥ+ḥayayḏux áydarbo fayiti bi+qriṯo? (06. 04)
contents.versio: 1.	I. First, I have an initial question: can you tell us about your life? Like, thirty years back, and until today. How has your life been in the village?

contents.textus: 2.	Malfono Isḥaq. Bări tleṯi+əšne?
contents.versio: 2.	M. Thirty years back?

contents.textus: 3.	I. ŭ ládyawma. ʕƏmrux kibe ... səmlux arbʕi+əšne.
contents.versio: 3.	I. And until today. Your age is ... you are 40 years old.

contents.textus: 4.	M. E, ʕəmri uʕdo tarte+ŭ+arbʕi+ə̀šneyo. Ono harke mawladno, bi+qriṯo, hawxa karyo domaṇṇo, ŭ qreli b̰mōr+Malke, yulfono suryoyo, ŭ bəṯr aṯino li+qriṯo, bʕəmro dəmmina dətraḥsar+əšne, bayn traḥsar+tlotaḥsàr, hawxa.
contents.versio: 4.	M. My age is now 42. I was born here, in the village, so I shall speak briefly, and I studied at Mor Malke, Syriac studies, and then I came back to the village, at the age of twelve, so to speak, between twelve and thirteen, like so.

contents.textus: 5.	Bəṯr məd aṯino šġili bu+bayto, fləḥli, šġili bu+bayto ʕam emi, ʕam babi, hēš baḥ+ḥàyene. Karme, šuġlo, mə‿dhowewa. Yani dawríwayna karme, hul úʕdoste k̬dawrina karme. ínaqqa d̥kəmmina karme – daʕ+ʕənwe, ʕənwe.
contents.versio: 5.	After I came back, I worked at home, I farmed, I worked at home with my mother, with my father, they are still alive. Vineyards, work, whatever there was. Like, we ploughed vineyards, even until now we plow vineyards. When we say ‘vineyards’, the grape ones, grapes.

contents.textus: 6.	Kə́twaylan u+zabnawo ḥaywoṯo, ʕam aḥ+ḥaywoṯo maṣre. ŭ bəṯr maṭino dəmmat ləštaḥsar+əšne, mede ʕəmro, aw šwaḥsar.
contents.versio: 6.	At that time, we had living creatures, we were bound to living creatures. And after I reached, you can say, sixteen years, some age, or seventeen.

contents.textus: 7.	Hawi sniquṯo li+madrašto. Malfone latwa. Azzə́n l Awrŭpa, dəmmina, l Awrifi. Edi ... maṣəṇṇo bi+madrašto yani. Bdeli bi+madrašto, maqreli, hul bəṯr ... hu‿laʕ+ʕəsri+əšne.
contents.versio: 7.	There was a dearth of an academy. There were no teachers. They went to Europe, so to speak, to Evropa. Then I got bound to the academy, like. I started at the academy, I taught, until after… until twenty years.

contents.textus: 8.	Me tamo azzí li+folḥuṯo Turkoyto, yani li+ʕaskariye du+Tərki. Simolan šato ŭ falge. Ŭ bəṯr məd daʕərno mi+folḥuṯo du+tərki, mi+ʕaskariye, mzawaġno ʕam i+baṯ+zawgayḏi, i+Yəldəz, ŭ hawxa.
contents.versio: 8.	From there I went for Turkish corvée, that is for Turkish military service. We did it for a year and a half. And after I came back from Turkish corvée, from military service, I espoused my spousal unit, Yəldəz, and so forth.

contents.textus: 9.	Aḥ+ḥayayḏi k̬mdawmi. Yani bgawe+dəḥḏoḏe, frišo məḥḏoḏe, kibux dəmmat, traḥsar+šnayo maqreli bi+madrašto. Ŭ hawxa bəṯr me zabno yani ba+tralfo+ŭ+ḥsar, kibi domaṇṇo ma+tralfo+ŭ+ḥsar, edi mi+maǧburiye, mi+sniquṯo di+maddiye, ŭ me qaṭre, me săbabe ḥrene, ġēr hawxa, edi ṭreli mena ba+tralfo+ŭ+ḥsar. Ŭ uʕdo baḥ+ḥaye du+bàytono, di+ʕayla, aḥ+ḥaye dəmmina ... e?
contents.versio: 9.	My life goes on. Like, altogether, but separate from one another, you can say, I taught twelve annuals at the academy. And so, after some time, like, in 2010, I can say, from 2010, then, out of necessity, out of a dearth of substance (i.e., wealth), out of entanglements, out of other causes, otherwise like so, then I left it in 2010. And now, I’m (engaged) in the life of the home, of the family, the life so to speak ... yes?

contents.textus: 10.	I. Bu+maktab di+dawle qrelux hīč, dəmmina?
contents.versio: 10.	I. Have you never studied at the public school, so to speak?

contents.textus: 11.	M. E, qreli ḥamməš‿šne, qreli ḥamməš‿šne, normál, šeṯ qreli, qreli šeṯ+əšne. Bas ḥḏo+manne zoyúṫṫowa, ǧizza, ʕal dluli diḳo rəšwa ... ha-ha-ha ... lu+malfonayḏan du+Turkoyo. Normál kašírowayno bi+qraye, bas ʕal dəṭləble diḳo, u+waxtawo ... mayko diḳo? Dobat mede lnošo ... Fəqriye, flān ... yani, laybux mdabrat ruḥux, kṭolab diḳo menux, aw mede ḥreno rəšwa, mede muklo. E, lulan, latwa, dəmmina, lulan. Qreli šato zoyuṫṫo, ṭowo yaləfno šato ḥreto, zoyuṫṫə́r.
contents.versio: 11.	M. Yes, I studied five years, I studied five years, (that’s) normal, (but) I studied six, I studied six years. But one of them was extra, punishment, because I didn’t give a rooster as a bribe ... ha-ha-ha ... to our teacher of Turkick. I was usually prosperous at studying, but because he demanded a rooster, that time ... a rooster from where? For you to give something to someone... Poverty, etc., like, you can’t support yourself, he demands a rooster from you, or some other kind of bribe, some kind of food. Yes, we didn’t give it, there wasn’t any, so to speak, we didn’t give it. I studied an extra year, I learned well another year, all the more.

contents.textus: 12.	I. Kmo lešone kuḏʕat?
contents.versio: 12.	I. How many languages do you know?

contents.textus: 13.	M. Lešone ... suryoyo ŭ turkoyo ŭ ʕaraboyo ŭ kurdóyoste, hawxa kibi mdabarno ruḥi.
contents.versio: 13.	M. Languages… Syriac, and Turkick, Arabick, and also Kurdick, I can manage like so.

contents.textus: 14.	I. ʕAraboyo kuḏʕat???
contents.versio: 14.	You know Arabick???

contents.textus: 15.	M. E, turkoyo ... Yani, e, kibi mdabarno ruḥi hawxa, e.
contents.versio: 15.	Yes, Turkick ... Like, yes, I can manage, like so, yes.

contents.textus: 16.	I. Šafiro!!!
contents.versio: 16.	I. Great!!!

contents.textus: 17.	S. ʕAraboyo? Mayko?
contents.versio: 17.	S. Arabick? From where?

contents.textus: 18.	M. Deboro hawxa lruḥi, hawxa. Xabro marke, ḥa me tamo, šeyolo, flān. Meqəm qoréwayno lruḥi, yalə́fwayno kṯawto du+ʕaraboyo bruḥi hawxa. Bbayto kə́twayli dəmmat, yani hawxa mărā́q du+ilofo, ḥubo mede, yalə́fwayno, bəṯr ṭreli. Qoréwayno kul+yawmo. Kibux dəmmat koṯáwwayno ŭ qoréwayno ... heš ... hawxa.
contents.versio: 18.	M. So, managing, like so. A word from here, another from there, a question, etc. Back then, I used to study on my own, I learned the Arabic script by myself, like so. At home, I had, you can say, like, such a curiosity to learn, a kind of love, I used to learn, then I abandoned it. I used to study every day. You can say, I used to write and read ... still ... like so.

contents.textus: 19.	I. Mən kuḏʕat ʕal u+tarī̀x, ʕal u+maktàbzabno d Arkaḥ? Dəmmina am+maʕəmronayḏa mánwayne? B̥ayna zabno ʕamiro? Mən iḏaʕ̥ṯo kətlux ʕal u+medano?
contents.versio: 19.	I. What do you know about the history, about the chronography of Arkaḥ? Let’s say who were its builders? At what time was it built? What knowledge do you possess about this matter?

contents.textus: 20.	M. Mətyaqán, maktabzabno, yani ...
contents.versio: 20.	Make sure, chronography, like ...

contents.textus: 21.	I. Yani, Arkaḥ. I+maʕnayḏa mənyo?
contents.versio: 21.	Like, Arkaḥ, What is its meaning?

contents.textus: 22.	M. Yani Arkaḥ, dəmmina yaqiḏo, normál, kmo+naqlat. Dəmmina baq+qaṭle, bam+medone dhawi, baq+qṭolʕame dhawi, kul+naqqa mhaǧriwa, əzzənwa, mahəzmiwa larwal. Ṭabi, Arkaḥ, kito eba, dəmmina, me qəryawoṯe, əšmone ġắlabe mšáḥəlfe, ṭabi, márkewayne, mahzamme, aw me larwal aṯən ʕabirila.
contents.versio: 22.	Like, Arkaḥ, let’s say, burned down, normal, several times. Let’s say during the killings, during the things that happened, during the genocides that happened, they relocated each time, they went away, they fled outside. Well, Arkaḥ has, so to speak, those from some villages, many diverse surnames, well, they were from here, they fled, or they came into it from outside.

contents.textus: 23.	Yani bam+mo mo kibux dəmmat latyo iḏiʕo. Hən manne meqəm me šwaʕmo+əšne, daʕirila me dukoṯo ġēr. Ŭ hən noqəṣṭə́r, ŭ hawxa. Yani hən me Maḥsarte ... kəmmina ... aḥna, kəmmi, me Maḥsártena. Kəmmilan be+Ṣaboġo.
contents.versio: 23.	Like, one hundred percent, you can say it’s not known. Some of them came back to it from other places seven hundred years ago. And some later, and like so. Like, some from Maḥsarte, let’s say us, they say, we are from Maḥsarte. They call us the Ṣaboġo family.

contents.textus: 24.	Ŭ kīt‿ənna kəmmi me Armū́n ... tamo mu+darbo ... yani mi+B̥šeriye, i+xasrayo, kəmmina b Baṭmán, Armū́n kīt tamo, lo? E, kətlan kmo+yaqroṯo me tamo. Dəmmina, k̬mitawmar hawxa. Ŭ hən arboye...
contents.versio: 24.	And there are some who say (some are) from Armun… there on the way from … like, from Bšeriye, on that side, we shall say in Batman, Armun is there, no? Yes, we have several households from there. Let us say, so it is said. And some Arboians...

contents.textus: 25.	Ŭ bu+šəklawo, yani, bam+mo mo kibi domaṇṇo laybe noše domar ‘aš+šaqṣani maʕmarre i+qriṯo’, e.
contents.versio: 25.	And that way, like, 100% I can say, nobody can say ‘these people built the village’, right.

contents.textus: 26.	I. Yani, dəmmina, komaḥwe, dəmmina, bu+maktàbzabno di+ʕito bi+aġlabiye. Dínaqqa dʔoṯənwa a+mšiḥoye, yani, dínaqqa dmaqəbliwa i+haymonuṯo də Mšiḥo, direk maʕəmriwa ʕito bi+qriṯayo. I+ʕitaṯxu dəmmina bu+zabno ... bu+doro da+kmo ʕamiro? Mayo komitawḏaʕ̥ d̥kətyo i+qriṯo məqqa ʕatəqto.
contents.versio: 26.	Like, shall we say, it seems, shall we say, predominantly in the chronography of the church. When the Christians would come, like, when they embraced the faith of Christ, they would immediately build a church in that village. Your church, so to speak, in the time ... in which century was it built? From that, it becomes evident (lit. ‘gets made known’) that the village is that old.

contents.textus: 27.	M. Hiye ʕal u+mede dməḷḷux kšofaʕ̥ dəmmina bi+Tašʕiṯo d Mōr Malke. Komar Ḥarbo d Ayle, Xărăbale komar, Xărăbale, aw Arkaḥ, Árkaḥste komar ... i+tašʕiṯo d Mōr Malke, harke tre+kilomàtrayo. Komar tamo, yani, kulle mġuše ŭ flān, yani. Látwalle hāž mi+haymonuṯo. Komar ínaqqa dʔaṯi Mōr Malke larke, bdele bi+haymonuṯo, flān, dəmṭalle lu+darbo. Ḥatta, komar, maʕmárralle i+dayro, yani mʕawanne bi+ʕmara di+dayro támoste, Mōr Malke.
contents.versio: 27.	M. What you talked about unfolds, so to speak, in the Life of Mor Malke. It says Ḥarbo d Ayle, it says Xărăbale, Xărăbale, or Arkaḥ, it also says Arkaḥ… the Life of Mor Malke, here, it’s two kilometres. There it says, like, all of them Magians and so on, like. They had no idea about the faith. It says when Mor Malke came here, he started with the faith, etc., to bring them on the way. They even, it says, built the monastery for him, like, they helped with the building of the monastery there too, Mor Malke.

contents.textus: 28.	I. Af+fayoše qamoye d̥arke, hənnək mġúšene, oromóyene, bas dínaqqa d̥koṯe Mōr Malke, Mōr Malke bu+doro da+tloṯo ŭ falge, da+tloṯo ... (M.: Tloṯo ŭ ruʕo mede hawxa, e), tloṯo ŭ falge, koṯe komaʕmar i+dayro. Ínaqlayo komaqəbli i+mšiḥoyuṯo, kowən mšiḥoye, kmaḥwe.
contents.versio: 28.	I. The first settlers here, they are Magians, they are Aramaeans, but when Mor Malke comes, Mor Malke in the middle of the fourth century, in the fourth … (M.: in the first quarter of the fourth, something like that, yeah), the middle of the fourth, he comes to build the monastery. At that time, they accept Christianity, they become Christians, it appears.

contents.textus: 29.	M. Hawxa komar bi+təšʕiṯayḏe d Mōr Malke, k̬maḥke hawxa. Ŭ i+ʕìtoste ṭábiki otomatík i+naqqayo híyaste k̬ʕəmro. Bəṯr məd mtalmḏi, məd mhaymanne.
contents.versio: 29.	M. It says so in the Life of Mor Malke, it tells it so. And naturally, the church is automatically built at the same time, too. After they discipled, after they believed.

contents.textus: 30.	M. I+ʕitayḏan, bas siqumo layt aʕla, maktábzabno lo+k̬maḥwe aʕla, dʔema ʕamiro, meqəm kə́twayla šurone ġắlabe rwiḥe, kə́pwalle tloṯo+mətrowat. E, ŭ bəṯr mḥatṯo, mšáḥəlfo, nafəq bgawa kefe baš+šuronayḏa, kefe daq+qəštoṯe dam+maḏəbḥe, kefe rabe, ʕatiqe. (12.22)
contents.versio: 30.	Our church, but there is no reckoning upon it, a chronography does not appear upon it, so when it was built back then, it had very thick walls, they were three metres thick. Yes, and later it was renovated, modified, stones emerged inside it, in its walls, stones from the altars’ arches, big stones, ancient ones.

contents.textus: 31.	Kito bdəkoṯe, bġắlabe qəryawoṯe manne. Kito, dəmmina, b̥ Ḥabsəs, kito b ʔAnḥəl, bdəkoṯe hawxa. Yaʕni hánəkste ksuhḏi d̥̚kətyo ʕatəqto. Bas latyo iḏiʕo, xud dməḷḷi. Yani latla hno, mṣákroyo, hak̇a maʔ+ʔiqoḏe dhawi, ŭ mu+tehzimo dmahəzmiwa mi+qriṯo.
contents.versio: 31.	There are some of them in some places, in many villages. There are, let’s say, in Ḥabsәs, there are in Anḥәl, in such places. Meaning, those also attest that it is ancient. But it is not known, like I said. Like, it doesn’t have a whatsit, it is lost, whether from the fires that happened, or from the times (lit. ‘flights’) they would flee from the village.

contents.textus: 32.	I. Kīt mede mġammone d͡ǧari? Yani, maḥšone d͡ǧari bi+qriṯo, dəmmina, xud u+Sayfo, xud i+Ġala, xud i+maḥtašiye, aw medone d͡ǧari d̥̚kətne makiwone lʕamo aw lšaqṣaṭ? Kīt u+medano d̥̚kuḏʕatte d̥šamiʕatte dbări minux ḥamši+əšne, bări mo+əšne? Dəmmina, mắsala, dəmmina ʕal u+Sayfo, bu+Sayfo bi+ Xărăbale mən ǧari, mən hawi bi+ Xărăbale bu+sayfo? (13.20)
contents.versio: 32.	I. Are there any tragic things that happened? Like, afflictions that happened in the village, let’s say, like the Genocide, like the Famine, like drought, or things that happened which cause pain to the people or to individuals? Is there this sort of thing, which you know, which you have heard, which were fifty years before you, one hundred years ago? Let’s say, for example, let’s say about the Genocide, during the Genocide in Xărăbale what happened, what occurred in Xărăbale during the Genocide?

contents.textus: 33.	M. Bu+Sayfo harke normál, mede lawi. U+ʕamo latəm b̰ Mōr Malke. Lu+gorā̀n, ṭabi, du+maḏʕo, du+šmoʕo, layimi b̰ Mōr Malke, ŭ tamo yani mdafaʕʕe ruḥayye ʕam ḥḏoḏe, aq+qəryawoṯe, yani...
contents.versio: 33.	M. During the Genocide, here was normal, nothing happened. The people gathered in Mor Malke. According to the information, to the rumours, they gathered in Mor Malke, and there, like, they defended themselves together, the villages, like...

contents.textus: 34.	I. Yani lṭaye lə+hǧəmme aʕlayye?
contents.versio: 34.	I. Like, the Muslims didn’t attack them?

contents.textus: 35.	M. Di+dukṯo? Du+hǧomo lo+koḏaʕno, normál hayo, laybi dobeno hno aʕla. Bas ínaqqa dəmmina d̥ Ḥaǧo, hawi, howewa ḥboṣo ġắlabe aʕlayye, ḥəb̥ṣíwanne. Ínaqqa d̥ Ḥaǧo d̥kətwe, yani bi+dukṯo d̥kətwe, dmamlaxwa ḥatta yani mḥéwayle, dəmmina bi+dayro d Mōr Málkeste. Topat, medone flān lədroyo, medone hawxa, ŭ ənnək mdafaʕʕe ruḥayye tamo. U+mede d̥kuḏʕina, yani, mdafaʕʕe ruḥayye.
contents.versio: 35.	M. The locals? About the attack, I don’t know, that one was normal, I can’t give a whatsit about it. But when we speak of Ḥaǧo, it happened, there was a great mobbing against them, they mobbed them. When Ḥaǧo, who was, like, in the place he was, that he ruled until, like, he had hit it, so to speak, in the Mor Malke monastery as well. Cannons, such and such things for shooting, such things, and they defended themselves there. The thing we do know, like, they defended themselves.

contents.textus: 36.	Azzalle noše, lazzé, əllah azzalle! Ínaqqa dlowe ... yaʕni lo+bi+hăwa mahzamme ltamo?! Mdafaʕʕe ruḥayye tamo, b̰ Mōr Malke.
contents.versio: 36.	People went to them, they didn’t, of course they went to them! If it weren’t ... like, did they flee there for no reason?! They defended themselves in Mor Malke.

contents.textus: 37.	Ŭ medone dəmmina baynə‿ḥḏoḏe, medone maḥišone lawi. Yani kə́twaylan ḥa, əšme Brahím, balki ono naʕímowayno, qṭíwalle lad+Daliniye, hawxa. Qay kə́twayle qay mahwo ŭ šqolo. Kətwa baq+qəryawoṯe ... dəmmíwayla barbăriye, kətwa fliġuṯo ... məḷḷi ŭ məḷḷux ... Kul+ḥa ksamle ḥawro ḥa tamo ḥa tamo. Yani qṭíwalle ḥa hawxa. Harke qṭíwalle bu+ṭuro. Yani xud dəmmat ruʕyo qṭəlle. Hənnək ŭ ad+Daliniye hawxa kə́twalle medone ʕam ḥḏoḏe. Məḷḷi ŭ məḷḷux naqqawā́t, ʕal‿awxa qṭíwalle. Ŭ bəṯr sə́mwalle bi+ḥarayto šayno, ŭ hawxa...
contents.versio: 37.	And some things, so to speak, among each other traumatic things didn’t happen. Like, we had someone whose name was Brahim, I was probably a child, the Dalinians killed him, like so. Probably, he had some business (lit. ‘giving and taking’). There was in the villages ... they called it feuding, there was division ... he said, she said. Everyone makes himself one ally here, one ally there. Like, they killed someone like so. They killed him here in the hill country. Like, you could say, they killed a shepherd. They and the Dalinians had issues with each other. He said, she said sometimes, for such they killed him. And later they finally made peace, and so on...

contents.textus: 38.	Dəmmina, bi+folḥuṯo, qṭəlle tloṯ‿arbʕo. Kibi domaṇṇo hánəkste balki ʕal i+tawdiṯo quṭlíwanne. Hawxa medone, kətwa ḥsome, medone du+medawo. Hən qariwe me diḏan ... flān ... be ʕammi, yani, támoste qṭīl noše, mayiṯi hawxa tamo, azzə́n lo+daʕiri, yani. Hawxa medone hawxa, bu+šklawo hawi. Ŭ medone ġēr baynə‿ḥḏoḏe, aḥna, daxəlī́ mede hawxa lawi. Mede maḥišone ġēr lawi, yani.
contents.versio: 38.	So to speak, in the corvée, they killed three–four. I can say they killed them perhaps for confessional reasons. Such things, there were feuds, things of that sort. Some relatives of ours ... whosit ... my paternal uncle’s family, like, there too people were killed, they died like so there, they went, they didn’t return, like. Such things like so, it happened in that way. And some other things between ourselves, internally such things did not happen. No other traumatic things happened, like.

contents.textus: 39.	Ínnaqa dəmmina, am+medone dlanne iḏiʕe du+ʕamo: d̥kəmmi muqḏiwa i+qriṯo, muqḏalle; quwérəšwa meqəm, kətwa quwerəš, yani, bote dəmmina ... kuḏʕat u+qarəš? Bote mu+qayso, bote mu+qayso, qarʕayye ʕafro, yani raġlote d̥qayso, ŭ qṭoro.
contents.versio: 39.	Now then, so to speak, the things that are unknown to people: those who say they would burn the village, they did burn it; back then, there were hovels, there were hovels, like, houses so to speak… Do you know hovels? Houses made of wood, houses made of wood, their tops – earth, like, wooden posts, and a ceiling.

contents.textus: 40.	I. Áydarbo howənwa hani ab+botani, aq+quwerəšani?
contents.versio: 40.	I. How were these here houses, these hovels?

contents.textus: 41.	M. E hani normál, ono yani lo+ʕayəšn‿appe, bas hul uʕdo hēš kito ḥa, kibi domaṇṇux hawxa d̥fayəš kmo+stunat me diḏe dnafəl. Hēš, e, hani gmoṭənne dəmmina qayse ḥlime mu+ṭuro. Hawxa yani fagone kəmmínanne, qayso fagono, yani dugliye, kīt hənna d̥kəmmi dugliye. Hano kurdóyoyo. Bas aḥna kəmmina fagono, qayso ḥlimo, fagono.
contents.versio: 41.	Yes, these ones were normal, I, like, I didn’t live in them, but until now there is still one, so I can tell you that there remain however many of its columns, from the one that fell down. Still, yes, these things, they bring them, let’s say thick logs from the hill country. So, we call them crutches, a crutch log, that is a fork, there are some who say a fork. This is Kurdick. But we say a crutch, a thick log, a crutch.

contents.textus: 42.	Ṭabi ‘maʕə̞mrat bayto xarke aw rab̥ṫə́r’ meqəm latwa yani, ‘kul+ḥa sāmle bayto rabo’, latwa. Xarke aw tarte+kore hawxa. Yani gmaḥat, moṭe mu+ṭuro qayse du+baluṭo, qawye, našife. Meqəm ṭurone kətwa, u+ʕamo dəmmat lo+masxewa d̥qoṭaʕwa. Yani kul+ḥa kə́twayle u+ṭurayḏe, i+ḥəmmayḏe kəmmina. Miqafewa, latwa xd‿uʕdo. Quṭʕiwa qayse mani, ya<ni> mu+ṭuro. Moṭanwa ánnaqqa kiban dəmmina, ḥḏo tamo, kul, kul+tre aw tloṯo+mətrowat, lu+gorā̀n du+ṭʕono. Yani, ono, u+medano lo+ʕayəšne bas ḥzalli ḥzoyo, bas ḥzoyo. (16.49)
contents.versio: 42.	Naturally, back then there wasn’t ‘you build a house like here or bigger’, there wasn’t ‘everyone builds a big house for himself’. Like here or twice as much. Like, he brings down, they bring strong dry oak logs from the hill country. Back then, there were hills, people, you might say, would spare cutting them. Like, everyone had his own hill, we call it his plot. They used to exist, it wasn’t like now. They used to cut such logs, like, from the hill country. They would bring, now we can say, one there, every, every two or three metres, depending on the load. Like, I, this thing, I didn’t experience it (lit. ‘live it’), but I saw things, just things (lit. ‘I saw them seeing, just seeing’).

contents.textus: 43.	Kul+tre, aw tloṯo+mətrowat, qayso mano hawxaaa, yani bi+ṣira, ḥa tamo, ḥa bu+falgo, ḥa lŭgab̥, lu+gorā̀n di+ʕmara, di+rabuṯo du+bayto. Ŭ bəṯr ʕal qarʕe, maḥtiwa qayse medone, qayse msawye hanək. Qṭore msáwyewayne, lanne hawxa xani, lo+hawxa yani brime, msawye. Ŭ maḥtiwa bəṯr maq+qaysani, ṭowo suxriwa i+dukṯo, ḥatta balki ṭárfeste, maḥtiwa aʕlayye, lăǧan dlo+ʕobar u+ʕafro. Mətyaqanno ṭárfeste, ŭ maḥtiwa ʕafro ʕal qarʕe, ʕafro ṣiṭo, zəd̥. Ŭ bəṯr bi+mandarune, aḥna kəmmina mandrune, aḥna mandrune kəmmina ...
contents.versio: 43.	Every two or three metres, one such log, that is in a line, one there, one in the middle, one over there, according to the construction, to the size of the house. And then on top of it, they would put log things, those sorts of flat logs. Ceilings were flat, so they are not like these, not like so, that is, curved, flat. And they would put after these logs, they would seal (lit. ‘close’) the place well, even maybe branches too, they would put over them, so that the earth doesn’t get in. I believe branches, too, and they would put earth on top of it, a handspan of earth, more. And then with the rolling pin, we say rolling pin, rolling pin, we say.

contents.textus: 44.	I. Aḥna, manduriye. (17.30)
contents.versio: 44.	I. As for us, roller.

contents.textus: 45.	M. E, hənna mandarune kəmmi, kəmmi manduriye xud d̥kəmmat, aḥna kəmmina mandrune. E, yaʕni, ḥayṣowa u+qṭoro, ínaqqa dhówewa rakixo, ṭino, flān, ínaqqa towewa ... lăǧan dlo+gorəš maye laltaḥ. Ínaqqa hawxa laf u+nšofayḏe bayziwa tawno, tawno lăǧan dlo+qōṯ u+ṭino bi+manduriye, dlo+qōṯ u+ṭino eba, d̥qušʕole, dmarfyole. Ánnaqqa, mandriwa i+goro bu+šəklawo. Yani, hanək, qwerəš hawxa. (18.00)
contents.versio: 45.	M. Right, some say rolling pin, they say roller, as you say, we say rolling pin. Yes, that is, it compressed the roof, when it was soft, mud, whosit, when it became… so that it does not pull water down (i.e., absorb it). So when they would spread straw for drying it, straw so that the mud does not touch the roller, lest the mud touches it, so it eradicates it, so it repels it. Now then, they would roll the roof that way. Like, those ones, such hovels.

contents.textus: 46.	Hawxa gawe bahro zătan latwa, bahro latwa, lámpawa. E, i+lampa, koṯe lboli, bu+gāz, gāz ... mən ... aḥna gāz əmmíwaynale ... doġā́l gāzyo, be mənyo, gāz kəmmínale. Ínaqlayo hawxa, baq+qəryawoṯe kul+ḥa kə́twayle lampa. Kulle bәḥḏo+oda dəmxiwa, bu+šəklawo.
contents.versio: 46.	So, inside it, there wasn’t any light, of course, there was no light, it was a lamp. Right, the lamp, I remember, with kerosene, kerosene ... what… we would call it kerosene… it’s natural gas or whatever it is, we call it kerosene. So that time, in the villages everyone had a lamp. They all used to sleep in one room, that way.

contents.textus: 47.	I. Ŭ bəṯr manək, maq+quwerəšanək, an+noše qalibi lab+bote d̥kətne ádyawma, d̥koməstaʕmli, ab+bote ʕatiqe d̥kəmmínanne. Qalibi lani, bas lani, klozamme ánnaqqa kalšo, kefe. Áydarbo misəmwa u+kalšano yani? (18.38)
contents.versio: 47.	I. And after these things, these hovels, people switched to the houses that now exist, that they use, the old houses, as we call them. They switched to these, but these, now then they need lime, stones. How was this lime produced, that is?

contents.textus: 48.	M. ʕAyni mede, yani, ono bas aḥ+ḥaroyoṯe, dəmmina, dəḥzeli bʕayni dmaʕəmriwa, naʕímowayno. Kibi domaṇṇo hawxa bi+qamayto ḥəfriwa gurtoṯe laltaḥ, gurtoṯe ʕamuqe, dnəfqo i+šeno, yani, i+šeno kəmmina, u+šoʕo, kəmmina i+šeno. Hul dməfqíwayla, mə́troyo, treyo, tlóṯoyo, lgorā́n di+dukṯo, məqqa ʕamə́qtoyo, lgorā́n məqqa kīt ʕafro, i+dukṯo məš‿šə́kəlyo, ḥufriwa. Dəmmina, maṯlo, i+qəštaṯe məqqa g̥̊ṭuʕno. Kul+tloṯo+mətrowat, raġlo, yani bi+arʕo, ḥufriwa i+arʕo hul dnəfqowa.
contents.versio: 48.	M. Same thing, like, I saw with my eyes only the last ones, so to speak, when they were building them, I was a young boy. I can thus say, in the beginning, they would dig pits down, deep pits, so the bedrock appears, that is, we call it bedrock, megalith, we call it bedrock. Until they expose it, it’s a metre, it’s two, it’s three, depending on the place, however deep it is, depending on however much earth there is, on what kind of place it is, they would dig. Let’s say, for example, that arch, however much it will bear. Every three meters, a footing, like, in the earth, they would dig up the earth until it appeared.

contents.textus: 49.	Bonanwa kefe hul lalʕal, məd maṭyowa lfoṯa di+arʕo. Yani hano dəmmat, i+ḥalo du+bàytoyo, məṭyowa li+ḥalo du+bayto. I+raġlayo, hayo, hayo hani d̥kənne taḥta di+arʕo, maʕlanne xəd məḷḷi. Ánnaqqa, bəṯr g̊ʶquṭrənne. G̊ʶquṭri mi+raġlayo ŭ layo qəšto, bak+kefe ŭ bi+čimənto, yani kalšo, ŭ mayo layo, bu+šəklawo, ʕam ḥḏoḏe.
contents.versio: 49.	They would build stones upwards, until it reaches the surface of the earth. Like, this is what you would call, it’s the floor of the house, it would reach the floor of the house. That footing, that one, that one, those that are under the ground, they raise them as I said. Then, afterwards, they would tie them together. They tie an arch from that footing to that one, with stones and cement, that is lime, and from that one to that one, that way, together.

contents.textus: 50.	Edi, ʕamani, g̊saymiwa qṭoro, u+qṭoro dəkḥozina. Kəbʕat hano laltaḥ howe, ŭ kəbʕat bayto lalʕal‿owe. Maṯlo, uʕd‿arke kito bayto lalʕal mano, ʕayni mede, baš+šurone dəkḥozina uʕdo. (20.05)
contents.versio: 50.	Then, with these, they would make a ceiling, the ceiling that we see. If you want, this goes below, and if you want, a floor (lit. ‘house’) goes above. For example, now there is a floor here above this one, the same thing, with the walls that we see now.

contents.textus: 51.	I. U+qṭorawo áydarbo misəmwa, dəmmina? U+qṭorawo, u+šəklano, áydarbo mōdwa u+šəklano, yani?
contents.versio: 51.	I. How would this ceiling be made, so to speak? That ceiling, this shape, how would it take this shape, that is?

contents.textus: 52.	M. E, u+qṭoro ánnaqqa hano, maṯlo, saymiwa bi+qamayto aš+šurone ha hawxa. U+ʕulyo daš+šurone, mə́qqane? Tre aw tloṯo+mətrowat gmaʕlat aš+šurone. Hani aš+šurònene. Bəṯr ánnaqqa maš+šurone kuṯyo i+məre, haṯe kəmmínala məre, dək̬maḥwyo. U+šuro lárkeyo. Marke ŭ ze, gbode.
contents.versio: 52.	M. Yes, the ceiling, now, this one, for example, they would first make the walls here like so. The walls, how high are they? Two or three meters, you would raise the walls. These are the walls. After the walls, now then, comes the lunette (lit. ‘mirror’), this one we call a lunette, the one which is seen. The wall is up to here. From here onwards, it starts.

contents.textus: 53.	Tamo ánnaqqa gmoṭanwa qayse ḥlime mu+ṭuro, yarixe, lgorā́n du+ʕulyo di+dukṯo, du+ʕulyo d̥arke, du+ʕulyo di+məre. Kayle kayle makilíwanneste, be mə‿kə́twanne ínaqqayo, wăki bu+ḥuṭo makiliwa, bmən makiliwa? Mətro latwa. Zaḥme d̥owalle mətro.
contents.versio: 53.	There they would then bring thick logs from the hill country, long ones, depending on the height of the place, on this here height, on the height of the lunette. Measure after measure (lit. ‘measures, measures’), they would measure them (i.e., the trunks), at that time, what would they have had, whether they measured with thread, with what did they measure? There wasn’t any metre. A metre would be difficult for them.

contents.textus: 54.	Quṭʕiwa qayse lgorā́n kmo glozamme, hostáwatwayne, yalífewayne. ʕAyni mede hawxa, Fagone, maṯlo, ḥa ltamo, dəmmina, i+ʕmara tre+mətròwatyo u+ʕulyayḏa. Ḥušwina tre+mətrowat, ḥa ltamo, ḥa larke, ḥa larke, ḥa larke, ŭ támoste hawxa. Ŭ bəṯr gməždiwa mxadde aʕle, yani stune daməxto, qayso ḥlimo mayo layo, ŭ maṯe lawo, hawxa. G̊saymalle xd‿i+ʕarzelo. Ánnaqqa dəmmina gdəmdawmiwa, lăǧan dməfqi u+hnawo. Me tamo ... ánnaqqa, hano qat, qayse. Bəṯr mano, disa gmoṭanwa qayse kreṫə́r, daqrone kreṫə́r. Yani fagone mani, qayse fagone, stune kəmmínanne. Disa naqqa ḥreto, qat ḥreno bu+šəklawo. ʕAyni xd‿at+taḥtoye. Mdawám hawxa, mu+rešo lu+rešo. Bu+fàlgoste, dəmmina maṯlo, ḥa tamo lu+gorā̀n d̥ṭoʕən.
contents.versio: 54.	They would cut logs as many as needed, they were craftsmen, they were knowledgeable. So, the same thing, crutches, for example, one over there, let’s say the construction, its height is two metres. Let’s count two meters, one over there, one here, one here, one here, and over there too, like so. And then they stretched a ‘pillow’ over it, that is, a column on its side (lit. ‘lying’), a thick log, from that one to that one, and from this one to that one, like so. They would make it like a ground bed. Now then, let’s say, they would continue so that they would bring out that whatsit (i.e., the scaffold). From there … now then, this one, a layer, logs. After that one, once again they would bring shorter logs, shorter braces. Like, some of these crutches, crutch logs, we call them a column. Once again, another time, another layer that way, the same as the ones below. Continue like so, from one end to the other. In the middle, too, let’s say for example, one there, according to what it carries.

contents.textus: 55.	Kibe dowe u+fəṯwaṯṯe, mətro ŭ falge baynaṯṯe howe, yăda mətro. Ak+kaylanək, laybi dománnanne. Lu+gorā̀n di+rwiḥuṯo du+bayto, tloṯo, tloṯo ŭ fálgene, árbʕone rwiḥe, bu+šəklawo. (22.03)
contents.versio: 55.	It could be that their width is, it could be a metre and a half between them, or a metre. As for those measurements, I cannot tell them. Depending on the width of the house, they are three, three-and-a-half, four wide, that way.

contents.textus: 56.	Naqqa ḥreto g̊ʶquṭriwa ḥreno bu+šəklawo, hani tre. Ŭ gəsəlqiwa hul lalʕal ebe bu+šəklawo, hōl dməfqiwa u+qalbano ... ánnaqqa ... dəbʕat... dməfqi u+qaləb, yani, u+šəkl. Maḥtiwa qayse ánnaqqa aʕlayye.
contents.versio: 56.	Another time, they would overlay another one in that manner, these two (i.e., layers). And they (i.e., the builders) would go upwards on it that way, until they created this shape (i.e., the ‘mirror’)... now then ... as you wish... to create the scaffold, that is, the form. They would put logs, now then, on them.

contents.textus: 57.	Dəmmina, bi+qamayto, maqəmme ḥa hawxa. Hano qātyo. Bəṯr gdoṯe ḥreno ha hawxa. Čik̇e čik̇e gmabərmile, mat+tarte xasrat: tre hawxa, bəṯər tre+ḥrene hawxa, hano qṭīr hawxa. Yani, xud ḥa domar, b̥šəkəl ʕắǧămi. (22:38)
contents.versio: 57.	So to speak, at the beginning, they raised one like so. This is a layer. Then there comes another, here like so. Bit by bit, they’ll round it up, from both sides: two like so, then the other two like so, this has been roofed over (lit. ‘tied’) like so. Like, as one might say, in an amateurish way.

contents.textus: 58.	Ánnaqa gmaḥti qayse damixe aʕle, gmolalle. Qayse damixe, maṯlo hawxa. Moṭənwa ba+ḥmore, dəmmina. Moṭənwa qayse normál dat+taʕne ... aʕlayye hul d̥saymíwayle brimo, qaləb kule. Yani ann+alʕoṯe dmaqəmme tre aw tloṯo+qátatyo, lu+goran di+ʕmara, d̥kətyo ʕelayto, xud məlli, hul dməṭyo li+qəšto, qayse damixe.
contents.versio: 58.	Now then, they’ll put horizontal (lit. ‘lying’) logs upon it, they’ll fill it up (i.e., enclose the roof). Horizontal logs, for example, like so. They would bring them with donkeys, so to speak. They would bring logs of the normal sort of loads (e.g., for heating)… on them until they would make it curved, the whole frame. That is, the ‘ribs’ that they raise up are two- or three-layered, depending on the building, whether it’s high, as I said, until it reaches the arch, horizontal logs.

contents.textus: 59.	Hawxa bu+fəṯwo, qayse damixe, ŭ hawxa bu+šəklano, hul dmabərmíwayle, nofaqwa brimo, e, ŭ bəṯr məd‿šīʕ ṭowo baq+qayse, məd hīw ele u+qaləb di+qəšto baq+qayse damixe dmaḥatte ʕul manək, maṯlo, dmaqəmlan, dar+raġloṯe, ṭrowe dar+raġloṯanək.
contents.versio: 59.	So in the width, horizontal logs, and so that way, until they would round it up, it would come out curved, yeah, and after it became well-covered by logs, after the shape of an arch was given to it (i.e., the house) with the horizontal logs they put above those ones, for example, that we raised, the footings, it should be those footings.

contents.textus: 60.	Ánnaqqa maḥtiwa ṭino, saymiwa ṭino, mgawliwa ṭino. Maḥtiwa tawno ébeste, saymiwa hawxa šallinat, šallinat kəmmina, hən kəmmi qoleʕe, šallinat, aḥna kəmmina šallinat hawxa, ŭ barbán dəḥḏoḏe ʕal aq+qaysanək.
contents.versio: 60.	Now then, they would put clay, make clay, mix clay. They would also put straw in it, they would make cob blocks like so, we call them cob blocks, some call them adobe blocks, cob blocks, we call them cob blocks like so, alongside each other on those logs.

contents.textus: 61.	Ṭabi, u+ʕamo mʕawanwa ḥḏoḏe. Mʕawniwa ḥḏoḏe yani ínaqqa dhówewa bi+qriṯo... kul+dukkoṯe kətwa u+medano, d̥owewa bayto ləsyomo, ínaqqa du+qṭorayḏe... faluṫa, saymiwa faluṫa. Mənyo i+faluṫa? ʕEwono, dəmʕawni ḥḏoḏe bălā́š, dlo+ḥaq. Kul+ḥa ema dmaʕmar, gmiʕawən bu+dawro. Adyawma ono gmaʕmanno, gdoṯən lu+qṭorayḏi, gəmʕawnili ʕəsri+šaqṣat, tleṯi, ḥamši, yani tešmiʕo di+qriṯo, gmašmʕiwa i+qriṯo. Kul+ḥa bu+šəklawo oṯənwa.
contents.versio: 61.	Naturally, people would help each other. They would help each other, like, when in the village there was… in each place there was this thing, when there was a house to build, when its roofing… a bee, they would have a bee. What is a bee? Help, when they help each other for free, without charge. Everyone, whenever he builds, would get helped in turn. Today I am building, they come to my roof, twelve, thirty, fifty folks would help me, that is, a village transmission, they would let the (whole) village hear. That way, everybody would come.

contents.textus: 62.	E, hawxa, mitáḥatwa u+ʕafro, xud dməḷḷi, bu+ʕewono dəḥḏoḏe, lăǧan dmiṣakri aq+qaysanək ṭowo ... e, ṭino ... bu+ṭino, yani, xud məḷḷan. Bam+maye mgawlíwayle, bam+maye hawxa ʕam ḥḏoḏe, saymíwayle šallinat, ŭ hawxa. Hən nuqliwa, ŭ hən maḥtiwa hul dmiswewa bu+ṭino. Šayʕíwayle hawxa.
contents.versio: 62.	Right, so, the soil would get put, as I said, with each other’s help, so that those logs would get covered well ... yes, clay ... with the clay, like, as we said. They would mix it with water, with water accordingly with each other, make it into cob blocks, and so on. Some would bring it, and some would put it until it would get level with clay. They would smooth it out like so.

contents.textus: 63.	ŭ bi+harayṭo, ánnaqqa u+ḥa dobaʕwa, d̥qodarwa, dowéwayle šaġole ... medone ... moṭéwayle nqurto ḥewərto, ḥəfríwayla bi+šawk̇e. Aḥna kəmmínala šawk̇e, kətla tre+reše ḥarufe, kiba hawxa yarəxto, ŭ šawyo xud u+nargo, bu+falgayḏa. Ŭ g̊ḥəfri. Kəmmínala šawk̇e.
contents.versio: 63.	And finally, now then, the one who wanted, who was able, who had workers ... things ... he would bring white aggregate for himself, he excavated it with a mattock. We call it a mattock, it has two sharp heads, it is yea long, and a handle like the axe, in its middle. And they would dig. We call it a mattock.

contents.textus: 64.	Ḥəfriwa nqurto, ánnaqqa, maḥtiwa háṯeste dəmsawalle, mšafrile dnofəq šafərṫə́r, yani, kīt, maḥti i+čmənto aʕle, lăǧan towe šafiro. Ánnaqqa məd msawalle hawxa, gdoṯe u+dawro li+kefo dquṭrile, bi+kefo, ŭ bu+kalšo, gdoṯe u+dawro li+kefo ŭ lu+kalšo. U+kalšo, dəmmina, me darbe di+čmənto duʕdo məstaʕmalwa.
contents.versio: 64.	They would dig aggregate, now then, they put that one too to level it, they refined it so that it came out finer, like, there is, they put cement on it, so it would be fine. Now then, when they levelled it out, the turn would come for the stone to roof (lit. ‘tie’) it, with stone, and with lime, the turn would come for the stone and the lime. Lime, as we call it, would be used in the way of today’s cement.

contents.textus: 65.	I. Áydarbo saymiwa u+kalšo?
contents.versio: 65.	I. How would they make the lime?

contents.textus: 66.	M. Kalšo ḥewórowe, čmənto ḥewə́rtowa, kəmmínala čmənto, bu+lešono duʕdo, e.
contents.versio: 66.	M. Lime was white, cement was white, in today’s language, we call it cement, right.

contents.textus: 67.	I. Mə‿šəkəl nəfqowa, yani, mə‿šəkəl howewa u+kalšawo? (25:30)
contents.versio: 67.	I. How would it appear, like, how would that lime come to be?

contents.textus: 68.	M. U+kalšo, ánnaqqa, háwoste kətle hno lruḥe. Xud dəmmat, foṯo lruḥe. Yani, mkamlina uʕdo haṯe, bəṯr gduʕrina lu+kalšo, mkamlínala. Ánnaqa dəmmina, gəd maydiwa, gəd ... məd qṭərre ... məd ḥaḏər lu+qṭoro, yani, lu+kalšo ŭ lu+teḥito di+kefo, dməqṭər b̥kefo ŭ bəčmənto, b̥kalšo. (25:51)
contents.versio: 68.	M. The lime, now then, that one also has a whatsit of its own. As you’d say, an appearance (lit. ‘face’) of its own. Like, let us now finish that (story), then we’ll come back to the lime, we’ll finish it. Now then, let’s say, they would take ... would ... after they roofed (lit. ‘tied’) ... after it was ready for roofing, like, the lime and the laying of stone, so it gets roofed with stone and cement, with lime.

contents.textus: 69.	Gbodanwa, mḥaḏriwa, mgawliwa, aw xulṭiwa u+kalšo ŭ i+nqurto bəḥḏoḏe. Nqurto ḥewərto, háyoste ḥəfríwayla, xud məḷḷi, mu+ṭuro, ʕafro ḥewóroyo, kəmmínale nqurto.
contents.versio: 69.	They would start, they would prepare, they would mix or put the lime and the aggregate together. White aggregate, so that one they would dig, as I said, from the hill country, it is white powder, we call it aggregate.

contents.textus: 70.	Ṭabi, hano kowe li+čmənto, lu+šyoʕo dab+bote, lu+bnóyowe. Xulṭíwayle bu+kalšo aw bi+čmənto du+waxtawo. Kəmmínale kalšo. Ánnaqqa gmaxlanwa saṭlo mawo ʕal u+ṭino, čmənto, yani, kalšo, ŭ kefo aʕle, kefe mə‿šəkəl d̥ḥakəm. Kefe nqiwe, šriqe, məqqa dhowən... hawxa dlowən ġắlabe šafire ŭ msawye ṭawtərne, lăǧan dzəbṭi ḥḏoḏe, dməsnodi ləḥḏoḏe, ʕam i+čmənto.
contents.versio: 70.	Naturally, this is for the cement, it was for smoothing the houses, for building. They would mix it with lime, or with cement of that time. We call it lime. Now then, they would empty a bucket of that onto the clay, cement, that is, lime, and a stone upon it, stones of whatever kind that came up. Pierced stones, hollow stones, however much (abraded) they may be, so, if they aren’t very beautiful and level, they’re better, so they catch each other, lean against each other, with the cement.

contents.textus: 71.	Maxlanwa, dəmmina, maṯlo, gbodən me tamo, gbode hosta mi+xasrayo, ŭ ḥa mi+xasraṯe. Gmaxlən ṣaṭlo dəčmənto. Kul+ḥa, u+šaġolayḏe gmoṭele u+kalšayḏe ŭ ak+kefayḏe. Gmaxle ṣaṭlo, xud d̥kətyo, gwilo ḥaḏiro, ŭ gmaḥat kefo aʕle. Gmaxle ḥreno barban diḏe, gdoṯe, gəmhalax hawxa hul lu+rešo.
contents.versio: 71.	They would empty, let’s say, for example, they’ll start from there, a craftsman will start from that side, and another one from this side. They’ll empty a bucket of cement. Each one, his worker brings him his lime and his stones. He’ll empty a bucket, as is, mixed and ready, and he’ll put a stone on top of it. He’ll empty another one next to it, he’ll come, he’ll go accordingly until the top.

contents.textus: 72.	Háwoste gmalax hūl dʕolən. Yani, latyo maǧbūr d̥owe bu+rēz, ayko drəkwo i+kefo. Hənnək gnŭkti ḥḏoḏe, ṣaṭlo dəčmənto ŭ kefo, ṣaṭlo dəčmənto ŭ kefo, e. Ham gdayši i+čmənto ʕal i+kefayo dmaḥatle, ham ʕal i+arʕo taḥta, ŭ barban diḏa bu+šəklawo: teʕliyo dak+kefe kulle ʕam čmənto xud məḷḷi, texliyo, ŭ kefe aʕlayye ḥḏo bəḥḏo, hul dmoṭewa li+ḥarayṭo. G̥fāšwa bi+ḥarayṭo dukṯe d̥kefo hawxa, hul dmaḥtiwa ḥḏo bi+ḥarayṭo, hawxa háyoste, čmənto taḥta xud dməḷḷi, ŭ g̊ṣuxriwa, xud dəmmat, i+kefo ḥarayto.
contents.versio: 72.	That one will also go until they get to the top (lit. ‘rise’). That is, it doesn’t have to be in a row, where the stone sits (lit. ‘rides’). They’ll hold onto (lit. ‘bite’) each other, a bucket of cement and stone, a bucket of cement and stone, right. Either they’ll trample the cement upon that stone he had put, or upon the earth beneath it, and beside it that way: to raise all the stones with cement, as I said, to empty, and stones on top of them, one by one, until he would reach the end. There would remain at the end a place for a stone, like so, until they would put one at the end, that one too, some cement beneath it, as I said, and they would close it up, as you’d say, the last stone.

contents.textus: 73.	I. Aḥna əmmíwayna i+kefayo i+kefo du+xətəm, i+kefo du+xətəm.
contents.versio: 73.	I. We would call this stone the capstone, the capstone.

contents.textus: 74.	M. E, i+kefo du+xətəm. E, ánnaqqa ŭ bu+šəklano, hano məd‿əqṭərre, bas kéfene hani, kefe bəčmə́ntone. Hēš lo+tayimo, hano qṭīr hawxa bak+kefe ŭ bi+čmənto, xud məḷḷan. Taḥtayye hawi čmənto, ŭ baynalle ŭ ləhḏoḏe čmə́ntoyo. Yani, fahimat? Me larwal gmaḥwe kefe, i+čmə́ntoste əšmo gədmaḥwyo. (28.06)
contents.versio: 74.	M. Right, the capstone. Yes, now then, and in this way, after they roofed (lit. ‘tied’) this one, these are only stones, they’re stones with cement. It hasn’t been finished yet, this has been roofed like so with stones and cement, as we said. Under them, there was cement, and it’s cement between and beside them. Like, do you understand? From outside, the stones would show, the cement would also show a bit.

contents.textus: 75.	Ánnaqqa, me tamo gmaʕlən, marke ... mu+ḥəkəm, yani, mi+hizaye, dəmmina, du+šuro dəgbədyo i+məre. Me tamo, ánnaqqa, larwal, ṭabi ʕal larwal gməǧġalno, ánnaqqa gmaʕlən əšto šawʕo rezat, hūl dʕolən, mi+xasraṯe ŭ maṯe, hul dʕolən lalʕal ʕam qarʕe du+qṭoro, ʕam u+meḥo, hul dʕolən lalʕal. Bas mənyo? Gawe hēš xályoyo, ánnaqqa. Kīto qṭoro hawxa, ŭ kito tre+šurone, ʕalən hul lalʕal, ánnaqqa bayn d̥ani, bayn d̥ani maḥtiwa ʕafro, bayn d̥ani mahtiwa ʕafro, lo? Dəmmina harke larwal, kito šuro mqabəl d̥ano, gʕole hul lalʕal, ʕam‿ano, me larwal, támoste ḥa, ʕayni mede, hul dʕole lalʕal, bəṯr gawayye ʕafro, kefe, mə‿šəkəl dḥakəm kefe, ŭ ʕafro, molanwa ʕam aš+šuronanək, ʕam u+qṭoro d̥owe hawxa.
contents.versio: 75.	Now then, from there they would raise it up, from here, from the range of, uh, from the level, let’s say, of the wall where the lunette would start. From there, now then, outside, naturally, I’m talking about the outside, now then, they would raise up six-seven rows, until they rise, from that side and that one, until they rise upwards with the shell (lit. ‘skull’) of the ceiling, with the cockloft, until they rise upwards. But what is it? Its inside is still empty, now then. There’s a ceiling like so, and there are two walls, they rose all the way upwards, now then, between these ones, between these ones, they would put earth, they would put earth, no? Let’s say, outside here, there is a wall facing this one, it will rise all the way upwards, with this one, from outside, and also there one the same thing, until it rises upwards, then earth inside them, stones, stones of whatever kind that came up, and earth, they would fill onto those walls, onto the ceiling so it would be like so.

contents.textus: 76.	Məd‿əmlewalle, msawéwaylan qarʕa bu+ʕafro, di+goro, ṭowo, ʕafro ṣiṭo, ŭ bəṯər maḥtiwa čmənto aʕle, kalšo mawo, čmənto, ŭ hawxa. Hən ṭoránwanne ʕafro, mandriwa bi+mandruniye, ŭ hən maḥtiwa čmənto aʕlayye, hawxa. Haṯe hawxa, dəmmina, u+bayto bu+šəklawo, matimíwayle. E, ṭabi bi+ḥarayṭo məd našəf, ánnaqqa g̥̊šəlḥi u+qaləb, gmaydile me taḥte, hedi hedi, bmaḏʕo, ŭ hawxa. Gnofal u+ʕafro kule laltaḥ, d̥kito tamo bu+qṭoro dəqṭərre, lo? Taḥt u+qaləb, taḥt dad+dafe dəqṭərre, hawxa. Hano hawxa.
contents.versio: 76.	After they had filled it, they would level its head with soil, the roof’s, well, a span of earth, and later they would put cement on it, lime of this sort, cement, and so forth. Some would leave them earth (i.e., uncovered); they would roll them with a roller, and some would put cement on them, like so. Such a thing as this, let’s say, the house that way, they would finish it. Right, naturally, at the end, after it dried, now then, they would take away the frame, they would remove it from below it, bit by bit, intelligently, and so forth. All the earth would fall downwards, so that it’s there on the ceiling they roofed, no? Beneath the frame, beneath the planks with which they roofed, like so. So this is it.

contents.textus: 77.	Ŭ ʕal u+kalšo, u+šeyolayḏŭx. Ánnaqqa u+kàlšoste disa malimiwa kefe me larwal, mu+ṭuro, kefe mə šəkəl dḥakəm, kefe. Saymiwa atuno, atuno, kəmmínale atuno. Malimiwa kefe, bonanwa bayto manne, bayto dlo+čimənto, dlo+ṫə+mede (CHECK). Ŭʕdo hēš kito bak+karme bote dlo+čimanto qṭire. (30.16)
contents.versio: 77.	And it’s about lime, your question. Now then, the lime as well, once more they would gather stones from outside, from the hill country, stones of whatever kind came up, some stones. They would make a kiln, a kiln, we call it a kiln. They would gather stones, they would build a house out of them, a house without cement, without anything. Today, there are still some houses in the vineyards that are roofed without cement.

contents.textus: 78.	Hawxa bu+šəklano hawxa mgarvne, e, mdawrne, hawxa qŭṭríwanne, maʕlánwanne, bi+àrʕoste maʕəmqíwanne, maʕəmqíwanne mətro, tre ŭ zədyo. Dəmmina, ḥa ŭ falge, mede, yani, kibi domaṇṇo hawxa, xud ḥa domar, ŭ maʕlə́nwayle lálʕalste, qŭṭríwayle ṭowo, ṭoranwayle šəbbak̇e, dgoraš hăwa, ŭ ǧŭġríwayle, lăǧan dmaḥti nuro bgawe.
contents.versio: 78.	So, in this way, rounded like so, right, ringed, they would roof them like so, they would raise them, they would also sink them into the ground, they would sink them a meter, two, or more. Let’s say, one and a half, something, like, I can say so, as one might say, and they would also raise it upwards, they roofed it well, they would leave it some windows, so that it draws air, and they would ignite it, in order to make fire inside it.

contents.textus: 79.	Ánnaqqa, i+nuro áydarbo mahtíwayla? Molanwa gawe, dak+kefani kulle, du+bayto dəqṭərre, molánwayle qayse. Balki hul šabṯo mede, ṣafro ŭ lalyo hul dnohar, dlo+dmoxo, yani bu+dawro, saymiwa nawba, nəṭríwayle bu+dawro. Kul+naqqa tlōṯ+arbʕo šaqsat kmo glozəm. ŭ nuqliwa hažžək̇at, qayse, mən d̥ḥakəm, maḥtiwa bgawayye, hōl šabṯo. (31.20)
contents.versio: 79.	Now then, the fire, how would they set it? They would fill its inside, of all these stones, of the house they roofed, they filled it with logs. Maybe for something like a week, morning and night until it dawns, without sleeping, like, in shifts, they would keep watch, they would watch it in shifts. Each time three-four individuals, however many are necessary. And they would transport twigs, logs, whatever came up, they would put them in their insides, for a week.

contents.textus: 80.	Ŭ haṯe, əmmíwayla uxlo, əmmíwayla uxlo. Ṭabi ono u+atuno lo+ḥzeli mə‿šəkəl saymiwa, bas kito aḥ+ḥarboṯaṯṯe d̥kənne nafile, d̥fayiši ʕamuqe, dnafili, flān. Əmmíwayla uxlo, hul šabṯo molanwa gawayye uxlo yani muklo, muklo. Obíwayle muklo hul dyuqḏi ak+kefanək kulle, hul šabṯo ǧuġríwanne bi+nuro bu+šəklawo, ŭ bi+ḥarayto, ánnaqqa hul d̥ḥawriwa ak+kefe, dhowənwa ḥewore, ḥawriwa ṭowo. (31.50)
contents.versio: 80.	And this, they would call it stoking, they called it stoking. Naturally, I haven’t seen the kiln, what kind they would make, but their ruins exist, which are fallen, of which the deep parts (i.e., those that were so deep that they were insufficiently calcinated) remained, which collapsed, etc. They would call it stoking, for a week they filled their insides with stoking, that is, food, food. They would give it food until all those stones burn, for a week they would set fire to them that way, and at the end, now then, until the stones would blanch, until they would become white, they would blanch well.

contents.textus: 81.	Ínaqqa dəbʕiwa dmaʕəmriwa, ánnaqqa ak+kefani, məd qayiri, ṭabi məd qayiri, gmaydiwa ak+kefani, gbayziwa maye aʕlayye, g̊fayxiwa, fəšriwa, fayxiwa, kəmmina fəšriwa.
contents.versio: 81.	When they wanted to construct, now then, these stones, after they cooled down, naturally, after they cooled down, they would take these stones, they would pour water on them, they would disintegrate, they melted; they disintegrated, we say they melted.

contents.textus: 82.	Məd fayixiwa, ánnaqqa kəppe məstaʕmlənne čmənto. Yani, i+čmənto me darba di+čməntaṯe duʕdo d̥saymi, dəmmina, i+fabriqa, ŭ moṭanwa, xu‿dməḷḷi, nqurto hewərto mu+ṭuro, ḥufriwa taḥta di+arʕo, i+dukṯo d̥kito ʕafro ḥewóroyo, qum, me darbe du+qum, ŭ xulṭiwa bu+kalšo, bu+kalšano, dhawi mi+kefo, mak+kefanək, ak+kefanək dyuqḏiwa howənwa xŭ‿dməḷḷi, čmənto—kalšo, kalšo əmmíwanne. Ŭʕdo čmə́ntoyo, mede ḥrénoyo. (32.35)
contents.versio: 82.	After they would disintegrate, they can now use them as cement. Like, cement in the way of this cement of today that they make, let’s say, the factory (one), and they would bring, as I said, white aggregate from the hill country, they would dig beneath the ground, it’s the place where there’s white earth, sand, in the way of sand, and they would mix it with lime, with this lime, that came from the stone, from those stones, from those stones, those stones that would burn up and become, as I said, cement—lime, we call them lime. Nowadays, it’s cement, it’s another thing.

contents.textus: 83.	Ŭ hanək, bəṯr me zabno yarixo, ínaqqa dhowanwa ... dmaḥtiwa ṭowwo bgawa di+nqurto, ŭ i+nqurto i+ḥawràṯṯeyo. Čmənto ŭ nqurto, yani, kalšo ŭ nqurto. Ínaqqa dmaḥtiwa ṭowwo zoyudo bgawa, čmənto ġắlabe, huyowa qwiṯo ġắlabe. ʕAm zabno, bəṯr me arbʕi əšne, kəmmi, ŭ šróloyoste, bəṯr me arbʕi+əšne, lo+g̥̊fərqat i+kefo ŭ hənnək me ḥḏoḏe, kowe kefo, u+kalšawo kowe kefo, miḏe dmi+kefo hawi, mi+kefo, mawqaḏḏe i+kefo, səmme mena.
contents.versio: 83.	And those ones, after a long time, when they would become … when they would put a good amount inside the aggregate, and the aggregate is their partner. Cement and aggregate, that is, lime and aggregate. When they put a good surplus inside it, lots of cement, it would become very strong. With time, after forty years, they say, and it’s also true, after forty years, you won’t distinguish the stone and those from each other, it becomes stone, that lime becomes stone, because it came from the stone, from the stone, they burned the stone, they made it from it.

contents.textus: 84.	ŭ ínaqqa dmitaswaʕ ṭowo, dhowe, yani, u+məšḥayḏe ṭowo, yani, dmitaḥat eba zoyudo, bi+nqurto, kowe xdi+kefo, law g̊fərqatle, bəṯr me arbʕi+əšne, ḥamši+əšne, d̥owe sawiʕo.
contents.versio: 84.	And when it gets well saturated, it becomes, like, its viscosity becomes good, that is, when an excess gets put in it, into the aggregate, it becomes like a stone, you won’t distinguish it anymore, after forty years, fifty years, if it becomes saturated.

contents.textus: 85.	Hawxa u+kalšo saymíwayle bu+šəklawo, kul+dəbʕiwa, naqqa gmaydíwanne, tloṯ+arbaʕ+kefe, ḥamməš+kefe manək, gbayziwa maye aʕlayye, gmafixíwanne ŭ gxulṭiwa nqurto appe ŭ mgawlíwayle bəḥḏoḏe, ʕam am+maye. Maḥtiwa dəmmina tre+nqurto, ŭ ḥa kalšo, yani, tre+sahmone mawo, ḥa mawo. Maṯlo, tănak mawo, ḥa d̥kalšo, tre mawo, ŭ ḥa d̥kalšo. Tre dənqurto, ḥa dkalšo, bu+šəklawo.
contents.versio: 85.	Like so, the lime, they would make it that way, whenever they wanted, immediately (lit. ‘the moment’) they would take took it, three-four stones, five of those stones (lit. ‘five stones from those’), they would pour water upon them, they would dissolve them and mix mortar with them and churn it together, with water. They would put, let’s say, two (parts) aggregate and one lime, like, two parts of that one, one of that one. For example, a can of that one, one of lime, two of that one, and one of lime. Two of aggregate, one of lime, that way.

contents.textus: 86.	Ŭ hawxa maʕəmriwa ab+bote, ŭ howanwa qawye ġắlabe, yani, i+kefo kuyo ... hiya ŭ hənnək ḥḏo. Ínaqqa dhowən sawiʕe xud məḷḷi, lo+gnəfli, yani, nfolo layt. (34:17) Dammər layt appe, hawxa lruḥáyyene, dammər layt, ṫə+mede. Ḥădī́d layto, dammər, ṫə+mede, ŭ hawxa bann+əšne ŭ bad+dore, hawxa.
contents.versio: 86.	And like so, they would build the houses, and they were very strong, like, the stone becomes ... it and they are one. If they become saturated, as I said, they will not collapse, like, there is no collapse. There isn’t any iron in them, so they were by themselves, there isn’t any iron, nothing at all. There isn’t any iron, iron, nothing at all, and so for years and centuries, like so.

contents.textus: 87.	Kə́twaylan, dəmmina, hostawat di+qriṯo, əzzanwa larwal, maʕəmriwa baq+qərya<woṯo> daṭ+ṭaye, dač+čəlkoye, larwal əzzanwa.
contents.versio: 87.	We had, let’s say, village craftsmen, they would go out, they would build in the villages of Muslims, Yezidis, they would go out.

contents.textus: 88.	Dam+məḏyoye oṯanwa larke, aḥ+ḥostawat dam+məḏyoye. Hawxa yani meqəm mani, meqəm mani, aq+quwèrəšwayne, xud məḷḷi. Aq+quwerəš, xud məḷḷi, d̥qáysowayne, stunat ḥlime, ŭ u+zabno, dəmmina, dʕamiri ab+bote, dəbdalle baʕ+ʕmarat u+ḥa dlatwa ʕamani a+ḥrene, ʕam am+mašəlmone d̥kə́twayne qawye, be+Ḥaǧo ŭ ġēr, lápwayle maʕmarwa bayto b̥kefe, wăk̇i gabayna lápwayle maʕmarwa bayto b̥kefe. (34:55)
contents.versio: 88.	Some Midyatians would come here, the Midyati craftsmen. So, um, before these ones, before these ones, there were hovels, as I said. The hovels, as I said, were from wood, thick columns, and the time, let’s say, when the houses got built, when they started the constructions, the one who wasn’t with these others, with the Muslims who were strong, the family of Hajo and the rest, he wouldn’t be able to build a house with stones, since he wouldn’t be able to build a house with stones in our neighborhood (lit. ‘beside us’).

contents.textus: 89.	Yasáq, mamnuʕyo. U+ḥa dlowe ḥawrayye, mi+xasraṯṯe, lápwayle maʕmarwa bote hawxa. Suč, lək+kowe, dəmmina, u+sayfaṯṯe qoṭaʕwa, biḏáyyewe, be+Ḥaǧo ŭ hawxa, ŭ aḥ+ḥawronaṯṯe, az+zabnanək. Yani, dlowe ḥa ḥawrayye, bayto mani lo+gmaʕmar, dəg̥̊fōš bu+ʕafro, bu+qarəš.
contents.versio: 89.	It is forbidden, prohibited. The one who wasn’t their friend, on their side, wouldn’t be able to build such houses. It was a crime, it wouldn’t happen, let’s say, the gloves would come off (lit. ‘their sword would cut’), it was under their control (lit. ‘hand’), the family of Hajo and so on, and their friends, those times. That is, if someone wasn’t their friend, he wouldn’t build one of these houses, so he would stay in the earth, in the hovel.

contents.textus: 90.	I. Fahimina haṯe, tawdi ġắlabe, kə́tlilŭx šŭwolo, tre+ḥrene. Kobaʕno ánnaqqa dfohamno meqəm, bări btleṯi+əšne, i+zariʕa áydarbowa, mən zərʕútuwa, áydarbo zərʕútuwa, áydarbo saymútuwa yani, áydarbo zərʕútuwa, áydarbo ḥŭṣdútuwa, áydarbo dayqútuwa, áydarbone hani?
contents.versio: 90.	I. (Now) we understand this, thanks a lot, I have a question for you, two more. Now then, I want to understand how it was before, thirty years ago, how farming was, what you would plant, how you would plant, how you would do, like, how you would plant, how you would harvest, how you would mill, how these things are?

contents.textus: 91.	M. Aḥ+ḥaye dmeqəm ʕəsri, bu+noqusu, ʕəsri əšne kiban dəmmina, aw tleṯi. Ínaqqa dəmmina bam+mo mo, dəmmina tleṯi+əšne. Kə́twalle tawre, lkul+ʕayla, kul+iqarṯo kə́twayla tawre, zawgo d̥tawre, tawre nēr, yani nēr dəmmínanne, dekro. Dawriwa ʕal at+tawre, ŭ kətwa tawroṯo barbán d̥ani, tawroṯo du+ḥalwo. Hániste, kul+ḥa kə́twayle tarte+tlōṯ lu+goràn di+iḥtiyaǧiyayḏe. I+fadonayḏe, dəmmina, du+dworo.
contents.versio: 91.	M. The life of at least twenty years ago, we can say twenty years, or thirty. If, shall we say, 100%, let’s say thirty years. They had bulls, each family, each household had bulls, a pair of bulls, male bulls, that is, we call them male, masculine. They would plow with bulls, and there were milch cows besides these ones. These ones as well, everyone had two-three according to their need. The team, let’s say, of ploughing.

contents.textus: 92.	Áydarbo dawriwa? Kətwa kəmmínala i+ale, ale mu+qayso, saymíwayna ale mu+qayso. Ánnaqqa haṯe áydarbo gmaḥkínala, i+ale du+qayso? Saymiwa dəmmina, maṯlo, qayso yarixo, tre+mətrowat, tloṯo+mətrowat yarixo, lo+g̊forəq, tloṯo. Hano əmmíwayle mašono. Quṭʕiwa qayso yarixo, taqriban ʕaṣro+sanṭime ḥlimo, mnaǧríwayle mgarvno, tre ŭ falge, tloṯo yurxo, lo+g̊forəq. (37.00)
contents.versio: 92.	How would they plough? There was what we call the plough, a plough (made) from wood; we would make a plough out of wood. Now then, this one, how shall we talk about it, the wooden plough? They made, let’s say, for example, a long log, two meters, three meters long, it doesn’t matter, three. This (log), they would call a shaft. They would cut a long log, approximately 10 centimetres thick, fashion (lit. ‘carpenter’) it round, two and a half, three (meters) in length, it doesn’t matter.

contents.textus: 93.	Hano, bəṯr saymíwayle barko, kəmmile barko. Ánnaqqa i+bàrkoste, ha bu+šəklano, qayso hawxa ʕwiǧo, qayso ʕwiǧo hawxa. Hano ánnaqqa gdəṯyo i+mašono dməḷḷan; gmitaṣro ebe, qayso ʕwiǧo. ŭ bəṯr marke ŭ ze, ḥa, tre, aw tloṯo+mətrowat, mitaṣər harke ebe. Ḥayṣiwa tre, dəmmat, ḥădī́d aw be mən kə́twalle, aw nuqwiwa, moḥanwa qayso ebe, ínaqqa dlatwalle ḥadī́d. Ḥădī́d latwa, moḥanwa qayso ebe. Haṯe i+bàrkoyo, haṯe i+mašònoyo. Xud məḷḷi, saymíwanne ḥa.
contents.versio: 93.	This one, then they would make a sheth for it, they call it sheth. Now then, as for this sheth, this here way, a piece of wood so curved, a piece of wood curved like so. This one, now then, there comes the shaft that we spoke about; it is tied to it, a curved piece of wood. And from hereon out, one, two, or three meters gets tied here onto it. They would fasten two, you might say, iron or whatever they had, or they would bore it, put a piece of wood in it, if they had no iron. There wasn’t any iron; they would put a piece of wood in it. This is sheth, and this is shaft. As I said, we made them one.

contents.textus: 94.	Breše di+mašono nuqwíwayle tre+naqwe, u+qayso hawxa ḥlímoyo, i+mašono d̥kəmmina, hawxa yarəxto masərto b̥áṯeyo, tre tloṯo+naqwe nuqwíwayla. Saymíwayla layoste qayso hawxa, dmanḥtíwayle bgawa, bgawa di+mašono, yani bgawe du+qayso dnoḥat laltaḥ. Ṭabi ánnaqqa dəmmina bi+qamayto da+tre+tawre kəmmínale u+niro. Maḥtiwa niro ʕal qarʕe da+tre, hánəkste ṭabi balki, ḥa dlowe bi+ṣərto, ḥa lə+qodar mafhamle.
contents.versio: 94.	In the head of the shaft, they would bore two holes in it, the wood is so thick, the shaft, let’s say, is so long tied to this one, they would bore two-three holes in it. They would make for this one too a piece of wood like so, which they would put inside it, into the shaft, that is, inside the piece of wood that goes beneath. Naturally, now then, let’s say, in front of the two bulls, we call it the yoke. They put the yoke on the head of the two, so those ones naturally, maybe, if one isn’t in the picture (Fig. 1), one cannot explain it.

contents.textus: 95.	Bas hánoste kətle qayso hawxa. Kibe dəmmina ʕasro ṣanṭime ḥlimo, ʕasro yarixo lu+goran da+tre tawre, dʕorən bgawe, se ḥḏoḏe. Hánoste kə́twayle lu+qaysano arbʕo qayse rafiʕe, tre ṣanṭime tloṯo+sanṭime ḥlime. Ḥa mi+xasraṯe ŭ ḥa maṯe, tre hawxa barbán dəḥḏoḏe, ŭ hárkeste tre, a+trani gʕəbri bqarʕe du+tawrano, ŭ a+trani gʕəbri bqarʕe du+tawro+ḥreno.
contents.versio: 95.	But this one too has such a piece of wood. It counts so to speak ten centimetres thick, ten long (i.e., thick), for the two bulls, so they fit inside it, alongside one another. So this one, this piece of wood would have four thin pieces of wood, two-three centimetres thick. One on this side and one on this one, the two like so opposite one another, and here as well two, these two would go in over head of this bull, and these two would go in over the head of the other bull.

contents.textus: 96.	Bi+ḥarayto gloqən ha hawxa bəḥḏoḏe hani; laltaḥ gmiḥəs aʕlayye ḥawlo. A+tre tawrani bu+šəklawo gmitawsri bgawe du+niro. Hano níroyo. Annaqqa lu+nirano kətle bu+falgàyḏeste qayso mgarvno, xud i+dayira. Gʕəbro i+ale dməḷḷan ebe, u+qaysawo dməḷḷan, gʕəbro bgawe, gmitaḥat u+qayso bgawe dlaw nofaq, hano hawxa.
contents.versio: 96.	Finally, these ones would meet one another here like so; underneath, a rope would be fastened to them. That way, these two bulls would be tied inside the yoke. This is a yoke. Now then, this yoke has, in its middle, too, a round piece of wood, like a ring. The plough (shaft) we mentioned would go into it (i.e., the ring, bafso in Fig. 1), that piece of wood we mentioned, it goes inside it, the piece of wood (the peg, qutribo in Fig. 1) would get put inside it (i.e., the shaft) so it doesn’t go out anymore, so this is it.

contents.textus: 97.	Ánnaqqa i+barko, áydarbo gəmdawmo? Gnuḥto laltaḥ, bəṯr koṯela ḥa marke, lăǧan ḥa dzobaṭle biḏe. Kowele kəmmínale sayfo, u+sayfo di+ale. Hano g̊zobaṭle u+daworo, ayko dəzzə́n at+tawre, kowe biḏe, kəmhalxi ŭ qošaʕ‿i+arʕo. Kətle mede lu+sayfano, qayso yaríxoyo hawxa. Gmičək b̥aṯe dgəzzá lŭgab̥, bi+barko, dkəmmínala barko, gmičək bgawa, hawxa bu+šəklano. (39:50)
contents.versio: 97.	Now then, the sheth, how would it go on (i.e., from the shaft)? It would go downwards, then another one comes to it from here, so that someone grabs it by its handle. It would have what we call a sword, the plough’s sword. This one, the ploughman grabs it, wherever the bulls go, it is in his hand, they go, and it carves up the soil. This sword has a thing, it’s a piece of wood, long like so. It would get into this one, which goes over there, into the sheth, what we call a sheth, it gets inside it, this way like so.

contents.textus: 98.	Haṯe gəmdawmo hawxa, reše du+sayfo gnoḥat bi+arʕo, gnoḥat bi+arʕo, gḥofar i+arʕo. Ínaqqa dəmhalxi at+tawre, hano dəgnoḥat bi+arʕo, g̊ḥofar i+arʕo, g̊ḥobašla, g̊sōmla hno hawxa, ǧiwo, gəmhalax bu+ḥaylo dat+tawre, hano u+dworo bu+šəklànoyo. Balki lo+qadərno mafhamno bam+mo mo, dawriwa me ṣafro hul ʕaṣriye, kul+ḥa bi+fadonayḏe. Zərʕiwa ḥeṭe, sʕore, kušne, ṭlawḥe… ḥəmṣe… daḥno ŭ hawxa medone, ŭ dawriwa ak+karme aʕlayye, u+karmo, aʕ+ʕənwe.
contents.versio: 98.	This thing continues like so, the point of the sword goes down into the soil, it goes down into the soil, it digs up the soil. When the bulls move, that one which goes down into the soil, it digs up the soil, it digs it out, it makes it such a whatsit, a furrow, it goes by the strength of the bulls, this is ploughing this way. Maybe I wasn’t able to explain 100%, they would plough from morning to night, each one with his team. They would sow wheat, barley, vetch, lentils… garbanzo beans… millet, and such things, and they would plough the vineyards on them, the vineyard, the grapes. (40:33)

contents.textus: 99.	I. U+dyoqaṯṯe, i+zariʕaṯe, áydarbo howewa?
contents.versio: 99.	I. Their crushing, this farming, how was it?

contents.textus: 100.	M. E ánnaqqa ṭabi bəṯr mu+zroʕo, gdoṯe, xud məllux, u+zaroʕo, gdoḏaʕ̥ u+ḥṣodo, gdəzzé lu+ḥṣodo bam+magzune, kə́twalle magzune, hawxa rabe… naʕime, kətwa hənna falge+dmətro, hən mətro yarixe, yani, ŭ hawxa, ŭ šawyo yarixo hawxa. Kobe quwwe du+brimo, xud u+ṣahro, xud u+ṣahro, ŭ gyorax, kowele šawyo. Hano hawxa, magzuno.
contents.versio: 100.	M. Right, now then, naturally after sowing, there would come, as you said, the sower, he would know the harvest(-time), he would go to the harvest with sickles, they had sickles, so big… small, there were some half a meter, some a meter long, like, and so on, and a handle so long. It (i.e., the arc) gives some force to the curve, like the moon, like the moon, and it extends, it has a handle. So this is it, a sickle.

contents.textus: 101.	Hano gzobaṭle dəmmina bi+iḏo du+yamino ŭ g̥̊ḥoṣad̥. Áydarbo g̥̊ḥosad̥? Məd našəf u+zād, as+sʕore aw aḥ+ḥeṭe, gmoyad u+magzuno biḏe, ṭowo glozam nəšfi, d̥owən ṭowo, dnəšfi lăǧan dməqrofi. Hano ʕawúdoyo, ḥarúfoyo, gəmḥalaqle bayne das+sʕore, ggorašše, gzobaṭṭe bi+iḏaṯe, gmoḥe lano gmoḥe, disa gmoṭe buqto+ḥreto, buqto yani falqo+ḥreno, buqto, gzobaṭṭe bi+iḏaṯe, gəzzé hawxa hul dməmloyo i+iḏo.
contents.versio: 101.	This one, he would grasp it, let’s say, by hand on his right, and he would harvest. How would he harvest? After the grain dries, barley or wheat, he would take the sickle in his hand, they must be well dried, so they become good, so they dry to get chopped up. This one is pointed, it is sharp, he would thrust it into the barley, he would pull them, he would grasp them with this hand, he would strike this (sickle), he would strike, once again it would bring another bunch, a bunch, that is, another bit, a bunch, he would grasp them with this hand, he would go like so until his hand gets full.

contents.textus: 102.	Ŭ kə́twalle, ono lo+ḥzeli, bas kə́twalle meqəm, dəmmina bu+zabno dbabi, šuġliwa babi, hēš baḥ+ḥáyeyo, kə́twalle qinaġe, əmmíwanne qinaġe, ṣawʕoṯe ddammər, farzlo, ṣawʕoṯe maḥtiwa breše+diḏoṯayye, kul+ḥḏo maḥtiwa ḥḏo eba, yurxiwa haqqa lăǧan dmaydi ġắlabe ínaqqa dḥuṣdi bu+magzuno, dmaydo ġắlabe, me darbe dmaydi haqqa bi+iḏo, gmaydi hawxa. (42.10)
contents.versio: 102.	And they had, I personally haven’t seen, but they had earlier, let’s say at the time of my father, my father used to work, he is still living (lit. ‘in life’), they had finger cots, they called them finger cots, fingers of iron, iron, they would put the fingers on the tips of their hands, on each one they would put one, they would extend so much to take a lot (more) when they harvest with the sickle, to take a lot, instead of taking as much as the hand, they would take like so.

contents.textus: 103.	E, ŭ ḥoṣadwa u+ḥaṣodo, dworo, yani u+ḥaṣodo d̥owe ṭowo, ḥoṣadwa fadono bu+yawmo, fadono me ṣafro hul ʕaṣriye, ḥoṣadwa fadono mdat+tawranək, ddawriwa, bu+magzunawo. Kulle bam+magzune, e, ḥuṣdíwanne. (42:25)
contents.versio: 103.	Yes, and the harvester would harvest, ploughing, that is, the harvester, if he is good, he would harvest an acre a day, an acre from dawn to dusk, he would harvest an acre from the ones of those bulls, that they would plough, with that sickle. All of them with sickles, right, they would harvest them.

contents.textus: 104.	Məd̥‿kaməl u+ḥṣodo, malimíwanne tamo, saymíwanne hənna rwəqto kəmmínala, hən‿əgdišo. Mənyo i+rwəqto? I+rwəqto, ínaqqa d̥kəmmina dəkḥuṣdi, aw d̥ḥuṣdíwayna, maḥtíwayna i+buqto dəmmina dmaləmli, gmaḥanna ʕal i+arʕo. Koḥoṣadno buqto+ḥreto.
contents.versio: 104.	When the harvesting was over, they would gather them there, they would make (what) some of us call a stack, some a bushel. What is a stack? The stack, when, let’s say, they harvest, or when we would harvest, we would place the bunch, let’s say, that I gathered, I would place it on the ground. I harvest another bunch.

contents.textus: 105.	Ánnaqqa gmadʕanno reša mqabəl da+ḥrene, buqto foṯa hawxa, ŭ ḥḏo hawxa, barbán dəḥḏoḏe hul d‿owe quflo. ŭ ínaqqa d̥xayifo dlo+mənqoliwa, saymíwayn‿awxa dəmmat tamo bi+arʕo, čík̇este hawxa dnəšfi, dmiḥoṣi bəḥḏoḏe. Ṣira, tarte, tlōṯ, ŭ bu+šəklawo, košə́nwanne ʕal ḥḏoḏe. Hano rwəqto. (43.10)
contents.versio: 105.	Now then, I turn its head facing the other ones: a bunch, its face so, and another one so, opposite one another, until it becomes a sheaf. And if it would not be transported quickly, we would put it like so, you might say, there on the ground, a bit so that they’d dry, so that they get firm together. A row, two, three, and that way, they would pile on top of each other. This is a stack.

contents.textus: 106.	U+gdišo: reše da+sʕore aw daḥ+ḥeṭe, maqimíwayle hawxa bi+arʕo. Hano qúfloyo, mədli quflo ḥsido, dəmmina, ḥšaw ḥṣədlan. Ánnaqqa g̊samne gdišo. Lăǧan mede dlo+roʕele, maḥtiwa rešayye laltaḥ, quflooo ʕal quflo hawxa, arʕe lalʕəl, ŭ a+sʕore laltaḥ, yani i+šəblo laltaḥ. Huuul dboramwa hawxa, u+quflo me hawiiir. Bi+ḥarayṭo, xud u+qtoro dab+bote dməḷḷan, u+quflo ḥaroyo briše, lalʕəl bqarʕe, məsxərwa u+gdišo, aš+šʕore kulle fayšiwa laltaḥ. Hánoste gdišoyo. 43.55
contents.versio: 106.	The bushel: the heads of barley or of wheat, they would stand it up like so on the bottom. This is a sheaf, I took a harvested sheaf, let’s say, consider that we harvested it. Now I shall make it a bushel. So that nothing grazes it, they would put their heads downwards, sheaf upon sheaf like so, the bottoms upwards, and the barley downwards, that is, the ear downwards. Until it would turn out like so, the sheaf all around. Finally, like the roof of the houses that we discussed, the last sheaf on its top, upwards on its head, the bushel would be closed, all the barley would stay downwards (i.e., on the inside). So this is a bushel.

contents.textus: 107.	Hul lu+yawmo du+nqolo, mitalimiwa; malimíwanne ʕal aḥ+ḥmore, baš+šale. U+šalo mənyo? Maršo, marše qṭiʕe, medone du+ṣaʕro, d̥saymiwa meqəm, marše du+ṣaʕro daʕ+ʕeze flān, ŭ dġayr medone, daḥ+ḥayewən, dʕuzlíwanne bi+iḏo. Ṭabi, ono lo+koṯe lboli dəʕzəllan. Kətwa hawxa tak tuk noše dʕuzliwa medone bu+kušo, əmmíwayle u+kušo.
contents.versio: 107.	Until the day of transporting, they would be gathered; they would gather them upon donkeys, in carpet bags. What is a carpet bag? A carpet, cut carpets, things made out of hair, which they made earlier, carpets of goat hair, and so on, and other things, animals, which they would spin by hand. Naturally, I don’t remember when we spun it. There were people here and there who would spin things by needle; they would call it ‘needle’.

contents.textus: 108.	Ayna d̥kə́twalle ṣaʕro zewudo, ḥəyewən, ʕeze, saymiwa maršo xano. Hano ḥəšwínale maršo manək, ṣaʕro, as+sappoṯayḏe maqimíwanne, ḥayṭiwa u+rešawo ŭ hawo, howewa bu+šəkl dəmmat yani du+qawro, kiban dəmmina xud u+qawro d̥owe ḥfiro, ḥa d̥ḥofar qawro. Maṯlo kobeno. Maḥtiwa u+zād bgawe du+šalawo, howewa rabo, kibe tre+mətrowat yarixo kiban dəmmina, yani gəšt ḥaste rwiḥo, molánwanne bgaweee. Ḥatta ánnaqqa, bəṯr ... ʕul mene, maʕlánwanne ʕul mene, háwxaste baq+qərnawoṯayḏe mdawsíwanne, yani mede šuġlo ḥiso qawyo, dlo+rəmši, ŭ bu+ḥawlo ḥayṣíwanne, hēš hiye ... ʕal i+arʕo hayṣiwa u+šalo ḥiṣo. (45.10)
contents.versio: 108.	Whoever had extra hair, animals, goats, would make a carpet like this one. This one, let’s consider it one of those carpets, hair, they would raise its edges, they would sow on top of that one (lit. ‘that head’) and that one, it would turn into the shape, you might say, like, of a grave, we could say like a grave that is excavated, as if someone digs a grave. I’m giving an example. They would put the grain inside this carpet bag, it would be big, it was two meters long, we could say, like, approximately also one wide, they would load (lit. ‘fill’) them up inside it. Even so, now then, after ... above it, they raise them up above it, this way they would also stamp them into its corners, that is, a hard, difficult work, so they don’t move, and they would compress by rope, it still … onto the ground they would press the carpet bag tightly.

contents.textus: 109.	Bəṯr me tamo, maṭəʕníwayle ʕal u+ḥmoro tre+šaqṣaṭ, mičokiwa taḥte, maqimíwayle hawxa, ḥa mi+xasrayo ŭ ḥa mayo. Ŭ obiwa iḏoṯayye ləḥḏoḏe ŭ ḥa gzobaṭ harke, ŭ ḥa hawxa, ŭ maʕlənwayle ʕal ḥaṣe du+ḥmoro, hul li+adro, əmblíwayle li+adro.
contents.versio: 109.	After that point (lit. ‘there’), they would load it on the donkey, two individuals, they would get under it (i.e., they would join their hands under it), they would lift it up like so, one from this side and one from this one. And they would extend (lit. ‘give’) their hands to each other, and one grabs here, and another one like so, and they lifted it up onto the donkey’s back, to the threshing floor, they would take it to the threshing floor.

contents.textus: 110.	Ṭŭḥníwanne tamo bi+adro. I+adro, i+dukṯo, dəmmina, dmitaḥat eba u+zād̥. Xud məḷḷi, ḥéṭene, aw sʕórene, aw ġayr medónene, bi+adro.
contents.versio: 110.	They would thresh them there on the threshing floor. The threshing floor, the place, let’s say, on which grain gets put. As I said, they’re wheat, or they’re barley, or they’re other things, on the threshing floor.

contents.textus: 111.	Ánnaqqa u+ṭḥono, disa baḥ+ḥayewən, naqla+ḥreto baḥ+ḥaywoṯo. Iḏa kətle ḥaywoṯo dmakfən, kətle. Lo, gəzzé ldu+ǧiranayḏe, gdobele tre+tloṯo, flān, ḥmoro, tawre ʕam hḏoḏe flān. Masríwanne ʕam ḥḏoḏe, saymíwanne tăqəm bu+ḥawlo, ḥa ḥawlo ʕal qarʕe d̥kulle, kul+ḥa quṭríwayle bu+ḥawlawo, kul+ḥa quṭriwa u+qamoyo, hul d̥saymiwa qaṭro+ḥreno dmabərmile bəqḏole d̥awo. Qaṭro+ḥreno bəqḏole d̥awo, yani, bu+šəklano. (46:11)
contents.versio: 111.	Now then, the threshing, again with the animals, one more time with the animalia. If he has animals that suffice, he has them. No, he would go for those of his neighbour, he would give him two, three, etc., a donkey, bulls, together, etc. They would tie them together, they would make them into a squad with rope, one rope on everyone’s heads, each one they would bind with that rope, each one, they would tie the first one, until they made another knot which they twist around the neck of that one. Another knot on the neck of that one, like, this way.

contents.textus: 112.	Xălăk̇eee, kul+ḥa ḥa manne, kulle saymíwanne ḥa ʕam ḥḏoḏe, ŭ a+sʕore ʕal i+arʕo. I+naqqayo hēš ṗaṫóz latwa, ṭăbi hano u+hno qamóyoyo, yani u+zabno ʕatiqo, dlatwa ṗaṫóz kəmmina, makkine latwa. Makərxíwanne; əmmíwayla i+druxto, druxto, madraxto, aw druxto, bas druxto əmmiwa. Ánnaqqa dəmmina aḥ+ḥayewənanək qulʕíwanne aʕla, ʕal u+zadawo dʕal i+arʕo. Yani, maḥtíwayle ʕal i+arʕo, mbarbzíwayle, yani dlowe hawxa ḥlimo mede, xud dəmmat xarke, aw zəd̥ṫə́r marke, lu+gorā̀n daḥ+ḥayewən d̥kito. Ánnaqqa gbərmiwa aʕlayye hul d̥ṭuḥníwayle braġloṯayye, dayšíwayle, dayšíwayle.
contents.versio: 112.	A ring, each of them one of them, they would all make one with each other, and the barley on the floor. At that time, there still wasn’t any threshing machine, naturally, this is the first whatsit, like, old times, when there was no combine harvester, let’s say, there weren’t any machines. They would make them go around; they would call it the grist, grist, bed or grist, we say only grist. Now then, let’s say, those animals, they would drive them upon it, upon that grain that is on the floor. Like, they would put it upon the ground, they would scatter it, that is, so it is not so thick, like you’d say like here, or more than here, depending on the animals that are there. Now then, they would run around upon them until they would thresh it with their feet, they would trample it, they would trample it.

contents.textus: 113.	Ŭ kətwa hənna dəmmina əmmiwa, əmmíwayle u+ǧarǧar. U+hnawo lo+ḥzeli, yani, lo+ḥzeli dməstaʕmalle, bas hawo, ab+bəregəl, əmmiwa, makərxíwayle hawxa, ʕayni mede ab+bəregəl makərxíwayle, kə́twayle xud am+maqaṣe ṭoḥanwa. Bas hano dəmmina daḥ+ḥəyewən ṭabiʕi dayšíwanne hawxa, sʕore, ṭlawḥe, kušne. Bəṯr mə dəṭḥini ṭowo, yawmo, tre, tloṯo, hul ṭowo dməṭḥoni, d̥owən dəmmat tawno yani, dmətḥoni ṭowo.
contents.versio: 113.	And there were some ... what we call ... they called ... they would call it the threshing sledge. That whatsit I haven’t seen, that is, I have not seen how they use it, but that one, the horses, they would call them, they would make it go around like so, the same thing the horses would make it go around, it had something like scissors, it would thresh. But this one with animals, naturally, they would thresh them like so, barley, lentils, vetch. After they got well threshed, a day, two, three, until they get well threshed, to become you can say chaff, that is, to get well threshed.

contents.textus: 114.	Ánnaqqa gəmdaranne, maydíwanne malḥoyo. Ánnaqqa u+malḥoyo, kiban dəmmina bu+šəkl du+rawšo, u+rawšo dmeqəm, ḥušwínale rawšo, kə́twayle ṣawʕoṯe mu+qayso. ʕAyn xd‿iḏo ŭ šawyo. Ŭ ánnaqqa maydiwa u+hno dətḥənne, u+zadawo, howewa xud u+tawno. Ánnaqqa mdaránwayle doṯewa hăwa qwiṯo. Ínaqqa dəmdaránwayle, u+zād noḥatwa laltaḥ, u+tawno, gzəʕfówayle i+hăwa lŭgab̥. Dmaʕlewa, i+hăwa gzə́ʕfowa u+tawno, a+sʕore, laltaḥ, hul dlaymiwa kulle tamo. (48.13)
contents.versio: 114.	Now then, they would winnow them, take along a pitchfork. Now then, the pitchfork, we can say it’s in the form of a shovel, the shovel of yesteryear, we consider it a shovel, it had tines (lit. ‘fingers’) of wood. Same as a hand and a handle. And now then, they would take the whatsit they threshed, that grain, it would become like chaff. Now then, they would winnow it while a strong wind was coming. When they were winnowing it, the grain would go downwards, the chaff, the wind would blow it away. When he would lift it up, the wind would blow the chaff, the barley, downwards, until all of them would gather there.

contents.textus: 115.	Ínaqqa dhăwa dloṯewa, klóyoyo. Klóyoyo. Yani dlowe hăwa dmandfole me ḥḏode, lo+kowe. Hawo bu+šəklàwoyo, u+deroyo ŭ u+tekrixo. Hawxa, deroyo bi+iḏo xud məḷḷi, malḥoye ŭ flān. Ŭ bəṯr məd nafiqi am+makinat, u+ṗaṫṓz, kəmmínale u+ṗaṫṓz, ṭabi u+ṗaṫṓz gmitaṣər bu+traktə̀r, bu+moṫṑr, traktə́r, traktə́r di+zràʕayo, du+dworo. Tamo ánnaqqa gmabram u+qarī̀š, gmiḥalaq lgawe di+makina, ŭ hiye gmabramle. Hano šuġlo, dəmmat, di+makinayo, hano, dann+əšne ḥaroye hul uʕdo, hul uʕdo bu+ṗaṫṓzyo.
contents.versio: 115.	When the wind wouldn’t come, it’s a standstill. It’s a standstill. Like, if there is no wind to purify it (i.e., them) from one another, it won’t happen. That’s that way, winnowing and threshing. Like so, winnowing by hand, as I said, the pitchfork and so forth. And after the machines came out, the combine harvester, we call it the combine harvester, naturally, the combine harvester gets hitched to a tractor, to a motor, it is an agricultural tractor, a ploughing one. There, now then, it makes the belt go around, it gets tossed inside the machine, and it makes it go around.
