That is a job, you can say, for a machine, that one, from the last few years until now, it’s by combine harvester until now.

contents.textus: 116.	Ŭ ḥṣódoste uʕdo lo+fāš bi+iḏo, lo+fāš bi+iḏo, hawi bu+traktə̀r. Meqəm yani u+zroʕo bi+iḏo, u+ḥṣodo bi+iḏo, u+ṭḥono bi+iḏo, u+nqolo bu+ḥmoro, hawi ḥmoro. Uʕdo hawi kul+mede: u+dworo bu+traktə̀r, u+ḥṣodo bu+traktor, u+nqolo li+adro bu+traktə̀r, u+teʕbiro du+zād lu+bayto, yani dəgnodəf háwoste bi+ḥarayto, naqqa+ḥreto hawi bu+traktə̀r. Ŭ meqəm kul+mede bu+ḥaywanwe, xud məḷḷi, dworo bu+ḥaylo du+ḥaywanwe, nqolo ŭ ṭḥono. (49.25)
contents.versio: 116.	And the harvesting as well, it’s no longer (lit. ‘it hasn’t stayed’) by hand, it’s no longer by hand, it became by tractor, Previously, like, sowing by hand, harvesting by hand, grinding by hand, transport by donkey, it became a donkey, now everything became ploughing by tractor, harvesting by tractor, transport to the threshing floor by tractor, housing of grain (lit. ‘the entering of the grain to the house’), that is, so that one would also clean up in the end, again it became by tractor. And previously, everything was by animal, as I said, ploughing by animal power, transport and grinding.

contents.textus: 117.	I. Meqəm ak+karme áydarbo saymútuwanne, dəmmina u+ʕ̥ṣoro, u+syomo dan+nabišoṯe, ak+kure, am+medonani, áydarbo saymútuwanne meqəm? Bayn meqəm ŭ ládyawma, mḥalaf medone ġắlabe aw? Bi+zariʕa fahimina, yani, nafəq taknike friše, nafəq, dəmmina, ʕabiri lu+ṗaṫṓz, mu+ṗaṫṓz ʕabiri lu+bičar, bas bu+hno, bak+karme, baʕ+ʕənwe komaṇṇo mede lo+mḥalaf?
contents.versio: 117.	I. Previously, how did you work the vineyards, let’s say pressing, making raisins, the furnaces (i.e., for evaporating molasses), these things, how did you make them previously? From previously until today, it’s changed a lot, some things, or? With crops, we understand, like, there appeared new technologies, there came out, let’s say, they went to the combine harvester, from the (pull-type) combine harvester they shifted to the (self-propelled) combine harvester, but with the whatsit, with the vineyards, with the grapes, I would say nothing has changed?

contents.textus: 118.	M. Lo, baʕ+ʕənwe ġắlabe mede lo+mḥalaf, u+ʕ̥ṣoro bi+ìḏoyo. Kibi domaṇṇo naqqa+ḥreto, u+ʕ̥soro daʕ+ʕənwe bi+ìḏoyo.
contents.versio: 118.	M. No, with the grapes, not a lot has changed, the pressing is by hand (i.e., by foot). I can say once more, the pressing is by hand.

contents.textus: 119.	I. Ayko koʕəṣrútənne?
contents.versio: 119.	I. Where do you press them?

contents.textus: 120.	M. Meqəm kətwa dəmmina bak+karme məʕ̥ṣoriwa, domaṇṇo hawxa, meqəm kətwa ʕarwo, aw kəmmina ʕarwo, ŭ hən kəmmi maʕ̥ṣarto, bas aḥna bu+zoyudo bu+lešono, dəmmina, kəmmina ʕarwo. Mi+šeno, ʕaməqto taḥta di+arʕo, mətro ʕaməqto ŭ mi+šènoyo, ŭ ʕuṣríwanne, ŭ kə́twayla lalʕal xud i+ṣəfro kefo, ʕuṣriwa aʕla bu+kiso, dăwamli bu+kiso ŭ bi+raġlo, dyošo bi+raġlo hul dnuḥtiwa am+maye kulle laltaḥ. Bi+ʕàrwowe bak+karme.
contents.versio: 120.	M. Previously, there was, let’s say, in the vineyards they would stomp, I’d say so, previously there was a basin, or we say a basin, and some say press, but we predominantly in the language, let’s say, we say basin. Out of rock, deep under the ground, it’s a meter deep, and out of rock, and they would press them, and it had down below a stone like a platter, they would stomp onto it with a sack, continuously with the sack and the foot, treading by foot until all the juice would go down below. It was by basin in the vineyards.

contents.textus: 121.	Bas uʕdo aʕ+ʕənwe k̬mitamṭən lu+bayto. Kul+ḥa k̬ʕoṣarre fāš bbayto. K̬ʕuṣrənne dəmmina u+ḥa. Kīt hənna d̥saymənne dukṯo, dáyïra mi+čmənto, dukṯo d̥sulqila dʕuṣri, ŭ dnuḥti am+maye laltaḥ. D̥owela marziwo bu+šəklawo. (51.08)
contents.versio: 121.	But now the grapes get brought home. Everyone stomps them at home nowadays. They stomp them, let’s say, on their own (lit. ‘the one’). There are some who make a place, a circle out of cement, a place to which they go up to stomp, and so the juice goes down. It’s so that there’s a gutter this way.

contents.textus: 122.	Ŭ kito hənna kməstaʕmli ... kətwa meqəm əmmíwaynale dălāv, mənyo dălāv? Hánoste əšmo xabro daḥna məstaʕmlínale gabayna: dălāv, qayso mi+dawmo, ṣahrónoyo, bu+šəkl du+ṣahro, taqriban xud u+ṣahro, balki latyo ġắlabe kamilo xud u+ṣahro.
contents.versio: 122.	And there are some who use ... earlier there was, they would call it ‘a trough’, what’s a trough? This is a name-word we use among us: a trough, a piece of wood from trees, it’s a crescent, in the shape of the moon, approximately like the moon, perhaps not really perfect like the moon.

contents.textus: 123.	Elo yani šəkl qəštonóyoyo, tre+mətrowat yarixo. Dəmmina, maṯlo mu+qurmo di+dawmo, ḥub̝̊šiwa gawa di+dawmo, kule, dawmo duyo sawto. Dawmo duyo maṯe, tlōṯmó+əšne, našifo yăda quṭʕila. Saymíwayla dălāv; gawa kule maydíwayle; fāšwa u+qayso baroyayḏa; kule əzzáwayle; gəmḥalqíwayle; fāšwa u+qayso dlarwal. Ánnaqqa hánoste ʕuṣriwa aʕle.
contents.versio: 123.	But, like, it’s a bow shape, two meters long. Let’s say, for example, from the tree stump, they would dig out the tree’s insides, all of it, a tree that would be old. A tree that would be two hundred, three hundred years old, it dried up, or they cut it down. They would make it a trough; all its insides, they would take; its external wood would stay; all of it (i.e., the insides) would go away; they would throw it away; the wood from outside would stay. Now then, so this one they would stomp on.

contents.textus: 124.	Gmaḥtile hawxa, ŭ aʕ+ʕənwe lalʕal, i+kəsto daʕ+ʕənwe, u+kiso daʕ+ʕənwe. Ŭ u+ʕaṣoro g̥̥̥̊solaq lalʕal, gʕoṣar, gnuḥti mu+dălāvawo, lgawe du+sefoqo, g̊d̥ówewa sefoqo, lăgan, mede, gnuḥti mu+dălāv. Hedi, yani, dălāv hawxa ... marziwo kəmmínale marziwo d̥qayso hawxa. Hánoste, mede bu+šəklawo, məstaʕmlíwayle, úʕdoste hēš kməstaʕmlənne hanək, yani ʕayni mede hawxa.
contents.versio: 124.	They would put it like so, and the grapes above, the pouch of grapes, the sack of grapes. And the stomper gets on top, he stomps, (the juice) would go down from that trough, to the inside of the vessel, there used to be a vessel, a basin, something, (the juice) would go down from the trough. Then, like, such a trough … we call it a gutter, a wooden gutter like so. So this one, something of that sort, they would use it, now, too, they still use them, those ones, that is, the same thing like so.

contents.textus: 125.	I. Məd‿əʕṣirənxu, mə‿g̊saymutu bam+mayanək?
contents.versio: 125.	I. After you stomped them, what would you do with that juice?

contents.textus: 126.	M. E bəṯr məd‿əʕṣiri hani, kīt də‿g̊saymənne ḥamro, u+ḥa d‿əg̊šote ḥamro g̊samme ḥamro. U+ḥamro hawxa, mede karyoyiṯ dəmmina. <G>mitaḥat bi+šəmšo, droṯaḥ bi+šəmšo hōl dkole u+raṯḥayḏe kule, hul dlaw, yani, hul dlaw roṯaḥ. ŭ bətr gmitaʕbar lawġul, gmaḥtile bas+sefoqe, dəmmina du+qaḥfo, sefoqe du+qaḥfo gdəmmínanne ḥeṣfo, qaḥfo, hani d̥kənne mu+ṭino ṭabi, muqḏe mu+ṭínone, xud i+kefo. Kowe b̥anək, lo+g̊ḥoraw. Hano u+ḥamro ṭabiʕi hawxa. (53.06)
contents.versio: 126.	Yes, after these were stomped, there are some would make them wine, everyone who would drink wine would make wine. Such wine, a few words (lit. ‘a thing succinctly’), let’s say. It would get put under the sun, so it ferments until all its fermentation stops, until no more, like, until it doesn’t ferment anymore. And later it would get decanted inside, they would put it in vessels, let’s say a jug one, a jug vessel, we call them an amphora, a jug, those ones that are (made out) of clay naturally, they are fired from clay, like stone. It will be in those ones, it doesn’t spoil. This is natural wine, like so.

contents.textus: 127.	Ŭ aʕ+ʕənwe dəmmina, am+maye, mam+maye, dəmmina, daʕ+ʕənwani. Ánnaqqa marṯḥíwanne. Úʕdoste, u+ḥa d̥kobaʕ̥ d̥soyam ʕayni mede, martḥíwanne, gmaḥti appe, dəmmina, qamḥo, gmaḥti qamḥo daḥ+ḥeṭe, u+ḥa dobaʕ̥ g̊soyam ḥărire mənne. I+ḥărire mənyo? Ḥalyuṯo qšiṯo, ḥalyuṯo našəfto qšiṯo, kiban dəmmina xud i+raḥa, raḥa xabro nuxróyoyo bas kəmmínala raḥa. Bas+sefoqe maḥtíwanne ... xud dməḷḷi, maqšən am+mayanək bu+qamḥo daḥ+ḥeṭe, ŭ kəmmínala ḥawdal. Ḥawdal haṯe kuyo ḥawdal normál, ḥawdal.
contents.versio: 127.	And the grapes, let’s say, the juice, from the juice, let’s say, of these grapes. Now then, they would boil them. Nowadays too, the one who wants to do the same thing, they would boil them, they would put in them, let’s say, flour, they would put wheat flour, the one who wants to make fruit leather from them. What is fruit leather? A solid sweet, a dry, strong sweet, we can say like ‘(Turkish) delight’, ‘delight’ is a foreign word, but we call it ‘delight’. They would put them in vessels … as I said, that juice solidifies with the wheat flour, and we call it ‘pudding’. This pudding becomes normal pudding, pudding.

contents.textus: 128.	Ánnaqqa ḥa dobaʕ̥ ḥarire g̊soyam, gmaxlela las+sefoqe. Məd našifo, g̊qoṭaʕla, g̊sāmla falqe, hayo kuyo ḥarire. (54.00) Ŭ dobaʕ̥ g̊sōm mena kəmmínanne ʕoliqe, hən kəmmi ʕqude, hániste xurziwa, dəmmina bu+ḥuṭo, luze aw gawze. Hániste u+ḥa dobaʕ̥, gġoyaṭṭe bgawe du+dəsto, bi+ḥawdalayo d̥kətyo mu+qamḥo ŭ maʕ+ʕənwe, yani gmišaḥno bi+nuro, balki lo+məḷḷi bi+nuro gmišaḥno, normál gmišaḥno hōl d̥qošən ʕam ḥḏoḏe, Ŭ ánnaqqa hawxa u+ḥa dobaʕ̥ d̥sōm ʕoliqe manne, gġayṭənne bgawayye, ŭ gmaydənne, gəmʕalqatte tamho, hul d, yani, nəšfi.
contents.versio: 128.	Now then, if a guy (lit. ‘a [male] one’) were to want to make fruit leather, he would empty it into the vessels. After it dries, he would cut it, he would make pieces of it, this one becomes fruit leather. And if he were to want to make from it what we call walnut rope, some say walnut knots, these ones they would thread, let’s say with a needle, almonds or walnuts. These ones, the one who wants, would dip them inside a vat, into that pudding that is (made) of flour and grapes, that is, it gets heated by the fire, maybe I didn’t say it gets heated by the fire, it gets heated the normal way until they solidify together. And now then, like so, if one were to want to make walnut rope from them, they dip them inside them, and they take them, you hang them over there, until, like, they dry.

contents.textus: 129.	Hániste, hawxa, lăǧan u+saṯwo saymíwanne ḥəzbe, lăǧan u+saṯwo, ḥšowe yani. Ḥălile, xud məḷḷi. (54.43) ʕOlíqene hani, mal+luze ŭ mag+gawze flān ŭ mat+tene hən saymiwa, mat+teneste, tene našife, nəšfiwa at+tene, maltmiwa, saymiwa mánəkste ʕayni mede, ġayṭíwanne bgawe di+ḥalilayo… di+ḥawdal. (55.00)
contents.versio: 129.	So these ones, like so, for the winter they would settle an account, for the winter, deposits, that is. Fruit leather, like I said. They’re walnut ropes, these ones, made from almonds or from walnuts, so and so, and from figs, some would make them, from figs too, dry figs, the figs would dry, they would collect them, they would make those too, the same thing, they would dip them inside that fruit leather… inside the pudding.

contents.textus: 130.	ŭ bəṯr, barbán d̥ani kito u+pastìq kəmmínale. Hánoste, naqqa+ḥreto, i+ḥawdalayo saymíwayla čik̇e raqəqto, dluyo ġắlăbe qšiṯo. Fərsíwayla ʕal aǧ+ǧule, ǧulo qumáš, dəmmina dlowe ġắlăbe ḥlimo, ŭ lo+raqiqo. Normál, tre+mətrowat tloṯo+mətrowat lo+kforaq. Tre+šaqṣat zəbṭi, kul+ḥa a+tre reše, ḥa harke, ŭ ḥa tamo, ŭ ḥa k̬maxle i+ḥawdal. ŭ ánnaqqa hani k̬mabərmila aʕle, hul dzobaṭ i+foṯo kula. Haṯe kuyo pastíq, maʕ+ʕənwe ŭ mu+qamḥo. Yani ínaqqa dək̬misəm, məxləṭ bəḥḏoḏe, k̬mitawmaḷḷa ḥawdal, xud məḷḷi, ḥawdal daʕ+ʕənwe k̬mitawmaḷḷa. Bu+šəklawo saymiwa pastíq, xud məḷḷi. Ḥalile, maḥtíwayla bas+sefoqe. Bəṯr quṭʕíwayla, nəšfowa, šabṯo, tarte, bi+šəmšo. Aʕ+ʕoliqe hawxa. Medone hawxa, bas u+ḥamro xud dməḷḷi lruḥe, hawo bi+šəmšo g̊kole ŭ g̊šoḥan mi+šəmšo, gmoyad dəmmat u+ḥaylayḏe mi+šəmšo, ṭabiʕi.
contents.versio: 130.	And then, at the side of these, there is what we call fruit roll-ups. This, too, once again, that fruit leather they would make a bit thin, so it isn’t very solid. They would spread it upon clothes, cloth is fabric, let’s say, so it’s neither very thick nor thin. Normally (i.e., on average), two meters, three meters, it doesn’t matter. Two people grasp it, each one the two ends, one here and one there, and one empties the pudding. And now then these ones circulate it on it, until it catches onto the whole surface. This one becomes a fruit roll-up, (made) from grapes and flour. Like when it gets made, it gets mixed together, one calls it pudding, as I said, grape pudding is what one calls it. That way, they would make fruit roll-ups, as I said. Fruit leather, they would put it into vessels. Then they would cut it, it would dry, a week, two, in the sun. Walnut rope, like so. Such things, but wine, as I said, on its own, that one would stay in the sun, and would heat up from the sun, it would take, you might say, its strength from the sun, naturally.

contents.textus: 131.	I. Tawdi ġắlabe.
contents.versio: 131.	I. Thanks very much.

contents.textus: 001. Meqəm ab+bote, komaṇṇo, balki ḥzalxu, ʕabiritu lbote, lo? Baq+qəryawoṯe flān... ab+bote+ʕatiqe. Aq+qṭoraṯṯe háwxane, bu+šəklànone.
contents.versio: 001. Formerly, the houses, I say, perhaps you have seen, entered such houses, no? In such-and-such villages… the old houses. Their ceilings are like this, they are in this shape.

contents.textus: 002. Meqəm… kəmmínale, ‘atuno’. ‘Atuno’, mənyo ‘atuno’? Saymiwa bayto… Uʕḏo hēš kito bote manne bak+karme, lo?
contents.versio: 002. Formerly ... we called it a ‘lime kiln’. ‘Lime kiln’, what is a ‘lime kiln’? They used to build a house … Nowadays there are still some of these houses in the vineyards, no?

contents.textus: 003. Ak+karme. Hēš kito bote dak+karme manne. Kəmmínanne ‘bote dak+karme’. Bayto du+karmo, nuṭriwa u+karmo.
contents.versio: 003. The vineyards. There are still some of these vineyard houses. We call them 'vineyard houses’. A vineyard house, they guarded the vineyard.

contents.textus: 004. Dǝmxiwa bu+qayṭo aʕle aw fayšiwa bgawe. Bayto b̥kefe našife, dlo čimənto, dlo tə+mede. Hēš kito manne.
contents.versio: 004. They used to sleep during the summer on top of it or stay within it. A house of dry stones, without cement, without anything. There are still some of those.

contents.textus: 005. Ánnaqqa saymiwa bayto manək… e, hawxa, mdawṛno, mgaṛvno, bu+šəklano. Kowele tarʕo, bas hiye kulle kéfeyo, xdi+qubo hawxa.
contents.versio: 005. Then they used to make one of those houses ... yes, like so, circular, round, in that shape. Apart from a door, it was entirely stones, like a dome.

contents.textus: 006. Hawxa qubo, balki ḥzalxu bad+dayre, iḏa azzoxu l Mor Gabriel, iḏa azzoxu lġēr dəkkoṯe, dayre… Kowe qube ha hawxa, bu+šəklànone, a+qṭoraṯṯe, tarʕo... Bas hani dkǝmmina, čimənto lo+maḥtiwa appe.
contents.versio: 006. A dome, like so, perhaps you have seen them in the monasteries, if you went to Mor Gabriel or you went to other places, monasteries. There are domes just like so, they are in that shape, their ceilings, a door. But those ones about which we speak, they did not put cement in them.

contents.textus: 007. Saymiwa hawxa ḥḏo … kul ḥa lu+goràn dməqqa glozamle čimənto. Yani kalšo, lăǧan dmaʕmar bak+kefe.
contents.versio: 007. They made one like so … everybody according to how much cement he would need. Like, quicklime, so that he can build with stones.

contents.textus: 008. Ksaymiwa ḥa hawxa. Molanwa gawe ṭarfe w qayse mdu+ṭuro. Quṭʕiwa qayse mdu+ṭuro, hažžəkat kəmmínanne.
contents.versio: 008. They would make one like so. They filled its inside with twigs and wood from those of the hill country. They cut some wood from those of the hill country, we call them brush.

contents.textus: 009. ‘Hažžəkat’ kǝmmina aṭ+ṭarfe dkowən mad+dawme, dquṭʕi qarʕe dad+dawme, dann+ilone. Hanək kəmmínanne ‘hažžəkat’, ar+rafiʕe. Manək w ma+ḥlime molanwa gawe du+baytawo.
contents.versio: 009. Brush is what we call the twigs that come from trees, when they cut off the tops of the trees, of the arbors. Those are what we call brush, the thin ones. With those ones and the thick ones they filled the inside of that house.

contents.textus: 010. Ṭoránwayle tarʕo w ṭoránwayle šəbbake naʕime. Šəbbake naʕime, hawxa čučḳín, hēš naʕǝm manək.
contents.versio: 010. They left a door for it and they left some small windows for it. Small windows, yea tiny, even smaller than those.

contents.textus: 011. Gədǧuġríwayle, molánwayle, tloṯo+arbʕo+yawme. Muqḏíwayle nuro.
contents.versio: 011. They would heat it, they had filled it up, three-four days. They set it on fire.

contents.textus: 012. Kul dnuḥtowa i+nuro, nuqṣowa, molánwayle hēš, hūl tloṯo+arbʕo+ḥamšo+yawme, balki šabṯo. Hūl dyuqḏiwa ak+kefanək, ḥawriwa, howanwa ḥeeewore, xdu+talgo.
contents.versio: 012. Every time the fire went down, it diminished, they filled it up again, for three-four-five days, maybe a week. Until those stones burned down, whitened, the became really white, like snow.

contents.textus: 013. Ánnaqqa hani, kulle ak+kefe, dəmmina, dmaʕmarre, kulle gyuqḏi. Məqqa dməǧġǝr, haqqa gyuqḏi kulle. U+bayto, dəmmina, kowe, dəmmina, haqqa. Kiban dəmmina, tloṯo aw arbʕo+mətrowat ʕeloyo. Kiban dəmmina, tloṯo aw árbʕoste rwiḥo, w mgaṛvno, w hawxa.
contents.versio: 013. Now then, these, all these stones, so to speak, that they built, all of them are burning. The hotter it becomes, the more all of them burn. The house, so to speak, is, so to speak, that big. We can say it is three or four meters high. We can say, also three or four wide, and circular, and so on.

contents.textus: 014. Ánnaqqa hano, mǝd yaqəḏ ṭowo, bəṯr me šabṯo dǧuġrile, kḥawri ak+kefe, kxayfi, kowən xayife. Dəmmina, i+kefo ḥamši kilowatyo, kfayšo ʕaṣro+kilowat, lo?
contents.versio: 014. Now then, this one, once it has burnt well, after they have been heating it for a week, the stones blanch, they get light, they become light. So to speak, a stone is fifty kilos, it preserves ten kilos, right?

contents.textus: 015. Kfayšo hawxa, kxayfo, kḥawro, gmaydo qalite dhuyo čimənto, zubṭo ak+kefe. Ínaqqa ḥa dmaʕmər, dzubṭo ak+kefe. Ínaqqa ḥa dbone, lo, dbone ak+kefe šuro flān.
contents.versio: 015. It becomes like so, it gets light, it blanches, it reaches the quality to become cement, to hold the stones together. When one builds, to hold the stones together. When one fabricates, right, to fabricate a wall or something with the stones.

contents.textus: 016. Ánnaqqa, ínaqqa dkəbʕi, gmaydi i+kefayo, kefe manək, mədkaməl u+šuġlo+ḥaroyo, zatan mədṭafi, <kfayšo> kfayši bdukṯayye, ya gnofəl, ya gədfoyəš hawxa. Kšurṭile, bi+ḥarayto kšurṭile.
contents.versio: 016. Now then, when they want, they take away that stone, one of those stones, once the last task has ended, basically once it has gone out, they stay in their place, either it falls down or it stays like so. They dismantle it, at the end they dismantle it.

contents.textus: 017. Ínaqqa dlo+nofəl, gmaydi ak+kefaṯṯe. Ínaqqa dlozəm, maḥtənne … maḥti mayye aʕlayye … maḥtənne bayn am+maye. Kfayxi, kfǝrdi xdu+ʕafro, lo?
contents.versio: 017. When it does not fall, they take away their stones. When it is necessary, they put them… they put water on them … they put them into water. They disintegrate, they crumble like soil, right?

contents.textus: 018. Dəmmina, u+ʕafro. Kfǝrdi, kowən čimənto, dəmmina, uʕdo kəmmina čimənto.
contents.versio: 018. So to speak, soil. They crumble, they become cement, so to speak, nowadays we call it cement.

contents.textus: 019. Kálšoyo, hiye kálšoyo, əšmayye hǝnnǝk kalšo mitawmárwalle.
contents.versio: 019. It’s lime, it is lime, as for their name, one used to call them lime.

contents.textus: 020. Ánnaqqa hawo, ḥəfriwa nqurto, ʕafro ḥeworo. Kḥəfríwayle meqəm bi+iḏo. Kə́twalle medone du+ḥforo: maqoro, dəmmina kəmmínale, hawxa moḥanwa aʕle, ḥəfriwa. Aw howéwalle mede biḏayye hawxa du+ḥforo: kə́twalle šawye, hawxa reše hawxa ʕawude.
contents.versio: 020. Now then, they used to excavate aggregate, pale dirt. Formerly they would dig it by hand. They had digging instruments: a chisel, so to speak as we call it, they beat upon it like so, they dug. Or they had some other such thing for digging in their hands: they had handles, serrations like so, sharp like so.

contents.textus: 021. Ḥəfriwa ʕafro ḥeworo, yani mu+ṭuro, mi+kefo. Mu+qatoro aw mi+šeno kəmmina. ʕAfro rakixo, mawo ḥeworo.
contents.versio: 021. They dug white dirt, like, from the hill country, from the stone. From a boulder or a crag, as we say. Soft dirt, from that pale type.

contents.textus: 022. Xulṭíwayle ánnaqqa pawo dsə́mwalle, pano dsəmme. Kowən tre+medone, lo? Tarte+maddat. Hayo kuyo čimənto, i+qamayto, w haṯe, dəkḥufri biḏayye, nqurto kəmmínala, nqurto.
contents.versio: 022. They then mixed it with that which they had made, with the one they made. There are two things, right? Two materials. That one becomes cement, the first one, and this one, which they dig with their hands, aggregate we call it, aggregate.

contents.textus: 023. Hayo ḥewərto w hawo ḥeworo, a+tre kowən ḥewore. Hayo čimənto, xud məḷḷan, nqurto, kxulṭənne, w maye aʕmayye. Li+ḳeliḳe dkəbʕi, məqqa dkəbʕi, kmaxlən mayye aʕlayye. Kfǝšri, kowən ʕafro.
contents.versio: 023. That one is pale and this one is pale, the two of them are pale. That cement, like we said, aggregate, they mix them, and water together with them. For the occasion they want, as much as they want, they unload water upon them. They melt, they become dirt.

contents.textus: 024. Ánnaqqa gawlənne bəḥḏoḏe šan dməxloṭi ṭawwo bayn+ḥḏoḏe. Kowən čimənto, kowən, gzəb̥ṭi yani.
contents.versio: 024. Then they churn them together, so that they merge with each other well. They become cement, they become, like, they stick.

contents.textus: 025. Kowən dabuqe, elastik, dəmmina hawxa mede. Gmaydi qalite, w maʕmriwa ab+bote appe.
contents.versio: 025. They become sticky, elastic, so to speak something like so. They reach a certain quality, and they built houses with them.

contents.textus: 026. Hayo i+čimə̀ntowa. Mḥaḏriwa i+čiməntaṯṯe hawxa. Yani, xduʕdo čimənto latwa.
contents.versio: 026. That was cement. They prepared their cement like so. Like, there was no cement like now.

contents.textus: 027. Uʕdo čimənto ḥaḏə́rtoyo. Ksaymila: mo+əšne, azzá. Bas u+kalšawo foyašwa, dəmmina, bi+ʕmara.
contents.versio: 027. Nowadays cement is ready-made. They make it: one hundred years, it is gone. But that lime lasted, so to speak, in the building.

contents.textus: 028. Ínaqqa dmaḥtiwa ṭowo kalšo zoyudo, yani xŭdəglozəm, bu+xarǧaṯṯe, bi+čimənto, bu+hno, bi+malzama du+bnoyo, bəṯr me arbʕi+əšne, mitawmər, bəṯr me arbʕi+əšne gməxloṭo hiya w i+kefo bəḥḏoḏe.
contents.versio: 028. When they put extra lime, like, as much as necessary, in their mortar, in the cement, in the whatsit, in the building material, after forty years, one might say, after forty years it and the stone merge together.

contents.textus: 029. Məqqa dʕutqo … ínaqqa dhuyo sawəḥto, i+čimənto, məqqa dʕutqo, arbʕi+əšne, mo+əšne, maṯe+əšne w zəd, ktuyo qwiṯo, kuyo hiya w i+kefo ḥa. Law kibux ḥozat i+kefo áynayo, i+čimənto áynayo. Fahimat?
contents.versio: 029. However much it ages, when it becomes cured, the cement, however much it ages —forty years, a hundred years, two hundred years and more —it becomes stronger, it and the stone become one. You can no longer see which is the stone and which is the cement. Do you understand?

contents.textus: 030. Yani larwal ḥzalxu kefe, lo? Law kibux fərqat ak+kefe w i+čimənto me+ḥḏoḏe.
contents.versio: 030. Like, you have seen stones outside, no? You can no longer distinguish the stones and the cement from each other.

contents.textus: 031. Miḏe dhawo ḥeworo w hanək ak+kèfeste, dəmmina, naturél, ḥewórene, gəšt taqriban w kowən ḥa, ḥəngi dkətwe ṭowo u+kalšawo.
contents.versio: 031. Since that pale one and those stones as well are, let’s say, naturel, pale, they almost exactly become one, so good was this lime.

contents.textus: 032. Ṭaw mi+čimənto duʕdo balfo+qènewe. Dəmmina, kito bote, ʕmarat dəkoṯe antik, alfo+əšne, tralfo+əšne, tloṯalfo+əšne. Fayiši maṣre bi+čiməntayo ʕam+ḥḏoḏe. ʕMara qwiṯo, lo+ǧarila mede li+čiməntayo, yani, lu+kalšo.
contents.versio: 032. It was one thousand times better than the cement of today. So to speak, there are houses, buildings, old-fashioned places, one thousand years, two thousand years, three thousand years. They have remained held together by that cement. A strong building, nothing has affected that cement, meaning the lime.

contents.textus: 033. Xud məḷḷi, i+čimənto duʕdo, ʕəmra šawʕi+tmoni+əšneyo, mo+əšneyo, kḥurwo. Šmaṭ u+dammǝr, ḥalaq u+ḥadīd kúlmede.
contents.versio: 033. As I said, the cement of today, at the age of seventy-eighty years, one hundred years it falls apart. Take out the iron, throw away the steel, everything!

contents.textus: 034. I+malzama du+waxtawo háyowa. Ánnaqqa uʕdo imkanat law+fayəš. Mḥaləf u+zabno, hawi modernleš... modérn. Ánnaqqa mədčimənto ḥaṯto w maʕmár! Bote fayiṭe, dəmmínanne, bote fayiṭe.
contents.versio: 034. The material of that time was like that. Now then, now such possibilities no longer remain. The times have changed, it has become moder... moderne. Now take new cement and build! Rotten houses, as we call them, rotten houses.

contents.textus: 035. Hayo i+čimə̀ntowa.
contents.versio: 035. That was the cement.

contents.textus: 036. Ánnaqqa u+šəkl du+bayto. U+bayto, u+šəklano diḏe. Yani mi+badaye, dəmmina, ḥəfriwa u+bayto.
contents.versio: 036. Now then, the type of the house. The house, this type of it. Like, at the beginning, so to speak, they dug the house.

contents.textus: 037. Maṯlo, hano báytoyo. Dəmmina, kibe ʕaṣro traḥṣar+mətrowat yurxo. Ḥufríwayle gurtoṯe taḥta di+arʕo.
contents.versio: 037. For example, this is a house. Let’s say, it is ten-twelve meters long. They dug for it footingings trenches under the earth.

contents.textus: 038. Məfqiwa i+šeno kəmmínala, i+kefo dkito taḥt u+ʕafro. Aḥna gabayna latyo xud Awrupa. Kito kefo, šeno, šeno qwiṯo.
contents.versio: 038. They took out what we call the bedrock, the stone which is under the earth. We, by us it is not like Europe. There is stone, bedrock, strong bedrock.

contents.textus: 039. Ínaqqa dḥufrat u+ʕafro, gmaḥwyo. Xud i+čimə̀ntoyo, taḥt i+arʕo.
contents.versio: 039. When you excavate the dirt, it appears. It is like cement, under the earth.

contents.textus: 040. Məfqiwa i+čimənto, yani i+šeno. Kul arbʕo+mətrowat, dəmmina, aw tloṯo+mətròwatyo.
contents.versio: 040. They took out the cement, um, the bedrock. Every four meters, let’s say, or it is three meters.

contents.textus: 041. Lu+goran du+štatik ḥəfriwa gurtoṯe, ‘raġloṯe’ kəmmínanne, aw kolone kmitawmarre. Aḥna kəmmínanne ‘raġlo’ bu+suryoyo.
contents.versio: 041. Depending on the foundation, they excavated footingings trenches, we call them ‘legs’, or one calls them ‘columns’. We call them ‘a leg’ in Ṭuroyo.

contents.textus: 042. Dəmmina, ḥfərre ḥḏo, ḥušwina tamhó. Ḥḏo harke, arbʕo+mətròwatyo baynoṯayye.
contents.versio: 042. Let’s say, they have excavated one, let us suppose over there. One here, it is four meters between them.

contents.textus: 043. Ánnaqqa gmolanwa tamo dmaʕmaqqe hul li+šeno, hul li+kefo, dtaḥte du+ʕafro. Molánwayle kule čimənto w kefe, yani kalšo mano dməḷḷan.
contents.versio: 043. Then they would fill there what they have deepened as far as the bedrock, as far as the stone which is below the dirt. They filled all of it with cement and stones, like, with lime of the sort we spoke about.

contents.textus: 044. Čimənto w kefe bonanwayle, maṯlo mətro hul lalʕal. Mǝd maṭi lu+ʕafro, li+arʕo, at+tarte maṭən, ánnaqqa qquṭri ʕal+qarʕayye qəšto.
contents.versio: 044. They built it up with cement and stones, for example, for a meter to the top. After it has reached the dirt, the earth, two have reached it, then they tie an arch on top of them.

contents.textus: 045. Xaṯe haṯe. Hēš ʕam i+foṯo di+arʕona. Hēš ʕam i+foṯo di+arʕona.
contents.versio: 045. This is like this one. We are still on the surface of the earth. We are still on the surface of the earth.

contents.textus: 046. I+raġlaṯe hayo w hayo. Ánnaqqa kmo glozamle lu+bayto mani? Kmo raġloṯe? Saymiwa u+hnayḏe, u+ḥšowayḏe.
contents.versio: 046. This footing – that one and that one. Now then, how many of these does it need for the house? How many footings? We made ... its whatsit ... its calculation.

contents.textus: 047. Mǝdkaməl u+bayto kule me hawīr taḥta di+arʕo, yani, maṯlo, harke glozəm tarte, tamo tarte, harke glozəm ḥamməš, tamo ḥamməš. Mǝdkamili hani kulle, qquṭríwanne, xǝd məḷḷi, ar+raġloṯe me+laltaḥ, čimənto flān, kefe.
contents.versio: 047. After the whole house is finished beneath the earth all around, like for example, here it needs two, there two, here it needs five, there five. After these are all finished, they tied them, as I said, the footings from below, cement, such-and-such, stones.

contents.textus: 048. Ánnaqqa hēžnú gdoṯalle ləḥḏo seviye ʕam+ḥḏoḏe … taraziye dəmmina, maṯlo, aw mizən.
contents.versio: 048. Now then, they have now become at one plane with each other … a level, let’s say, for example, or a balance.

contents.textus: 049. Ánnaqqa gmaḥtiwa čimənto aʕlayye, kalšo mawo dməḷḷan. Hedi gbodanwa dbonanwa kefe ḥeḏore du+bayto hul lalʕal. Kefe, xǝdəkḥozina me larwal, lo, ak+kefe dlarwal.
contents.versio: 049. Now then, they would put cement on them, lime of that sort we mentioned. Then they would begin to build up stones around the house upwards. Stones, as we see from outside, right, the stones outside.

contents.textus: 050. Me lawġul kefe w me larwal kefe. Hul dʕole, tloṯo+mətròwatyo, treyo, hən árbʕoyo, məqqa dkəbʕi, maʕlən u+bayto, lo?
contents.versio: 050. Stones on the inside and stones on the outside. Until it rises, whether it is three meters, two meters, or some even four meters. As much as they want, they raise the house, right?

contents.textus: 051. Bəṯr me tamo ánnaqqa gdoṯe lu+qṭoro. Uʕdo hawi {arbaʕ} arbʕo+šurone.
contents.versio: 051. After that point it now comes to the roof. Now it has become four walls.

contents.textus: 052. Ánnaqqa gdoṯe u+qṭoro. Məksaymi? Əzzanwa lu+ṭuro, maydiwa qayse yarixe, bu+šəklano, dkənne hawxa. Ayna? Xduʕdo diḏi hawxa, dkətte hawxa.
contents.versio: 052. Then it comes to the roof. What do they do? They went to the hill country, they took long beams, of that type, which are like so. Which ones? Such as mine nowadays, which are like so.

contents.textus: 053. Quṭʕíwanne <d>ʕəsri, tleṯi, arbʕi, zədtə́r. Maḥtiwa ánnaqqa bah+hawire daš+šuronanək, sundə́nwanne hawxa.
contents.versio: 053. They cut for themselves twenty, thirty, forty, more. Then they put them in the precincts of those walls, they leaned them like so.

contents.textus: 054. Bəṯr maḥtiwa aʕlayye hǝnna damixe. Yarixe, arbʕo+mətròwatne, ḥámšone. Məqqa dkito, maḥtiwa aʕlayye.
contents.versio: 054. Afterwards they put on them some horizontal ones. Long ones, they are four meters long, they are five. As many as there are, they put them upon them.

contents.textus: 055. Maḥtiwa dəmmina du+falgo yarixe, laǧan dsaymi u+šəklano.
contents.versio: 055. They put, so to speak, some long middle ones, in order to make it this shape.

contents.textus: 056. Kəmmina, tamo kiba tre. I+ḥreto ktuyo, ṣira ḥreto, ktuyo tloṯo. Du+falgo ktuyo arbʕo, ṣira hawxa.
contents.versio: 056. Let’s say, over there it has two. The other one will be, the other row, it will be three. The middle one will be four, a row like so.

contents.textus: 057. Məd húwalle u+šəklano, ánnaqqa maḥtiwa qayse aʕlayye, qayse damixe, hul dṣuxriwa qarʕe dah+hnanək, i+iskalayo.
contents.versio: 057. After they gave it this shape, then they put beams upon them, horizontal beams, until they enclosed the top of those whatsits, that scaffold.

contents.textus: 058. Uʕdo, dəmmina, bi+qamayto kuyo ftəḥto hawxa, xduʕdo diḏi, lo? Ánnaqqa kṣuxríwanne baq+qayse, qayse yarixe.
contents.versio: 058. Now, so to speak, at the beginning, it is open like so, like mine now, right? Then they would close them with beams, long beams.

contents.textus: 059. Hedi gmaḥtiwa aʕlayye ʕafro — ṭino, mgawliwa u+ṭino bu+ʕafrano. Howewa hawxa falqe, saymíwayle falqe.
contents.versio: 059. Then they would put dirt upon them — mud, they mixed the mud with this dirt. Like so they became clumps, they made it into clumps.

contents.textus: 060. Mʕawniwa ḥḏoḏe. Meqəm kulle mʕawniwa ḥḏoḏe. Əzzewa hano ʕammawo, hawo ʕammawo, ḥreno ʕammawo, mḥalfiwa. Ayna doḏaʕwa u+šuġlano, əzzewa u+ḥreno aʕme laǧan doṯe maʕmər u+baytayḏe. Zuze latwalle, bu+šəklawo.
contents.versio: 060. They helped each other. Formerly everybody helped each other. This one went with that one, that one with that one, another one with that one, they alternated. Whichever one knew that job, the other one accompanied him so that he would build his house. They had no spondulix, in this way.

contents.textus: 061. Mǝd maḥátwalle u+ʕafrawo ʕal qarʕayye, ṣuxriwa kulle qarʕayye daq+qaysanək, laǧan i+čimənto dlo nuḥto laltaḥ, lo? Me darbe dad+dafe, lo, ad+dafe, dkəmmina, dafe, qayse. Ad+dafe, dkənne uʕdo, dəkḥozina.
contents.versio: 061. After they put that dirt on top of them, they closed all the tops of those beams, lest the cement go down, right? In place of planks, right, planks, so we say, planks, beams. The planks that are there now, which we are seeing.

contents.textus: 062. Bəṯr mayo maḥtiwa nqurto maṯe, dməḷḷi, ḥewərto, dḥufríwayla. Haṯe d <gmitaḥto>, dmaḥtila bayo, bgawe di+čimənto aw du+kalšo.
contents.versio: 062. After that they add this kind of aggregate, as I said, the white one, which they had dug out. This is the one that is being put, which they put in that one, into the cement or the lime.

contents.textus: 063. Maydiwa nqurto mayo, ánnaqqa bayziwa aʕla, msawanwa qarʕe du+bayto kule, dnofaq u+qṭoro šafiro, lo?
contents.versio: 063. They took that kind of aggregate, then they poured it upon it, they levelled the top of the entire house so that the roof comes out beautiful, right?

contents.textus: 064. Mǝdəfrəsse šafiro hawxa, mlalle kule nqurto. Hawi hawxa, hawi hawxa ʕam u+yurxayḏe kule.
contents.versio: 064. After they plastered it so beautifully, they filled all of it with aggregate. It became like so, it became like so along its entire length.

contents.textus: 065. Bəṯr ánnaqqa gmaḥti i+čimənto, ak+kefe. Qquṭri qarʕe ʕal u+qalǝbawo b̥kefe, b̥čimənto.
contents.versio: 065. Then afterwards they would put this cement, the stones. They would tie its top according to that pattern with stones, with cement.

contents.textus: 066. Gmoṭǝlle kefe, dkənne nqiwe, hawxa dlanne kefe ṭowe, kefe nqiwe, ḥariwe, laǧan dzubṭi ḥḏoḏe, kefe hawxa dnukti ḥḏoḏe.
contents.versio: 066. They would bring stones for it, which are pierced, like, the ones that are not good stones, pierced stones, destroyed ones, so that they catch one another, such stones that ‘bite’ each other.

contents.textus: 067. Maḥtiwa čimənto. Dəmmina, gbode, gbode, dəmmina, marke, maṯlo. Gbode marke, gmaḥət rēz harke w gborəm hawxa, hul dkomalwa.
contents.versio: 067. They applied cement. Let’s say, he would begin, he would begin, so to speak from here, for example. He would begin from here, he would put a row here and would turn around like so, until it was complete.

contents.textus: 068. Čimənto, kefo aʕla. Ṣaṭlo dčimənto, kefo aʕla, barbán dəḥḏoḏe. Kulle moḥanwanne bəḥḏoḏe hawxa, hul dʕolewa, məqṭarwa kule bi+ḥarayto.
contents.versio: 068. Cement, with a stone on it. A bucket of cement, with a stone on it, next to one another. They slammed all of them together, like so, until it rose, everything would get tied up at the end.

contents.textus: 069. Fāšwa naqwo. Hawxa gmaḥatwa čimənto, maḥatwa aʕle sale, fāšwa, dəmmina, ʕəsri+yawme mede u+qaləb̥, yani aq+qayse, am+medonani taḥte di+hno, taḥte di+ʕmara, taḥte du+bayto dsaymiwa.
contents.versio: 069. There remained a hole. Like so, he would put cement, he put a basket on it, there remained, so to speak, for some twenty days, the frame, meaning the beams, the things under the whatsit, under the building, under the house that they were making.

contents.textus: 070. ʕƏsri+yawme, flān, balki yarḥo, lgoran di+hawa, dəmmina. Dowe saṯwo, klozəm dfayši ġắlăbe, dowe qayṭo — gnəšfi xayifo.
contents.versio: 070. Twenty days, such-and-such, maybe a month, according to the weather. If it is winter, they need to stay for long, if it is summer — they dry quickly.

contents.textus: 071. Bas kefe, dlo dammər, ḥadīd layt, kefe w kalšo lḥuḏayye. Yani aq+qṭoronani kulle, duʕdo dəǧġilina aʕlayye, kulle, dḥufratte, layt appe lo ḥadīd w lo dammər, lo barʕayye w lo b̥qarʕayye. Lo bar+raġloṯe taḥte di+arʕo w lo baš+šurone kīt ḥadīd, dammər, w lo bu+qṭoro, bu+saqaf.
contents.versio: 071. Only stones, without iron, there is no steel, stones and lime on their own. Meaning, all these roofs about which we were just speaking, all of them, if you dig into them, there is neither iron nor steel in them, neither in their bottom nor in their top. Neither in the footings beneath the earth nor in the walls is there any steel, iron, and not in the roof, in the ceiling.

contents.textus: 072. Kulle kéfene. Maḥtiwa bgawe daš+šurone. Aš+šurone mə́trone, mətro.
contents.versio: 072. Everything is stones. They put them inside the walls. The walls are a meter, a meter.

contents.textus: 073. Maḥtiwa bgawayye, mgawliwa ṭino. Maʕlūm, čimənto latwa dmaḥti ġắlăbe, yani, kəbʕela kalla ġắlăbe. Mgawliwa u+ṭino, ʕafro maḥtíwayle bgawayye.
contents.versio: 073. They put them inside them, they churned mud. Obviously, there wasn’t a lot of cement to put, like, it required lots of money. They churned mud, they put dirt inside of them.

contents.textus: 074. Bgawe du+mətro. Mǝd dbnalle u+rezano u+hano, ánnaqqa bgawayye buġre. Buġre, kefe naʕime, buġre. W čimənto, domanno, ʕafro, gawlíwayle.
contents.versio: 074. Inside the meter. After they built this row, this one, then pebbles inside of them. Pebbles, small stones, pebbles. And cement, let me say, dirt, they churned it.

contents.textus: 075. Ham kowe šaḥuno u+bayto, bu+ʕafro, kowe mede ṭabiʕí, naturel bayto, yani kowele klima ṭabiʕí.
contents.versio: 075. The house becomes both warm and … with the dirt, it becomes something natural, a naturel house, like, it has natural air conditioning.

contents.textus: 076. Lo? Naturel… klima. Bu+ʕafrawo. W mə́troste rwíḥene, kowən fayuḥe bu+qayṭo w šaḥune bu+saṯwo.
contents.versio: 076. Right? Naturel... air conditioning. With this dirt. And they are also a meter wide, they are cool in summer and warm in winter.

contents.textus: 077. U+ʕafrawo, me darba di+čimənto, molánwanne gawayye, aš+šurone.
contents.versio: 077. That dirt, in place of the cement, they filled them, their interiors, the walls.

contents.textus: 078. W bu+qṭòroste kito ʕafro, lalʕal, bu+qṭoro. Bəṯr mǝd našəf, gmaydi ánnaqqa u+qalbawo. Kḥayrat: kle ánnaqqa u+qṭoro dfayəš, fayəš hawxa lruḥe.
contents.versio: 078. And on the roof too, there is dirt, up above, on the roof. After it has dried, then they took away that frame. You take a look, now here’s the roof that remained, remained like so on its own.

contents.textus: 079. Lo ḥadīd, lottə́mmede kīt ebe ġer mi+čimənto w mak+kefe. Hăma qay? ʕAl dkətyo hawxa, kkole, miḏe dkətyo hawxa.
contents.versio: 079. There’s no iron, no nothing in it other than the cement and the stones. But why? Because it is like so, it stands, since it is like so.

contents.textus: 080. W kito hənna, háwxaste kkolən, kito háwxaste qṭore msawye, kkolən. Hánəkste kətte mimariye lruḥayye.
contents.versio: 080. And there are a few, they also stand like so, there are level roofs also like so, they stand. As for those too, they have an architecture of their own.

contents.textus: 081. Hánəkste b̥teqliḏo: kefo gzəb̥ṭo ḥreto, kefo gdumxo ʕal i+kefo, kefo gdumxo ʕal i+kefo. Mi+xaṣrayo w mayo, hul dʔoṯe lu+falgo. Maḥtiwa kefo rabṯo, kulle ṭuʕniwa ḥḏoḏe ak+kefe. Yani kīt háwxaste. Bas bu+zoyudo háwxane.
contents.versio: 081. These too by means of ‘keystoning’: a stone catches another, a stone lies on the stone, a stone lies on the stone. From that side and that one, until it comes to the middle. They put a big stone, all of them stones bore each other. Like, there are also ones like so. But predominantly they are like so.

contents.textus: 082. Hawxa kfayši bəṯr lruḥayye, mede ṭabiʕí, lo. Mede ṣuni layt yani, mede dkətyo simo layt. Kúlmede ṭabiʕí, šafiro, kowən fayuḥe, ġắlăbe basime. Uʕdo, dəmmina, dʕubrina lab+botayḏan aʕ+ʕatiqe w dəzzán laḥ+ḥaṯe, lanne ʕayni.
contents.versio: 082. So they remain afterwards on their own, something natural, right. There isn’t anything artificial, meaning there isn’t anything that is done. Everything natural, beautiful, they are cool, very pleasant. Nowadays, so to speak, when we enter our old houses and when we go to new ones, they are not the same.

contents.textus: 083. D̥ḥayrina baʕ+ʕatiqe, bu+teknik+ʕatiqo, w dḥayrina bu+ḥaṯo lanne ʕayni. Lanne fayuḥe, xdaʕ+ʕatiqe.
contents.versio: 083. When we look at the old ones, with the old technique, and when we look at the new one, they are not the same. They are not cool, like the old ones.

contents.textus: 084. W lanne šaḥúneste bu+saṯwo, hani aḥ+ḥaṯe. Kowən ǧamude mu+ḥadīd, mu+betòn, me kúlmede.
contents.versio: 084. And they are also not warm in winter, those new ones. They become cold because of the metal, because of the concrete, because of everything.

contents.textus: 085. U+kalšawo dməḷḷi, dboniwayna ak+kefe ebe … dbonánwanne ... kowe šaḥúnoste. Ġēr me dkətyo ṯabuto, gzobəṭ i+čimənto, lo+gmarfela, yani gzobəṭ ak+kefe, lo+gmarfalle, gzobəṭ, ṭaw mi+čimənto dúʕdoyo. ʕAm dhowewa qawyo, lo+gmarfe ak+kefe, kowe šaḥúnoste, šaḥúnowe.
contents.versio: 085. That lime that I mentioned, with which we built the stones ... which they built ... it is also warm. Apart from being durable, it keeps the cement, it does not release it, meaning it keeps the stones and does not release them, it keeps them, it is better than today’s cement. Along with being strong, it does not release the stones, it also becomes warm, it was warm.

contents.textus: 086. W bəṯr qolabwa li+kefo, law miḏaʕwa, laybux furšatle bəṯr me zabno dḥamši+əšne aw mo+əšne, edi howewa xdi+kefo. Laybux dəḏʕat, lo i+kefo áynayo, w lo ayna loyo. Ktowe msawyo ʕam+ḥḏoḏe, lo+kfərqatle. Laybux furšatle me ḥḏoḏe.
contents.versio: 086. And after it turned into stone, it was no longer recognizable, you cannot distinguish it after a period of fifty years or a hundred years, then it has become like stone. You cannot recognize either which is the stone or which is not. It becomes equal to one another, you cannot separate it. You cannot distinguish one from another.

contents.textus: 087. Yani hano u+sistèm dméqəmyo. Bdéwalle ġắlăbe šafiro w mazbūṭ. Yani uʕdo fayišina bi+ḥaṣra dsaymina mede hawxa, law kiban. Qay? U+zabno mšaḥləf, i+ḥzayto mšaḥlfo.
contents.versio: 087. Like, this is the former system. They began very beautiful and orderly. Like, today we still yearn to do something like so, we no longer can. Why? The times have transmogrified, the vision has transmogrified.

contents.textus: 088. Mawxa. Hano u+šəkl di+ʕmara dméqəmwe. W xud məḷḷi, ánnaqqa saymiwa, dəmmina, lak+kàrmeste bote bu+šəklawo. Hani bote, dʕayši bak+karme.
contents.versio: 088. That’s why. This was the type of building that was before. And, as I said, then they made, so to speak, houses of that type for the vineyards as well. These are houses, in which they lived in vineyards.

contents.textus: 089. Meqəm kətwa ganowe, kətwa ḥăramiye. Lo? Ganowe, gunwiwa aʕ+ʕənwe, gunwiwa ann+afšoṯe, kummínanne, kuḏʕitu ann+afšoṯe, lo? Ann+afšoṯe, ak+karme.
contents.versio: 089. Formerly there were thieves, there were robbers, right? Thieves, they stole grapes, they stole raisins, we call them, you know raisins, right? Raisins, vineyards.

contents.textus: 090. Dəmmina, meqəm iʕ+ʕayaša ʕal u+karmowa, ʕal aʕ+ʕənwewa. W kətwa noše, u+ʕamo kafínowe, ánnaqqa, dəmmina, nuṭriwa ak+karmaṯṯe, dloṯe ḥaramiye, ganowe, dgunwi aʕ+ʕənwe, dmaydənne.
contents.versio: 090. So to speak, formerly the livelihood depended upon the vineyard, depended upon grapes. And there were folks, people were hungry, then, so to speak, they watched their vineyards, so that robbers, thieves, those who steal grapes, who take them away, do not come.

contents.textus: 091. Aʕ+ʕənwaṯṯe, dəmmina, meqəm quṭfíwanne mas+sate, mak+karme. Ġayṭíwanne bam+maye, šəkəl dmaye, saymiwa šəkəl dmaye. Maye du+zeyoto kummínanne.
contents.versio: 091. Their grapes, so to speak, formerly we used to pluck them from vines, from vineyards. We dipped them in water, a kind of water, we made a kind of water. We call it a cold dip.

contents.textus: 092. W ánnaqqa ġuṭ bam+maye aʕ+ʕənwe w fras, ġuṭ w fras. Howanwa, xud me tamo larke kule, xdu+dawšak, xdu+lḥef.
contents.versio: 092. And then dip the grapes into water and spread them, dip and spread. They would be… as if all from over there to here, like a mattress, like a quilt.

contents.textus: 093. Šab̥ṯo tarte nušfiwa. Ánnaqqa nuṭríwanne, maydíwanne u+zaynaṯṯe, u+silaḥaṯṯe, kə́twalle meqəm zayno. Nuṭríwanne, fayšiwa blalyo bak+karme.
contents.versio: 093. They dried for a week or two. Then they watched them, they took their armaments, their weapons, formerly they had armaments. They watched them, they stayed overnight in the vineyards.

contents.textus: 094. Fayšiwa tamo, aḥ+ḥayaṯṯe támowayne. Yani meqəm i+dukkanaṯṯe, u+šuġlaṯṯe, u+ʕamlaṯṯe, u+dahwaṯṯe, yani aḥ+ḥayaṯṯe kulle rakíwewayne ʕal u+karmo, w bəṯr ʕal u+ḥaywan.
contents.versio: 094. They stayed there, their life was there. Meaning, formerly their shops, their work, their labour, their gold, meaning, their whole life was riding upon the vineyard, and furthermore upon the animals.

contents.textus: 095. U+ḥaywan larwal howewa. Yani bu+qayṭo, uʕdo qáyṭoyo, noše ḥyewən lo+moṭewa li+qriṯo, lu+bayto. Bu+ṭuro ʕayšiwa, ṭabiʕí, ḥaye ṭabiʕí, naturél.
contents.versio: 095. The animals were outside. Meaning in summer, now it is summer, people did not bring animals back home to the village. They lived in the hill country, natural, a natural life, naturél.

contents.textus: 096. Muklo w štoyo kúlmede organík, ḥaḏiro, w mu+ṭuro w me larwal. A+ḥyewən larwal, w a+nsane larwal. Yani ab+bote, ínaqqa dowǝnwa xalye, oṯǝnwa, fayšiwa appe. Dlowənwa xalye, bgawe dab+bote lo+fayšiwa.
contents.versio: 096. Food and drink, everything organic, ready-made, both from the hill country and from outside. The animals outside and the people outside. Like, the houses, when they became free, they came, they stayed in them. If they were not free, they did not stay inside the houses.

contents.textus: 097. Dayəm maṣre bu+šuġlaṯṯe: kármoyo, árʕoyo, flānyo, larwal. Ánnaqqa ab+bote, dsaymiwa bak+karme, laǧan ddumxi appe aw dmaḥti aʕ+ʕənwaṯṯe bgawayye, dma…, yani, dmičoki bgawe dtolən ruḥayye appe. Bote, dəmmina, du+karmo. Laǧan kúlmede, lkul ḥǝtyaǧiye dməstaʕmli tamo.
contents.versio: 097. They are constantly bound to their work: it is a vineyard, it is a field, it is some such thing, outside. Now then, the houses which they made in the vineyards, in order to sleep in them or in order to put their grapes in them, to …, like, so that they slip into it to shelter themselves in them. Houses, so to speak, of the vineyard. For everything, for every necessity that they used there.

contents.textus: 098. Hanək dlo čimə́ntowayne. Lo+koḏaʕno, lo+ḥzalxu manne aw lo. Bas dlo čimə́ntone. D̥ḥozatte, mede dumoro hawxa.
contents.versio: 098. Those were without cement. I do not know whether you saw one of them or not. But they are without cement. If you see them, such a fantabulous thing.

contents.textus: 099. Háwxane. Towalxu zabno, əzzáwayna lak+karme, dḥozítuwa məšə́kl̩ne, mede ʕuǧbo. D̥ḥozatte, dəmmat, áydarbo kolən hawxa dlo čimənto, dlo tə́mede? Yani čimənto layt appe, Kleber layt appe.
contents.versio: 099. They are like so. If you had time, we would go to the vineyards, so you would see what type they are, something wonderful. If you see them, you would say, how do they stay like so without cement, without anything? Meaning there isn’t any cement in them, there isn’t any Kleber in them.

contents.textus: 100. Bas kefe hawxa, disa bnoyo, bnoyo, bnoyo, ḥḏo, ḥḏo, bram hawxa. Hul lu+qarʕo, taq! Fayšiwa hawxa, dlo čimənto ăma.
contents.versio: 100. Only stones like so, once again building, building, building, one by one, turn around like so. Up to the top, thwack! They stayed like so, even without cement.

contents.textus: 101. Hano bote du+karmo. Hēš kənné kulle dlo ... Hani mowat dəšne dʕamiri. Ġắlăbe manne kanné qime w lo+nafili.
contents.versio: 101. This is vineyard houses. All of them are still without... These are the ones that were built hundreds of years ago. Many of them are standing and have not fallen.

contents.textus: 1. Kətwa ŭ latwa, ṭaw m Aloho latwa, ḥaq!
contents.versio: 1. There was and there wasn’t, there was none greater than God, truth!

contents.textus: 2. Kətwa, domaṇṇux, ʕammo... (Afrem: Bi+qamayto, ayna gmaḥkatla? Amár, ayna čiro...). Du+Quz̥ko. (Afrem: I+măsale, i+qəṣṣa, i+čirok̇e du...) I+qəṣṣa du+Quz̥ko, e. (Afrem: Du+Quz̥ko, e.)
contents.versio: 2. There was, let me tell you, an ‘uncle’... (Afrem: First of all, which one will you tell? Say, which fab...) About Marty. (Afrem: The matter, the story, the fable of...) The story about Marty, right. (Afrem: About Marty, yes.)

contents.textus: 3. Haṯe latyo šrolo, ăma čirók̇eyo. (Afrem: Hawxa daḥ+ḥănak̇e, du+tegḥixo). E. Hayo šróloyo, haṯe lo.
contents.versio: 3. This one isn’t true; rather, it’s a fable. (Afrem: So about jokes, about inducing laughter). Yes. That one is true, this one isn’t.

contents.textus: 4. Hiye… ŭ kə́twayle, dəmmina, ʕammo. B̥ḥa bayto howənwa, ŭ ṗirat mede látwalle.
contents.versio: 4. He… and he had, let’s say, an uncle. They were (living) in a single house, and they didn’t have any wives whatsoever.

contents.textus: 5. Ŭ əzzənwa lu+ṣaydo. U+ṣàydosi, əzzənwa lu+qṭolo dak̇+k̇irošk̇at, dat+taʕle, dam+medone. Mən dəmḥayṣliwa, ʕaṣriye uxli... šəlḥiwa qarʕayy, ŭ uxlə́nwanne.
contents.versio: 5. And they would go hunting. As for the hunt, they would go kill hares, foxes, and things. Whatever they caught, in the evening they would ea... cut off its head, and they would eat them.

contents.textus: 6. Bu+šəklano, fayiši zamā́n hawxa tavda.
contents.versio: 6. In this way, they spent some time together like so.

contents.textus: 7. Hánosi, mək‿kosaymi? Ŭ ḥa yawmo, u+braziyayḏe, yani, xud‿dəmmat, u+abro, lo... u+bràziyo, komaḷḷe lu+ʕammo, ʕámmoyo, brazi kowe. Omar, ‘Kuḏʕat omaṇṇo?’ Omar, ‘Mənyo?’ Omar, ‘ʕAǧəzno bu+ṣaydo, kobaʕno obat foṯi laff briṯo’.
contents.versio: 7. So this one, what do they do? And one day, his nephew, that is, like you’d say, the son, no... he’s the nephew, he says to the uncle, it’s an ‘uncle’, he’s a nephew. He says, ‘You know what I’m going to say?’ He says, ‘What is it?’ He says, ‘I am fed up with hunting, I want you to let me face the world (lit. ‘give my face to the world’)’.

contents.textus: 8. Gəzzino bəbriṯo, g̊koraxno, ḥozina, mək‿kīt, məl‿layt, ḥozina!’
contents.versio: 8. I’ll go into the world, I’ll go around, let’s see, what there is and what there isn’t, let’s see!

contents.textus: 9. Hánosi, koqaymi, koḥṓr bu+ʕammo druḥe, bay+yawme komanqəṣ u+ʕammo. ‘ʕAmmo, qay hawxa?’ Flān behvā́n. Omar, ‘Mṭelux baḥs du+mazlo, oṯayli ṣabr ebux, kəmmat, “Əḷḷáh gəzzino”.’
contents.versio: 9. So this one, they get up, he looks at his own uncle, his uncle is weakening daily. ‘Uncle, why is it so?’ So on and so forth. He says, ‘You brought up (lit. ‘you brought word of’) leaving, you made me happy (lit. ‘delight would come to me through you’), (and) you say, “By God, I’ll leave”’.

contents.textus: 10. Hule daṣṭə́r diḏe, hule daṣṭə́r diḏe, azzé bəbriṯo, ŭ fāš u+ʕammo bu+bayto. Azzé ləqriṯo, dəmmina, xud i+qriṯaṯe diḏan.
contents.versio: 10. He gave him his permission, he gave him his permission, he went into the world, and the uncle stayed at home. He went to a certain village, let’s say, like this village of ours.

contents.textus: 11. E, ma nuxróyoyo, ma gəzzé se man? Qrele, omər, ‘U+šaqṣ‿d̪zobaṭli ruʕyo, baqoro, greʕo, gəzzano qmaʕ+ʕezaṯṯe ya qmarw... gréʕosi d̥oweno bu+bayto’.
contents.versio: 11. Yes, isn’t he a stranger, to whom shall he go? He called out, he says, ‘The person who takes me as a herdsman, a cowherd, a servant, we’ll (i.e., I’ll) herd their goats or catt... even to become a servant in the house (lit. ‘even a servant, to become in the house’)’.

contents.textus: 12. Hánosi, lbayto mə́ḷḷele, bayto qarabáləġwa, omər, ‘Tux lsidi. G̊d̥owat greʕo?’ Omar, ‘Qay lə+g̊weno?’ ‘Mən dəmmina, g̊saymat ban diḏan?’ Omər, ‘E’. Omər, ‘Aḥna bu+baytayḏan ġəbn layt. U+šaqṣ d̥ṭore lebe dəḥḏoḏe, lazəm lo+məġbən’. Omar, ‘Ġəbn layt’.
contents.versio: 12. So this one, a household told him, it was a chaotic house, he says, ‘Come over to me. Will you become a servant?’ He says, ‘Why wouldn’t I?’ ‘Whatever we say, you’ll do it for us?’ He says, ‘Yes’. He says, ‘As for us, in our house there are no hard feelings (lit. ‘there’s no offense’). The person who offends one another, he mustn’t get angered’. He said, ‘No hard feelings!’

contents.textus: 13. Ăḷo fayiši tavda. Fayiši, ʕaṣriye... kə́twalle k̇ačk̇e, baxyo.
contents.versio: 13. Gosh, they stayed together. They stayed, one evening... they had a daughter, she cried.

contents.textus: 14. (Xud uʕdo, dádlalyo, əmmat, ‘Ma i+twalè áykoyo?’ U+bayto dam+maye. Omaṇṇo, ‘Kalá’. Meqəm twalat latwa).
contents.versio: 14. (Like now, if tonight, you were to say, ‘The toilet, where is it?’ The outhouse (lit. ‘the house of water’). I would say, ‘Here it is’. Formerly, there were no toilets.)

contents.textus: 15. Mərre, əmmi, ‘Quz̥ko!’ Omər, ‘Mənyo?’ Əmmi, ‘I+k̇ačk̇ayḏan kobuxyo, zux, mbala lam+maye, mofeqa larwal’. Omər, ‘ʕAl at+tarte ʕayne!’
contents.versio: 15. They said, they say, ‘Marty!’ He says, ‘What is it?’ They say, ‘Our girl is crying, go, take her to the water, take her outside’. He says, ‘At your service!’ (lit. ‘On both eyes’)

contents.textus: 16. Hánosi, mə‿kosōm? Komofaqla, dəmmina, bəṯr u+tarʕo. Kətle, kətle msallat, medone mani, d̥koḥayṭi aǧ+ǧule. Komoḥela braġla di+k̇ačk̇e, kobuxyo.
contents.versio: 16. So this one, what does he do? He takes her outside, let’s say, past the door. He has, he has packing needles, things of that sort, with which people sew clothes. He pricks the girl’s foot with it, she cries.

contents.textus: 17. ‘Quz̥ko, qay kobuxyo i+k̇ačk̇ayḏan?’ Omər, ‘Ašə́r, i+k̇ačk̇aṯxu, ak+kalbe bi+tarayo konawḥi, (xud̥‿ani diḏan, duʕdo daṯitu, aṯəlxu). Ak+kalbe konawḥi, i+k̇ačk̇e kobuxyo’.
contents.versio: 17. ‘Marty, why is our girl crying?’ He says, ‘Really, your girl, the dogs in that neighbourhood are barking (like these ones of ours, which when you came now, they approached you). The dogs are barking (so) the girl is crying!’

contents.textus: 18. Állesi‿mmi, qḥiri, əmmi, ‘Mḥaya bu+šuro, ŭ tux!’ Mədle, həzle i+k̇ačk̇e, hizole ŭ məḥyole bu+šuro, simole mo+parčayat—qṭilole.
contents.versio: 18. They themselves then say, they get angry, they say, ‘Knock her upside the head and get back!’ He took her, swung the girl, swung her, threw her at the wall, made her a hundred pieces—he killed her.

contents.textus: 19. Koṯe, koʕobər, kəmmi, ‘Quz̥ko, áykoyo i+k̇ačk̇e?’ Komər, ‘Lo alxu əmmutu, “mḥaya bu+šuro, ŭ tux”? Ăḷo, məḥyoli bu+šuro, qṭiloli, ŭ aṯino’. Omar, ‘Ma ġbinutu?’ Əmmi, ‘Məḷḷan, əmmina, ġəbn layt bi+măsăle’.
contents.versio: 19. He comes back, he enters, they say, ‘Marty, where is the girl?’ He says, ‘Didn’t you yourselves say “knock her upside the head and come back!” Gosh, I knocked her upside the head, killed her, and came back’. He says, ‘Are you angry?’ They say, ‘We said, we say, there are no hard feelings about the issue’.

contents.textus: 20. U+lalyawo azzé. U+lalyawo azzé, u+lalyo da+tre. Qām hánosi, mə‿kosaymi? U+k̇urk̇àṯṯesi baxi.
contents.versio: 20. That night passed. That night passed, the second night. So this one got up, what does he do? Their son started crying too.

contents.textus: 21. U+k̇urk̇àṯṯesi baxi, ‘Mənyo, mə kobaʕ̥?’ Əmmi, ‘Mbale lu+bayto dam+maye’. Disa mḥele a+msallanək bu+k̇urk̇osi, baxi. ‘Qay koboxe?’ Omər, ‘Ak+kalbe bi+tarayo koboxən, hiye harke... konawḥi, hiye harke koboxe’.
contents.versio: 21. Their son started crying too, ‘What is it, what does he want?’ They say, ‘Take him to the outhouse (lit. ‘house of water’)’. Once again, he pricked him with packing needles, and he cried. ‘Why is he crying?’ He says, ‘The dogs in that neighborhood are crying, here he is… they are barking, and here he is crying’.

contents.textus: 22. Əmmi, ‘Mḥaye bu+šuro, ŭ tux’. Mḥele bu+šuro háwosi, qṭile, ŭ aṯi. ‘Áykoyo u+k̇urk̇ayḏan?’ Omər, ‘Ăḷo, qṭili’.
contents.versio: 22. They say, ‘Knock him upside the head and come back’. He knocked that one too upside the head, killed him, and came back. ‘Where is our boy? He says, ‘Gosh, I killed him’.

contents.textus: 23. ‘E, qṭilux? Ma əmmina “qṭale!”?’ Omər, ‘Alxu mərxu. Ma ġbinutu?’ Əmmi, ‘Lo!’
contents.versio: 23. ‘Right, you killed him? Did we say “Kill him!”?’ He says, ‘You yourselves said so. Are you angry?’ They say, ‘No!’

contents.textus: 24. U+lalyàwosi azzé. Bəṯr mək‿kosaymi? Azzənne... kə́twayle emo.
contents.versio: 24. That night also passed. Then what did they do? They went... he (i.e., the head of the family) had a mother.

contents.textus: 25. Kə́twayle emo, omər, ‘Yade!’ Əmmo, ‘Mənyo?’ Omər lu+more du+bayto, omər, ‘Lano g̊ʶqošaʕlan!’ ‘E, ba məs‿saymina?’
contents.versio: 25. He had a mother, he says, ‘Mother!’ She says, ‘What is it?’ The owner of the house says, he says, ‘This one will wipe us out’. ‘Yes, but what can we do?’

contents.textus: 26. Omər, ‘Zax ʕal i+tuṯo, qray, amár, “kQawlé <šəvāna>k …”, amár, “U+qawl dar+ruʕye, dab+baqore, da+greʕe tayəm”. Kīt dəmšayeli, doṯe, domər “Mənyo?”, gdomaṇṇo, “K̇úndoyo, koquryo!”’. K̇undo mani, d̥koquryo, kummo ‘ṭuṭwiyu, ṭuṭwiyu’, bu+šəklawo.
contents.versio: 26. He says, ‘Get on top of a mulberry tree, call out, say, “kThe contract term ofk …”, say, “The contract term of the herdsmen, of the cowherds, of the servants is finished”. If he asks me, if he comes, he says, “What is it?”, I’ll say, “It’s an owl, it’s hooting!”’. One of these owls, that hoots, it says, ‘Hoo, Hoo’, in this way.

contents.textus: 27. Omər, ‘Gdomaṇṇo, “Ḥḏo mánəkyo, yasiqo ʕal i+tuṯo, ŭ hawxa kəmmo”.’
contents.versio: 27. He says, ‘I’ll say, “It is one of those things, it got on top of the mulberry tree and it goes (lit. ‘says’) like so”.’

contents.textus: 28. Nahər, i+šira di+emo. Ha ha blalyo, u+… u+… ani, u+abro di+emo qām maʕlele i+emo ʕal i+tuṯo.
contents.versio: 28. The day broke, the mother’s (i.e., the son’s) advice. Right away at night, the… the…, like, the mother’s son up and lifted the mother onto the mulberry tree.

contents.textus: 29. Ŭ koquryo, kəmmo, ‘Qawl dar+ruʕye, dab+baqore, da+greʕe, d̥kul+mede tayəm’.
contents.versio: 29. And she calls out, she says, ‘The contract of the herdsmen, of the cowherds, of the servants, of everything is finished’.

contents.textus: 30. Azzé omər, ‘ʕAmmo, ʕammo!’ Omər, ‘Mənyo?’ Omər, omər, ‘Kīt mede koqore ʕal i+tuṯo, mə́nyaṯe?’ Omər, ‘Ašə́r k̇úndoyo’. Omər, ‘Hedi klay, uʕdo gnofaqno me ḥaq diḏax’.
contents.versio: 30. He went, he says, ‘Uncle, uncle!’ He says, ‘What is it?’ He says, he says, ‘There is something crying out on top of the mulberry tree, what is this thing?’ He says, ‘Surely, it’s an owl’. He says, ‘Wait a minute, I’ll go out on your behalf’.

contents.textus: 31. Azzé, mə́dlelux tarte+kefe rabe ṭawwe ŭ mḥele. Mḥele bi+emo, dəryole me támova, bqárʕava naḥito mʕal i+tuṯo, mayiṯo.
contents.versio: 31. He went and took you some two good, big stones and threw them. He threw them at the mother, knocked her down from over there, she fell down headwise from the mulberry tree, she died.

contents.textus: 32. ‘K̇uro, qṭilux, émiyo!’ Omər, ‘Elux əmmat “k̇úndoyo”, lo+məḷḷux “émiyo”. Ăḷo, qṭiloli’. Háyose azzə́n təlyalle. Tlalle háyosti.
contents.versio: 32. ‘Boy, you killed her, it’s my mother!’ He says, ‘It was you who say “it’s an owl”, you didn’t say “it’s my mother”. Gosh, I killed her!’ So that one, they went to bury her. They buried that one too.

contents.textus: 33. Omər, ‘Quz̥ko!’ Omər, ‘Mənyo?’ Omər, ‘Ádyawma gəmšadrínalux lu+dworo’. Omər, ‘ʕAl at+tarte+ʕayne!’
contents.versio: 33. He says, ‘Marty!’ He says, ‘What is it?’ He says, ‘Today, we’re going to send you out to plough’. He says, ‘At your service! (lit. ‘upon the two eyes’)’

contents.textus: 34. Lu+dworo. Omər, ‘Kətlan tre+tawre ŭ kətlan ṭažíyesi. Gəmḥalqat a+tre+tawre bəṯr i+ṭažiye.
contents.versio: 34. To plough. He says, ‘We have two oxen and a greyhound too. You’ll send the two oxen after the greyhound’.

contents.textus: 35. Ayko drawiʕo, tamo gdawratlux arbʕo+xṭuṭe, gdoṯat ʕaṣriye lu+bayto. Məd aṯat lu+bayto, məd áṯatsi, g̊saymatlux ṭaʕno d̥qayse ŭ gmaṭaʕnatte ŭ gdoṯat.
contents.versio: 35. ‘Wherever she lies down, plow yourself four furrows there, you’ll come back home in the evening. Once you’ve come home, once you’ve come back, you’ll gather yourself a load of brush, load them up, and (then) you’ll come back’.

contents.textus: 36. Ṭaʕno d̥qayse, mani du+ṭuro. Mad+dawmani du+ṭuro qṭaʕən, ŭ maṭʕan ṭaʕno d̥qayse ʕal i+ḥmarto ŭ gmotatte’. Omər, ‘ʕAl at+tarte+ʕayne’.
contents.versio: 36. ‘A load of brush, of those ones from the hill country. Cut them from those trees of the hill country, and put (lit. ‘load’) a load of brush on the jenny, and you’ll bring them back’. He says, ‘At your service! (lit. ‘upon the two eyes’)’

contents.textus: 37. Ṣafro mḥalle i+ṭažiye b̥qamayte, ŭ malaxle u+zlām. Me... me ṣafro hul ʕaṣriye, i+ḥaywanayo lo+rawiʕo, ŭ komalxo, komaləx bəṯra.
contents.versio: 37. In the morning, they put the hound in front of him, and the man walked. From the … from the morning until the evening, that animal didn’t lie down, but she walks, he walks behind her.

contents.textus: 38. Híyesi maq+qaḥrat omər, ‘Hawi ʕaṣriye ŭ lo+rawiʕo. U+mede dmə́rralli, lo+rawiʕo’. Mə́dlelux kefo, qṭile i+ṭažiye.
contents.versio: 38. So he says out of anger, ‘It has become evening (already) and she hasn’t lain down. What (lit. ‘the thing’) they told me, she didn’t lie down’. He took a stone, he killed the hound.

contents.textus: 39. Qṭile i+ṭažiye, ŭ bəṯr mi+ṭažiye dəqṭilole… Ánnaqla, bəṯr məd‿əqṭilole, koqṓm towər i+ale ŭ u+niro.
contents.versio: 39. He killed the hound, and after he had killed the hound… Now then, after he had killed her, he up and breaks the plough and the yoke.

contents.textus: 40. Ŭ kosamme qayse ŭ komaḥatte ʕal i+ḥmarto, koḥoyaṣṣe ŭ koṯe lu+bayto.
contents.versio: 40. And he makes them brush and he puts them on the jenny, he binds them and comes home.

contents.textus: 41. ʕAṣriye koṯe, ‘Šoooš’, k̬maqləb aq+qayse. Komər, ‘Zoxu, maʕberu aq+qaysaṯxu, komṭéləlxu qayse’.
contents.versio: 41. In the evening he comes, ‘Stoppp!’, he unloads the brush. He says, ‘Go, bring your brush inside, I have brought you brush’.

contents.textus: 42. Kəmmi, ‘I+ṭažiye ayko?’ Komər, ‘Ăḷo, qṭiloli’. ‘Qayyo? Qay qṭilolux?’ Omər, ‘Əmmutu, “Ṭro malxo, malxo, malxo”. Malaxla hul ʕaṣriye’, omər, ‘lo+rawiʕo ŭ mede lo+səmla, əmmutu “gdawrat!”’
contents.versio: 42. They say, ‘The hound, where is it?’ He says, ‘Gosh, I killed her’. ‘Why?! Why did you kill it?’ He says, ‘You say, “Let her walk, walk, walk”. She walked until the evening’, he says, ‘she didn’t lie down and didn’t do anything, (yet) you say “You’ll plough!”

contents.textus: 43. E, ónoste qayəmno mḥélila kefo, bəṯr məd lo+rawiʕo, qṭiloli. Əmmutu qáysesi, čōlwa’, omər, ‘lo+qayse ŭ lo+dawme kətwa.
contents.versio: 43. ‘Right, so I, I up and hit her with a stone, after she didn’t lie down, I killed her. You say brush too, it was a plain’, he says, ‘there was neither brush nor trees’.

contents.textus: 44. Qāmno, i+ale ŭ u+niro twirili, maḥtili aʕla, ʕal i+ḥmarto, ŭ aṯino lu+bayto’. ‘Hawxa?’, əmmi. ‘E’.
contents.versio: 44. I got up, the plough and the yoke I broke, I put them on her, on the jenny, and came home’. ‘Is that so?’ they say. ‘Yes’.

contents.textus: 45. Ánnaqla omər, ‘Ăḷo i+ṭažiye qṭiloli ŭ komṭeli aq+qayse, ŭ mede d̥sámnolxu?’ Omər, ‘Ma ġbinutu?’ Əmmi, ‘Lo’.
contents.versio: 45. Now then, he says, ‘Gosh, the hound I killed, and I have brought you some brush, and (is there) something that I can do for you?’ He says, ‘Are you angry?’ They say, ‘No’.

contents.textus: 46. Háyosi azzá. U+yawmo dbəṯr, əmmi, ‘Quz̥ko!’ Omər, ‘Mənyo?’
contents.versio: 46. That one was gone too. The next day (lit. ‘the day of after’), they say, ‘Marty!’ He says, ‘What is it?’

contents.textus: 47. Dəmmina, ag+gorani, dəmmina, aʕ+ʕatiqe, meqəm kətwa kawwe daṣ+ṣopat. Ḥa koǧoġər aṣ+ṣopat, ak+kawwe lálʕəlva konəfqi.
contents.versio: 47. Let’s say, these roofs, let’s say, the old ones, formerly they had stovepipes. Someone heats up the stove, and the pipes go out upwards.

contents.textus: 48. Hánosi, kəmmile, kəmmi, ‘Zux, maštáy u+tawro ʕal qarʕa di+goro’. E, u+tawro áydarbo g̊solaq ʕal qarʕa di+goro, g̊šote? Hənnək áxrab mínewayne!
contents.versio: 48. Then they say to him, they say, ‘Go, water the ox on the rooftop’. Right, the ox, how will it go up on the rooftop, will it drink? They were worse than him!

contents.textus: 49. Hánosi, koqōm kuzzé, koqōm kuzzé, košoləḥ qarʕe du+tawro. Ŭ komaḥət qarʕe du+tawro bi+kawwo, ʕal qarʕa di+goro, komər ‘Rrrhoo!’ Ani ‘štay!’
contents.versio: 49. So this one, he up and goes, he up and goes, he cuts off the ox’s head. And he puts the ox’s head into the pipe, on the rooftop, he says, ‘Rrrhoo!’ That is, ‘drink!’

contents.textus: 50. Kəmmi, ‘Hano, šuġle m Alóhoyo, du+zlamano. Áydarbo mosaqle u+tawro, ŭ áydarbo komašte u+tawro, komər ‘rrrhoo’, ṭrošote maye. Mášaḷḷa, məqqa! Hul ʕayne čəkle bam+maye! Hul ʕayne du+tawro kočakle bi+kawwo’.
contents.versio: 50. They say, ‘This one, his is God’s work (i.e., it’s incredible), this man’s. How did he raise the ox, and how is he watering the ox, saying ‘rrrhoo’ — ‘let it drink water!’ Amazing (lit. Mashallah), how far! Up to his eyes, he stuck him in the water! Up to the ox’s eyes, he has stuck him in the stovepipe’.

contents.textus: 51. Kuzzə́n, koḥayri, kəmmi, ‘Məs‿səmlux, Quz̥ko?’ Komər, ‘Mašteli u+tawro hul ʕayne, čiki bam+maye’. Koḥayri, konḥəḷḷe u+tawro ŭ maḥatle qarʕe bi+kawwo.
contents.versio: 51. They go, they look, they say, ‘What have you done, Marty?’ He says, ‘I have watered the ox up to its eyes, they’re deep (lit. ‘they penetrated’) in the water’. They look, he has slaughtered the ox and put its head in the stovepipe.

contents.textus: 52. Háwosi azzé. Háwosi azzé. Fayiši bu+bayto. Fāšle lu+mērk̇o barṯo ŭ i+aṯto, ŭ hiye, tloṯo fayiši.
contents.versio: 52. So that one was gone. So that one was gone. They stayed in the house. For the husband, there was left for him a daughter and his wife, and he, three were left.

contents.textus: 53. Ánnaqla komaṣəṯ ʕal more du+bayto, u+Quz̥ko, kalé talyo, komaṣəṯ. Mək‿kosaymi? Hánosti, kəmmile, kəmmi, ŭ more du+bayto komaḷḷa li+aṯto, komər, ‘Xalaṣbune latlan mu+šaqṣano’.
contents.versio: 53. Now he’s listening to the homeowner, Marty, see, he’s hidden, he’s listening. What are they doing? So this one, they say to him, they say, and the homeowner says to his wife, he says, ‘There’s no getting rid of this character for us’.

contents.textus: 54. ‘Səmlan tanuro dlaḥmo ŭ mlay i+xurǧazine laḥmo, ŭ hay hiye haw kiban aʕle. Mən d̥kosaymina, kibe aʕlan’.
contents.versio: 54. ‘Make us an oven of bread, and fill up a saddlebag with bread, and anyway we can’t prevail over him anymore. Whatever we do, he prevails over us’.

contents.textus: 55. Səm laḥmo, aḥna blalyo, məd̥‿d̥awi i+saʕaye traḥṣar dəblalyo, aḥna gmahəzmina. Aḥna gmahəzmina me qume, ŭ ṭrofṓš u+bayto laǧane!’
contents.versio: 55. Make bread, as for us at night, after midnight (lit. ‘the hour has become twelve of in the night’), we’ll run away. We’ll run away from him, and let the house stay for him (alone)!’

contents.textus: 56. Hánosi, hánosi, bimomo kosaymo u+laḥmo ŭ fahəm be mən mərre, mək‿kosaymi məl‿lə+ksaymi.
contents.versio: 56. So this one, so this one, during the day she’s making bread, and he realized what they had said, whatever they’re doing (lit. ‘what they are doing, what they aren’t doing’).

contents.textus: 57. Axər harke ŭ tamhok̇é kowe, lə+k̬makuno qarʕux, falge dlalyo, hənnək kodəmxi.
contents.versio: 57. Finally, it’s all over the place (lit. ‘here and over there’), I don’t want to give you a headache, the middle of the night, they are sleeping.

contents.textus: 58. I+žənk̇e, u+mērk̇o, i+barṯàṯṯesi mṭiṯo, damíxene. Híyesi kuzzé. Ánnaqla i+xurǧk̇e, dəmmina, rábṯoyo. Məlyalle laḥmo, dlo+kufni.
contents.versio: 58. The wife, the husband, their mature daughter too, were asleep. As for him, he’s going. Now then, the saddlebag, let’s say, is big. They filled it with bread, so they won’t starve.

contents.textus: 59. Komofəq u+qa+laḥmawo me tamo, komičək bi+xurǧk̇e ŭ maḥət tarte+ṭalme, tlaṯ+laḥmo ʕal qarʕe druḥe, dnoše lo+forəq ebe.
contents.versio: 59. He takes out so much of that bread, he sneaks into the bag and puts two loaves, three loaves on his own head, so people wouldn’t pick him out.

contents.textus: 60. Kuyo i+saʕaye traḥṣar dəblalyo, u+mērk̇o komər, ‘Žənk̇e, žənk̇e!’ Kəmmo, ‘Mənyo?’ Komər, ‘Qum, mahəzmina me qmu+Quz̥ko!’
contents.versio: 60. It’s midnight (lit. ‘the hour is becoming twelve of in the night’), the husband says, ‘Wife, wife!’ She says, ‘What is it?’ He says, ‘Get up, let us run away from Marty!’

contents.textus: 61. Komaḥat i+xurǧazine ʕal katfa di+aṯto, yaqúrtoyo. (E, u+Quz̥ko xōrtyo, dəmmina, kibe xoṯi, xdu+Afrəm, xoṯux. Yaqúroyo, u+laḥmo latyo haqqa yaquro!)
contents.versio: 61. He puts the saddlebag on the woman’s shoulders, it’s heavy (right, Marty is a young man, let’s say, he’s built (lit. ‘there is in him’) like me, like Afrem, like you. He’s heavy, the bread isn’t so heavy!)

contents.textus: 62. Kəmmo, ‘Mērk̇o, qṭíluxli!’ Komar, ‘Maláx, d̥xulṣina me qume’.
contents.versio: 62. She says, ‘Husband, you are killing me!’ He says, ‘Get walking, so we escape from him’.

contents.textus: 63. Ánnaqla koṭuʕni u+Quz̥ko. U+laḥmo komaxlele, kosāmle nadyā́r, tarte+ṭalme komaḥat ʕal qarʕe. Dəmmina, markeee kuzzé tart‿tlaṯ+qəryawoṯe, koroḥaq. Kuzzə́n ləqriṯo.
contents.versio: 63. Now then, they are carrying Marty. The bread, he empties it, he makes it disappear, he puts two loaves above his head. Let’s say, from here, he is going through two–three villages, he is getting farther. They are going to a village.

contents.textus: 64. I+qriṯàyosi, mək‿kosaymi? Koṯalle ḥamš‿što+kalbe. Ánnaqla simənne ġắlăbe šapərzá.
contents.versio: 64. So this village, what do they do? Five–six dogs come to them. Now then, they made them very miserable.

contents.textus: 65. Hánosti, mək‿kosaymi? Komər, ‘Aaax, aaax uʕdo d̥owewa u+Quz̥ko harke! G̊folatwa bəṯr aq+qa+kalbani’. Omər, ‘ʕAmmo!’ Omər, ‘kAz čaʕve ṫáma,k kalí!’
contents.versio: 65. So this one, what do they do? He says, ‘Ah, ah, if only Marty were here now! He would chase after so many of these dogs!’ He says, ‘Uncle!’ He says, ‘kI am with youk (lit. ‘I am your eye’), here I am!’

contents.textus: 66. Naḥət, ŭ mlele qəm ṣadre kefe, ŭ rahəṭ lak+kalbe. I+aṯto kəmmo, ‘Lo mə́ḷḷilux, əmmono, u+qa+yuqrano latyo laḥmo, ŭ ḥur, nafəq hiye’.
contents.versio: 66. He came down, filled up stones against his chest, and ran to the dogs. The woman says, ‘Didn’t I tell you, I say, so much of this heaviness isn’t bread, and look, it turned out it’s him!’

contents.textus: 67. ‘E, ba ánnaqla məs‿saymina?’ Əmmo, ‘Ăḷo, haw kiban aʕle’. Omər, ‘Naysa’.
contents.versio: 67. ‘Yes, now then, what do we do?’ She says, ‘Gosh, we can’t prevail over him anymore’. He says, ‘Anyhow’.

contents.textus: 68. Mtahtahle ak+kalbe, azzənne ŭ malaxxe tavda. Árbʕone. Hiye ḥayo ŭ u+zlām, dmore du+bayto, ŭ i+aṯto ŭ i+barṯo.
contents.versio: 68. He dispersed the dogs, they went and walked together. The four of them. He is one, and the man, so the homeowner, the woman, and the daughter.

contents.textus: 69. Azzənne u+yawmawo, malaxxe hul ʕaṣriye. Bəṯr məd malaxxe, hánosti koqoyəm, komoṭən lmaye ʕamuqe, dəmmina, baḥar.
contents.versio: 69. They went that day, they walked until the evening. After they walked, so that one gets up, they reach deep water, let’s say, a sea.

contents.textus: 70. Mə́ḷḷela li+aṯto (disa komaṣəṯ aʕle). Omər, ‘Kuḏʕat?’ Əmmo, ‘Mənyo?’ Omər, ‘Hak̇a kətlan at+tarte+ṭalmanək, gmaḥəšmina tavda ŭ gdəmxina qmam+mayani.
contents.versio: 70. He said to the woman (he’s listening to him again). He says, ‘You know what?’ She says, ‘What is it?’ He says, ‘Since we have these two loaves, let’s dine together and sleep by these waters’.

contents.textus: 71. Məd̥ hawi lalyo, gəzzano, gmaḥəsnax’, mə́ḷḷela li+aṯto, ‘Məd daməx, ono gmādno liḏoṯe ŭ hat məd lraġloṯe, gəmḥalqínane lam+maye’. Əmmo, ‘Ăḷo haṯe mede ṭáwoyo’.
contents.versio: 71. After it becomes night, we’ll go, I’ll wake you up’, he told the woman, ‘After he falls asleep, I will take his arms and you take his legs, and we’ll toss him (lit. ‘them’) into the water’. She says, ‘Gosh, this is a good thing’.

contents.textus: 72. Maṭən lam+maye, am+maye ʕamúqene, báḥaryo, ŭ maḥatte tamo. Kətte tarte+ṭalme dlaḥmo, xilənne, maḥšamme.
contents.versio: 72. They reached the water, the water is deep, it’s a sea, and they got down there. They have two loaves of bread, they ate them, they had dinner.

contents.textus: 73. Ŭ ṭábiki nvine mede layt aʕmayye, qmu+baḥar damixi. Hawi falge dlalyo. E, u+k̇urk̇o žīrwa: bari məd̥‿saymi i+ḥarakayo, u+k̇urk̇o maqəmle i+žənk̇e. Lályowa, ʕútmawa, ǧayrane, xud uʕdo, latwa.
contents.versio: 73. And, of course, they did not have any kind of beds with them, they slept by the sea. It became midnight. Right, and the boy was clever: before they made this move, the boy made the wife get up. It was night, it was dark, there wasn’t, like now, any electricity.

contents.textus: 74. Omər, ‘Žənk̇e, žənk̇e!’ Əmmo, ‘Mənyo?’ Omər, ‘Qum mḥalqina u+Quz̥ko lam+maye’. Ánnaqla u+Quz̥ko komaḷḷa li+ṗire du+zlām).
contents.versio: 74. He said, ‘Wife, wife!’ She said, ‘What is it?’ He said, ‘Get up, let’s toss Marty into the water’. now then, Marty says this to the man’s wife.

contents.textus: 75. Ínaqla d̥komaydi lu+zlām, komər, ‘Žənnək̇e, ónono, u+zlamàyḏaxno!’ Komər, ‘Lo!’ Komər, ‘Mḥaláq, mḥaláq! Dlo+mḥalqat, gˠqoṭaṇṇax!’. Komḥalqo u+zlām druḥa aʕme, háwosi, lam+maye, koməḥnəq.
contents.versio: 75. When they grab the man, he says, ‘Wife, it’s me, I’m your husband!’ He says, ‘No!’ He says, ‘Toss him, toss him! If you don’t toss him, I’ll kill you!’ So she tosses her own man with him, that one too, into the water, he drowns.

contents.textus: 76. Kofayšo i+žənk̇e, ŭ i+barṯo. I+žənk̇e kəmmo, ‘Mə‿g̊saymat eban?’ Komər, ‘Ánnaqla mḥalequ bəṯri, aṣəl ónono’. Komḥalqi bəṯre, komadʕarre su+ʕammo druḥe, su+ʕammo druḥe.
contents.versio: 76. The wife remains, and the daughter. The wife says, ‘What will you do with us?’ He says, ‘Now follow me, I’m the one who is the real deal’. They follow him, he brings them back to his own uncle, to his own uncle.

contents.textus: 77. Ínaqla d̥komadʕarre su+ʕammo druḥe, komoḥe ʕal u+tarʕo. Ínaqla d̥komaḥət ʕayno ʕal u+brazi druḥe, azzé mətro aʕle maʕ+ʕəšqat.
contents.versio: 77. When he brings them back to his own uncle, he knocks on the door. When he sets eyes (lit. ‘he puts an eye’) on his own nephew, he is on cloud nine (lit. ‘a meter went on him out of passions’).

contents.textus: 78. Azzə́n lfoṯe dəḥḏoḏe, flān, yatiwi, harke ŭ tamhok̇é. Omər, ‘Hani mánnani?’ Omər, ‘Kuḏʕat, mánnani?’ Omər, ‘E?’ Omər, ‘Hani, hawino greʕo lbayto ŭ nafəqno bi+ṣəfənk̇e d̥kulle, haṯe i+barṯoyo ŭ haṯe i+emo. Emo ŭ bárṯone.
contents.versio: 78. They went to face each other, and so on, they sat down, here and over there. He says, ‘Who are these ones?’ He says, ‘Do you know who these ones are?’ He says, ‘Yes?’ He says, ‘These ones, I became a servant in one house and swept the floor with them (lit. ‘I came out with the broom of them all’), this is the daughter and this is the mother. They are mother and daughter’.

contents.textus: 79. I+ṗire du+bayto laǧanux, ŭ i+barṯo laǧani. Hani haw gˠquṭlinanne, ṭrofayši bu+bayto.
contents.versio: 79. ‘The woman of the house is for you, and the daughter is for me. These ones we won’t kill anymore, let them remain in the house’.

contents.textus: 80. Ánnaqla, xe meqəm, ono ŭ hat gəmdawmina. Gəzzán lu+nečirayḏan, ŭ hənnək g̊saymi u+muklayḏan, u+štoyayḏan, ŭ bu+šəklano’. Omər, ‘Mo+kore ʕomər baytux’. Nšəqle ʕayne du+brazi druḥe ŭ mdawamme u+nečiraṯṯe. Ṫə žmə́ra sāġ. (Afrem: Tə saġtə́r!)
contents.versio: 80. ‘Now then, like before, you and I are going to keep going. We will go hunting, and they will make our food, our drinks, and that sort of thing (lit. ‘in this manner’)’. He says, ‘A hundred times, thank you (lit. ‘may he build your house’)!’ He kissed his own nephew’s eyes and they continued their hunt. God bless you! (Afrem: You as well!)

contents.textus: 1. Kətwa ŭ latwa, ṭaw̃ m Aloho latwa. (Ḥaq!) I+čirok̇aṯe d̥ Xaláf Aġayo, gdománanxuyo.
contents.versio: 1. Maybe it happened, maybe it didn’t (lit. ‘there was and there wasn’t’), there was none greater than God. Truth! This story is about Halaf Agha, I shall tell it to you.

contents.textus: 2. Xaláf Aġá, dəmmina, u+rabo di+barriye d̥ Súriyawa.
contents.versio: 2. Halaf Agha, let’s say, was the leader of the Syrian plain.

contents.textus: 3. Ani, xud dəmmat, hánosi rabo man d̥ Súriyawa. (AA: Aġawa.) Aġawa.
contents.versio: 3. Like, like you’d say, now this one was one of the chiefs of Syria. (AA: He was an agha.) He was an agha.

contents.textus: 4. I+barriye d̥ Xaláf Aġá kula díḏewa. Xud dəmmat, falga d̥ Súriya taḥt u+k̇ontrolàyḏewa.
contents.versio: 4. The whole plains of Halaf Agha belonged to him. Like you’d say, half of Syria was under his control.

contents.textus: 5. Hánosi kə́twayle ṗire, latwa ṭawto.
contents.versio: 5. As for this one, he had a wife, she wasn’t a good woman.

contents.textus: 6. Omər, ‘Gnoḥaṇṇo, gəzzí mu+băladayḏi, noḥatno, gəzzino lbălā́d ḥreno. Ḥozina, mək‿kīt, məl‿layt!’
contents.versio: 6. He says, ‘I shall go down, I’ll go from my country, let me go down, I’ll go to another country. Let’s see what there is and isn’t!’

contents.textus: 7. Axər, harke ŭ tamhok̇é, hánosi kuzzé, konoḥət mu+aṯrayḏe, konoḥət, kuzzé lwaṯro ḥreno.
contents.versio: 7. Finally, here and over there (i.e., some time passed), as for this one, he goes, he goes down from his land, he goes down and goes to another land.

contents.textus: 8. Kuzzé lwaṯro ḥreno. Tamo, tamo, ánnaqla bu+aṯrawo kofṓš.
contents.versio: 8. He goes to another land. There, there, now then, he stays in that land.

contents.textus: 9. Ŭ kofoyəš bu+aṯrawo, kuzzé ldukṯo, dəmmina, kuzzé taḥte k̇one daʕ+ʕarab.
contents.versio: 9. And he stays in that land, he goes to a place, let’s say, he goes within (lit. under) the tent of the Arabs.

contents.textus: 10. Kuzzé taḥte k̇one mani dak̇+k̇očàr, dam+medone, balki kuḏʕutu, d̥kosaymi săwā́l, medone, harke ŭ tamhok̇é.
contents.versio: 10. He goes within one of those nomad tents, of the things, maybe you know, those who deal with livestock, things, here and over there (i.e., some time passed).

contents.textus: 11. Kofṓš tamo. Harke ŭ tamhok̇é, kosaymi... kofṓš tamo … kuzzé koṯe … korowax ʕal səsyo ŭ kuzzé, ŭ koṯe talgo ġắlăbe aʕle.
contents.versio: 11. He stays there. Here and over there (i.e., some time passed), they deal... he stays there, he goes back and forth, he gets on a horse and sets off, and a lot of snow falls (lit. ‘comes’) on him.

contents.textus: 12. (AA: Yawmo du+tàlgowa.) E, bu+zamā̀n du+talgo, sáṯwowa. Ŭ ad+darbe mṣakri me qume.
contents.versio: 12. (AA: It was a snow day.) Yes, in the season of snow, it was winter. And the roads disappeared from before him.
