contents.textus: 009. Naqqa koviye komáhəzmo mbayn i+ṭalane, koʕurqo máhəzmo. Aḥna kəmmina ‘koʕurqo’ hatu kəmmutu ‘máhəzmo’. Axər, mahzamla mbayn i+ṭalane.
contents.versio: 009. Once a wild nanny goat was escaping out of the thicket, it was fleeing, escaping. We say ‘she flees’, you say ‘she escapes’. Finally, it escaped through the thicket.

contents.textus: 010. Kuzzeyo, ga kal kīt zʕuro! Kalkawi barmə́lk̇, hawxa kəmfaraǧ ʕal ap+pallat, i+hawa komǝḥyo ʕal ap+pallat di+dawmo, kəmfaraǧ hawxa məfṣəḥ appe, məštaʕe aʕmayye. Iḏoṯe nafiqi mbayn ap+pačk̇at; he raġloṯe kanné bayn ap+pačk̇at.
contents.versio: 010. He goes, look, there’s a baby here!  Here he’s become an infant, he is looking at the leaves like so, the wind beats against the leaves of the tree, he is looking like so, he is happy with them, he is playing with them. His hands went out from the swaddling clothes; his legs are still there within the swaddling clothes.

contents.textus: 011. Ánnaqqa ba u+zlām hăma ṭrele maq+qanyonayḏe, mədle li+pečak̇e ŭ rahəṭ lu+bayto. ‘Žənk̇e, žənk̇e, komṭeli u+abrayḏax.’
contents.versio: 011. Now then, didn’t the man then leave his cattle, he took the bundle and ran home. ‘Wife, wife! I have brought your son’.

contents.textus: 012. Əmmo, ‘Ooo, u+abrayḏi, áykoyo u+rabbano, u+abrayḏi?’ ‘Kalé kalé!’  Kəmmo, ‘Ooo rabbano, u+abrayḏi kə́pwayle haqqa, kálkawi hano mášaḷḷa xortyo!’
contents.versio: 012. She says, ‘Ooo, my son, where is he, the poor thing, my son?’ ‘He’s here, he’s here!’ She says, ‘Ooo, poor thing, my son was yea large, here this one’s become a young boy, amazing (lit. ‘mashallah’)!’

contents.textus: 013. Omar, ‘De ḥur baǧ+ǧulayḏi!’ Koḥayro, kəmmo, ‘Ăḷa ak+kənǧ̊k̇àyḏine, aǧ+ǧəlk̇àyḏine’. Omar, ‘Rabbane, i+ʕezo+koviye mamṣówayle, hawi rabī́ṭ, maqbele, i+ʕezo+koviye maməṣla, maynaqla, ŭ hawi barmə́lk̇’. Ánnaqqa maḥatte əšme Kovi, Kovi, u+Kovi, u+Kovi. Azzé quryole i+emo Kovi, u+Kovi.
contents.versio: 013. He says, ‘Come on, look at my (i.e., his) clothes!’ She looks, she says, ‘Gosh, these are my articles of clothing, these are my fabrics’. He says, ‘Poor thing, the wild nanny goat would suckle him, he became a toddler, he has flourished,  the wild nanny goat suckled him, she nursed him from her teat, and he became an infant’. Then they gave him the name a billy goat, a billy goat, Billy, Billy. The mother went and called him a billy goat, Billy.

contents.textus: 014. Lu+šulṭono hawile zan. Koqorǝn li+emo d… li+emayḏe, komar, ‘Žənk̇e, mǝn i+măsalayḏax, mənyo? Kəmmatle lu+abrayḏax Kovi...’  Kəmmo ḥāl ŭ mắsala, ‘Ašə́r l Ăḷo hule, damixono, qayimono, ga, lo+abro ŭ lo+mede! Kuzzé hak̇a yarḥo hak̇a tre, kuzzé u+baqoro, ga kalkó i+ʕezo+koviye máhəzmo mbayn i+ṭalane, ŭ koḥayrina… koṯe koḥōr, ga kalé u+zʕurayḏan! Mṭele lu+bayto, kalkawən aq+qeprayḏe ha hawxa’.
contents.versio: 014. The Sultan had a supposition. They summon the mother of… his mother, he says, ‘Woman, what’s your problem, what is it? You call your son a billy goat…’ She says what happened (lit. ‘the state and the situation’), ‘Really, God gave him, I was asleep, I got up, look, no son or anything! Either a month or two passes, the cowherd goes, look, a nanny goat escapes out of the thicket, and we see… he comes, he sees, look, here’s our child! He brought him home, here his limbs had become just like so’.

contents.textus: 015. Fahəm, omar, ‘Uʕdo lə+gbàtliyo, sōmne greʕo? Hăma g̊sōm k̇elik̇at ʕal iḏi. Kəmmutu Kovi, Kovi, xile u+ḥalwo dak+koviyat, čalangyo žeháṫiyo, g̊sōm k̇elik̇at ʕal iḏi. Faqírehatu, gdobénanxu kallawat.’
contents.versio: 015. He understood, he says, ‘Now won’t you give him to me, I’ll make him a servant? Well, he will do chores for me (lit. ‘on my hand’). You say a billy goat, a billy goat, he ate the milk of nanny goats, he is quick, he is diligent, he will do chores for me. You are poor people, I’ll give you money’.

contents.textus: 016. Əmmo, ‘Ăḷa, komilaʕina!’ Ánnaqqa səmla greʕo šan u+šulṭono, səmla greʕo šan u+šulṭono, ‘ha Kovi hawxa, ŭ ha Kovi hawxa, ŭ ha Kovi hawxa, ŭ ha Kovi hawxa’, kosōm k̇elik̇at ʕal iḏayye, kosōm k̇elik̇at ʕal iḏayye, hul‿u+yawmo di+məštuṯo.
contents.versio: 016. She says, ‘Gosh, we are begging (for it)!’ Now then, she made him a servant for the sultan, she made him a servant for the sultan, ‘Just like so Billy, and just like so Billy, and just like so Billy, and just like so Billy’, he does chores for them (lit. ‘on their hand’), he does chores for them, until the wedding day.

contents.textus: 017. U+yawmo di+məštuṯo komarle, komar, ‘Kovi, izzúx li+bax…’  Komarle lu+ǧanono di+baxča, ‘Oṯe u+abrayḏi―šlaḥ qarʕe. U+abrayḏi buxwa doṯe―šlaḥ qarʕe’. Komar, ‘Tamā́m. Elux mʔamallux’. Qām hedik̇a kuzzeyo, kobe čalṭa biḏe du+Kovi, komar, ‘Zux mṭilan fire, medone mi+baxča’.
contents.versio: 017. On the wedding day, he says to him, he says, ‘Billy, go to the gard…’ He says to the groundskeeper (lit. ‘the gardener of the garden’), ‘My son comes along―cut off his head! If my son himself comes along―cut off his head!’ He says, ‘OK! It was you yourself who ordered it!’ Then he up and goes discreetly, he puts (lit. ‘gives’) a bag in Billy’s hand, he says, ‘Go, bring us fruits, things from the garden’.

contents.textus: 018. U+zʕùroste, Aloho komaṭʕele. Kuzzé bayn an+naʕime məštaʕe. Kuzzé bayn an+naʕime koməštaʕe, ŭ axər bu+qadr ŭ bi+maʕrifa məštaʕe ʕam an+naʕime. Wáxtak̇e kuzzeyo, u+abro du+šulṭono kuzzé koḥoyar, kuzzeyo―u+ǧanono košolaḥ qarʕe.
contents.versio: 018. So the boy, God makes him forget. He goes among the children to play. He goes among the children, he plays, and after with all due respect (lit. ‘with power and recognition’) he plays with the children. A certain time passes, the sultan’s son goes, he sees, he goes―the gardener cuts off his head.

contents.textus: 019. U+ǧanono košolaḥ qarʕe. Kuzzeyo zamának̇e, naqqa u+zʕuro koṯe lbole. De lo mu+hno d Alóhoyo?! Kəmmi, Kčalk̇á xayə́na žə paḥnəyá wáya’.K Mede dlo m Aloho lo+kowe!
contents.versio: 019. The gardener cuts off his head. A certain time passes, at once the boy remembers it (lit. ‘it comes to his mind’). Well, isn’t it from God’s whatsit?!  They say (in Kurdish), ‘they are hoisted by their own petard’. Nothing happens except from God (lit. ‘a thing that isn’t from God doesn’t happen’)!

contents.textus: 020. Ăḷa, aṯi lbole, ‘Hak̇, Ăḷa, lu+šulṭono mtaráswayleli li+baxča!’ Kuzzé hedik̇a komole i+čalṭayḏe fire ŭ medone di+baxča, ŭ kəm… mbele, maḥatte qmu+šulṭono.
contents.versio: 020. Gosh, he remembered, ‘Oh! Gosh, the Sultan had sent me to the garden!’ Then he goes discreetly, he fills his bag with fruits and garden things, and he … he brings it, he puts them in front of the sultan.

contents.textus: 021. ‘Hak̇, hul uʕdo áykowayt, laṯat?’ Omar, ‘Ašə́r azzíwayno, ṭaʕíwayno ruḥi, azzí bayn an+naʕime, məštaʕeli, uʕdo aṯyo lboli’. Kuzzé koḥōr kalé u+abro, qṭíloyo.
contents.versio: 021. ‘Oh, where have you been until now, didn’t you come?’ He says, ‘Really, I was going, I forgot myself, I went among the children, I played, now I remembered it’. He goes, he looks, here’s his son, he has been killed.

contents.textus: 022. Háyoste hawxa šamiʕalla, hak̇a šrolo hak̇a štaġaliye hawxa, hawxa šamiʕalla háyoste.
contents.versio: 022. So that one, I heard it like so, whether it’s the truth or such chatter, I heard it like so, that one too.

contents.textus: 023. I. E, u+abro qṭīl, ánnaqqa u+zʕuro?
contents.versio: 023. Yes, his son was killed, now then, the boy?

contents.textus: 024. N. U+zʕuro hawyo i+k̇ačk̇e šane.
contents.versio: 024. As for the boy, the girl became his.

contents.textus: 025. I. E, mdawam! Kamilo?
contents.versio: 025. Right, continue! Is it done?

contents.textus: 026. N. Kamilo, haw kuḏʕalla, i+k̇ačk̇e fayišo šane.
contents.versio: 026. It is done, I don’t know it anymore, the girl stayed his.

contents.textus: 001. Nisane: E, gdəmmono ánnaqqa ʕal i+ġala, ʕal u+kafno. E, u+kafno, meqəm ġálawa, ǧala, i+ġala+ḥarayto koṯe lboli. Əzzáwayna lu+Čōl, laq+qălačani ḥeḏər Mārbobo. Əzzáwayna, ḥoṯi... əəə ... babi ḥoṣadwa – miḥaṣən miṯayxu, ăḷo mḥasalle – ŭ ḥoṯi maydowa šəble ŭ luqṭowa. Ono ḥamməš+šnaye, emi mayiṯo. Fayišono yatəmto, qašti sə́mlalan more.
contents.versio: 001. Yes, I’ll talk about the Famine, about the hunger. Yes, the hunger, formerly it was a famine, a famine, I remember the last famine. We used to go to the Lowlands, to the slopes around Mārbobo. We used to go, my sister… uh… my father used to harvest—Let your dead ones be blessed, may God bless them!—and my sister picked and gleaned wheat spikes. My mother died when I was five. I stayed an orphan. My grandmother took care of us.

contents.textus: 002. Arbʕo+aḥunone ŭ tarte+ḥwòṯewayna. U+naʕimo tloṯo+yarḥe, ŭ mayiṯo emi, mḥasyo. H̱oṯi makərxówayle. I+naqqayo mammək̇at ŭ ḥalwo di+ḥkume, medone latwa, makərxówayle ʕal aṗ+ṗirat. Aṗ+ṗirat d̥kə́twalle dargəšyoṯe, mamṣə́nwayle. Mkamele tarte+šnaye, d̥owutu sāġ, hule aḥ+ḥaye laḥ+ḥaḏire! Háwoste bi+ḥazbe, ṣohrək̇at kəmmina ḥazbe, háwoste māṯ. Fayišina tloṯo+aḥunone ŭ tarte+ḥwoṯe.
contents.versio: 002. We were four brothers and two sisters. The youngest was three months old and my mother died, she passed away. My sister carried him around. At that time, baby bottles and powdered milk, there weren’t such things, she carried him around to the women. The women who had cradles suckled him. He became two years old, God bless you, he gave up the ghost! This one too, from measles, we call rubeola measles, this one also died. We three brothers and two sisters survived.

contents.textus: 003. Ánnaqqa lu+qamṣo tarte+tlaṯ+šnaye xile u+zād, i+raqqək̇e ŭ u+qamṣo. U+ʕamo hawi šăpərzá. Əzzáwayna, xŭd wáxtak̇e əzzənwa l Almanya, əzzáwayna lu+Čōl, əzzənwa lu+Čōl, l Mārbobo, nuḥtiwa l Súriya. Ma u+ahl d̥ Súriya kule me Tərkíyayo!? Kulle ʕIwardnoye, Arboye, Əḥwoye, Qusnoye, Kfarzoye, ḥaḥoye, kulle u+ahl d̥árkeyo! Azzə́n fayiši bač+čolanək.
contents.versio: 003. Now then, the locust ate up the grain for a few years, the sunn pest, and the locust. The people became destitute. We used to go, like once they used to go to Germany, we used to go to the Lowlands, to Mārbobo, we went down to Syria. Is everyone in Syria from Turkey!? All the ʕIwardians, Mārbobians, Əḥwians, Beqŭsyonians, Kfarzeans, Ḥāḥians, all of them are people from here. They went to stay in those lowlands.

contents.textus: 004. Veǧa, əzzənwa, babi ḥoṣadwa, ŭ ḥoṯi mnaqyowa hawxa šəble. Maltmowa hoool ʕaṣriye. Saymówalle boqoṯe hawxa, ŭ maltmowa. Kətwa lavlavk̇e ba+frezanək, may+yarixanək d̥kuzzá hawxa. Layfowa aʕlayye, saymówalle. ʕAṣriye məḥyówalle b̥ḥaṣa, bi+ṗəštiye mṭówalle, maḥtówalle b̥k̇aviye dadro manək dam+mārbabiye, hoool dmkamalwa u+ḥṣodo. Babi kəmmono b̥kallawat ḥoṣadwa. Hedik̇a gədmdaqəd̥qowa aš+šəblanək, mdaríwaynanne, howənwa ṭaʕno, əmṭíwaynanne lal+labaniyat.
contents.versio: 004. Then, they used to go, my father harvested, and my sister picked spikes like so. She used to go gathering until the evening. She made them into sheaves like so, and she gathered them. There was a bindweed in those stubble fields, one of those long ones, one that goes like so. She wrapped it around them, she made them. In the evening she put them on her back, she brought them in a bundle, she put them into a corner of one of those threshing floors of the Mārbobians, until he finished harvesting. I would say my father harvested for money. Then he pounded those spikes, and we winnowed them, it became a load, we brought them for yogurt cream.

contents.textus: 005. Aḥna harke, šəlḥíwayna baluṭe. Baluṭe, kuḏʕat mənne, ab+baluṭe? Bad+dàwmene. Əmṭíwaynanne, šəlqíwaynanne ŭ məsqíwaynanne li+goro. Mən‿nəšfiwa gəmṭíwaynanne, tawríwayna xud al+luze d̥kosaymínanne uʕdo ʕoliqe. Tawríwaynanne, disa ṣaṭfe gməsqíwaynanne li+goro.  Mən‿našifiwa, g̥̊ḥurkíwaynanne bu+ḥurako, ŭ ṭowo dhowənwa, ŭ layšiwa, maḥtiwa haqqa d̥qamḥo da+sʕore baynaṯṯe, ŭ saymíwayle laḥmo (laḥmo latwa, qamḥo latwa!). E, ăḷo u+laḥmaṯṯe … u+qamḥaṯṯe basímowa, elo u+laḥmaṯṯe ġắlăbe náxwašwa. Xili laḥmo dab+baluṭe, xili di+ṭolək̇e, xili du+ǧaǧəq, xilan ṣawmo+rabo, ŭ xilan du+ṭamṭam, d̥kowe bu+ṭuro, qmaq+qunk̇at dad+dawme. Hawo, ṭaʕme basímowa. ŭ xilan răzala ġắlăbe.
contents.versio: 005. Here, we used to pick acorns. Acorns, do you know what acorns are? They are on trees. We brought them back, boiled them, and brought them up to the roof. When they dried, we brought them back, crushed them like the almonds we now use to make walnut rope. We crushed them and once again brought pieces up to the roof. When they dried, we ground them with a grinding stone, and so they became fine [flour], and they kneaded it, put so much barley flour in them, and made bread with it (there wasn’t any bread, there wasn’t any flour!). Yes, gosh, their bread … their flour was pleasant [to make], but their bread was very bad. I ate acorn bread, I ate mallow bread, I ate cacık [bread], we ate during our Lenten fast, and we ate mullein bread, which grows in the hill country, by tree stumps. As for that one, its taste was pleasant. And we ate a lot of crow.

contents.textus: 006. Ilyas: I+ǧaǧəq mənyo?
contents.versio: 006. I. What is cacık?

contents.textus: 007. N. ǧaǧəq, hano d̥komšaḥni ad+dawġe, maḥtile bu+kiso. Uʕdo, komaḥti gweto bu+kiso. Kəmšaḥnina ad+dawġe. Mayʕina u+qaṭiro, saymínanne, dawġe. Ad+dawġanək gəmšaḥnínanne ŭ maḥtíwayna u+ǧaǧqawo bu+kiso, xud uʕdo d̥komaḥtina i+gweto bu+kiso, ŭ ʕəsrínanne, hul dnəšfo. Edi, uʕdo kosaymínala šərṫān.
contents.versio: 007. N. Cacık, that one, when they heat up buttermilk and put it into the pouch. Nowadays they put cheese into the pouch. We heat up buttermilk. We churn yogurt, we make it, buttermilk. This buttermilk, we boiled it and we used to put that cacık into the pouch, like now when we put cheese into the pouch, and squeeze it, until it becomes dry. Thereupon we make it into kashk patties.

contents.textus: 008. I. Bas áydarbo howewa laḥmo mayo?
contents.versio: 008. I. But how would bread have come from it?

contents.textus: 009. N. E, ánnaqqa maḥtíwayna qamḥo, gelone, ṭolək̇e, medone baynaṯṯe, ŭ ləzqówayle qašti bu+tanuro.
contents.versio: 009. N. Yes, now then, we used to put flour, herbs, mallow, some (other) things among them, and my grandmother used to stuck it to the oven.

contents.textus: 010. I. Fahəmno.
contents.versio: 010. I. I understand.

contents.textus: 011. N. E, ʕiš du+kàfnowa.
contents.versio: 011. N. Yes, it was a labour of hunger.

contents.textus: 012. N. E, hawxa səmlan, răzala hawxa xilan, mašraṭ. Naqqa, aḥuni naʕímowa―gdəmmono kula, latyo ʕaybo ŭ latyo k̇emayiye, azzeyo―məd̥‿tolewa ... Aḥuni ánnaqqa hawo, māṯ u+naʕimo, drab mine, híyeste čúčk̇owa. Ha hawxa, məd̥‿ torewa u+dexono, əzzewa ʕal at+tanure, kafínowa. Káfnowa. Ánnaqqa d̥saymiwa u+laḥmo, obə́nwayle ha haqqa. Oṯewa, qašti fəlġówayle kul+ḥa haqqa aʕlayna. Uxlíwayna, ŭ aḥuni, əzzənwa, əmmiwa k‘Golək̇ván!’k Əzzənwa qmann+arwonk̇at du+ḥalwo b̚ Mārbobo, ḥa mənne, ŭ ḥa mənne howewa ʕam u+baqoro əmmíwayle Mahmado. Kə́twalxu hátuste Kfarzoye tamo... Use, əmmíwayle Use, Use, ŭ Farida. ŭ hánəkstene Kfarzóyewayne, kuḏʕono. Hăma am+Mārbabiye falgayye Kfarzóyene. U+babo du+məlfonano, məlfono ʕIsa, d̥kətyo b̚ Mar Gawriye, híyeste Kfarzóyoyo, Muqsi ḥanno. Be Gabre Kfarzóyewayne.
contents.versio: 012. N. Yes, we did so, so we ate crow, believe it or not. Once, my brother was a child―I will say everything, there isn’t any shame, there isn’t anything wrong with it, it’s over―when it would go up … My brother, now then, that one who was older than the baby who died, he was also little. Just like so, whenever the smoke would go up, he would go to the ovens, he was hungry. It was a famine. Now then, when they would make bread, they would give him so much. He would come back, my grandmother would divide it up, so much for each of us. We would eat it, and my brother, they would go, they would say, ‘Calf herder!’ They would go in front of the suckling calves in Mārbobo, one of them, and the other one would be with the cattle herder whose name was Mahmado. You also had you Kfarzeans there… Use, his name was Use, Use, and Farida. Those were also Kfarzeans, I know. But the Mārbobians, half of them are Kfarzeans. The father of that teacher, ʕIsa the teacher, who is at Mor Gabriel, he is also a Kfarzean, Ḥanno Muqsi. The Gabre family were Kfarzeans.

contents.textus: 013. Hawxa l Aloho hawxa səmle hul dwáxtak̇e: bu+qayṭo oṯíwayna ʕal aʕ+ʕənwe l Bequsyone, ŭ bu+saṯwo əzzáwayna. Babi howewa mrebá, dowarwa b̥ḥaq, dowarwa b̥sahmo, b̚mən? Be u+mrebà mənwa? Howewa mreba, hawi l Rašid dbe Kele, hawi l Zahre i+emo d̥ ḥanno, d Muqsi ḥanno, dowarwa, əzzewa lu+šuġlo, əzzewa lu+šuġlo.
contents.versio: 013. So God made things like so, until a little while later: in the summer we would come back to Bequsyone for grapes, and in the winter we would go back. My father used to be a sharecropper, he would farm for a salary, he would farm for a share, for what? What was the sharecropper? He used to be a sharecropper, he was Rašid Kele’s, he was Zahre’s, the mother of Ḥanno, Ḥanno Muqsi, he would farm, he would go to work, he would go to work.

contents.textus: 014. I. Mreba mən-yo?
contents.versio: 014. I. What is a sharecropper?

contents.textus: 015. N. Mreba dowarwa, dowarwa, edi be áydarbo, lo+bḥaq dowarwa, b̥sahmo dowarwa, be áydarbo – lo+kuḏʕono. Dowarwa baq+qanyonaṯṯe hăma hiye dowarwa baq+qanyonaṯṯe. Xud duʕdo dəmmat, ṣaydatlux greʕo, lo+saymat šuġlo, masimat u+šuġlo ebe, hawxa. Əzzewa li+Qaməšlo, kə́twayle barṯo dʕammo bi+Qaməšlok̇e, əzzewa lu+šuġlo ltámoste. Axər l ăḷo hawxa səmle, aṯina edi waxt daʕ+ʕənwe, oṯíwayna ʕal riše daʕ+ʕənwayḏan lak+karmayḏan. L ăḷo hawxa səmle, hak̇a əšmo hak̇a ġắlăbe. Tlaṯ, arbaʕ, ḥamməš, šeṯ+šnaye aṯina li+qriṯo, aṯina li+qriṯo, babi dowarwa.
contents.versio: 015. N. A sharecropper would farm, he would farm, but how, whether he would farm for a salary, he would farm for a share, how, I don’t know. He would plough with their oxen, yeah, he would plough with their oxen. Like you now say, you get yourself an employee, you don’t do the work, you make him do the work, like so. He would go to Qamishli, he had a cousin in Qamishli, he would go there for work as well. Finally, God made things like so, we came then at the time of the grapes, we would come to our grapes, to our vineyards. God made things like so, either a little bit or a lot. Three, four, five, six years we came back to the village, we came back to the village, my father would farm.

contents.textus: 016. I. Bəṯr məd̥‿fayito i+ġala kmaḥwe.
contents.versio: 016. I.: After the Famine was over, it seems.

contents.textus: 017. N. E, aṯyo ... aṯi li+qriṯo, babi dowarwa. Kə́twayle tre+aḥunone qəfərkoliye, ḥəfriwa bu+nargo, quṭliwa u+gelo. Ma qăfare lə+ḥzelux dwərre baq+qanyone? Hawxa, ŭ u+zadayḏan howewa. ŭ u+naʕimo howewa qmaʕ+ʕeze. E, mašraṭ, edi sawiʕina. Ŭ babi lə+mṭele niše, babi lə+mṭele žənbave ʕal rišan. Fayišo ḥoṯi, hul dhawyo rab̥ṯo, k̇avnaxooort, səmla zəd me ḥamməš ŭ tleṯi+šnaye, lam+mene ḥewore mḥalaqqe lqarʕa, líwole. Səmme lo+səmme, əmmi, ‘Hawa bəḥḏo lruḥux!’ Omar, ‘Ono bəxwá lo+kəmṭ<eno>, ḥzeli u+dard di+žənbave’. Omar, ‘ăḷa, i+žənbavàyḏiste, ăḷa, ṭáwtowa, elo lo+kəmṭeno žənbave ʕal a+zʕurayḏi. B ăḷo doṯeno ga kal komṣaʕro lan+naʕime, li+emo dan+naʕime, g̊ˠqoṭanna. Hăma lo+kobaʕno niše’. Ánnaqqa hul dhawyo ḥoṯi rab̥ṯo.
contents.versio: 017. Yes, she ... he came to the village, my father would farm. He had two brothers, field clearers, they would dig with the pickaxe, they would kill weeds. Haven’t you seen a stony field that they ploughed with oxen? Like so, and our grain would appear. And the youngest would be in front of the goats. Yes, believe it or not, then we became satisfied. My father didn’t bring back any women; my father didn’t inflict a stepmother upon us (lit. ‘bring a stepmother upon our heads’). My sister stayed, until she became grown up, a spinster, she became older than thirty-five, white hairs struck her head, he didn’t give her up. They tried and tried, they said to him, “Exchange her for one for yourself!” He says, ‘I won’t bring one back for myself, I saw the pain of a stepmother’. He says, ‘Gosh, my stepmother was a good person, too, but I won’t bring back a stepmother for my children. By God, if I come and there she is, disparaging the children or the mother of the children, I will kill her. Anyway, I don’t want any women’. Now then, until my sister became an old maid.

contents.textus: 018. Kə́twaylan abrə‿dʕammo b̥ Surya. ʕAskar du+Farànsawa, du+Hənglīzwa. Aṯi mi+ʕaskariye, məḷḷe li+emo, omar, ‘Yade, ma i+barṯo dʕammi kofayšo?’ Omar ... əmmo, ‘E’. Bi+qrìṯowa hiya, ŭ hənnək láltaḥwa<yne>, Mulla ʕAbbas, bar+Ruṭa, ba+d̥koṯànəkwayne. Omar, ‘ṭlábliyo!’ L Aloho hawxa səmle, ṭlibole ŭ azzá ʕal u+naṣibayḏa.
contents.versio: 018. We had a cousin in Syria. He was a soldier of France, of England. He came back from the military and told his mother, saying, ‘Mommy, is my cousin available (lit. “does she remain [single]”)?’ He says ... she says, ‘Yes’. She was in the village, and they were down below, in Mŭlla ʕAbbas, in al-Ruṭa, in those places. He says, ‘Ask for her (hand) for me!’ God made things like so, he asked for her (hand), she went to her destiny.

contents.textus: 019. Hul dmaṭyono lu+šuġlo ... maṭyono lu+šuġlo ónostene. E, šoḏíwayna qəšto, ketono. Koṯe lboli qŭmā́š latwa, saymíwayna, əzzənwa a+zlamayḏan, aḥunoni ŭ babi, əzzənwa lu+čərrə̀k̇. Be edi lo+kuḏʕono lo ... kmo+kìlowat lmore du+ketono ŭ ḥa alle...
contents.versio: 019. Until I started working ... I started working, me too. Yes, we used to card with a bow, cotton. I remember, there wasn’t any cloth, we would make it, our men used to go, my brothers and my father, they used to go the gin. Then, don’t I know ... however many kilos went to the owner of the cotton and one to them…

contents.textus: 020. I. Čərrə́k̇ mənyo?
contents.versio: 020. What is a čərrə́k̇?

contents.textus: 021. N. U+čərrə̀k̇ du+dulabo ... dhawxa kosaymi ... ánnaqqa dammər dahino ŭ manduriye du+qayso. ʕAyn xud aṗ+ṗirani d̥komarqi u+laḥmo šk̇ăvá, ánnaqqa u+ketono maḥtíwayle tamo ŭ ʕuzliwa hawxa. U+ketono əzzewa ltamhó ŭ fayšiwa aḥ+ḥabbat harke xud aḥ+ḥəmse kome. Kmo+kìlowat lmore du+ketono ŭ kilo alle, əmṭənwa šawʕo+tmanyo+kìlowat. (07: 57)
contents.versio: 021. The roller gin… which they do like so… now then, an oiled iron rod and a wooden roller. Just like these women who flatten unleavened bread, now then, they put the cotton there and they would spin like so. The cotton would go over there and cotton seeds would stay here like black chickpeas. However many kilos for the cotton’s owner and one kilo for them, they brought back seven-eight kilos.

contents.textus: 022. Ánnaqqa aw+watre du+săwā̀l, am+maʕye, ḥăramani, da+Kfarzoye zawnə́nwanne, xurṭíwaynanne xurṭíwaynanne xurṭíwaynanne xurṭíwaynanne, hul dəzzənwa bu+xurmo du+mḥaṭo, di+msalle. ŭ saymíwaynanne də ṭa ŭ se ṭa ŭ bərmíwaynanne, mʕalqíwayna sapṯo harke ŭ ḥḏo harke, maḥtíwayna ʕoqəlyoṯe daḥ+ḥmore ŭ kefe ŭ medone, mʕalqíwayna appe dməmxən, dməmxən hul dnəšfi. Əmmíwayna watre.
contents.versio: 022. Now then, catgut, intestines, these godawful things, those that the Kfarzeans would buy, we would scrape, scrape, scrape, scrape them, until they would pass through the eye of a needle, of a packing needle. And we would make them double thread and triple thread, and twist them, we would hang up a hook here and one here, we would put donkey carrying frames and stones and some things, we would hang them on them so they would stretch, so they would stretch until they dry. We would call them catgut.

contents.textus: 023. I. E, bəṯr məd nəšfi, mə‿g̊d̥owən? Bəṯr məd nəšfi, mə‿g̊saymutu appe?
contents.versio: 023. Right, after they dry, what do they become? After they dry, what would you do with them?

contents.textus: 024. N. Ánnaqqa gdəmmallux. Ánnaqqa hanək ... Edi gduhníwaynanne, he ṭawo lo+našifi, b̥ṗāčk̇e ṭowo saymíwaynanne, xud u+məšḥo. G̊saymíwaynanne qəqlo. Ínaqqayo kə́twaylan qəšto, əmmiwa i+qəšto.
contents.versio: 024. Now then, I’ll tell you. Now then, these… then we would oil them, they still had not dried completely, in a cloth we would put them good, like butter. We would make them a coil. That time, we had a bow, they would call it a bow.

contents.textus: 025. I. Qəqlo mən-yo?
contents.versio: 025. What is a qəqlo?

contents.textus: 026. N. Hawxa layfíwayna gullok̇e, ánnaqqa saymíwaynanne. Ánnaqqa kətwa i+qə̀štoste, qáysowa. Kə́twayla dapk̇e haqqa bi+qunk̇ayḏa, ŭ kə́twayla tloṯo+dārk̇at ha hawxa briša, maḥtíwaynanne ha tamo, maḥtíwayna u+hno tamo, bərmíwaynanne ʕal ad+dārk̇anək, ŭ kə́twayla xud i+tarišk̇e bi+qunk̇ayḏa, lo bi+dapk̇e. ŭ guršíwayna i+watro ʕal i+dapk̇e, miḥoṣowa. Kə́twayla dastk̇e ʕayn doquqto du+tumo. Veǧa šoḏíwayna hawxa u+ketono, šoḏíwayna ... Ma bu+talavəzyṑn lə+ḥzalxu, lo+koḥozutu? Əmmiwa i+lăbudiye. Šoḏíwayna ha hawxa, saymíwaynale xud am+maye u+ketono.
contents.versio: 026. So, we would roll them into balls, now then, we would make them. Now then, there was also a bow, it was wood. It had a dowel yea long in its butt, and it had three sticks here like so at its head, we would put them over there, we would put the whatsit there, we would twist them upon those sticks, and it had something like a strip on its butt, not on the dowel. And we would pull the catgut onto the dowel, it would stretch. It had a little handle just like a garlic pestle. Then we would card cotton like so; we would card … Haven’t you seen it on TV, don’t you watch? They would call it spinning. We would card just like so, we would make cotton like lightning.

contents.textus: 027. ŭ kətwa ánnaqqa čitat mani du+bačik, du+daḥno. Saymíwayna dārk̇at. Maḥtíwayna kul+naqqa haqqa ʕal u... ʕal u+kesoyo, saymíwayna hawxa ftalat, a+ftalanək bərmíwaynanne. Ánnaqqa gʕuzlíwaynanne bu+dulabo, ʕuzlíwaynanne bu+dulabo hawxa, ŭ saymíwayna u+ʕazlawo kule.
contents.versio: 027. And then there was one of these stalks of yellow millet, dark millet. We would make little sticks. Every time we would put yea many on the ... upon the covering, we would make spindle like so, we would twist those spindles. Now then, we would spin them with a spinning wheel, we would spin them with a spinning wheel like so, and we would make all that yarn.

contents.textus: 028. Ma lo+Kfarzoye saymiwa bădā́l? Hăma lemux lo+maḥkélalux? Səmme bădā́l: mu... me falge du+kilo saymíwayle ʕəsro+kìlowat. ʕUzliwa ŭ əzzənwa, obənwayle u+kilo+du+ʕazlo, obənwayle bətré+ketono, bu+məqamawo hnənwa. ŭ edi səmme šuqo, ánnaqqa g̊saymile šuqo, aḥuni bəxwá zaqorowa.
contents.versio: 028. Didn’t Kfarzeans barter? Didn’t your mother tell you? They bartered: from ... from half a kilo, they would make ten kilos. They would spin it and go, they would give one kilo of yarn, they would give it for two of cotton, in this way they would whatsit. And then they made some gauze, now then, they’ll make some gauze from it, my brother himself was a weaver.

contents.textus: 029. I. Ayko? Harke aw b Bequsyone?
contents.versio: 029. I. Where? Here or in Bequsyone?

contents.textus: 030. N. B Bequsyone. Hawxa mašfaʕlan ʕəmran bu+məqamawo, xud d̥kəmmat. Aḷḷah, kəmmono mə́ḷḷilux. Ánnaqqa maʕmaḷḷan... ʕəmri, əmmat, ‘ma ʕəmrax?’ ʕəsri+šnaye, ʕəmri šwaʕ̥sar+tmonaʕ̥sar+šnaye, ṭrowe ʕəsri. Mbelan ʕəmran, šoḏíwayna, ʕuzlíwayna ŭ quṣríwayna i+šuqáyoste, mahtíwaynala bayn aš+šarʕe du+rabəʕ, əmblíwaynala li+rawmo, ḥawṭíwaynala, huyowa xud i+čərre du+ḥalwo. ŭ aq+quttək̇k̇at xud uʕdo... (10: 35)
contents.versio: 030. N. In Bequsyone. So, we spent our life, in this manner, like you say. By God, I believe I told you. Now then, we built… My age, you say, ‘Your age?’ Twenty years, I was seventeen-eighteen years old, let it be twenty. We spent our lives, we would card, spin, and also wash the linen, put it into springtime cow patties, bring it to the pond, beat it, it would become like powdered beestings. And waistcoats like now…

contents.textus: 031. I. Šuqo, lo+fahəmno áydarbo misomowa.
contents.versio: 031. I. Linen, I don’t understand how it would get made.

contents.textus: 032. N. Bi+gumṯo, ma uʕdo kozuqruṭu? Lo+kosaymutu bandok̇e, medone? Ma lo a+Kfarzoye kuḏʕutu?
contents.versio: 032. N. With a loom, don’t you weave now? Don’t you make saddlebags, things? Don’t you Kfarzeans know?

contents.textus: 033. I. Bele.
contents.versio: 033. I. Yes.

contents.textus: 034. N. Hayoste hawxa hawxa hawxa saymínawa.
contents.versio: 034. N. We used to do this and this way.

contents.textus: 035. I. Uʕdo mu+ʕazlo saymútuwayla, latyo hawxa?
contents.versio: 035. I. Now then, you would make it from yarn, isn’t it so?

contents.textus: 036. N. E, saymíwaynala, šuqo.
contents.versio: 036. N. Yes, we would make it, broadcloth.

contents.textus: 037. I. Saymútuwayla, šuqo ... kəmmat ʕal i+rawmo, mə saymíwayna eba?
contents.versio: 037. I. You would make it, broadcloth… you talk about the pond, what would we do in it?

contents.textus: 038. N. Ánnaqqa maḥtíwayna bu+rabəʕ̥, maltmíwayna aš+šarʕe yaroqe du+rabəʕ‿daq+qanyone. Maḥtíwaynanne dəmmina blăgan. Maḥtíwayna ṣeniye dmaye aʕlayye ŭ maḥtíwayna i+šuqayo baynaṯṯe, maḥtíwaynanne baynaṯṯe, hul dyurqowa. Qădar hul d̥xolíwayna, qădar falge+d̥saʕaye, ŭ gəmblíwaynala ġayṭíwaynala bi+rawmo. Ġayṭíwaynala dlo+ḥwoṭo, ġayṭíwaynala bi+rawmo bi+rawmo bi+rawmo tarte+tlaṯ+kore, ŭ bəṯr edi g̊ḥawṭíwaynala hul dhuyowa sibore. Nofalwa ḥuṭe ḥewore eba, huyowa aḥwar mu+hizarano duʕdo.
contents.versio: 038. N. Now then, in spring we would put, we would collect green cow patties. We would put them, let’s say, in a basin. We would put a serving bowl of water onto them and place that broadcloth within them, and we put it within them until it became green. For a while, until we would become free, around half an hour, and we would take it to immerse it in the pond. We would immerse it without beating, we would immerse it in the pond, in the pond, in the pond two-three times, and then we would beat it until it would become multicoloured. White threads would appear (lit. ‘fall’) in it, it would become whiter than this whitecloth of today.

contents.textus: 039. ŭ aq+quttək̇at muslí əmmíwaynanne, xṭuṭo ḥeworo ŭ ḥa komo. Ak+kome, mtarsíwaynanne li+dano, makimə́nwanne b Məḏyaḏ, ŭ mašqiwa hən kome ŭ hən ḥewore. Əmmənwa quttək̇at, hanək edi howənwa, saymíwaynanne, quttək̇at muslí. Gəmlak̇e latwa i+naqqayo. E, háwoste hawxa...
contents.versio: 039. And the waistcoats, we would call them Mosulite, a white thread and a black one. The black ones, we would send them for dyeing, they would blacken them in Midyad, and they would dye some of them black and some white. They would call them waistcoats, this way they would come into being, we would make them, Mosulite waistcoats. There were no shirts at that time. Yes, that’s about it (lit. ‘this too is like so’).

contents.textus: 040. I. Quttək̇at kəmmənne?
contents.versio: 040. Do they call them waistcoats?

contents.textus: 041. N. Quttək̇at. E, gumlak̇e, gumlak̇e, gumlak̇e, elo ləmmíwayna gumlak̇e. Quttək̇at.
contents.versio: 041. Waistcoats.  Right, shirts, shirts, shirts, but we did not call them shirts. Waistcoats.

contents.textus: 042. I. Quttək̇at yani xŭd a+elak̇e?
contents.versio: 042. Waistcoats, that is, like vests?

contents.textus: 043. N. Ašə́r də+ṭa saymíwaynanne, ṭawwe šuqo, ŭ ṭawwe manək, saymíwaynanne qupčat harke ŭ harke, ŭ saymíwaynanne gere, ŭ ḥayṭíwaynanne. Yani xud uʕdo xud ag+gumlak̇e duʕdowayne, háwoste hawxa.
contents.versio: 043. N. Really, we would make them double-layered, a layer of gauze, and one of those layers (lit. ‘a layer of those ones’), we would make hook and eye clasps here and here, and we would make cuff links, and sew them together. That is, like today, they were like the shirts of today, that’s about it (lit. ‘this too is like so’).

contents.textus: 044. I. Bas mu+marʕeze?
contents.versio: 044. I. Only from goat wool?

contents.textus: 045. N. Lo, lo, lo, ketono.
contents.versio: 045. N. No, no, no, cotton.

contents.textus: 046. I. Hani mu+ketono howənwa?
contents.versio: 046. These would have been from cotton?

contents.textus: 047. N. Dam+marʕeze, kăsaxat ŭ ʕăbáyatwayne, hanək.
contents.versio: 047. N. Those of goat wool, they were short coats  and robes, those ones.

contents.textus: 048. I. Kăsaxa mənyo, kăsaxa mənyo?
contents.versio: 048. What is a short coat? What is a short coat?

contents.textus: 049. N. Hee kăsaxa bu+šəkəl dač+čaketani, hanək. ánnaqqa mu+marʕeze saymíwaynale.
contents.versio: 049. Yeah, a short coat is like (lit. ‘in the form of’) these jackets, those ones. Now then, we would make it of goat hair.

contents.textus: 050. I. Bas hanək lo+ḥaykiwa?
contents.versio: 050. I. But those, wouldn’t they itch?

contents.textus: 051. N. Hee?
contents.versio: 051. N. Yeah?

contents.textus: 052. I. Lo+ḥaykiwa u+marʕezawo, yani i+naqqa dlawšíwayle?
contents.versio: 052. Wouldn’t that goat har itch, like when they would wear it?

contents.textus: 053. N. E ʕal aǧ+ǧule lowašwayle, uʕdo u+čaketayḏŭx kalé ʕal u+gəmlak̇.
contents.versio: 053. Yes, they would wear them over the clothes, now there’s your jacket over the shirt.

contents.textus: 054. I. Yani lo+hnənwa bi+laše?
contents.versio: 054. So they wouldn’t whatsit the body?

contents.textus: 055. N. Lo, lo, lo+hnənwa bi+laše. Elo, bele, mašraṭ, di+lašestene, miḥasən miṯayxu, u+mḥasyo dbabi omarwa, ‘Aʕ+ʕeze kome, ánnaqqa aʕ+ʕeze, zəvrayo čik̇e; daṣ+ṣafure, dag+gisk̇at, dəmmina he dlawəlle...’ Qoyaṣwalle, omarwa, ‘De k̇ačam, ʕzale, hano rakíxoyo, lo+koxal i+lašayḏan’. Beǧamat i+naqqayo latwa, ánnaqqa gʕuzlówayne, rafiʕo, rafiʕo, rafiʕo, hawxa saymówayne, hul d̥komalwa. Tre+šalat, tloṯo+šalat: babi ḥa, ŭ aḥunoni kul ḥa ḥa. Ánnaqqa u+ʕazlàwostene g̥̊saymíwaynale gəgle, ŭ háwoste bi+bəṣṣayle, u+dahwo daṗ+ṗirat daṭ+ṭaye kule...
contents.versio: 055. No, no, they wouldn’t whatsit in the body. But, yes, believe it or not, about the body, blessed be your dead, my late father used to say, ‘Black goats, now then, the goats, a bit harsh; that of bucklings, of yearlings, let’s say those that haven’t birthed yet…” He would shear them, he would say, ‘Come on, my girl, spin it, this is soft, it it doesn’t not eat our body’. At that time, there were no pajamas, now then I would spin it, thin, thin, thin; so I would do until it would be done. Two pairs of trousers, three pairs of trousers, one for my father, and one for each of my brothers. Now then, as for that yarn, we would make it into skeins, and also that one with the bulb, all the gold of Muslim women …

contents.textus: 056. I. I+bəṣṣayle mənyo?
contents.versio: 056. What is the bulb?

contents.textus: 057. N. I+bəṣṣayle xud ar+riše du+tumo, kuyo bu+ṭuro. əzzənwa, baḷo, Naro dbe ḥaǧo, a+bnoṯe d Brahime Xalaf, yani ġắlăbe noše əzzewa. Aḥna bəxwá azzán li+bəṣṣaylayo: šəlḥíwaynala, pəčqíwaynala, dayqíwaynala, ŭ šəlqíwaynala. Ínnaqqa d̥kəmmi, ‘flān mede xud i+bəṣṣayle ...’ huyowa ġəre, huyowa ġəre, ṣaydowa bu+hno, ánnaqqa lo+məqṭəʕwa u+ʕazlo, lo di+šuqo ŭ lo di+tašiye.
contents.versio: 057. N. The bulb is like heads of garlic, it’s in the hill country. They would go, gosh, Naro Ḥaǧo, the daughters of Brahime Halaf, that is, lots of people would go. We ourselves went for that bulb, we would pluck it, grind it, crush it, and boil it. When they say, ‘Such a thing is like the bulb ...’ it would become laminate, it would become laminate, it would catch on the whatsit (i.e., the needle), now the yarn would not tear apart, either in the gauze or on the spindle.

contents.textus: 058. I. Maquyówayle, saymówayle qawyo?
contents.versio: 058. I. Would it strengthen it (i.e., the yarn), make it strong?

contents.textus: 059. N. Maquyówayle, howewa xud at+telat, xud at+telat, ŭ edi saymíwayne. ḥa ʕIwarnoyo əšme Sáfarwa, zaqoro dak+kăsaxat ŭ daʕ+ʕăbàyatwa, edi aṯi l Bequsyone bekár, huwalle ḥḏo qusnayto ŭ ftəḥle gumṯo b Bequsyone, sōmwa kăsaxat ŭ ʕăbayat. Edi hanək ḥayṭənwanne, he kəmmənne i+mḥaṭo daʕ+ʕăbayat, a+mḥaṭe xašunanək, kəmmina a+mḥaṭe daʕ+ʕăbak̇e, hánəkste saymíwaynale hawxa. Mbelan ʕəmran bu+məqamawo, hul uʕdo.
contents.versio: 059. N. It would strengthen it, it would become like wires, like wires and then we would make it. A certain Iwardian, whose name was Safar, he was a weaver of short jackets and robes, then he came to Bequsyone as a bachelor, they gave him a Bequsyonian girl and he opened a weavery (lit. ‘a loom’) in Bequsyone, he produced short jackets and robes. Then those would sew, they still call them robe needles, those thick needles, they call them short robe needles, those too we would make it (i.e., the yarn) like so. We have spent our life in this way until now.

contents.textus: 060. Uʕdo ánnaqqa ŭ aq+qaḥfuroṯe, kəmmalŭx ... fəḏre ... saymíwayna qəweləb du+ṭino, ha hawxa. ŭ ánnaqqa gəzzáwayna lu+ṭuro, əmṭíwayna fəḏre, mdaqəd̥qíwaynanne, hawxa šežən naxwəštə́r mdu+fəḏro layt.
contents.versio: 060. Then the utensils, I tell you… ox tongues… we used to make forms from clay, just like so. And when we would go to the hill country, we would bring back ox tongues, we would pound them, there is no such toil worse than that of the ox tongue.

contents.textus: 061. I. Fəḏro, hawo mənyo? Géloyo? Əšme?
contents.versio: 061. Ox tongue, what is this? Is it a plant? Its name?

contents.textus: 062. N. Tadro kəmmútəlle, ʕaynənto! Hawoste šəkəl dgéloyo, xud a+šrule kowe, mdaqəd̥qíwaynanne, naxwəštə́r mu+syomayo layto, mdaqəd̥qíwaynanne ŭ bi+manduriye edi, ʕal i+šeno bi+manduriye hul dhowənwa aw+wariḏayḏe ḥuṭe.
contents.versio: 062. You call it tadro, ʕaynənto! This is also a kind of plant, it is like melon leaves, we would pound them, there is nothing worse than that work, we would pound them and with a stone roller then, against the rock with a stone roller, until its veins would become threads.

contents.textus: 063. ŭ ánnaqqa u+qaləb̥ste g̥̊saymíwaynale, quršíwayna ... əmṭíwayna ánnaqqa qaṣmono dat+tanure: qáṭmoyo, qaṣmono? Gnuḥlíwaynale, g̊saymíwaynale ḥawdal, ŭ guršíwaynale ha hawxa, ʕal u+qalbawo.
contents.versio: 063. And then we would make a mold, we would cover… we would then bring soot from the oven: is it ashes, soot? We would sieve it, we would make it (like) grape pudding, and we would pull it out just like so, over that mold.

contents.textus: 064. ŭ maḥtíwayna, edi g̊saymíwayna af+fəḏre ha hawxa, mdahníwayna. Maḥtíwayna aʕle, ʕawwəli hawxa gurovár, xud u+dawqo, hawxa ʕal qarʕe, bəṯr edi xud u+damso, hawīr gəblíwayna ŭ šuqlíwayna ebe hul d̥owewa ḥa. Bəṯr g̊saymíwaynanne k̇avik̇at ŭ čəmbəlk̇at, ŭ bəṯr gəmnaqšíwaynale bu+kalšo, ʕawwəli ḥamməš, bəṯr tlaṯ, ŭ bəṯr tarte, ŭ bəṯr ḥḏo. Uʕdo kito naqqəš bu+šəklawo, hawxa konəqši.
contents.versio: 064. And we would place, then we would put a layer of ox tongues just like so, we would smooth it. We would put it on it, so first a circle, like the griddle, like so on its top, afterwards then like the ring, we would bring it around and transfer on it until it would become one. Then we would make for them edges and handles, and then we would adorn it with lime, first five, then three, and then two, and then one. Now there is decoration in that type, they decorate like so.

contents.textus: 065. I. Hánine aq+qaḥfəryoṯe d̥saymútuwanne?
contents.versio: 065. Are these the vessels you would make?

contents.textus: 066. N. Aq+qaḥfuroṯe, ánnaqqa məd̥‿kamili, tmanyo+yawme, təšʕo+ʕəsrò gmaydíwaynanne. Ánnaqqa u+qaṭmawo gmarfewa, marfewa, g̊šəlḥíwaynanne, mdahníwayna hawxa arʕa di+ḥolo, bayn i+arʕo, dəmmina bu+ṭyoro, bayn i+baxča.
contents.versio: 066. The vessels, when they got finished, eight days, nine or ten, we would take them. Then those ashes peeled off, they peeled off, we would take them off, we would smooth like so the surface of the ground, on the surface, let’s say in the courtyard, in the garden.

contents.textus: 067. ŭ maḥtíwaynanne harke. ŭ qaḥfərto ḥreto. Gmolíwaynanne ʕafro, hul dəzzewa qădar ʕəsro+yawme, ṭowo dnəšfiwa dlo+miqarmči. Ánnaqqa edi bi+maglo, hak̇a bi+skino, mdawrí[way]na ak+k̇avik̇aṯṯe, mʕadlíwaynanne, fərxíwayna ǧulo mede čike appe, aḷḷa hešste mičokiwa ak+kube. Laylonat latwa, kise latwa, nuqlíwayna u+zadayḏan baq+qaḥfuroṯe mi+adro.
contents.versio: 067. And then we would place them here. And another vessel. We would fill them with earth, until around ten days passed, until they would dry well so they don’t wrinkle. After that with a sickle, or with a knife, we would round off their edges, we would fix them, we would rub on them with some kind of cloth for a short while, gosh, even then the thorns would still stick out. There weren’t any nylons, there weren’t any sacks, we would carry our grain in the vessels from the threshing floor.

contents.textus: 068. ŭ ak+kore, mə́ḷḷilux, saymíwayna kore du+ṭino, maqimíwaynanne, əzzéwalle tleṯi+arbʕi+ʕelab, ḥamši+ʕelab, gnuqlíwayna ba+qaḥfuroṯanək, əmṭíwayna mi+adro, məlyówayno tarte, makəlwa bi+ʕulbe, tarte maḥatwa bi+hno, maṭʕánwayli, əṯyówayno maxlówayno bi+koro, maxlówaynanne li+barmale, dəmmina li+ḥolo.
contents.versio: 068. And the bins, I told you, we would produce clay bins, we would set them up, they contained thirty, forty, fifty bushels, we would transport it with those vessels, we would bring it from the threshing floor, I would fill two up, he would measure by the bushel, he would put two into the whatsit (i.e., the vessel), load it on me, I would come and empty it into the bin ... I would empty them in the antechamber, let’s say on the ground.

contents.textus: 069. Hăma háyoste gmafəhmallux, d̥šaḥino mi+adro doṯe, gnəflo i+qalmo ebe. Ánnaqqa maḥtíwaynanne lawġul, maxlíwaynanne bi+ḥolo lawġul, xud dmaxlínanne harke, hoool d̥fayḥi, hul dəzzíwayno ko mlele i+ḥreto, gmaṭʕánwayli hayo, əmṭówayno maxlówayna lawġul. Məd əzzíwayno ga ko mlele i+ḥreto. Bu+məqamawo nuqlíwayna u+zadayḏan mi+adro hoool d̥fayḥi. Məd̥‿fayiḥi, edi bəḥḏo xāfto məlyówayno edi ono lruḥi, maxlówayno bi+koro, ha hawxa əzzənwa lar+rəḥye. Hawxa laḥmo d̥sʕore uxlíwayna.
contents.versio: 069. But I’ll explain to you this too, when it comes hot off the threshing floor, lice fall into it. Now then, we would put them (i.e., the bushels of grain) inside, we would empty them upon the ground inside, like we empty it here, until they cool down, until I would go, he had already filled another, he would load that one on me, I would bring it to empty inside. When I would go back, he had already filled another one. In that manner we would transport our grain from the threshing floor until it (lit. ‘they’) cooled down. When they cooled down, then I’d fill it in one light one then by myself, I would empty it into the bin, just like so they would go to the mills. So we would eat barley bread.

contents.textus: 070. I. Wăki b Bequsyone kətwa gumoṯe, ftəḥwalle gumoṯe yani?
contents.versio: 070. I. So there actually were looms in Bequsyone, they had opened looms, that is?

contents.textus: 071. N. Ho ho u+bayto xud uʕdo dəmmat lma‿d̥kətle dukkano du+dahwo i+gumṯo háyowa. Aṭ+ṭaye ləḏʕiwa, qāṣ daʕ+ʕarabiyani qalibiwa ʕal Bequsyone. Xalila, Basəqqəl, ag+gərk̇ani kulle, d̥kəmmo me Dareǧa, k̇arboran kulle, əzzənwa l Beqŭsyone.
contents.versio: 071. Ho, ho! The family, like now, you might say, whoever has a gold shop, the loom was that one. The Muslims didn’t know the entirety of the ʕArbayans turned to Bequsyone. Xalila, Basəqqəl, all these burgs, as she (Gule) says from Dareǧa, all of Kerboran, would go to Bequsyone.

contents.textus: 072. ṭaye loḏaʕwa zoqar, anǧax əmbliwa baṣle, əmbliwa tumo, əmbliwa baǧanat, əmbliwa šan more di+gumṯo. Naqqa qašti, – veǧa aḥuni bi+ḥaraytaṯe iləfle, moḥewa, sṓmwayla ṭawto, – qašti əmmo, ‘Nafiqono mi+ʕito, naqqa ləḥḏo, kalkó əzzə́n lu+bayto, kəmmo, mədla li+qeməstayḏi, məḷḷa, “Xuzzí u+abrayḏax sṓmwayli i+šuqayḏi!” Dṓqwayla hul d̥qodarwa, dṓqwayla sṓmwayla qwiṯo
contents.versio: 072. Muslims, he didn’t know how to weave, they only brought onions, they brought garlic, they brought eggplants, they brought them for the loom owners. Once my grandmother, – then my brother in the last times learned it, he would work (lit. ‘hit’, i.e., the loom), he would make it very good, – my grandmother says, ‘I went out of the church, once a woman, here they are, going home, she says, she grabbed my dress, she said, “If only your son had made my cloth for me!”’ He would pound it as much as he could, he would pound it to make it strong.

contents.textus: 073. Veǧa kətwa hən, ha ha ha ha, saymiwa hawxa, hăma maqiṯíwayla bəḥḏoḏe, xoṯayxu, dəmmina, da+Kfarzoye. Hawxa hun žməra sāġ…
contents.versio: 073. Now there are some, here here here here, they would work like so, so they would make the threads touch each other, like yours, let’s say, of the Kfarzeans. So, may you be well for me...

contents.textus: 1. Kətwa, latwa, rab̰‿m Aloho latwa, ḥaq!
contents.versio: 1. Maybe it happened, maybe it didn’t (lit. ‘it was and it wasn’t’), there wasn’t anyone greater than God. Truth!

contents.textus: 2. Əmmi, kətwa ṗire ŭ zlām, láwəlle naʕime, láwəlle naʕime. Uʕdo, kuḏʕútuste kīt noše lo+kowalle naʕime, ġắlăbe kowǝn‿mšahye l Aloho. Qurbane d Aloho!
contents.versio: 2. They say, there was a woman and a man, they had no children, they had no children. Now, you also know, there are some people who don’t have any children, and they are greatly longing for God. Thanks to God (lit., ‘[may I be] God’s sacrifice’)!

contents.textus: 3. Hedik̇a kuzzé u+merək̇, u+zlām, li+rəḥyo. Ŭ i+žənk̇e koḥəzyola farrūčk̇e xušk̇e, gḏayto kəmmina. Komaḥtola bi+dargəšto, zawnola dargəšto, maḥtola ... mxamlo i+dargəšto, maḥto ab+band aʕla ŭ kohayzola. Meqǝm, ‘daydi, daydi, daydi’.
contents.versio: 3. Then the husband, the man, goes to the mill. And the wife finds herself a beautiful chick, we call it a hen. She puts her in a cradle, she buys her a cradle, she puts her… she spruced up the cradle, she puts swaddling upon her, and rocks her. Back then, ‘Rock-a-bye baby, rock-a-bye baby, rock-a-bye baby’.

contents.textus: 4. Koṯe u+zlamayḏa, komar, ‘Tax, ʕawalli, manəḥtina u+ṭaʕno di+rǝḥyo!’ Kəmmo, ‘De ay<na>... i+k̇ačk̇aṯe kobuxyo! Anḥat u+ṭaʕno!’ Ba ánnaqqa, ínaqqa domar, ‘I+k̇ačk̇aṯe kobuxyo’, aṯile ʕəšq, hiye məḷḷe, ‘Šróloyo’.
contents.versio: 4. Her husband comes, he says, ‘Come, help me, let’s unload (lit. ‘bring down’) the mill baggage!’ She says, ‘Wh<ich> ... this girl is crying! Unload the baggage (yourself)!’ So, now then, when he (i.e., she) says ‘This girl is crying!’, he became happy (lit. ‘passion came to him’), that one (lit. ‘he’) said, ‘It’s the truth’.

contents.textus: 5. Komoḥe u+xurǧo du+qamḥo b̥kaṯpe, komaʕballe lawġul, lə+kṭore i+žənk̇e rəmšo, kuzzé, maʕle i+dəsmale me ʕal foṯa, omar, ‘Ho mayṯat! Ho mayṯat! Rabbane, lə+gḏàytoyo?’ Əmmo, ‘Hăma, ṭray mina. Balki, Alóhoyo, huyo k̇ačk̇e!’
contents.versio: 5. He puts the saddlebag of flour upon his shoulder, he brings it inside, he doesn’t let his wife stir, he goes, he raises the scarf from upon her face, he says, ‘Oh, go to Hell (lit. ‘may you die’)! Oh, go to Hell! What a wretched thing, isn’t it a hen?’ She says, ‘Enough, leave her alone. Probably, it’s God, she’ll become a girl!’

contents.textus: 6. Hizola, hizola, hizola, baq+qudrat d Aloho, hawyo k̇ačk̇e. Hawyo k̇ačk̇e xud i+šmamok̇e, hawyo k̇ačk̇e xud i+šmamok̇e. Ánnaqqa gəzzayo, kuzzá bayn aḥ+ḥawrone, məštaʕyo, hawyo rabṯo.
contents.versio: 6. She rocked her, rocked her, rocked her, by the power (lit. ‘powers’) of God, she became a girl. She became a girl like a peach (lit. ‘the tigger melon’, i.e., beautiful), she became a girl like a peach. Now then, she would go, she goes together with friends, she plays, she grew up.

contents.textus: 7. Kito meqəm məbliwa ad+dolabaṯṯe, i+qəštaṯṯe lǝškaftək̇e, hawxa ḥeḏər i+qriṯo. Ak̇+k̇ačk̇at, žboyi dməštaʕən ŭ məǧġoli, dəmmənne čirok̇at ŭ guḥxi ŭ ʕuzli u+dolabaṯṯe, šorən i+qəštaṯṯe, ʕuzli u+dolabaṯṯe…
contents.versio: 7. It happens that earlier they would take their spinning wheels, their bow to a cave, such (as those) around the village. The girls, in order to play and chat, to tell stories and laugh and spin their spinning wheel, to card with their bow, to spin their spinning wheel …

contents.textus: 8. Véǧare ánnaqqa əmmi, əmmo, ‘Yade, ónoste’. ‘Yade, lo!’ Flān behvā́n. Əmmo, ‘Ăḷa, gəzzí’. ‘E, zax! Lo+kuḏʕat...’
contents.versio: 8. Well, now then, they say, she says, ‘Mommy, me too’. ‘Daughter (lit. ‘mommy’), no!’ So on and so forth. She says, ‘Gosh, I’ll go’. ‘Yes, go! You don’t know (i.e., how to spin, etc.)’

contents.textus: 9. Ánnaqqa kə́twalle baxča. Me kul ṭaʕmo kə́pwayla, me kul ṭaʕmo kə́pwayla. Ánnaqqa əmmi, əmmi, ‘Hăma Farrūčk̇e, izáx mṭilan ṣallək̇e d̥fire mi+baxčayḏax. Aḥna gʕuzlina u+ketonayḏax, g̊šoḏínale, ʕuzlínale’. Əmmo, ‘Ṭrowe!’
contents.versio: 9. Now then, they had a garden. It contained every type (i.e., of fruit), it contained every type. Now then, they say, they say, ‘Oh Chick, go, bring us a basket of fruits from your garden. We’ll spin your cotton, we’ll card it, we’ll spin it’. She says, ‘Let’s do it (lit. ‘let it be’)!’

contents.textus: 10. Mədla li+ṣalk̇e, azzá. Ánnaqqa u+tarʕo di+ṣàlkeste… di+bàxčaste, ǝmmiwa, ‘Šaltaḥ maltaḥ, qarʕax laltaḥ, raġloṯax lalʕal’, məsxarwa. Dəmmiwa, ‘Šaltaḥ maltaḥ’, xayo, ‘raġlax laltaḥ ŭ raġloṯux lalʕal’, məftaḥwa.
contents.versio: 10. She took the basket, she went. Now then, the door of the basket… of the garden, they would say, ‘Groundwards downwards, your head down, your feet up’, it would get closed. If they said, ‘Groundwards downwards’, like that one, ‘your foot (i.e., feet) down and your feet (i.e., head) up’, it would get opened.

contents.textus: 11. Azzá hawxa, məḷḷa, ftəḥla, mlela i+ṣalk̇ayḏa fire ŭ azzá dísane, nafiqo, əmmo, ‘Šaltaḥ maltaḥ qarʕux laltaḥ ŭ raġloṯux lalʕal’.
contents.versio: 11. She went like so, she said, she opened it, she filled her basket with fruits and went again, she went out, she says, ‘Groundwards downwards, your head down, your feet up’.

contents.textus: 12. Bu+mqamawo məblowa ŭ fəlġowa ʕal ak̇+k̇ačk̇at, ak̇+k̇ačk̇at ʕəzliwa u+ketonayḏa, ǝṯyowa. Ánnaqqa i+emo aṯila ʕǝšq. Əmṭowa u+ketono, saymówayle ʕazlo, ǝmṭówayle lu+bayto. Hak̇a ġắlăbe ŭ hak̇a əšmo, hawxa madəmla be məqqa.
contents.versio: 12. In that way, she would take it and distribute it among the girls, the girls would spin her cotton, she would come back. Now then, the mother became happy (lit. ‘passion came to her’). She would bring cotton, she would make it yarn, she would bring it back home. Whether it was a lot or a little, she kept doing so for however long.

contents.textus: 13. Naqqa u+fardo di+šəmk̇ayḏa fayəš bu+tarʕo di+baxča. U+abro du+aġàstene azzeyo lu+serangə̀h. Koḥoyar kalé fardo d̥tarlə́k tamo bayn am+maye. Komar, ‘Dluyo i+marta di+tarlikaṯe, lo+kobaʕno noše’. Šəmək̇e kəmmutla, tarləke kəmmutla ... mǝ‿kəmmutla li+šəmk̇e?
contents.versio: 13. Once, a single one of her slippers remained at the door of the garden. The son of an agha also went for a walk. He sees there’s a single room shoe there in the water. He says, ‘If it won’t be the mistress of that room shoe, I don’t want anybody’. You call it a slipper, you call it a room shoe… what do you call slippers?

contents.textus: 14. AA. Šəmə́keste, šəmək̇e yaʕni…kəmmina šəmk̇e, di+raġlo? Šəmək̇e kəmmina.
contents.versio: 14. A slipper too, a slipper, like… we say a slipper, of the foot? A slipper, we say.

contents.textus: 15. NE. E, b̥ Suriya kəmmi Ašqaṭa.A
contents.versio: 15. Right, in Syria they say Ašqaṭa.A

contents.textus: 16. AA. E, šəmək̇e. Tarlə́k bu+tə̀rkiyo.
contents.versio: 16. Right, a slipper. It’s a room shoe in Turkish.

contents.textus: 17. Aṯən, aṯi lu+bayto. Omar, ‘Dlowe i+marto d̥aṯe, lo+kobaʕno’.
contents.versio: 17. They came, he came home. He says, ‘If it’s not the mistress of this one, I don’t want her’.

contents.textus: 18. Koṭəlbi ak̇+k̇ačk̇at di+qriṯo kuuula, koṭəlbənne, ŭ maltmənne. Hayo kəmmo, ‘Díḏiyo’, hayo kəmmo, ‘Díḏiyo’. Lawyo ʕal raġle d̥ḥa mənne.
contents.versio: 18. They ask the girls of the entire village, they ask them, and they gather them. That one says, ‘It’s mine’, that one says ‘It’s mine’. It wouldn’t go on any of their feet (lit. ‘on a foot of any one of them’).

contents.textus: 19. Kəmmi, ‘Ăḷa, fayišo i+Farrūčk̇e’. Ba ánnaqqa i+Farrūčk̇e xud i+šmamòk̇eyo! Azzə́n, məṭyalle, hawyo ʕal raġla, əmmo, ‘Ăḷa, díḏiyo!’ Ha i+emo, u+babo, Kǧār bār!K əmmo, ‘Ăḷa, díḏiyo’.
contents.versio: 19. They say, ‘Gosh, (the one) left is Chick’. Now then, isn’t Chick like a peach (lit. ‘tigger melon’)! They went, they brought her, it fit (lit. ‘became’) on her foot, she says, ‘Gosh, it’s mine!’ Here the mother and father Kraise a fussK (lit. ‘warning blast’)! She says, ‘Gosh, it’s mine’.

contents.textus: 20. Edi mḥawlalle, háwoste mḥawlole, mblole šan ruḥe. KŬ hun žǝ mə ra sāġ.K Haw kəḏʕono.
contents.versio: 20. Then they moved her, it was that one who moved her, he took her for himself. KAnd you be well for me.K I don’t know anymore!

contents.textus: 1. Kәtwa latwa, rab̰‿m Aloho latwa. Ḥaq!
contents.versio: 1. Maybe it happened, maybe it didn’t (lit. ‘it was and it wasn’t’), there wasn’t anyone greater than God. Truth!

contents.textus: 2. Kәtwa zlām ŭ ṗire, híyaste b̥ṭáʕnowa. Azzá bdarbo, laqyo b̥qatte dremuno. I+ṗire du+ṭaʕno, leba kuzzé lar+remune. Mәdla, xila, mәḷḷa, ‘Xuyaaay! Ăḷa, fāḥ lebi! D Aloho dobeli k̇ačk̇e, gmaḥtono әšma Ḥabәrmán Xatun’.
contents.versio: 2. There was a man and a wife, as for her, she was pregnant. She went along a road, she encountered a piece of pomegranate. The woman, out of pregnancy, craves pomegranates (lit., ‘her heart goes to pomegranates’). She took it, she ate it, she said, ‘Yum! Gosh, what a relief (lit. ‘my heart was refreshed’)! If God gives me a girl, I will call her Lady Pomegranate Seed’.

contents.textus: 3. L Ăḷo maqḏele la+tre. Be mən hawi, l Ăḷo sәmle. L Ăḷo húlela k̇ačk̇e, maḥatla әšma Ḥabәrmán Xatun.
contents.versio: 3. God made it come to pass for the two. Whatever happened, God did it. God gave her a girl, she called her (lit. ‘put her name’) Lady Pomegranate Seed.

contents.textus: 4. Hawyo barmə́lk̇, xud uʕdo mani diḏux. I+emo mayiṯo. I+emo mayiṯo, lu+babo mṭele ḥreto, mṭele ḥreto. Komasәḥyola, bu+msarqo daʕ+ʕeze … hatu a+Kfarzoye sәrqútuwa u+ṣaʕro hawxa. Msarqo hawxa ʕawudo, koməḥyo b̥qarʕa!
contents.versio: 4. She became an infant, like one of yours now. Her mother died. Her mother died, her father brought back another one, he brought back another one. She grooms her, with a goat carding comb <she combed her> ... you Kfarzeans used to comb your hair like so. Such a sharp comb, she beats on her head!

contents.textus: 5. Kәmḥalaq u+admo, komaḥto zark̇e dmaye raaaṯuḥe aʕla. Ánnaqla am+maye… u+msarqo makula… ŭ maḥto am+maye raṯuḥe, bašilo. Kәmmo, ‘Ya Mōr! Ya Mōr! Hăma d̥yówayno ṭayro, fayrówayno mbayn… i+žәnk̇e, miḏa… mbayn iḏa di+zolumtaṯe, ma mәnwa?
contents.versio: 5. The blood springs forth, she pours a bowl of *seething* water on her. Now then, the water… the comb hurts her… and she pours seething water on her, she got boiled. She says, ‘O Lord! O Lord! If only I were a bird, I would fly out from between… the woman, from her hand… out from between the hands of this torturess, what would have happened?’

contents.textus: 6. L Aloho maqbele i+dәʕwiṯayḏa, hawyo ṭayro. Hawyo ṭayro, fayiro, fayiro, azzá, azzá, azzá, azzá, hawyo… azzá ʕal feme d̥čām, maḥatla ʕal dawmo. Maḥatla ʕal dawmo, aṯi u+abro du+šulṭònostene mu+sayrangə̀h. Košote u+sәsyayḏe, košote. Koḥōr u+sәsyo, koḥōr, koḥoze ṣәrṭa bayn am+maye.
contents.versio: 6. God accepted her prayer, she became a bird. She became a bird, she flew, she flew, she went, went, went, went, she became… she went up to the mouth of a brook, she put down on a tree. She put down on a tree, meanwhile the sultan’s son came along the promenade. His horse drinks, he drinks. The horse looks, he looks, he sees her image within the water.

contents.textus: 7. I. Əmmat ‘mu+sayrangə̀h?’
contents.versio: 7. You say ‘along the promenade?’

contents.textus: 8. N. E, yani kuzzə́n li+gazma. Azzeyo maštele u+sәsyayḏe. U+sәsyo koḥṓr i+ṣәrṭayḏa bayn am+maye, koḥozele. U+sәsyo koḥṓr, ḥōr, ḥōr, lә+kšote. Koḥṓr bayne qarne ... aḏne du+sәsyo, koḥṓr, híyeste koḥoze, koḥṓr: kalayo ʕal i+dawmo rafto. Mḥalaqle iḏe sida, omar... əmmo, ‘Baxt diḏux d Ăḷo, zalṭoníṯono’.
contents.versio: 8. Yes, that is, they went strolling. He went to water his horse. The horse looks at her image within the water, he sees it. The horse looks, looks, looks, he doesn’t drink. He looks between the horns… ears of the horse, he looks, he also sees it, he looks, here she is, perched on the tree. He stretched his hand towards her, he says… she says, ‘Honest to God (lit. ‘your honor (and) God’s’), I am naked’.

contents.textus: 9. Omar, ‘Ġamo layt, gmaḥannax taḥt u+čaket’. Maḥatle taḥt u+čaketayḏe, məṭyole lu+bayto, ŭ malwašalla ǧule, ŭ hawyo rabṯo.
contents.versio: 9. He says, ‘Don’t worry, I will put you under my jacket’. He put it under his jacket, he brought her home, they dressed her in some clothes, and she grew up.

contents.textus: 10. Hawyo rabṯo. Ánnaqqa, i+žәnbave kul+naqqa gdәzzá gdәmmo, ‘Ṣahrooo, ṣahrooo! Mini me Ḥabәrmán Xatun?’, komar, ‘Qaṭmo ʕal qarʕax, Ḥabәrmán Xatun kočiko bu+bayto du+Aġà. Ăḷa, lә+gbəlla bi+ruḥo druḥayye’.
contents.versio: 10. She grew up. Now then, every time the stepmother goes to say, ‘O Moon! O Moon! Which out of me and Lady Pomegranate Seed (i.e., who is the more beautiful)?’, it says, ‘Shame on you (lit., ‘ashes on your head’), Lady Pomegranate Seed has sneaked into the agha’s house. By God, they won’t give her up for their own soul’.

contents.textus: 11. E, haaa olā́m ḥreno, disa gәzzé waxt, gәzzá gdәmmo, ‘Ṣahrooo, ṣahrooo! Mini me Ḥabәrmán Xatun?’ Komar, ‘Qaṭmo ʕal qarʕax, Ḥabәrmán Xatun hawyo rab̥ṯo, fāš u+abro du+šulṭono kobaʕ mbaraxla ʕal ruḥe sōm daʕwo’.
contents.versio: 11. Yeah, there’s another stint, again some time passes, she goes, she’ll keep saying, ‘O Moon! O Moon! Which out of me or Lady Pomegranate Seed?’ It says, ‘Shame on you, Lady Pomegranate Seed has grown up (lit. ‘she became big’), and the sultan’s son has started (lit. ‘stayed’) wanting to marry (lit. ‘bless’) her, to have a wedding’.

contents.textus: 12. Ha qadark̇e hawxa, kul+waxt gәzzayo gdәmmo, ‘Ṣahró, ṣahró! Mini me Ḥabәrman Xatún?’ Gdomar, ‘Ḥabәrmán Xatun mḥawlalle, hawyo i+kalo du+šulṭono’.
contents.versio: 12. A while more just like so, every time she goes she’ll say, ‘O Moon! O Moon! Which out of me or Lady Pomegranate Seed?’ It’ll say, ‘Lady Pomegranate Seed, they’ve moved her (i.e., into the new household), she has become the sultan’s daughter-in-law’.

contents.textus: 13. Ha qadark̇e ḥreto, disa gәzzá gdәmmo, gdәmmo, ‘Ṣahró, ṣahró! Mini me Ḥabәrmán Xatun?’ Gdomar, ‘Ḥabәrmán Xatun, l Ăḷo húlela zʕuro’.
contents.versio: 13. Another while more just like so, she’ll go again, she’ll say, she’ll say, ‘O Moon! O Moon! Which out of me or Lady Pomegranate Seed?’ It’ll say, ‘Lady Pomegranate Seed, God has given her a boy’.

contents.textus: 14. Gәzzé zamā́n ḥreno, disa gәzzá gdәmmo, ‘Ṣahró, ṣahró! Mini me Ḥabәrmán Xatun?’ Gdomar, ‘L Ăḷo húlela ḥreno’.
contents.versio: 14. Another time would go by, she’ll go again, she’ll say, ‘O Moon! O Moon! Which out of me or Lady Pomegranate Seed?’ It’ll say, ‘God gave her another one’.

contents.textus: 15. Axәr hawәn arbʕo, hawәn arbʕo+abne, hawәn bәlṭə́k̇, xud ak̇+k̇ačk̇ani diḏux, rab, mašəkla bann+aḥunone kokurxi aʕla, šawʕo+aḥunone kə́twayla. Qayimo húlalle arbʕo+kaʕbe, arbʕo+aḥunone... arbʕo+abne kə́twayla, húlalle arbʕo+kaʕbe. Ak+kaʕbe kuḏʕat mәnne, hanәk du+săwā̀l? Áḥnaste meqәm mәštaʕíwayna, a+zlamat ž̥xwa, i+qәmaraṯṯe áppewa.
contents.versio: 15. Finally, there were four, there were four sons, they became toddlers, like your girls, older, she noticed her brothers were going around for her, she had seven brothers. She up and gave them four knucklebones, she had four brothers ... four sons, she gave them four knucklebones. Knucklebones, do you know what they are, those of livestock? We would also play it before, the men themselves, their gambling was with them.

contents.textus: 16. Húlalle arbʕo+kaʕbe. Əmmo, ‘Zoxu!’ Maḥtila kul+ḥa bəšqoqo mdi+walaye. ‘Maru, “Qəm, kaʕbo! U+abro d̥ Ḥabәrmán Xátunno, Ḥabәrmán Xatun i+ḥoṯo d̥šawʕo+aḥunòneyo!” Balki mәtfoqutu bәḥḏoḏe’.
contents.versio: 16. She gave them four knucklebones. She says, ‘Go!’ She put each on one of the city’s streets. ‘Say, “Get up, knucklebone! I’m the son of Lady Pomegranate Seed, Lady Pomegranate Seed is the sister of seven brothers!” Perhaps you will run into each other’.

contents.textus: 17. Ánnaqqa hula ann+arbʕo+kaʕbe biḏe dann+arbʕo+zʕurayḏa, kuzzə́n ba+šqoqone. Kәmmi, ‘Qәm kaʕbo, u+abro d̥ Ḥabәrmán Xátunno, Ḥabәrmán Xatun i+ḥoṯo d̥šawʕo+aḥunòneyo’. Hawxa.
contents.versio: 17. Now then, she gave the four knucklebones to her four sons, they go in the streets. They say, ‘Get up, knucklebone! I’m the son of Lady Pomegranate Seed, Lady Pomegranate Seed is the sister of seven brothers!’ Like so.

contents.textus: 18. Ḥa mәnne tfīq ḥa mәnne, kalko hawxa komar. Komaṣәṯ aʕle, maṣәṯ aʕle, komar, ‘Qəm kaʕbo, ono u+abro d̥ Ḥabәrmán Xátunno, Ḥabәrmán Xatun, Ḥabәrmán Xatun i+ḥoṯo d̥šawʕo+aḥunòneyo’.
contents.versio: 18. One of them ran into one of them, saying it here like so. He listened to him, he listened to him, he says, ‘Get up, knucklebone! I’m the son of Lady Pomegranate Seed, Lady Pomegranate Seed is the sister of seven brothers!’

contents.textus: 19. Komar, ‘De mar, mә‿mәḷḷux, mә‿mәḷḷux?’ Komar, ‘Hat, ḥarulux mini?! Hak, qay hat ḥarulux mini? Ono komanno hawxa, “Qəm kaʕbo, ono u+abro d̥ Ḥabәrmán Xátunno, Ḥabәrmán Xatun i+ḥoṯo d̥šawʕo+aḥunòneyo”.’
contents.versio: 19. He says, ‘Come on, say it, what did you say, what did you say?’ He says, ‘You, what concern am I to you (lit. ‘it ruined you by me’)? Wow, what concern am I to you? I myself say it so, “Get up, knucklebone! I’m the son of Lady Pomegranate Seed, Lady Pomegranate Seed is the sister of seven brothers!”’

contents.textus: 20. Ánnaqqa aḏәʕle, aḏәʕle. Mәdle, ṭʕәlle, mbele lu+bayto, mbele lu+bayto. Qralle lәḥḏoḏe, ŭ ann+arbʕo naʕimayḏa, ŭ hiya, ŭ ann+aḥunone latimi lәḥḏoḏe, aḏiʕi lәḥḏoḏe.
contents.versio: 20. Now then, he got acquainted with him, he got acquainted with him. He grabbed him, he carried him, he took him home, he took him home. They called out to each other, and her four children, she, and the brothers gathered together, they got acquainted with each other.

contents.textus: 21. Əmmi, ‘Ma lo+koṯat rišo lu+bayto?’ Əmmo, ‘Ma áydarbo gdәṯyono qmiḏa di+zolumtayo, ašər lo+kuṯyono lu+bayto. Kalko ḥzélәlxu harke. Toxu! I+k̇elik̇e dhatu oṯutu gnәṭrono u+darbaṯxu. Šanayxu u+bayto də́ṯxuyo, elo Ăḷo baḥ+ḥaye lo+kuṯyono qmiḏa di+žәnbavayo.
contents.versio: 21. They say, ‘Won’t you come visit the house?’ She says, ‘How could I come into that torturess’s hands, I’m really not coming home. I’ve just seen you here. Come back! The moment you come back, I’ll be waiting for your footsteps (lit. ‘path’). For your sake, the house is yours, but by God, I’m not coming back into that stepmother’s hands alive’.

contents.textus: 22. Ha hawxa háyoste.
contents.versio: 22. That one also is just like so.

contents.textus: 23. kHun žə mә ra sāġ!k Hawxa hayo šamiʕono, balki kiba ġálṭoste, hawxa košəmʕono.
contents.versio: 23. kYou be well for me!k I’ve heard that one like so, probably there is a mistake too, I hear it so.

contents.textus: 001. M. Aḥna gəmšaylínalax kmo+šuwole ʕal aḥ+ḥayayḏax.
contents.versio: 001. M. We are going to ask you some questions about your life.

contents.textus: 002. N. ʕAl aḥ+ḥayayḏi? E yade, uʕdo dəmaḷḷux yani, b̥šayno aṯutu, elo uʕdo . . . i+moda dwáxtak̇e, dʕumrayna bášqayo, ŭ uʕdo bášqayo. ʕUmrayna, laḥmo dəsʕore uxlíwayna, koṯe lboli i+Ġala, laḥmo dǧaǧəq, dag+gelone, dab+baluṭe uxlíwayna. Ŭ faqiríyewa, hăma ʕayšíwayna ʕal u+săwā̀l, ŭ baṭ+ṭurone lag+gelone, ŭ dawriwa bi+ḥaraytaṯe, edi dawríwayna. Yani, azzano lu+čōlste mu+kafno.
contents.versio: 002. N. About my life? Yes my dear, now I’ll tell you, like, welcome, but now…  the custom of former times, of our life is different, and it’s different now. Our life, we used to eat barley bread, I remember the Famine, we used to eat kashk bread, herb (bread), acorn (bread), we used to eat them. And there was poverty, but we used to live off livestock, and from herbs in the hill country, and later they used to plough, then we used to plough. Like, we went to the Lowlands too out of hunger.

contents.textus: 003. Aṯina lu+ṭuro, ŭ babi dowarwa, ŭ aḥunoni ḥəfriwa hawxa qăfare, ŭ ḥuṣdíwayna. Edi hawina čik̇e . . . raġlan aṯyo quman, sawiʕina, sawiʕina. Hawxa mbelan ʕumran, ṣawmo ŭ ṣluṯo, mṣalíwayna, li+ʕito əzzáwayna, əḏʕíwayna bi+qima di+ʕito, du+qašo. Aš+šamoše oṯənwa li+ʕito kul+ḥušabo, ŭ hawxa mašfaʕlan ʕumran bi+xwašiye.
contents.versio: 003. We came to the hill country, and my father used to plough, and my brothers also used to dig stony patches of land, and we used to harvest. Then we became a little… we got on our feet, we got enough, we got enough. We spent our life in this way, fasting and prayer, we would pray, we would go to church, we would know the value of the church, of the priest. Deacons would come to the church each Sunday, and in this way we spent our life in goodness.

contents.textus: 004. Hăma čik̇e hani am+mašəlmone saymiwa năḥaqqiye aʕlan, ŭ hawxa mbelan ʕumran hul uʕdo, xud komar ʕAziz. Ṭəlbíwaylan, lo+ḥozìwayna a+zlamā̀t, lo+ḥozìwayna ḥḏoḏe, u+mede deman ŭ baban dəmmiwa, tămāmwa. Dəmmiwa obə́nwaylan ləḥḏoḏe, tămāmwa. Yani maqablíwayna u+mamro deman ŭ dbaban. Lo+ḥozìwayna ḥḏoḏe, lo+məǧġolìwayna ʕam ḥḏoḏe dlo miḥawlíwayna.
contents.versio: 004. But these Muslims would do some injustice against us a bit, and so we have been spending our life until now, as Aziz says. They used to ask for us, we would not see the men, we would not see each other, the thing that our mothers and fathers said, it was OK. If they said they would give us to each other, it was OK. Like, we would accept what our mother and father say. We wouldn’t  see each other, we wouldn’t speak with each other unless we would get married.

contents.textus: 005. E, uʕdo ánnaqqa kokurxi ʕam ḥḏoḏe, kohnə́n. Ŭ mqapṭéwayna ha xud uʕdo, mqapṭéwayna, dəsmalat ʕal qarʕayna, aǧ+ǧule hawxa yarixe aʕlayna. He i+modayḏan háyoyo, he i+modayḏan háyoyo. Ak+kaloṯe dmiḥawliwa . . . kə́twaylan əmmíwayna bušiyat dabrisam kome, ʕal haqqa mnaqšéwayne čəzgəliyat yaroqe, šaʕuṯe, pamba, ar+rišikaṯṯe haqqa, bərmiwa tloṯo+hne hawxa ʕal qarʕayna, ŭ quṭrə́nwanne harke, ha qarʕayna howewa ha hawxa, maḥtiwa dəsmale šaʕəṯto ʕal foṯayna, ŭ fuṭa. Ayna d̥kə́twayle kallawat, abrisam; dlatwa, šuqo, disa damlí mnaqašto, maḥtiwa ha hawxa.
contents.versio: 005. Yes, now then, nowadays they make the rounds together, they whatsit.  And we would be covered up just like now, we would be covered up, scarfs upon our heads, the clothes so long upon us. Our custom is still this way, our custom is still this way. The brides that would get married ... we had, we would say, black bridal veils of silk, that would be embellished so much with green, yellow, and pink stripes, their fringes so long ... they would twist three whatsits around our heads, and tie them here, and our head would became like so, they would put a yellow headscarf upon our face and a head covering.  Whoever had money, silk; and if there wasn’t, linen, it was once again checkered and embellished, they would put it just like so.

contents.textus: 006. U+yawmawo məḷḷi, gaḥixi, ha hawxa maḥtíwayna qarʕan bi+arʕo, nəfqíwayna əmmíwayna, ‘Di+dawla dbabayna ləṯyo aʕmayna’. ŭ lo+nəfqìwayna tloṯo+yàwmeste me lawġul, lo+qaymìwayna lo+nəfqìwayna, əmmíwayna, ‘Ḥṭíṯoyo, barbʕina, ŭ lo+hno’. Ánnaqqa uʕdo konəfqi ak+kaloṯe. Kǝmmi, ‘lək lək!!’ guḥxi, ʕam ax+xelvaniye, hawxa koguḥxi. Hawxa medone hawxa, saymíwayna.
contents.versio: 006. The other day, I said it, they laughed, just like so we held our head down to earth (i.e., modestly), we went out, we said, ‘May our father’s luck not come along with us’, and we would not go outside for three days, we would not get up and go out, we would say, ‘It’s a sin, we are in quarantine, and don’t whatsit’. Now then, now the brides go out. They say, ‘Ha Ha!!’ they laugh, with the family of the groom, they laugh like so. So, we used to do such things.

contents.textus: 007. Y. ʕAziz u+abràyḏaxyo?
contents.versio: 007. Is Aziz your son?

contents.textus: 008. N. U+ḥaṯnàyḏiyo. Ono i+emo d Ḥánano, e. Ono me Derqúbeno, aṯyono ádyawma, Ndaṯáloyo. Aṯyono, səmli qəṣ̂d‿i+Ndaṯalo, i+emo də‿Mšíḥoyo, səmli. Ádyawma, dəmṣalyono bgawa—oballa nahire, mṣalina bgawa—aṯyono qəm raġla di+Ndaṯalo, hawxa. Haṯe i+Ndaṯalo ḥaqiqi háṯeyo, i+Maryamane, i+emo də‿Mšiḥo, háṯeyo.
contents.versio: 008. He is my son-in-law. I am the mother of Hanna, yes. I am from Derqube, I came today, it is the Theotokos. I came, I decided to go to [the Church of] the Theotokos, she is the mother of Christ, I did. Today, in order to pray inside it—I give her candles, we pray inside it—I came to the foot of the Theotokos, like so. This one is the Theotokos, the real one is this one, Mother Mary, the mother of Christ, it’s this one.

contents.textus: 009. M. Aʕ+ʕeḏe di+ʕito áydarbo kowən?
contents.versio: 009. How are the church feasts?

contents.textus: 010. N. Áydarbo, aʕ+ʕeḏe di+ʕito? Aʕ+ʕeḏe di+ʕito kosaymínanne disa ʕeḏe, ʕeḏo naʕimo lázǝmyo, u+ʕeḏano, ʕeḏo zʕuro, u+mawlodo də‿Mšíḥoyo, ŭ nuḥrina ṣafure, saymina i+ k̇ŭrbune də‿Mšiḥo, ŭ gǝdnuḥrínanne, ŭ g̊saymina marga ŭ rezo, ŭ gdobina səkkar šakar lan+noše ayna doṯe.
contents.versio: 010. How, the church festivals? The church festivals, we do them, once again, the festivals, Christmas is necessary, this festival, the small festival, is the birth of Christ, and we slaughter kids, we celebrate the Nativity of Christ, and (then) we’ll slaughter them, and we’ll make stew and rice, and we’ll give sugar candy to the people, whoever comes.

contents.textus: 011. Koṯe mašəlmone maq+qəryawoṯani diḏan kulle. Koṯən gaban lu+ʕeḏo, kəmyaqrina u+ʕeḏo ġắlăbe. Kobínale šakar, kobínanne medone. U+ʕeḏano meqəm lo+ḥayfìwayna hul ḥamšaḥṣar+yawme, lo+maḥtìwayna maye ʕal qarʕan, hul lu+yawmo dmaʕmaḏ Mšiḥo, u+yawmo dmaʕmaḏ Mšiḥo. Henú gmaʕmḏina, g̊ḥayfina, maḥtíwayna maye ǧamude ʕal qarʕayna, bu+šəkl di+murən.
contents.versio: 011. Along come Muslims from all these villages of ours. They come to us for the festival, we have a lot of respect for the festival. We give him candy, we give them things. This festival, formerly we did not wash for fifteen days, we did not put water on our heads, until the day Christ was baptized, the day Christ was baptized. Then we’ll baptize, we’ll wash up, we put cold water on our heads, in the manner of myrrh (or like our lord?).

contents.textus: 012. Ono buxwá he hawxa kosaymono, lo aǧ+ǧulayḏi lo ad+dəsmalayḏi, ŭ lo+ḥəfli, mu+ʕeḏo hul lalye du+danḥo. Lalye du+Danḥo əmmono, ‘Ya Rab xud dəsləglux u+mohr d‿Adam bə‿Mšiḥo, dhat səlgat a+ḥṭohayḏan’, ḥəfli ŭ qayimono falge dlalyo i+saʕa ba+traḥṣar, ḥəfli ŭ maḥatli maye ǧamude ʕal i+lašayḏi, ŭ lwəšli aǧ+ǧulayḏi, hawxa.
contents.versio: 012. I myself still do it this way, neither my clothing nor my headscarves, and I didn’t wash from Christmas to Epiphany. The night of Epiphany, I say, ‘Lord, as you have erased the seal of Adam through Christ, may you erase our sins!’—I washed and got up at midnight, at twelve, I washed and put cold water upon my body and wear my clothes, like so.

contents.textus: 013. Ŭ ha ádlalyoste i+Ndaṯàloyo, disa aṯina, sǝmli qəṣ̂d‿Aloho. Aṯənwa an+naʕime lu+ʕeḏayḏan, aṯən, aṯyono aʕmayye, saymina u+ʕeḏaṯṯe, lalye di+Ndaṯàloyo. Doṯən ádlalyo, gdoṯe u+qašo me Bequsyone, harke qašo layt, gdoṯe me Bequsyone, gəmṣale, gəmṣalina harke ŭ gdoʕina, ŭ ṭəlbina mi+Ndaṯalo.
contents.versio: 013. And this here night is the Theotokos, we came once more, I decided to go to God. The children had come to our festival, they came, I came back with them, we are celebrating their festival, it is the night of the Theotokos. Those who come tonight, the priest from Beqŭsyone will come, there is no priest here, he will come from Beqŭsyone, he will pray, we will pray here and supplicate, and we will petition the Theotokos.

contents.textus: 014. ʕEḏo+rabo, ʕeḏo+rabo, ánnaqqa gədmaṣuʕina beʕe, šəlqina beʕe ŭ maṣuʕinanne šəklat šəkl. Ŭ gdoṯən dísane ag+gundi, aq+qariwe, raḥuqe, ṭaye, gdoṯən, gdobínanne tarte+tarte, tlaṯ+tlaṯ, arbaʕ+arbaʕ, ḥamməš+ḥamməš, hawo ʕeḏo di+fṣiḥùṯoyo, də‿Mšiḥo.
contents.versio: 014. Easter, Easter, now then, we’ll colour eggs, we boil eggs and colour them in all kinds of ways. And once more the villagers will come, the relatives, non-relatives, the Muslims, they’ll come, we’ll give them, sometimes two, sometimes three, sometimes four, sometimes five, this is a joyful festival of Christ!

contents.textus: 015. Ŭ yawme+dəʕrəfto di+sqifuṯo, kosaymina i+sqifuṯo, dlaǧ+Ǧəhu ṣluwe Mšiḥo, disa kuzzán li+ʕito b̥ḥəznití, kǝmṣalina. Disa ǧule kome maqalbe. U+ḥasyo, u+qašo kolowaš i+badle maqlabto ʕar‿ruḥe. Aḥna k̬lawšina ǧule maqalbe yani ḥəznina də‿Mšiho, dlaǧ+Ǧəhu ṣluwe. E, fāš tloṯo+yawme bu+qawro, ŭ saləq li+šmayo, e ánnaqqa maškrina Aloho. I+heviyayḏan ʕal Aloho dlo+qoṭaʕlan mu+diwanayḏe. Dáḥnastene bu+šəklayḏe kosaymina, he aḥna am+modayḏan d̥arke, he lə+mdag̊šilan, he lə+mdag̊šilan. Hawxa.
contents.versio: 015. And on the Friday of the Crucifixion, we reenact the Crucifixion, when the Jews crucified Christ, once more we go to the church mournfully, we pray. Once more, inside-out black clothes. The bishop, the priest wears the suit inside out upon himself. We wear some clothes inside out, like, we are sad that Christ ... that the Jews crucified him. Yes, he remained three days in the grave, and went up to Heaven, so we thank God. Our hope upon God is that he will not cut us out of his presence. Since we also do it in his way, it is still our customs from here, we still haven’t changed it, we still haven’t changed it. Like so.

contents.textus: 016. M. Kibi mšālnax kmo+šuwole, əšmax, ŭ əšma di+ʕaylayḏax mǝnyo?
contents.versio: 016. Can I ask you a few questions, your name, and what is your family name?

contents.textus: 017. N. I+ʕaylayḏi, əšmi buxwá, əšmi Nisáneyo.
contents.versio: 017. My family name, my own name, my name is Nisane.

contents.textus: 018. ʕUmrax mə́qqayo?
contents.versio: 018. What is your age?

contents.textus: 019. N. ʕUmri, arbaʕ+ŭ+tmoni.
contents.versio: 019. My age is eighty-four.

contents.textus: 020. M. Ayko hawat?
contents.versio: 020. Where were you born?

contents.textus: 021. B Bequsyone hawyono, ŭ mḥawlono l Derqube, i+kalo dad+Derqubìyeno.
contents.versio: 021. I was born in Bequsyone, I got moved to Derqube, I’m the daughter-in-law of Derqubians.

contents.textus: 022. M. Ayko koʕayšat aġlab? Harke?
contents.versio: 022. Where do you live mostly? Here?

contents.textus: 023. Lo! Koʕayšono b Derqube, ádyawma ʕam an+naʕime aṯyono, haṯe i+barṯàyḏiyo, hano u+ḥaṯnàyḏiyo, aṯən lu+ʕeḏayḏan lriša di+šato, aṯyono aʕmayye, səmli qəṣd d Aloho ŭ di+Ndaṯalo ádlalyo. Haṯe i+Ndaṯàloyo, gəmṣalina bgawa, gdoṯe u+qašo me Bequsyone, gmoḥe lu+noqušo, gdoṯina mṣalina ádlalyo bgawa, ŭ ṣafro bgawa, edi ya hənnək gəmblili, ya gdoṯe u+zʕurayḏi mbeli, hawxa.
contents.versio: 023. No! I live in Derqube, today I came with the children, this is my daughter, this is my son-in-law, they came to our feast at the beginning of the year, I came with them, tonight I visited God and the Theotokos. This is the Theotokos [Monastery], we shall pray in it, the priest will come from Bequsyone, he will ring the bell, we shall come to pray in it tonight, and then in the morning in it, then either they will take me, or my son will come and take me, like so.

contents.textus: 024. M. Azzáx li+madrăse di+ʕito?
contents.versio: 024. Did you go to the parochial school?

contents.textus: 025. N. La‿ʔašə́r lazzí, madrăse ínaqqayo latwa, maketəb latwa, latwa ínaqqayo, elo koṯən  aq+qaše, koṯən aq+qaše koqorən təšʕiṯo, qorən at+tešʕəyawoṯe daq+qadiše, e, komarfono aḏni aʕlayye, ko..., yani, kohnanne, kofǝhmono mənne.
contents.versio: 025. Not really, I didn’t go, there wasn’t any parochial school at that time, there were no public schools, there weren’t any at that time, but priests come, priests come, they read a story, they read stories about saints, yes, I lend my ears to them, I ..., like, I whatsit them, I understand them.

contents.textus: 026. M. Babax ŭ emax manne?
contents.versio: 026. Who are your father and mother?

contents.textus: 027. N. Babi Barṣáwmowa. Emi, ono ḥamməš+šnaye, emi mḥasyo. Lqašti tlélali ŭ maḥátlali, moráwlalan, tarte+k̇ačk̇at ŭ arbʕo+abne. Abro mdiḏa, aḥuni, tloṯo+yarḥe, emi mḥasyo. Ḥoṯi makǝrxówayle ʕal aṗ+ṗirat, meqǝm ḥalwo ŭ mamməkat medone latwa, mamṣə́nwanne me ṣadrayye. Makraxla ʕal aṗ+ṗirat, sǝmla . . . səmle tarte+šnaye, māṯ bi+ḥazbe, kewo, kətwa ḥazbe, daqqat semoqe <how>ewa bi+laše du+ənsā̀n. Taxetǝr latwa, māṯ eba.
contents.versio: 027. My father was Barṣawmo. My mother, I was five years old, my mother passed away. My grandmother took me and put me up, she raised us, two girls and four boys. One of her sons, my brother, three months old, my mother died. My sister would make the rounds with him to the wives, at that time there wasn’t any milk and things like baby bottles, they used to suckle them from their breasts. She carried him among the wives, she became… he became two years old, he died of measles, a disease, there was measles, red spots would appear on the person’s body. There were no doctors, he died from it.

contents.textus: 028. Ŭ a+tloṯo+aḥunone ŭ ono ŭ ḥoṯi. Ḥoṯi kamə́ltowa, ŭ ono ʕəmri ḥamməš+šnàyewa, ŭ babi fayəš hul hani kibe, he laybe, arbʕi+šnaye. Hăma, me ʕəmre d ʕAbdǝl+Masī̀ḥ bábiste mḥase. Aḥúniste hani arbaʕ̥+ḥamməš+šnaye mḥase, Muqsi Šamʕən, ŭ kətli he tre+aḥunone sāġ, ŭ ono. Ha kanné hanək b Bárčiqa, lanne harke aḥunoni.
contents.versio: 028. And it’s the three brothers, I, and my sister. My sister was grown-up, and I was five years old, and my father lasted until some forty years ago more or less. So, around the birth of Abdel-Masih my father also passed away (lit. ‘was blessed’). My brother also passed away some four or five years ago, Muqsi Šamʕən, and I have two more brothers alive, and myself. See, those ones are there in Belgium, my brothers aren’t here.

contents.textus: 029. N. Kətli ḥḏaḥsar+naʕime, ḥamməš+k̇ačk̇at ŭ əšto+abne. Əšmayye, əšme du+rabo Abrohom, ŭ dnaʕəm Musa, ŭ dnaʕəmṫə́r Gabriyel, ŭ dnaʕəmṫə́r Bənyamen, ŭ dnaʕəmṫə́r ʕAbdǝl+Masī̀ḥ, ŭ u+naʕimo Əndrawos. I+k̇ačk̇e i+rabṯo Sayde, ŭ dnaʕəm Səṫṫo, ŭ dnaʕəm Maǧida, ŭ dnaʕəm Gule, ŭ haṯe Ḥana, hawxa.
contents.versio: 029. I have eleven children, five girls and and six sons. As for their names, the name of the elder is Abrohom, and the younger is Musa, and the even younger is Gabriel, and the even younger is Benjamin, and of the even younger is Abdel Masih, and the youngest is Endrawos. The eldest daughter is Sayde, and the one who is younger is Sitto, and the one who is the younger is Majida, and the one who is younger is Gule, and this one is Hanna, like so.

contents.textus: 030. M. Ayna lišone məǧġəlwa babax?
contents.versio: 030. What languages did your father speak?

contents.textus: 031. N. Lešono suryoyo xoṯi, suryoyo məǧġalwa. Kurdóyoste məǧġolina bayn ḥḏóḏena, kurdóyoste koḏaʕwa, elo ṣuroyo məǧġolíwayna aḥna. Aḥna ŭ ak+kuldoye kalán bayn ḥḏoḏe ǧiránena. Aq+qəryawoṯo d̥ḥeḏoran kulle kuldóyene, yalifina koməǧġolina b̥kuldóyoste.
contents.versio: 031. Syriac language, like me, he spoke Syriac. We speak Kurdick to each other, he knew Kurdick as well, but we spoke Syriac. We and the Kurds, here we are, neighbors with each other. The villages around us all Kurdick, we learnt speaking Kurdick as well.

contents.textus: 032. M. Əšme dǧəddax mənwa?
contents.versio: 032. What was your grandfather’s name?

contents.textus: 033. N. Lo+babi? Ǧəddi Gawríyewa, u+babo dǧəddi Úsowa.
contents.versio: 033. Not my father? My grandfather was Gawriye, my grandfather’s father’s name was Uso.
