contents.textus: 034. M. Ayko hawi?
contents.versio: 034. Where was he born?

contents.textus: 035. N. B Bequsyone.
contents.versio: 035. In Bequsyone.

contents.textus: 036. Y. Mənyo əšma d̥qaštax?
contents.versio: 036. What was your grandmother’s name?

contents.textus: 037. N. Qašti Máryamwa. emi Xázmewa, emi Xázmewa, qašti Máryamwa.
contents.versio: 037. My grandmother was Maryam. My mother was Xazme, my mother was Xazme, my grandmother was Maryam.

contents.textus: 038. Y. Me Bequsyónene?
contents.versio: 038. Are they from Bequsyone?

contents.textus: 039. N. Me Bequsyone, Bequsyone.
contents.versio: 039. From Bequsyone, Bequsyone.

contents.textus: 040. Xanəme. Kəmmi maḥkí i+ǧuwanitiyayḏax, i+ʕlaymuṯayḏax.
contents.versio: 040. They say, tell abour your youth, your juvenescence.

contents.textus: 041. N. I+ʕlaymuṯayḏi, i+ǧuwanitiyayḏi?
contents.versio: 041. My  juvenescence, my youth?

contents.textus: 042. X. Qaruto, bu+waxtawo mə‿kətwa? Dəmmina, me ḥeḏorayxu an+noše mə‿saymiwa, áydarbo howewa?
contents.versio: 042. Auntie (lit. ‘godmother’), what was there at that time? Let’s say, around you, what did people do, how was it?

contents.textus: 043. N. E ma mə‿kəmmanne? Dawríwayna, ŭ ḥusdíwayna, ŭ săwā́l kə́twaylan, ʕayšíwayna ʕal u+săwā̀l, əzzáwayna marʕíwayna aʕ+ʕeze, aq+qanyone, ʕaṣriye ḥulwíwaynanne, maḥtíwayna bu+gawdo, hawxa mayʕíwayna, makina latwa, mayʕíwayna hawxa.
contents.versio: 043. Yes, what shall I tell them? We would plough, and we would harvest, and we had livestock, we lived off the livestock, we went to graze goats, cattle, in the evening we would milk them, we put it in a goatskin, so we would churn, there were no machines, we would churn like so.

contents.textus: 044. Əmmíwayna: kəlmašk̇e dbe baqoro, nafəq məšḥo xud̥‿qatoro, hawxa mayʕíwayna.
contents.versio: 044. We would say, The churn-rocking of a cowherd’s home, butter went out like a stone. like so we would churn.

contents.textus: 045. X. A+bnoṯo ema məṭlobiwa? Bakmo+əšne bu+waxtaṯxu?
contents.versio: 045. When were girls betrothed? At what age in your time?

contents.textus: 046. N. A+bnoṯe! Aḥna kə́twaylan šuġlo, ṭaʕnan yaqúrowa. Ṭrallan ʕəsri+ʕəsri, tarte+ŭ ʕəsri+šnaye, hawxa, ṭoríwaynanne, yani, šuġlíwaylan šanan. U+babaṯṯe čik̇e nafás darləġí kətwa aʕle, xud u+kayìwowa. Ánnaqqa an+naʕìmeste əzzənwa lu+maktab, edi mašəġlíwayna bak̇+k̇ačk̇at ha ha Ḥana.
contents.versio: 046. The girls! We had work, our burden was heavy. We allowed them to go at around twenty, at twenty two years old, like so, we would release them, like, they would work for us, on our behalf. Their father, he had a bit of asthma, he was like a sick man. Now then, the children also went to the public school, and then we would direct the girls to help with the work, here’s Hanna right here!

contents.textus: 047. M. Kuḏʕat zmaryoṯe ḥrene?
contents.versio: 047. Do you know other songs?

contents.textus: 048. N. Zmaryoṯe? Lo+məfqatli ba+zmaryoṯe, me Almanya kəmdaʕən aʕli bi+hăvale! Lo, lo, hayo lo+maḥtatla bi+ḥolo!
contents.versio: 048. Songs?  Don’t expose me with songs, from Germany they are demanding Hevala from me. No, no, don’t put it into play (lit. ‘on the floor’)!

contents.textus: 049. X. Bele bele qay? Dəḏʕat, mar kmo+xabre karye.
contents.versio: 049. Yes, yes, why? If you know it, say a few short words.

contents.textus: 050. N. Lo+kuḏʕono, ʕáyboyo.
contents.versio: 050. I don’t know, it’s a shame.

contents.textus: 051. G. Na na na ʕáyboya!
contents.versio: 051. kNo, no, it’s not a shame!k

contents.textus: 052. N. Ínaqqa dəmḥawalle i+kalo du+abrayḏi u+rabo, d Abrohom, ṭləbbe zmarto mini, i+hăvale, mḥalle ... ŭ mbaṭalle u+müzìk tamo bu+ṣalòn, ŭ mḥalle u+hnawo hawxa qəm femayye, əmmi, ‘Ánnaqqa mar!’
contents.versio: 052. When they were transporting the daughter-in-law of my elder son, Abrohom, they demanded the Hevala from me, they put ... and they stopped the music there in the hall, and they put that whatsit (i.e., the microphone) like so in front of their mouths, they say, ‘Now then, say it!’

contents.textus: 053. Əmmono, Yade, Marqus henu, raṣṭa!  Yade, qurbān, henu, raṣṭa! ya go ṫa dvibu diya ṫa ŭ bave ṫa ž̥tara guhastən.  Lilililili,
contents.versio: 053. I say, Daughter, the newly-wed Mark, it’s real! Daughter, my precious, the newlywed, it’s real! He is a lamb fed (lit. made) on milk, yoghurt, The one whom you were desiring, your mother and your father brought to you, Lilililili,

contents.textus: 054. Čuma xana, dreda hăvale, Az hatəma xana, dəreda hăvā́l dălale, Čəl zavak̇i ṫeda, hăvale, Čəl zavak̇i ṫeda hăvā́l dalale! Lilililili,
contents.versio: 054. I went to a roadside inn on the way, friend, I came to a roadside inn on the way, dear friend, There are forty bridegrooms in it, friend,  Forty bridegrooms in it, dear friend! Lilililili,

contents.textus: 055. Zavak̇ē ma l ḥamū wa zēda, Zavak̇ē ma l ḥamū wa zēda. Hawxa.
contents.versio: 055. Our little bridegroom is the greatest of them all, our little bridegroom is the greatest of them all. Like so.

contents.textus: 056. M. Kətwa zmaryoṯe suryoye?
contents.versio: 056. Were there any Syriac songs?

contents.textus: 057. N. E, e, zəmriwa, ínaqqayo kəmmono xud u+k̇urmanǧiwa.
contents.versio: 057. Yes, yes, they would sing them, at that time, I would say, it was like Kurdish.

contents.textus: 058. A. Bu+suryoyo lo+zəmriwa?
contents.versio: 058. Didn’t they sing in Syriac?

contents.textus: 059. N. Lo, i+zmarto ʕal u+k̇urmanǧiwa. Lo+fāš mede?
contents.versio: 059. No, the singing was in Kurdish. Is there anything else (lit. ‘doesn’t something remain’)?

contents.textus: 060. N. Ġálawa, məblíwayna an+nabišoṯe... An+nabišoṯe, kuḏʕat mənne? Nabišoṯe – layto? Nabišoṯe ʕə́nwene, komaḥtínanne bu+qayṭo, koġayṭínanne bad+darmone, maḥtina bi+šəmšo, kowə‿nabišoṯe. Məblíwaynanne lə Sʕert, hul dəmzabníwaynanne. Qayṣíwayna u+marʕeze daʕ+ʕeze, u+ṣaʕro daʕ+ʕeze, qayṣíwaynale, əmblíwaynale lə Sʕert, mzabníwaynale.
contents.versio: 060. It was the Famine, we would take raisins ... Raisins, do you know what they are? Raisins – you know what (lit. ‘there isn’t’, i.e. in your knowledge)? Raisins are grapes, we put them out in summer, we dip them in chemicals, we put them out in the sun, they become raisins. We would take them to Siirt, until we would sell them out. We would cut goat wool, goat hair, we would cut it, we would took it to Siirt, we would sell it.

contents.textus: 061. Ínaqqayo ba+ḥmore, baḥ+ḥayewən əzzáwayna, ʕárabat latwa, baʕ+ʕarabat zanwa. U+dibəs, əmblíwaynale lə Gziro, háwoste, koʕuṣrile hawxa, dayši aʕlayye, ʕuṣrənne aʕ+ʕənwe, ʕuṣrənne, ŭ k̬maḥtínanne bab+baredəš, mbašlínanne, ŭ maḥtina darmone baynaṯte, mbašlínanne, qayšina i+kafaṯṯe, bəšli bəšli bəšli bəšli, hul d̥owe qašyo, d̥owe hawxa. Maʕlina i+mqašiye, d̥owe ṭarfo, edi‿ak̇a g̊d̥owe ṭarfo, gmanaḥtínale. Dibəs, háwoste əmblíwaynale lə Gziro mzabníwaynale.
contents.versio: 061. At that time we would go on donkeys, on animals, there weren’t any cars, we would(n’t) go by cars. The grape molasses, we would take it to Cizre, that one, they press it like so, they trample them, they press the grapes, they press them, and we put them in cooking pots, we cook them, and we put chemicals among them, we cook them, we skim off the foam, they boil, boil, boil, boil, until it becomes hard, it becomes like so. We lift the skimmer, when it becomes a leaf, then if it becomes a leaf, we take it down. Grape syrup, that one too we would take to Cizre, we would sell it.

contents.textus: 062. Harke kosaymina qawite, muqḏina bi+ṣaymənto Xədəlyás, muqḏina aḥ+ḥeṭe bu+dawqo, mqalínanne, ŭ gursínanne, ŭ matrínanne bam+maye ḥalye, bəṯr maḥtina dibəs aʕlayye, layšínanne, saymina i+qawite di+Xədəlyase, kəmmina aḥna u+ṣawmo d Nənwe, u+ṣawmo d Nənwe, hənna harke... kəmmina i+Xədəlyase.
contents.versio: 062. Here we make kavut, we burn it during the Hıdırellez fast, we burn wheat in a skillet, we roast them, and we grind them, and we moisten them with sweet water, then we put grape molasses on them, we knead them, we make Hıdırellez kavut, we call it the Fast of Nineveh, the Fast of Nineveh, some people here ... we call it Hıdırellez.

contents.textus: 001. .... (the recording begins in medias res; before this: I. mawxa ʕal hawxa košŭġli ‘so they work upon this <the Turoyo language>’)
contents.versio: 001. .... (the recording begins in medias res; before this: I. mawxa ʕal hawxa košŭġli ‘so they work upon this <the Turoyo language>’)

contents.textus: 002. Nisane: E alo msaʕadde.
contents.versio: 002. May God help them.

contents.textus: 003. Ilyas: Tawdi, miḥase babax. Veǧa, ono gyotawno harke, qamayto gabax, gəmšalnax kmo+šŭwole.
contents.versio: 003. Thank you, may your father be blessed. Now then, I’ll sit here, before your side, I’ll ask you a few questions.

contents.textus: 004. N. Ma he laṯən larke hani?
contents.versio: 004. And these ones hadn’t come here before?

contents.textus: 005. I. Bele, bele.
contents.versio: 005. Yes, yes, they have.

contents.textus: 006. N. Haṯe Gúleyo, haṯe Gúleyo?
contents.versio: 006. Is that one Gule, is that one Gule?

contents.textus: 007. Gule: E, e.
contents.versio: 007. Yeah, yeah!

contents.textus: 008. I. Haṯe Gúleyo.
contents.versio: 008. That one is Gule.

contents.textus: 009. N. E, aṯyo naqqa ḥreto.
contents.versio: 009. Yes, she came another time.

contents.textus: 010. I. Haṯe Gúleyo, naqqa ḥreto aṯyo.
contents.versio: 010. This is Gule, she came another time.

contents.textus: 011. N. Ŭ hawhə́n hani?
contents.versio: 011. And those over there?

contents.textus: 012. Sergey: ónoste naqqa ḥreto ...
contents.versio: 012. Me too, another time …

contents.textus: 013. N. Hawhó he laṯi?!
contents.versio: 013. That one hadn’t come before?

contents.textus: 014. I. Lo, hawo álmanyo.
contents.versio: 014. No, that one is German.

contents.textus: 015. N. álmanyo, e.
contents.versio: 015. He’s German, right.

contents.textus: 016. I. Haṯe k̇arboraníyeyo.
contents.versio: 016. This one is a Kerboranian girl.

contents.textus: 017. N. Kuḏʕono, me Dareǧa. E.
contents.versio: 017. I know, from Dereca, yes.

contents.textus: 018. I. Hawo me Rúṣyayo,  hawo me Almányayo.
contents.versio: 018. That one is from Russia, that one is from Germany.

contents.textus: 019. N. E, ʕal aʕ+ʕayne, ʕal aʕ+ʕayne.
contents.versio: 019. Yes, anything for you (lit. ‘upon the eyes’), anything for you!

contents.textus: 020. Əndrawus: B̥šayno aṯutu!
contents.versio: 020. You are welcome (lit. ‘you have come in peace’)!

contents.textus: 021. I. Tawdi ġắlabe, tawdi, ma hat bu+bayto kofayšat? Hēš lo+ḥzèlilux.
contents.versio: 021. Thank you so much, thank you, do you live in this house? I haven’t seen you yet.

contents.textus: 022. Nisane. E. Lo, lo! Hiye bu+bàytoyo, bu+bàytoyo. Kuzzé dawran daʕ+ʕeze, ksōm k̇elik̇at bu+bayto.
contents.versio: 022. Yes. No, no! He is at home. He takes our turn with the goats, he does small jobs at home.

contents.textus: 023. I. Ya, ṭawwo, ṭawwo, šafiro. Ma Xačo latyo bu+bayto? (01: 05)
contents.versio: 023. Oh, good, good, beautiful! Isn’t Xačo at home?

contents.textus: 024. N. Xáčostene, hawile ʕăza b Midən, azzeyo.
contents.versio: 024. Xačo too, he had a wake in Midən, he went.

contents.textus: 025. I. Aṯməl aḥna támowayna. Aṯməl azzáwayna li+ǧănaze l Midən. Aṯməl ono azzíwayno.
contents.versio: 025. I. Yesterday we were there. Yesterday we went to Midən for the funeral. I went yesterday.

contents.textus: 026. N. Di+qrìṯowa ya me dawlat aṯyowa?
contents.versio: 026. Did it belong to the village or had it come from abroad?

contents.textus: 027. I. Mṭówalle m Almanya.
contents.versio: 027. They brought it from Germany.

contents.textus: 028. N. Dmanwa?
contents.versio: 028. Whom did it belong to?

contents.textus: 029. I. Ḥanno Məšk̇e əmmíwayle.
contents.versio: 029. His name was (lit. ‘they used to call him’) Ḥanno Məšk̇e.

contents.textus: 030. N. Ooo, Ḥanno Məšk̇e...
contents.versio: 030. Oh, Ḥanno Məšk̇e...

contents.textus: 031. I. Ḥanno Məšk̇e.
contents.versio: 031. Ḥanno Məšk̇e.

contents.textus: 032. N. ăḷo kəmmanne, kəmmono, ‘Baḥ+ḥaye lo+koṯutu, uʕdo lmə‿kəmṭuṭu ak+kalašaṯxu ʕal rišan!’
contents.versio: 032. God, I tell them, I say, “You don’t come alive, now why do you bring your carcasses down upon our heads!”

contents.textus: 033. I. Háwxayo, háwxayo, háwxayo
contents.versio: 033. It’s like so, it’s like so, it’s like so… 02.07

contents.textus: 034. I. Ma, ḥulto, hat bu+ʕaslayḏax márkehat? Aw me dəkkoṯe hēšhat?
contents.versio: 034. Auntie, are you originally from here? Or are you from yet other places?

contents.textus: 035. N. Qusnáytono.
contents.versio: 035. N. I am a Bequsyonian.

contents.textus: 036. I. Hat qusnáytohat!
contents.versio: 036. I. You’re a Bequsyonian!

contents.textus: 037. N. Qusnáytono mbe Múqsino.
contents.versio: 037. I am Bequsyonian from the Muqsi family.

contents.textus: 038. I. Be Muqsi?
contents.versio: 038. The Muqsi family?

contents.textus: 040. I. Marke gawirat?
contents.versio: 040. Did you marry someone from here?

contents.textus: 041. N. E, be Danḥo, be Danḥo ad+derqubiye, be Ṣaliba Danḥo, ad+derqubiye hani, gawirono. Hani kli ḥamməš+ŭ+əšti+šnaye daṯyono larke. ʕƏmri ḥamməš+ŭ+tmoni+šnàyeyo.
contents.versio: 041. Yes, the Danho family, the Derqubian Danhos, the Saliba-Danho family, these Derqubians, I got married. See, it’s been (lit. ‘here they are’) 65 years since I came here. I’m eighty-five years old.

contents.textus: 042. I. Hat bi+qriṯo... dínaqqa dgawirat, bəkmo+ə̀šnewayt?
contents.versio: 042. I. You in the village... when you got married, how old were you?

contents.textus: 043. N. Bʕəsri.
contents.versio: 043. Nisan: Twenty.

contents.textus: 044. I. ʕƏsri+əšne! Xayifo lo+gawirat! Ġắlăbe noše bu+waxtawo xayifo gawriwa.
contents.versio: 044. Twenty years! You didn’t get married early! Many people at that time got married early.

contents.textus: 045. N. Yani dəmmono di+raṣtiye šwaʕ̥ṣar+tmonàʕ̥ṣarwayno. Ono ṭrowe ʕəsri. Hani dəmmina ḥamməš+ŭ+əšti daṯyono larke. ʕƏmri ḥamməš+ŭ+tmòniyo.
contents.versio: 045. I mean, to tell the truth, I was 17–18. For me, let it be 20. It’s been (lit. ‘they are’), let’s say, 65, since I came here. My age is eighty-five.

contents.textus: 046. I. Bele, šafiro. Kmo+naʕime kətlax? Bəṯr məd gawirat dəmmina kmo+naʕime hawilax?
contents.versio: 046. Yes, fine. How many children do you have? After you got married, let’s say, for you, how many children did you have?

contents.textus: 047. N. L ăḷo húleli arbaʕ̥ṣar+naʕime. Tloṯo māṯ, kīt – howən sāġ – kətli hēš ḥḏaʕ̥ṣar sāġ, əšto+k̇urrək̇at ŭ ḥamməš+k̇ačk̇at.
contents.versio: 047. God gave me fourteen children. Three died, there are – may they be healthy – I still have eleven living, six boys and five girls.

contents.textus: 048. I. Aloho morax ʕəmre das+sāġ, ŭ Aloho mḥase am+miṯe.
contents.versio: 048. May God prolong the life of the living, and may God bless the dead.

contents.textus: 049. N. Mḥásyene. Miḥasən am+miṯayḏux, ŭ Aloho ṭore dəṯxu, tavda.
contents.versio: 049. They are blessed. May your dead be blessed, and may God spare (lit. ‘abandon’) you, together (with mine).

contents.textus: 050. I. Miḥasyo i+emo ŭ u+babayḏax, tawdi ġắlăbe. Dínaqqa d̥kətwayt bi+qriṯo, dəmmina bәʕ̥ṣar+ə̀šnewayt, bәtraʕ̥ṣar+əšne, b̥ḥamšaʕ̥ṣar+əšne, mən šuġlo saymatwa bi+qriṯo, áydarbo ʕayšatwa bi+qriṯo?
contents.versio: 050. May your mother and father be blessed, thank you very much. When you were in the village, let’s say, when you were ten, twelve, fifteen, what kind of work would you do in the village, how would you live in the village?

contents.textus: 051. N. Bi+qriṯo u+šuġlo di+k̇urmanǧiye, di+qrìṯowa, kuḏʕat?
contents.versio: 051. In the village it was the work of Kurds, of the village, you know?

contents.textus: 052. I. Yani mən šuġlo mắsala, xud mən?
contents.versio: 052. Like, what kind of work, for example, like what?

contents.textus: 053. N. Ḥulwíwayna, kunšíwayna, mayʕíwayna, əzzáwayna lak+karsone dak+karme. Ḥzelux, ṭowíwayna, mṭíwayna pəštiyat. Ak+karsone, mṭíwaynanne lu+bayto bap+pəštiyat. Əzzáwayna lah+hažžək̇at bap+pəštiyat, əzzáwayna laṭ+ṭarfe bap+pəštiyat, ŭ mzaytíwayna ŭ ḥuṣdíwayna ŭ ʕuǧfíwayna. Gursíwayna ŭ dayqiwa, ḥzelux u+bərġəl? Mu+bərġəl bəṯr mnašfíwayle ŭ gursíwaynale bi+gorəsto... Dayqiwa, əmmiwa u+zmoro du+dyoqo ‘ḥe haye dayna ŭ haye.’ Əmmiwa hayo. Ŭ bəṯr gursíwayna i+gorə̀stostene, gursíwaynale, háyowa. Šuġle du+bayto...
contents.versio: 053. We would milk, clean up, make butter, go out for vine shoots. You’ve seen it, we would bind them, bring the bundles. The shoots, we would bring them back to the house in bundles. We would go out for twigs in bundles, to go out for branches in bundles, to make raisins and harvest or weed. We would grind and crush, have you seen bulgur? From the bulgur, after they dried it and we ground it in the handmill... They would crush it, they would sing the crushing song ḥe haye dayna w haye. They would say this. And then we would turn (lit. ‘grind’) the handmill too, we would turn it, it was like this. Housework...

contents.textus: 054. I. ǧġeni mu+dyoqo, dínaqqa dəmmiwa, ḥzelax, dəmmiwa ḥe haye... ʕam u+dyoqo, kə́twalxu hatu čirok̇at aw mắsayəl ḥrene dəmmūtwa aʕmayye? Dəmmina, kito hənna ʕam u+ḥṣodo kəmmi?
contents.versio: 054. Besides crushing, when they would say, you know, they would sing ḥe haye... with the crushing, did you have any other stories or sayings that you used to sing with them? Let’s say, are there some who say them while harvesting?

contents.textus: 055. N. Ašǝ́r əmmiwa zmaryoṯe ʕam u+dyoqo, ŭ bəṯr mu+dyoqo əmmiwa, ʕam u+gròsoste əmmíwayna. Mḥawliwa ak+kaloṯe əmmíwayna i+Hăvale.
contents.versio: 055. Really, they would sing songs with the crushing, and after the crushing they would sing, with the grinding too we would sing. They would relocate brides, we would sing Hevala.

contents.textus: 056. I. Dəmmina, ʕam u+groso mən əmmūtwa?
contents.versio: 056. Let’s say, with the grinding what did you sing?

contents.textus: 057. N. Əmmíwayna: Da bhēr, da bhēr dayəkē! ṫa ṫə žməna, xwəhik̇ē? Azē ṫa bəma nəšuk̇e! Nəšuk̇a, Mənuke ya!
contents.versio: 057. We would sing: Now grind, now grind, o Mother! What is it to you from me, o Sister? I will take you to the bath! It is the bath, Mənuke!

contents.textus: 058. Ax+xortin di+qriṯo, kulle ḥa b̥ḥa, əmmíwayna əšmayye. E, flānkasyo, hən əmmíwayna, ‘yaríxoyo lo+kubʕìnale!’ Hən əmmíwayna, ‘Káryoyo lo+kubʕìnale!’ Hən əmmíwayna, ‘Kómoyo lo+kubʕìnale!’ Hən əmmíwayna, ‘ḥewóroyo lo+kubʕìnale!’ Mṭíwayna k̇emayiyat aʕlayye. Latwa hawxa? ‘E, ma navek. Flānkás k̇əna, mə nave, flānkás dəreža, mə-navek. Hawxa čirok̇at. Hat Gule ... kuḏʕo b̥k̇urmanǧí.
contents.versio: 058. The lads of the village, each of them, one by one, we would say their names. Right, it’s So-and-So, some of us would say, ‘He’s tall, we don’t want him!’ Some of us would say, ‘He’s short, we don’t want him!’ Some of us would said, ‘He’s black, we don’t want him!’ Some of us would say, ‘He’s (pale) white, we don’t want him!’ We would find fault with them. Wasn’t it so? ‘Well, we don’t want him, So-and-so is short, I don’t want him, So-and-so is tall, I don’t want him’. Such sayings. You Gule ... she knows Kurmanji.

contents.textus: 059. I. Hani du+groso, ǧġeni me du+groso? Dəmmina, kətwa, dəmmina, xud̥‿kəmmat du+dyoqo du+bərġəl, ŭ du+groso, bašqa?
contents.versio: 059. These are grinding ones, something other than grinding? Let’s say, there was, let’s say, like you say about crushing bulgur, and about grinding, anything else?

contents.textus: 060. N. Du+dyoqo du+bə̀rġəlstene:
contents.versio: 060. About crushing bulgur as well:

contents.textus: 061. Ḥe haye! Dayna  ŭ haye!  Ḥəmma ŭ haye! Šarra, šarra, šarra! Xēra, xēra! ʕAl u+xēr! Hawxa əmmíwayna!
contents.versio: 061. Heave ho! Dump and ho! Heave and ho! It’s evil, it’s evil, it’s evil! It’s good, it’s good! For goodness’s sake! We would sing so!

contents.textus: 062. I. Bašqa dəmmina, ʕam u+ksoḥo, ʕam u+dworo?
contents.versio: 062. Anything else, let’s say, with the pruning, with the plowing?

contents.textus: 063. N. Ksoḥo, dworo lazzano, ləmmíwayna. Hanək ləmmíwayna aḥna. Bele, ag+gawre əmmiwa ʕam gab u+ḥṣodo bi+barriye, hayo, hayo lu+hno. Elo ak+kalòṯestene, məd mḥawlíwayna, əmmíwaynanne i+Hăvale.
contents.versio: 063. We didn’t go pruning (and) plowing, we wouldn’t sing. We wouldn’t sing those. Yes, the men would along with the harvesting in the wilderness, that (song), that one, for the whatsit. But the brides as well, when we relocated them, we would sing Hevala to them.

contents.textus: 064. I. Áydarbo əmmūtwa yani?
contents.versio: 064. How would you sing, like?

contents.textus: 065. N. Kakkō, zavā hēnū, raṣta! Qurbān, hēnū, raṣta! Barxə́ki šərkərí masṭa, Barxə́ki šərkərí masṭa, Ya go ṫa dvibū ma ž̥tara guhasto! Ya go ta dvibu, ma ž̥tara guhasto! Lili, lili, liliiii ...
contents.versio: 065. Brother, a groom newlywed, it’s real! Dear, a newlywed, it’s real! He is a lamb fed (lit. made) on milk, yoghurt, He is a lamb fed (lit. made) on milk, yoghurt, The one you were desiring, we brought (her) to you! The one you were desiring, we brought (her) to you! Lilii liilii liii

contents.textus: 066. Tawdi, ǧġeni mani ...
contents.versio: 066. Thank you, apart from these…

contents.textus: 067. Em, čūma Diyarbakər, Čūma xana bireda, havalē! Az hatəma xana bireda, havalē dalalē! Čəl zavak̇i tēda,havalē! Čəl zavak̇i tēda, haval dalalē! Zavák̇ēma lḥamūwa zēda, havalē! Zavák̇ema lḥamūwa zēda, havalē dalalē! Lili, lilii, liliiii
contents.versio: 067. As for us, I went to Diyarbakir, I went to a roadside inn, friend!  I came to a roadside inn, dear friend! Forty grooms were in it, friend! Forty grooms were in it, dear friend! Our little bridegroom is the greatest of them all, friend! Our little bridegroom is the greatest of them all, dear friend! Liili Liilii Liilii

contents.textus: 068. I. Tawdi, tawdi ġắlăbe. Haṯe k̬makfo. ǧġeni mani, bu+səryoyo? Hani dmərlax am+medone, dmirilax, aġlab mənne bu+kùrdine, bu+lešono, bu+k̇urmanǧì.
contents.versio: 068. Thank you, thank you very much. This is enough. Apart from these, in Aramaic? These ones you said, these things that you said, most of them are in Kurdish, in the language, in Kurmanji.

contents.textus: 069. N. E, šxwa, lo+maqballe, əmmiwa, ‘B̥səryoyo mar’
contents.versio: 069. Yes, of course, they didn’t accept it, they would say, ‘Say it in Səryoyo!’

contents.textus: 070. I. Bu+səryoyo dilok̇at hawxa aw zmaryoṯe hawxa hīč ləmmūtwa?
contents.versio: 070. Would you never sing such songs or such chants in Səryoyo?

contents.textus: 071. N. A+ḥrene uʕdo dməḷḷi, Gule, hani dmirili malə‿kanné gabayxu mqayde?
contents.versio: 071. The other ones I have now sung, Gule, these ones that I sang, aren’t they here recorded by you?

contents.textus: 072. I. Gabayye, hənnək, kətte hawxa čirok̇at alle.
contents.versio: 072. By them, they, they have such stories.

contents.textus: 073. I. Koguršo i+dəqqayḏi d̥kuḏʕat ġắlăbe lešono kurdí, k̇urmanǧi!
contents.versio: 073. It strikes me that you know Kurdish very well, Kurmanji!

contents.textus: 074. N. Kuḏʕono, kuḏʕono, ṭaw mak+k̇urmā̀nǧ, kuḏʕono.
contents.versio: 074. I know, I know, better than Kurds, I know it.

contents.textus: 075. I. Mayko yalifat, áydarbo?
contents.versio: 075. Whence did you learn it, how?

contents.textus: 076. N. Ono naʕəmto, i+šato di+ġala, b̚ Mārbobo ṭaye ŭ ṣuroye baynə‿ḥḏoḏéwayna.
contents.versio: 076. As a young girl, the year of the famine, the Muslims and Syriacs, we were together in Mārbobo.

contents.textus: 077. I. b̚ Mārbobo.
contents.versio: 077. In Mārbobo.

contents.textus: 078. N. E, b̚ Mārbobo i+šato di+ġala, laḥmo latwa duxlina. Lu+qamṣo ŭ li+raqqək̇e xəlle u+zād.
contents.versio: 078. Yes, in Mārbobo, the year of the famine, there was no bread for us to eat. The locust and the sunn pest ate the grain.

contents.textus: 079. I. Harke?
contents.versio: 079. Here?

contents.textus: 080. N. E aḥna naʕime, ha háwxawayna. Azzán l Mārbobo, ḥuṣdiwa, babi əzzewa ḥoṣadwa. Emi, ono ḥamməš+šnayo, mayiṯo. Babi ḥoṣadwa bu+magzuno. Xud̥ kəmmat, zəmriwa, ŭ ḥoṯi rab míniwa, kətwa tre+tloṯo+naʕime bayn eli ŭ ela, mnaqyowa aš+šəble hawxa, šəblo+šəblo. Lu+laqṭo, əmmíwayna.
contents.versio: 080. Yes, we as small children, we were like this. We went to Mārbobo, they would harvest, my father would go and harvest. My mother died when I was five years old. My father would harvest with a sickle. Like you say, they would sing, and my sister was older than me, there are two or three children between me and her, she would pick ears of grain like so, ear by ear. To glean, we would call it.

contents.textus: 081. I. Laqṭo?
contents.versio: 081. Gleaning?

contents.textus: 082. N. E laqṭo. Ánnaqqa saymiwa boqoṯe hawxa. Kətwa, ḥzelux, lavlavk̇e mi+yarəxtayo da+freze, layfiwa aʕlayye, saymiwa ʕoruwwo. Ánnaqqa ínaqqa d̥saymiwa u+ʕoruwwawo...
contents.versio: 082. Yes, gleaning. Then they would make sheaves like so. There was, you have seen, bindweed from that long <kind of bindweed> of the stubble fields, they would wrap it on them, they used to make ʕoruwwo. Then, when they made that ʕoruwwo...

contents.textus: 083. I. ʕOruwwo mənyo?
contents.versio: 083. What is ʕoruwwo?

contents.textus: 084. N. ʕOruwwo boqoṯe hawxa... ánnaqqa mxalfə́nwanne ʕal ḥḏoḏe, məḥyówayla b̥ḥaṣa xud i+pəštiye, əmṭowalle li+adro. E! U+yawmo dəmkamliwa u+ḥṣodo, mdaqd̥qówalle, howənwa ṭaʕno d̥ḥeṭe. E.
contents.versio: 084. ʕOruwwo are sheaves like so… now then, they would intertwine them together, she (i.e., her sister) would put it on her back like a bundle, she would bring them to the threshing floor. Right! The day they would finish the harvest, she would thresh them, they would become a load of wheat. Right.

contents.textus: 085. I. U+mawsimayḏa, dmaləmla kul+mede ṭaʕno d̥ḥéṭewa?
contents.versio: 085. Her season, what she collected, the whole thing, was a load of wheat?

contents.textus: 086. N. E, ṭaʕno, yani u+ḥṣodo kule. Ṭaʕno d̥ḥeṭe gəmṭowa, ŭ hawxa. Tamo hedi yalifono, ono naʕə́mtowayno. Kətwa čalkoye, kətwa ṭaye. Hḗšstene ono d̥kuzzí l Mārbobo, uʕdo azzí ltarte+ʕăzāt l Mārbobo. Yani an+nošaṯxu dbe Gabre, aḥna ŭ hənnək yakrə́ḥwayna, hənnək ŭ be babi. Hul uʕdo kanné b Balčiqa, he kuzzə́n ʕal riše dəḥḏoḏe.
contents.versio: 086. Yes, a load, like, it’s the whole harvest. She would bring a load of wheat, and so forth. There I slowly learned it, I was a child. There were Yezidis, there were Muslims. Until now, whenever I go to Mārbobo, I just went to two wakes. Like, your people, the Gabre family, we and they were intimates, they and my father’s family. Even now, they’re over there in Belgium, they still keep visiting each other.

contents.textus: 087. I. Koḏaʕno, ḥzili b Balčiqa.
contents.versio: 087. I know, I saw them in Belgium.

contents.textus: 088. N. Ánnaqqa hawxa, yalifono kŭrmanǧí.
contents.versio: 088. So this way, I learned Kurmanji.

contents.textus: 089. I. U+kŭrmanǧíyayḏax ṭáwwoyo ġắlabe.
contents.versio: 089. Your Kurmanji is very good.

contents.textus: 090. N. E, ašǝ́r ṭaw mənne kŭḏʕono.
contents.versio: 090. Yes, really I know it better then they do.

contents.textus: 091. I. Bele, bəṯr məd daʕirutu me Mārbobo ... áydarbo daʕirutu me Mārbobo?
contents.versio: 091. Yes, after you returned from Mārbobo… How did you return from Mārbobo?

contents.textus: 092. N. Daʕirina ... tarte+tlaṯə+šnaye, koṯe lboli, məd moṭənwa aʕ+ʕənwe, oṯíwayna ʕal aʕ+ʕənwe, ŭ bu+saṯwo disa‿zzáwayno l Mārbobo. Aḥuni‿zzewa qmann+arwonk̇at dam+Marbabiye. Golək̬vanwa. Ŭ aḥuni u+ḥreno, kə́twaylan ḥaməš‿što qanyone, əzzewa ʕam u+baqoro, əmmíwaynale Mḥammado, ṭayo. Əzzewa aʕme, ánnaqqa kul+ʕrəfto … lo kul+ʕrəfto ŭ lo kul+lalyo. Xano i+barṯo kurxowa ʕal u+laḥmo, kurxowa ʕal u+laḥmo, kul+naqqa gdomarwa ‘Haw ḥamməš+šeṯ+ṭalme l Dawudo! Kotoʕab aʕmi, komʕawalli baq+qanyone.’ Əmṭówaylan ḥamməš+šeṯ+ṭalme dlaḥmo. Ba lo+kafìnewayna! Ġálawa! Hawxa.
contents.versio: 092. We returned… during two-three years, I remember, when the grapes ripened, we would come back for the grapes, and in the winter we went again to Mārbobo. My brother would herd the calves of the Mārbobians. He was a calfherd. And my other brother, we had five cows, he went with the shepherd, they called him Mohammed, a Muslim. He went with him, now then, every Friday … either every Friday or every evening. Xano the daughter went for bread, she would go for bread, and each time he would say, “Give five-six rings to Dawudo! He toils with me, he helps me with the cattle…” She would bring us five-six rings of bread. Oh, were we not hungry?! It was a famine! Like so.

contents.textus: 093. I. Bəṯr ann+əšne di+ġala d̥fayiti, daʕirutu me Mārbobo?
contents.versio: 093. After the years of famine that passed, did you return from Mārbobo?

contents.textus: 094. N. E, e, daʕirina l Mārbobo, daʕirina l Mārbobo, hedi babi azzé li+ʕaskăriye. Babi bi+ʕaskăriye, mayiṯo emi. Aṯi mi+ʕaskăriye, aḥunoni hawən rabe, edi babi dwəḷḷe ŭ aḥuni, aḥunoni ḥəfriwa qăfare hawxa. Kuḏʕat vega?!
contents.versio: 094. Yes, yes, we returned to Mārbobo, we returned to Mārbobo, then my father went to the military. With my father in the military, my mother died. He came from the military, my brothers grew up, then my father farmer and my brother, my brothers dug stony patches like so. So, you know?

contents.textus: 095. I. Qufre?
contents.versio: 095. Stony patches?

contents.textus: 096. N. Qufre … E, ŭ hedi hawina more ... hawən aḥ+ḥeṭayḏan, fayšiwa lderṫə́r šato, ŭ a+sʕorayḏan hawxa, edí sawiʕina! Haw azzán l Mārbobo, sawiʕina!
contents.versio: 096. Stony patches… Yes, and then we took care … our wheat reappeared, it lasted till the next year, and our barley like so, then we had enough! We no longer went to Mārbobo, we had enough!

contents.textus: 097. I. Fayišutu b Bequsyone?
contents.versio: 097. Did you stay in Bequsyone?

contents.textus: 098. N. E, fayišina b Bequsyone huuul uʕdo, hul uʕdo. Ba+šnayani dazzə́n l Barčiqa ... ono ... hedi aṯən larke. U+năṣibayḏi aṯi larke. Húwalli larke, ŭ hə́nnəkstene mṭalle tarte mi+qriṯo, tlaṯ mi+qriṯo, mṭalle šan aḥunoni, ŭ ṫə žməra sāġ!
contents.versio: 098. Yes, we stayed in Bequsyone uppp to now, up to now! In these years that they went to Belgium… I ... then they came here (to Derqube). My fate brought me here (lit. my fate came here). They gave me (in marriage) here, and they also brought two from the village, three from the village (Bequsyone), they brought them for my brothers, and that’s the end of the story!

contents.textus: 099. I. Aḥunonax hani uʕdo b Awrúpane?
contents.versio: 099. Are your brothers now in Europe?

contents.textus: 100. N. E, ḥa mənne mḥase...
contents.versio: 100. Yes, one of them passed away (lit. ‘was blessed’)…

contents.textus: 101. I. Ăloho mḥasele!
contents.versio: 101. God bless him!

contents.textus: 102. N. Miḥase miṯux! Kalé Dawudo ŭ Marawge b Awrupa, b Bárčiqa. Aḥuni uʕdo more d̥kíboyo, kalé ʕal ab+baḥare bə Sṭambəl. Ŭ u+Dawudo kalé b Bárčiqa. Yawme d̥ḥušabo səmme i+qandelayḏe. Ŭ aḥuni azzé lu+Qŭdəs. Kəmmi ‘Be Muqsi Šaʕo’, aḥna u+ahlayḏan. Ánnaqqa aḥuni bəšme d Muqsi Šáʕowa. Omar, ‘Bə́šmeno, gəzzí lu+Qŭdəs!’ Azzé háwoste lu+Qŭdəs, səmle u+qud̥sayḏe, ŭ aṯi bəṯr mu+Qŭdəs, tarte+šnayo mḥase háwoste. Miḥase miṯux. Ăḷo mḥasele. Ŭ kanné an+naʕimaṯṯe b Bárčiqa. E, hawxa.
contents.versio: 102. Let your dead be blessed! Dawudo and Marawge are there in Europe, in Belgium. Now my brother has an infirmity, he is there on the seas in Istanbul. And Dawudo is there in Belgium. On Sunday they gave him last rites. And a brother of mine went to Jerusalem. They say ‘the Muqsi Šaʕos’, us and our family. Now then, my brother went the name of ‘Muqsi Šaʕo’. He says, ‘I (already) go by its name, I’ll go to Jerusalem!’ That one also went to Jerusalem, he made his pilgrimage, and then came back from Jerusalem, and two years ago that one also passed (lit. ‘was blessed’). Let your dead be blessed! God bless him. And their children are there in Belgium. Yes, it’s like so.

contents.textus: 103. I. Koṯən naqqawoṯe larke?
contents.versio: 103. Do they come here sometimes?

contents.textus: 104. N. E, koṯən, koṯən, koṯən.
contents.versio: 104. Yes, they come, they come, they come.

contents.textus: 105. I. An+naʕimayḏax, hani, láḏəʕnanne?
contents.versio: 105. Your children, these ones, didn’t I know them?

contents.textus: 106. N. An+naʕime ... hano u+rabo dmə́ḷḷilux díḏiyo, ŭ hawhok̇é d̥kətyo smixo li+hno du+abràyḏiyo, ŭ hano d̥kətyo yatiwo di+barṯàyḏiyo, ŭ hawhok̇este di+barṯo du+abro dbarḥmayo.
contents.versio: 106. The children ... this big one I told you about is mine, and as for that there one who is propped up against the whatsit (i.e., the wall) is my son’s, and this one who is sitting is my daughter’s, and that there one too, he’s my brother-in-law’s son’s daughter’s.

contents.textus: 107. I. Yani, harke kofayši?
contents.versio: 107. Like, are they living (lit. ‘staying’) here?

contents.textus: 108. N. Lo! Lo! Diḏan hárkene, elo hano kowe b̥ Ḥāḥ, bi+Ndaṯalo̥ d̥ Ḥāḥ. U+babo ŭ i+emo xodúmene.
contents.versio: 108. No! No! Ours are here, but this one is in Ḥāḥ, at the Church of the Theotokos. His father and his mother are caretakers.

contents.textus: 109. I. u+ʕAzī́z?
contents.versio: 109. Aziz?

contents.textus: 111. I. Koḏaʕne ṭawwo.
contents.versio: 111. I know him well.

contents.textus: 112. N. U+ḥaṯnàyḏiyo.
contents.versio: 112. My son-in-law.

contents.textus: 113. I. Koḏaʕne ṭowo lu+ʕAzī́z.
contents.versio: 113. I know Aziz well.

contents.textus: 114. N. Ŭ hawhéstene kowe b Bequsyone. U+aḥuno du+šamošo dwáxtak̇eyo, u+babayḏe. Háwoste, u+babayḏe məlfónoyo. Hánoste, ǧare dlo+kowe ḥaḏiro, hánoste məlfono. Hano diḏan qrele maktab, mkamele u+maktab. Uʕdo lu+dayroyo Aḥo di+Der Ġəzalk̇e ṭləble, omar, ‘Kobaʕno doṯe gabi’. Kowe qəm iḏe.
contents.versio: 114. N. That there one is in Bequsyone. He is the late deacon’s brother, his father. That one as well, his father is a teacher. This one too (i.e., his father), it happens that he isn’t present, this one too, he’s a teacher. This one of ours studied at school, he finished school. Now the monk Aḥo of Der Ġəzalk̇e asked, saying, ‘I want him to come to me’. He is with him.

contents.textus: 115. I. Šafiro, šafiro.
contents.versio: 115. Beautiful, beautiful.

contents.textus: 116. N. Omar, ‘Gmaqrene Făransawi ŭ Həngilisí ŭ ṣluṯo’. I+ṭămayiyayo səmlan.
contents.versio: 116. He says, ‘I will teach him French, English, and prayer’. That became a great attraction for us (lit. ‘we committed that act of greed’, no irony is implied).

contents.textus: 117. I. Ṭawwo.
contents.versio: 117. Good!

contents.textus: 118. N. Me ṭawwuṯux kəmmat. U+yawmawo azzano gabe, əmmono, ‘Abuna dayroyo, Ăloho lo+ḥošawlan kəbariye, ašǝ́r lo mi+faqiriye mtaraslan, ašǝ́r latwa zeyúdoste, hăma əmmat, ‘Səmxu mayliye’. Maḥatlan tre mənne, kanné b Mor Awgín koqorən suryoyo. Əmmat, ‘Yade, kosaymat mayliye, mtaraslax an+naʕimayḏax l Mor Awgín ŭ ono fāšno tăne. Edi hăma əmmina ... əmmat, ‘Gmolafne Faransawi ŭ Hənglisi ŭ ṣluṯo..’. Ăḷa latwa zeyudo. Mašraṭ u+yawmo dәmṭele larke, azzé l Kárboran, mṭele əšto+šawʕo+ʕiščiye, u+yawmaṯṯe obéwalle tmoni+malyune. Mnagliwa i+arʕo məqmi+kapča. Veǧa, hawxa.
contents.versio: 118. You speak from your goodness. That day we went to him, I said, ‘Father Monk, may God not count it as arrogance towards us, really we sent him not out of poverty, really he wasn’t a burden (lit. ‘superfluous’) either, but you say, ‘You were partial’. We placed two of them (i.e., the grandchildren), here they are in Mor Awgin, studying Syriac. You say, ‘Mommy, you are being partial, you sent your children to Mor Awgin, and I have stayed on my own’. But then we say ... you say, ‘I will teach him French, English, and prayer…”’ Gosh, he wasn’t a burden. Believe it or not, the day he brought him here, he (i.e., the grandson) went to Kerboran, he brought back 6–7 workers, and gave them eight million daily. They cleared the field with the excavator. Now then, it’s like so.

contents.textus: 119. I. Ṭawwo, šafiro! Kətxu šəwole mede dəmmutu hatu?
contents.versio: 119. Good, beautiful! Do you have more questions to ask?

contents.textus: 120. N. Kibi dəmmanxu i+ṭafṭafòreste, lo+kowe?
contents.versio: 120. I can also tell you the ‘Ṭafṭafore,’ or not?

contents.textus: 121. I. Lo, aḥna kəbʕina dəmšaylina, aḥna kəbʕina dəmšaylina ʕal aḥ+ḥayayḏax.
contents.versio: 121. No, we want to ask you, we want to ask you about your life.

contents.textus: 122. N. ʕAl aḥ+ḥayayḏi?
contents.versio: 122. About my life?

contents.textus: 123. I. Aḥ+ḥayayḏax. Fahəmno, aṯat, maṭat hul dgawirat. Bəṯr məd gawirat, aṯat fayišat bi+Derqube, áydarbo morawxu an+naʕime? Áydarbo an+naʕime yariwi, mən šəkəl?
contents.versio: 123. Your life. As I understood, you came, you got as far as you got married. After you got married, you came to stay in Derqube, how did you all raise the children? How did the children grow up, in what way?

contents.textus: 124. N. Hayo ġắlăbe, ġắlăbe ṣáʕbowa.
contents.versio: 124. This was very, very difficult.

contents.textus: 125. I. Mə‿šəkəl yani ʕayšūtwa aḥ+ḥayani?
contents.versio: 125. How did you live this life?

contents.textus: 126. N. Mašraṭ, mašraṭ əzzáwayna lu+ḥṣodo, qaymíwayna. Mašraṭ məʕli, ḥluli aʕ+ʕeze ŭ aq+qanyone, ŭ qayimono, saliqono li+goro... ḥzelux. Kəmmi saxmat daqrone, aḥna ... kəmmi saxma. Mayʕiwa bu+gawdo.
contents.versio: 126. Believe it or not, believe it or not, we would go harvest, we would get up. Believe it or not, I churned, I milked goats and cattle, and I got up, I went up to the roof… you’ve seen it. They call them churns, we ... they say ‘churn’ (lit. ‘pole’), they churned in a goatskin.

contents.textus: 127. I. Saxma, bele.
contents.versio: 127. ‘Churn’, yes.

contents.textus: 128. N. Hawxa dmayʕiwa bu+gawdo.
contents.versio: 128. They churned in a goatskin like so.

contents.textus: 129. I. Bele, bele, koḏaʕno ṭawwo.
contents.versio: 129. Yes, yes, I know it well.

contents.textus: 130. N. Mašraṭ tlaṯ+kayat məʕli hul dnafəq u+yawmo.
contents.versio: 130. Believe it or not, I churned three times before the sun came out.

contents.textus: 131. I. Tlaṯ+kayat? Ġắlăbe xayifo qaymatwa.
contents.versio: 131. Three times? You would get up very early.

contents.textus: 132. N. E, qaymówayno falge+dlalyo. Hăma d̥solaqwa u+kəkwo dənhoroṯe qaymówayno ŭ hawxa əzzáwayna saymíwayna i+labaniye, saymíwayna u+laḥmo, saymíwayna ak̇+k̇elik̇ayḏan. Əzzáwayna ʕam a+zlamat lu+ḥṣodo. E, ínaqqa dləzzáwayna lu+ḥṣodo, doṯewa, nuqlíwayna aš+šale, nuqlówayno šáleste li+adro. Məd aaa... aš+šale, nqililan li+adro, tux mar lu+ʕaql! Saymíwayna u+šuġlayḏan, disa kunšíwayna ŭ maqərṭíwayna u+ḥalwayḏan, saymíwayna ŭ mayʕíwayna, hníwayna, hul doṯənwa aq+qanyone d̥falge dyawmo, kuḏʕat! Hedika gəd... gəzzíwayno məṣrówaynanne. Məṣrówaynanne, bi+kalle d̥falge+dyawmo, i+saʕaye ba+ṭraḥṣar. Makərxíwayna, makərxíwayna baq+qanyone bi+adro...
contents.versio: 132. Yes, I would get up at midnight. When the morning star rose, I would get up and so we would go to make ‘labaniye’, we would make bread, we would do our chores. We would go with the men to harvest. Yes, when we wouldn’t go to harvest, when (the time) would come, we would carry the sacks, I would carry sacks as well to the threshing floor. When we carried the sacks to the threshing floor, forget about it. We would do our work, over and over we would sweep, and we would curdle our milk, we would do it and churn, we would whatsit, until the cattle would come at noon, you know! Then we will ... we would go, we would tie them up. We would tie them up, at the peak of noon, 12 o’clock. We would thresh, we would thresh with the cattle on the threshing floor…

contents.textus: 133. I. Bi+gera?
contents.versio: 133. While threshing?

contents.textus: 134. N. Bu+ḥemo.
contents.versio: 134. In the heat.

contents.textus: 135. I. I+gera?
contents.versio: 135. Threshing?

contents.textus: 136. N. E, i+gera. Bu+ḥemawo, dəmmina, huuul dmirastqo, i+saʕaye hăka tlaṯ+arbaʕ, u+baqoro qore, ‘Heee azzá i+baqro, arfewu aq+qanyone!’ Henú g̥̊šəryówayno aq+qanyone maʕl‿i+draxa, qulʕówaynanne lu+ṭuro. Əṯyówayno, disa saymówayno ak̇+k̇elik̇ayḏan. Ma ʕəmro mašfaʕlan!? Ġắlăbe ṣáʕbowa, ŭ ʕam gab an+naʕime.
contents.versio: 136. Yes, threshing. With that heat, so to speak, uppp until (the cattle) head straight out around 3–4 (p.m.), the cowherd calls, ‘Heeey! The cattle’s gone, let the cattle go!’ Then I would release the cattle from upon the threshed stuff, I would drive them to the hill country. I would come back, I would do our chores again. Were we leading a life!? It was very hard, in addition to (lit. ‘alongside’) the children.

contents.textus: 137. I. ʕAm u+medano, ʕam u+šuġlano haqqa yaquro, áydarbo saymūtwa an+naʕime?
contents.versio: 137. In this way, with work so burdensome, how would you handle the children?

contents.textus: 138. N. An+naʕime, hăša dəṯxu, du+kăramaṯxu, xud aǧ+ǧewə̀rk̇atwayne. Mašraṭ saymiwa bruḥayye ŭ dəmxiwa aʕlayye. Gəm+gəm dad+dədwone aʕlayye, ma răzala ḥzelan! Ánnaqqa ma hawo tăne!? Əzzáwayna lu+ṭuro, əmṭíwayna fədrat, kəmmutu tadre ... be mə‿kəmmútәnne?
contents.versio: 138. The children, excuse me, with all due respect to you, they were like puppies. Believe it or not, they would go on themselves and sleep on it. The buzz-buzz of flies upon them, didn’t we see the worst of it!? Now then, just that!? We would go to the hill country, we would bring back ox tongues, you call them tadre… What do you call them?

contents.textus: 139. I. Fadrat mənne?
contents.versio: 139. What are ox tongues?

contents.textus: 140. N. Fəḏre – gelo, uʕdo xud a+šrule kowən, fəḏre...
contents.versio: 140. Ox tongues – a plant, now they are like creepers, ox tongues…
141. Right.

contents.textus: 142. N. Hatu kəmmutu tadre, be mə kəmmútənne? Xud a+šrùlene, kowən ha maṭ+ṭuronānhò, əzzáwayna, bap+pəštiyat əmṭíwaynanne ...
contents.versio: 142. You say tadre, how do you call them? They are like vines, they grow up in yon mountains there, we would go, we would bring them back in bundles.

contents.textus: 143. I. Hano gelo lu+săwā̀l əmṭúṭuwayle?
contents.versio: 143. This plant, you would bring it for the livestock?

contents.textus: 144. N. Lo, lo. Mdaqdəqíwaynanne bak+kefe, šežən naxwašṫə́r mdəṯṯe layto. Kəmmina ʕaynənto, ŭ ánnaqqa ḥurkíwaynanne bu+ḥurako, bi+manduriye hawxa, hul d̥owənwa xud u+muḥo. Saymíwayna qaweləb du+ṭino, guršíwayna i+ḥame aʕlayye, ḥame du+qaṭmo guršíwayna aʕlayye ŭ maḥtíwayna af+fəḏranək aʕlayye ŭ saymíwaynanne qaḥfuroṯe. Ma lə+ḥzelux qaḥfuroṯe?
contents.versio: 144. No, no. We would crush them with stones, there is no toil (lit. ‘nature’) worse than theirs. We say ʕaynənto, and, now then, we would grind them with a grinding stone, with a stone roller like so, until they would become like brain. We would make clay molds, we would smear them with sludge, ash sludge we would smear upon them and would place (a paste made from) those ox tongues upon them and we would make grain vessels from them. Haven’t you seen grain vessels?

contents.textus: 145. I. Qaḥfurat, qaḥfure ...
contents.versio: 145. Grain vessels…

contents.textus: 146. N. E, qaḥfurat.
contents.versio: 146. Right, grain vessels.

contents.textus: 147. I. Qaḥfure, fahəmno!
contents.versio: 147. Grain vessels, I understand!

contents.textus: 148. N. Ánnaqqa, saymíwaynanne nəčk̇at hawxa, kaviyat, saymíwaynanne arbaʕ+nəčkat ha hawxa bi+xaṣraṯe ŭ b̥aṯe, ŭ haṯe hawxa. Arbaʕ+nəčkat.
contents.versio: 148. Now then, we would make them handles, like so, edges, we would make them four handles, here like so, on this side and on this one, and this one as well. Four handles.

contents.textus: 149. Ánnaqqa nuqšíwaynanne, balki ḥzallux. Bu+kalšo edi. Hənnək hē hənnək taʔile, nuqšíwaynanne bu+kalšooo. ʕAwwǝ́li ḥamməš, bəṯr tlaṯ, bəṯr tarte, ŭ bəṯr ḥḏo.
contents.versio: 149. Then we would paint them, maybe you saw them. With lime, then. While they were still wet, we would paint them with lime. First five (markings), then three, then two, then one.

contents.textus: 150. Uʕdo hē kit naqšat du... du ... naqšat ....I+kalayo dan+naʕime. Áykoyo? Hayo d̥kətyo ... dəmṭolux me Məḏyaḏ, i+qamayto.
contents.versio: 150. Now there are still markings… of… of ... markings … The children’s doll. Where is it? That one that’s ... which you brought from Midyat, the first one.

contents.textus: 151. Hawxa nuqšíwaynanne, hul tmanyo+yawme, ʕəṣro+yawme... Maydíwaynanne meʕal u+qālbawo, gawayye he taryo, gmolíwaynanne ʕafro. Msawíwayna hawxa i+arʕo, maḥtíwayna hawxa arʕayye bdŭkṯo rakuto, molíwaynanne ʕafro. Howewa arʕayye ha hawxa, qaḥfuro ltarte+ʕelab zād. B̥awo nuqlíwayna u+zād! Ḥzelux talisat latwa, ŭ naylonat mani lə+nfəqle. B̥anək, ăḷo, iḏan məmlənwa kube hul dmixarǧiwa. Ŭ b̥anək nuqlíwayna.
contents.versio: 151. We would paint them like so, till eight days, ten days ... We would take them off that mold, their insides still wet, we would fill them with soil. We would level the ground like so, we would put their bottoms like so on a flat spot, we would fill them with soil. Their bottom was like so, a vessel for two bushels of grain. In that one we would transport grain. You see (lit. ‘you saw’), there were no sacks, and these nylon bags hadn’t come out. Because of those ones, gosh, our hands were filled with thorns until they were inured. And with those ones we would transport (grain).

contents.textus: 152. Saymíwayna ṭino: əmṭíwayna ʕafro, matríwaynale ŭ layšíwaynale braġlan ŭ bəṯr saymíwaynale feləḥyoṯe du+ṭino hawxa. Ŭ bəṯr mraqqíwaynale, saymináwayna kore. Moṭənwa lu+qṭoro. Əzzewa tleṯi+arbʕi+ʕelab, əzzéwalle, ma lə+ḥzallux?
contents.versio: 152. We would make mud: we would bring soil, we would wet it, we would knead it with our feet, and afterwards we would make them into mud bricks like so. And after that we would thin it, we would make grain bins. They would reach the ceiling. It would fit (lit. 'it would go’) 30–40 bushels, it would fit them, haven’t you seen them?

contents.textus: 153. I. Bele, ak+kore ḥzili.
contents.versio: 153. Yes, grain bins, I saw them.

contents.textus: 154. N. E, hánəkste...
contents.versio: 154. Yes, those ones also…

contents.textus: 155. I. Bas i+koro ḥəzyoli, i+dəkke, áydarboyo?
contents.versio: 155. But the grain bin I have seen, the dəkke, what’s it like?

contents.textus: 156. N. I+dəkke mənyo?
contents.versio: 156. What is the dəkke?

contents.textus: 157. I. I+dəkke.
contents.versio: 157. The dəkke.

contents.textus: 158. N. I+dəkke. Dəkkánatne hanək dəmxiwa aʕlayye.
contents.versio: 158. The dəkke. Dəkkanat (‘ledges’) are those upon which they would sleep.

contents.textus: 159. I. Mani bu+šəklano.
contents.versio: 159. One of these sort of things (lit. ‘in this shape’).

contents.textus: 160. N. E, e, hanək ... šan dmolənne hawxa, maḥti rezat d̥kefe ŭ buġre, ŭ bəṯr g̊šayʕiwa hawxa ŭ yətwiwa aʕlayye. Xud uʕdo bdukṯe d̥ani.
contents.versio: 160. Yes, yes, those ... in order to fill them like so, they put rows of stones and pebbles, and then they would plaster them like so, and would sit upon them. Like now, instead of these things.

contents.textus: 161. E, at+tanùreste, saymówayno tanúreste. At+tanùreste ʕayn bu+šəkl dak+kore, hăma ʕafro ṭowo. ʕAfro ṭowo dlowe buġurk̇at ebe, glayšíwaynale mgawlčíwaynale hawxa hawxa hawxa biḏoṯan, čik̇e dbuġurk̇o xud riše dəmḥaṭo lo+ṭorina ebe. ŭ g̊saymówayne tloṯo+damse, arbʕo+damse, g̊fōšwa feme ldērṫə́r yawmo. Dērṫə́r yawmo g̊saymíwayna fémeste, g̊fōšwa qădar ʕəṣro+ʕəṣri+yawme... lgorā́n di+šəmšo, hul dəḏʕina našəf. Maydínale maḥtínale bu+šuro, ŭ čík̇ənk̇e ha hawxa d̥owe ṣṭān. ŭ šayʕiwa, šayʕíwaynale arʕe, ŭ maḥtíwayna šayʕíwaynale, dək ... saymíwaynale dəkkane hawxa xud̥‿kəmmat, dukṯe du+tāšt, dukṯe di+ṣeniye dam+maye, ŭ mədə‿ǧġəḷḷan, kaməl. Edi gəmblina u+layšo dawqina ebe. Ha kəpxu vega əzzoxu, ha klehé tamhó zoxu lqule. Hawxa, háwoste hawxa saymíwayna.
contents.versio: 161. Yes, the tannoors as well, I would also make tannoors. The tannoors too, exactly like the grain bins, but good soil. Good soil, so there are no small pebbles in it, we would knead it, we would mess it up like so, like so, like so with our hands, a bit of a small pebble like a needle head, we wouldn’t leave in it. And I would make three rings, four rings, and its mouth would wait until the next day. The next day we would make its mouth as well, it would wait roughly ten-twenty days, depending on the sun, till we learned that it had become dry. We take it, we put it by the wall, so that it is slanted a little bit like so. And they plastered over, we plastered over its bottom, and we would put it and plaster over it, we would make it a dəkkane like you say, a place for a basin, a place for a water bowl, and when we fired it up, it became finished. Then we take the dough to stick in it. Here you can now go, here it is over there, go over to it (lit. ‘in front of it’). So, that one too, we would make like so.

contents.textus: 162. Ŭ at+tavnat: ʕuzlíwayna <b>i+taši<ye>, ʕuzlíwayna <b>i+tašiye, blalyo ŭ bimomo i+tašiye bíḏanwa. Mkamlíwayna u+ʕazlo, mašqíwaynale, saymíwayna tavnat bu+hap. Saymíwayna tavnat bu+hap. Maló kətyo ḥzelux?
contents.versio: 162. And carpets: we would spin with a spindle, we would spin with a spindle, night and day the spindle was in our hands. We would finish the yarn, we would moisten it, we would make carpets with a weaving comb. We would make carpets with a weaving comb. Haven’t you seen it?

contents.textus: 163. I. Bele.

164. N. Hawxa, ha ʕumran hawxa mašfaʕlan. Ánnaqqa uʕdo lə+kˠqaymi hul dlo+nofaq u+yawmo qumṯo. Myoʕo lo+fāš, makkínayo. Knošo lo+fāš, makkínayo. Layšo makkínayo, tešiġo daǧ+ǧule makkínayo. I+naqqayo faqiríyewa. Me yawme tre hul yawme d̥šabṯo mraqʕíwayna aǧ+ǧəlk̇at dan+naʕimayḏan. Moḥíwaynanne ruqʕe. Quṭʕíwayna ḥa, moḥíwaynale lḥa, moḥíwaynale ruqʕe. Hawxa.
contents.versio: 164. So, we led this life of ours like so. Now then, nowadays they do not get up until the sun rises head-high (lit. ‘a height [of a person]’). Churning didn’t last, it’s a machine. Sweeping didn’t last, it’s a machine. Kneading is a machine, clothes-washing is a machine. That time was poverty. From Monday to Saturday we would patch our children’s clothes. We would put patches on them. We would cut one, we would put it on one, we would put patches on it. Like so.

contents.textus: 165. I. Uʕdo swóʕoyo, háwxayo, u+ʕamo sawíʕoyo, məqqa dəmmat. Latyo xud meqəm.
contents.versio: 165. Now it is plenty, it’s like so, people are satisfied, so to speak. It is not like earlier.

contents.textus: 166. N. Škur mine d Ăḷo, ǧule qṭiʕe haw kolawšina.
contents.versio: 166. Thank God for it, we don’t wear torn clothes anymore.

contents.textus: 167. I. Am+mayaṯxu áydarbo saymū́twanne bu+zabnawo? Gúbewayne? Məš‿šəkl u+hnaṯxu?
contents.versio: 167. How would you get water at that time? Were they cisterns? What kind’s your whatsit?

contents.textus: 168. N. E, ašǝ́r gúbewayne.
contents.versio: 168. Yes, they really were cisterns.

contents.textus: 169. I. Kulle gúbewayne?
contents.versio: 169. Were all of them cisterns?

contents.textus: 170. N. Kulle gúbewayne.
contents.versio: 170. All of them were cisterns.

contents.textus: 171. I. Nuqlūtwa maye?
contents.versio: 171. Would you transport water?

contents.textus: 172. N. E, ašǝ́r nuqlíwayna, mašraṭ. U+gubayḏan, kəmmina čalá ḥažire, kalé harke. U+yawmo ḥḏaʕ̥ṣar+gḏone dmaye məṭyówayno, yawme d̥šabṯo.
contents.versio: 172. Yes, for sure we used to bring (it) back, believe it or not. Our cistern, we call (it) çala ḥejîrê, here it is. On one day, I would bring back eleven jugs of water, Saturdays.

contents.textus: 173. I. Ba+gḏone nuqlūtwa?
contents.versio: 173. Would you transport it in jugs?

contents.textus: 174. N. Ba+gḏone ʕal kaṯpan, ŭ mašraṭ ha u+baytano dlaltaḥ, du+săwā̀l, maḥtówayno ḥa ʕal ḥaṣi ŭ ḥa ʕal kaṯpi. Məd̥‿d̥owewa maḥtašiye, bas+sablat ŭ bat+tanak̇e me k̇arborán, me Daywán nuqlíwayna. Hawxa.
contents.versio: 174. In jugs on our shoulders, and believe it or not, this here house down there, the livestock one, I would bring one on my back, and one on my shoulder. Whenever there would be a drought, we would transport it in donkey saddles and containers from Karboran, from Daywan. Like so.

contents.textus: 175. E, uʕdo škur mene d Aloho, d̥owutu sāġ! Kalkó hawyo ʕayno. Kalé u+məslə̀q lawġul, məqqa dəbʕat.  An+naʕimayḏan bi+pelaṯe mḥalle u+paṭòz̥. Ha ha, kul tre+xabre gdoṯənwa moḥənwa ruḥayye qmu+dūš! E l Aloho maʕmaḷḷe i+arʕo!
contents.versio: 175. Right, now thanks to God, God bless you (lit. ‘may you be well’)! Now a well has appeared. Here’s a tap inside, as much as you want. Our children recently worked the threshing machine. Hey, hey, every other minute (lit. ‘every two words’), they would come and take a shower. Yes, God built the earth.

contents.textus: 176. I. Háwxayo.
contents.versio: 176. It’s like so.

contents.textus: 177. N. Ánnaqqa be áydarbo gdobina u+ǧăwabayḏan?!
contents.versio: 177. Now then, how are we going to give our response (to God)?

contents.textus: 178. I. E, bəṯr məd aṯat, dəmmina, me Bequsyone, hani am+medonani kulle, ʕayišatte bi+Derqube?
contents.versio: 178. Right, after you came here, so to speak, from Bequsyone, all these things, you experienced them in Derqube?

contents.textus: 179. N. E, Aḷah!
contents.versio: 179. Yes, by God!

contents.textus: 180. I. Hani kulle bann+əšne d̥fayiti, yani?
contents.versio: 180. All these in the years that have passed, that is?

contents.textus: 181. N. E, Aḷah!
contents.versio: 181. Yes, by God!

contents.textus: 182. I. Ḥamši+əšne, yani?
contents.versio: 182. Fifty years, that is?

contents.textus: 183. N. Hani, kibe əšti+šnaye ...
contents.versio: 183. These, it could be sixty years …

contents.textus: 184. I. Əšti+šnayo bu+šəklano...
contents.versio: 184. Sixty years, more or less (lit. ‘in this form’) …

contents.textus: 185. N. E, hani əští, ḥamməš+ŭ+əšti+šnaye daṯyono larke. Ánnaqqa mi+zuḥṯo mu+ṭăraf di+ṭayuṯo, Aloho maṣtar! Kul+yawmo ḥăramiye, kul+yawmo, hani ánnaqqa bu+waxtano ... Ánnaqqa məḷḷi ... U+yawmawo, kətwa hən armnoye, ləḏʕayno d̥kənne armnoye. Aṯən hánəkstene, yani, KfaqiraK, səmme šeyolo mini. Xačo aṯi sə́mleli terǧămaniye. Ləḏʕayno armnóyene. Ǧġilina disa, əmmono, ‘Ašǝ́r aq+qoruǧiyani lo ʕal aṭ+ṭălăba kəmšayli, ʕal am+măramaṯṯe. Kəmmi, ‘tre+bote ṣuróyene, maḥtina mede bəqḏolayye, dmaṭaʕni, fayšo i+qriṯo elan’.
contents.versio: 185. Yes, these sixty, sixty-five years since I came here. Now then, out of the fear for the sake of Islam, God forbid! Every day thieves, every day, these one, now then at this time … Now then, I said ... That day, there were some Armenians, I didn’t know that they were Armenians. Along came those ones, like, Kthe poor things,K they asked me a question. Xačo came and translated for me. I didn’t know they were Armenians. We spoke once more, I say, ‘Really, these village guards don’t seek insurgents, (but rather) their own ends. They say, ‘These are two Syriac houses, let’s pin something on them, so that they get packing, the village would be left to us.’

contents.textus: 186. I. Grəšxu ġắlăbe zaḥme maq+qoruǧiye?
contents.versio: 186. Did you get a lot of trouble from the village guards?

contents.textus: 187. N. Ooo ma mede! Ašǝ́r maḥəšmíwayna, lo+mašrìwayna dmaqərṭina, maqərṭíwayna lo+mašrìwayna dmaḥəšmina... moḥə́nwaylan! ‘Yaḷḷa, kobútənne laḥmo?’ Bad+dugle ba+hne ... Hul úʕdoste, hul úʕdostene, hul úʕdoste kəmmi, u+qŭnaġaṯṯe Bequsyono ŭ Derqúbeyo. Əmmono: ḥeḏoran hawír, Ăḷo, kosaymi gəlh dəḥdóḏeste, xəlle ḥḏoḏe, qṭəlle ḥḏoḏe. Hawxa, li+bəṭriye xila galdayye. Hawxa, mašfaʕlan ʕəmran hawxa.
contents.versio: 187. Oh, The thing (we suffered from village guards)! Really, were we to have dinner, we wouldn’t hope to have breakfast. Were we to have breakfast, we wouldn’t hope to have dinner … they would beat us! ‘By God, do you give them bread?’ By lies, by whatsit … Until now, until now, until now they say that Bequsyone and Derqube are their safe house (lit. ‘hotel’). I say, everywhere around us, gosh, they make complaints about each other too, they ate each other, they killed each other. So, affluence ate them up. So, we spent our life like so.

contents.textus: 188. I. Yani, ḥaye lo+basime mašfaʕxu bi+qriṯo di+Derqube?
contents.versio: 188. That is, you spent an unpleasant life in the village of Derqube?

contents.textus: 189. N. E, ašǝ́r, lo+basime mašfaʕlan, d̥owutu sāġ, uʕdo ʕəmro basímoyo.
contents.versio: 189. Yes, really, we spent an unpleasant one, God bless you, now life is pleasant.

contents.textus: 190. I. Uʕdo basímoyo?
contents.versio: 190. Now it’s pleasant?

contents.textus: 191. N. E, uʕdo basímoyo, škur mine d Ăḷo, hul uʕdo basímoyo. Ǧaylā́n aṯi, u+darbo hawi, maye kito, ŭ aq+qanyonayḏan bal+lalyani ševadarne. Gnune, ḥaramiye lo+fāš! Ăḷo bu+lalyo+ḥreno, lu+dewo nkətle tre, arwonk̇o ŭ tərto, me diḏan, bramšəl mdarmníwayla. Kanné ba+d̥koṯani márfyene. ŭ zyónestene, haw kodawrina, ḥəngi kosaymi a+zyonayḏan. E, i+dukṯo d̥kətyo tele, səmlan marke tele hawī́r ʕal i+čawraṯe hul doṯe qmi+ʕito. Bgawa di+tele zrəʕlan ḥeṭe, ḥəmṣe ŭ karme, wăki a+ḥrene marfəllan bdav du+săwā̀l. Zyóneste haw kowe.
contents.versio: 191. Yes, now it is pleasant, thanks to God, up to now it is pleasant. Electlicity came, the road appeared, there is water, and our cattle spend these nights outside. Thievery and thieves disappeared! Gosh, last night a wolf bit two (animals), a calf and a cow, of ours, last night they treated the latter. Over there, in these places, they are ranging free. And crop damage too, we do not plough it anymore, since they damage our crops. Right, the place where there is a wire fence―we made from here a fence all around the neighbourhood till it comes to the front of the church―inside the fence we sowed wheat, chickpeas, and grapevines, while the others we abandoned to the livestock. There is no more crop damage, too.

contents.textus: 192. I. Ǧġeni mu+lešono suryoyo ŭ mu+kurdi mən lešone+ḥrene kuḏʕat?
contents.versio: 192. Beside Syriac and Kurdish, what other languages do you know?

contents.textus: 193. N. Ašǝ́r lo+kuḏʕono tə+mede...
contents.versio: 193. I really don’t know anything else.

contents.textus: 194. I. Tərki kuḏʕat?
contents.versio: 194. Do you know Turkish?

contents.textus: 195. N. Lo, e, lo, lo.  ínaqqa doṯənwa i+ʕaskar, ǧare ... ġəlbá əṯyowa i+ʕaskar larke. Yani hawxa kofəhmono xabre, naxwa lo+kuḏʕono.
contents.versio: 195. No, right, no, no. When the military came, sometimes … the soldiers often came here. Like, so I understand some words, otherwise I don’t know.

contents.textus: 196. I. Bas an+naʕimaṯxu kulle qralle, an+naʕime?
contents.versio: 196. But all your children studied it, the kids?

contents.textus: 197. N. E, škur m ăḷo, škur m ăḷo, qralle, qralle kulle.
contents.versio: 197. Yes, thanks to God, thanks to God, they studied it, all of them studied it.

contents.textus: 198. I. Uʕdo bas u+ʕAvdo kətlax harke?
contents.versio: 198. Now, you have only ʕAvdo with you here?

contents.textus: 199. N. ʕAvdo ŭ ha hano Əndrawos.
contents.versio: 199. ʕAvdo and this here Əndrawos.

contents.textus: 200. I. A+trene, a+trene?
contents.versio: 200. Both are, both are?

contents.textus: 201. N. Hano u+faqir bēkaryo, ŭ hawo kətle, d̥owat sāġ, əšto+šawʕo+naʕime.
contents.versio: 201. This poor thing is a bachelor, and that one, God bless you, has six or seven children.

contents.textus: 202. I. ăḷo ṭoralle.
contents.versio: 202. May God permit them (their share).

contents.textus: 203. N. ăḷo ṭore sáhmuxste.
contents.versio: 203. May God permit your share too.

contents.textus: 204. I. U+ḥolo kfoyaš? Yani u...
contents.versio: 204. Is Uncle alive? Like the…

contents.textus: 205. N. Mḥase, hani šwaʕ+əšnaye.
contents.versio: 205. He passed away, these seven years (ago).

contents.textus: 206. I. Mḥase. Ăḷo mḥasele!
contents.versio: 206. He passed away. May God bless him!

contents.textus: 207. N. Šawʕo bəšwəṭ māṯ, ŭ hul uʕdo ... hani šwaʕ ... uʕdo koqolab ba+tmone.
contents.versio: 207. He died February 7th, and until now… these seven… now it’s turning eight.

contents.textus: 208. I. Ăloho mḥasele!
contents.versio: 208. May God bless him!

contents.textus: 209. N. Miḥasən miṯux!
contents.versio: 209. May your dead be blessed.

contents.textus: 210. I. Mən kiban dəḏʕina ʕal emax ŭ babax? Yani, u+mede dəḥzelax mənne, áydarbowayne? Áykowayne?
contents.versio: 210. What can we learn about your mother and father? That is, the things that you saw from them, how were they? Where were they?

contents.textus: 211. N. E, ma lo+kəmmallux ʕəmri!? ʕƏmri ḥamməš+šnaye, emi mayiṯo. Edi qašti maḥkowa, qašti maḥkowa: bu+Fərmā̀n kǝ́twayle lbabi ṗire+ḥreto. Mayiṯo mi+ wazaṭiye, mi+bexwaditiye, mi+raziliye, mayiṯo. Bu+Fərman, u+zlām d̥qašti qṭīl bu+Fərman. ŭ qašti kə́twayla tre+aḥunone. Azzəhən. Ḥa mballe lu+safarballə̀k, lo+daʕər. ŭ ḥa, kə́twayle k̇urrək̇o ʕal u+ʕarbolo, māṯ. Makə́mwayla ruḥa híyaste xud dayrayto. Makəmla ruḥa xud dayrayto. Fayišo, ínaqqa dʔemi ... edi, kə́twayla tarte+k̇ačk̇at, ŭ qṭīl u+zlamayḏa. Əzzawa l Məḏyaḏ. Šoḏənwa meqəm, balki kuḏʕat! Hawxa, ketono, ʕuzliwa. Dulabo hawxa. Gursiwa hul dobə́nwanne haqqa dlaḥmo, uxliwa. Uxliwa, k̇ačk̇e me diḏa b Mə́ḏyaḏste mayiṯo. Fayišo emi. Maqḏalle hawxa hul daṯən aq+qusnoye li+qriṯo. Aṯən aq+qusnoye li+qriṯo, aṯyo li+qriṯo.
contents.versio: 211. Yes, am I not telling you my life!? Age five, my mother died. Then, my grandmother used to tell a story, my grandmother used to tell a story: during the Firman, my father had another wife. She died from exhaustion, from estrangement, from deprivation. During the Firman, my grandmother’s husband was killed in the Firman. And my grandmother had two brothers. They went away. One, they conscripted him, he did not come back. And the other one, he kept a boy on a sieve, he died. She had dressed herself in black (lit. ‘she made herself black’) like a nun. She dressed herself in black like a nun. She stayed, when my mother ... then, she had two daughters, and her husband was killed. She used to go to Midyat. Back then, they would card, maybe you know! So, the cotton, they would spin. A spinning wheel, like so. They would grind until they would give them this much bread, they would eat it. They would eat it, one of her daughters died in Midyat, too. My mother survived. They managed like so until the Bequsyonians came back to the village. The Bequsyonians came back to the village, (so) she came back to the village.

contents.textus: 212. I. Qay? Ma aq+qusnoye áykowayne?
contents.versio: 212. Why? Where were the Beqŭsyonians?

contents.textus: 213. N. Azzə́n, tayihi ínaqqa du+Fərmā̀n!
contents.versio: 213. They went away, they fled at the time of the Firman!

contents.textus: 214. I. Ha, bu+Fərmā̀n tayihiwa hǝ́nnəkste ...
contents.versio: 214. So, during the Firman those ones had scattered as well ...

contents.textus: 215. N. E, tayihi, azzehən, fayiši ... Bequsyone xliṯo ... Bu+Fərmā̀n, əmmi, əmmi ‘g̊ˠqom u+Fərman!’ Eeee... ḥəmyoni ŭ u+aḥuno Ṣaliba sayġiwa ... i+naqqayo ... uʕdo ... latwa xud uʕdo ... i+goro di+ʕito, qay kə́pwayla qəmṯo (u+maḏbḥo... i+məqbara ʕeláytowa, tlalle uʕdo u+ʕafro mina). Kosayġila baʕ+ʕole.
contents.versio: 215. Yes, they scattered, they went away, they stayed... Bequsyone empty... In the Firman, they said, they said, ‘The Firman is coming!’  Yesss, my father-in-law and his brother Saliba were fortifying … that time … now… it was not like now… the roof of the church, it hardly had any height (the altar ... the cemetery was high up, now they have taken the soil from it). They were fortifying it with briars.

contents.textus: 216. I. Bmən?
contents.versio: 216. With what?

contents.textus: 217. N. Baʕ+ʕole, bad+dərrəhā̀t!
contents.versio: 217. With briars, with brambles!

contents.textus: 218. I. Bad+dərrəhā̀t!
contents.versio: 218. With brambles!

contents.textus: 219. N. E, aṯi. Lu+mŭdūr ṭləble. Ḥaǧi Aġá. Aġá dbe Ḥaǧoye Xortə́k̇. Howewa harke qariwo bi+Mărank̇e. Mtarasle bəṯre, omar, ‘Tux!’ Azzeyo, omar, ‘Danḥo, Ṣaliba mə‿kosaymutu?’ Bi+àdroda xaləṣ, ʕal i+səstayḏe rawixo. Omar, ‘Mə kosaymu... ʕal me ... mə‿kosōm?’ Əmmi, ‘ăḷo, kosōm?’ Kəmmi, ‘Fə́rmanyo, kosayġina i+goro dʕoṣina eba...’ Omar, ‘De kazzí gab u+mŭdū̀r, hul doṯeno.’ Azzé gab u+mŭdū̀r, ‘Mŭdū́r afandí,’ drele šlomo.  – ‘KHūnK b̥xēr aṯat, flān...’
contents.versio: 219. Yes, he came. The superintendant summoned him. Haǧi [Rasho?] Agha. Agha of the Ḥaǧo Xortək family. He used to live near here, in Maranke. He sent for him, he said, “Come!” He went and said, “Danḥo, Saliba what are you doing?” He passed by the threshing floor, riding on his horse. He says, “What are you do... upon ... what is he doing?” They say, “Gosh, ‘he is doing?’!” They say, ‘It is a Firman, we are fortifying the roof in order to fight back on it…’ He says, ‘I am going to the superintendant, (wait) until I come back.’ He went to the superintendant. ‘Mister superintendant, sir,’ he greeted him.  – ‘You are welcome, etc…’

contents.textus: 220. Omar, ‘Mŭdū́r afandí mə‿kubʕat? Xēryo mtaraslux bəṯri?’
contents.versio: 220. He (Haǧi Aġa) says, “Mister superintendant, sir, what do you want? It’s a good thing you sent for me?” (26.21)

contents.textus: 221. Omar, omar, ‘Kətlux tlaṯ+qəryawoṯe ṣuroye. D̥ḥa mənne romaš gəmfašaṇṇo riṣaṣ ŭ maḥatno bəqḏolux...’ Omar, ‘Ónoste ʕal hawxa kəmšayalno! Komaṇṇo be ema xulṣina mənne? B̥ḥila šərʕí! Məd nafəq, omar, ‘Komaṇṇux, — henuka mofaqle u+maktùb qrele, omar — “D̥ḥa mənne romaš, gəmfašaṇṇo riṣaṣ, maḥatno bəqḏolux!”’ Hedika nafəq <me> gab u+mŭdū̀r.
contents.versio: 221. He says, he says, ‘You have three Syriac villages. If one of them stirs, I will melt tin and pour it down your throat!’ He says, ‘Me too, I am seeking such a thing! I say, when are we going to get rid of them?’ As a white lie (lit. ‘justified ruse’)! As he left, he says, ‘I am telling you’ — once more he took out the letter, he read it, he says — ‘If one of them stirs, I will melt tin and pour it down your throat!’ Then he left the superintendent.

contents.textus: 222. Əmmiwa be Laḥdə́k̇ b̥ k̇árboran. Prū́ṭwayne. Húlalle xabro. Omar, ‘Lázəmyo...’  (d̥owat sāġ! Hánoste ḥawráyxuyo? B̥xēr aṯat yade!). Omar, ‘Lázəmyo dʔoṯutu ádlalyo li+Mărank̇e!” Mərle lbe Laḥdə́k̇ b̥ k̇árboran.
contents.versio: 222. They called them the Laḥdək̇ family in Karboran. They were Protestants. He brought word to them. He says, ‘You must (Be well, is this also your friend? You are welcome dear!) He says, ‘You must come to Mărank̇e tonight!’ He told the Laḥdək̇ family in Karboran.

contents.textus: 223. W aṯi məḷḷe élanstene, lḥəmyoni ŭ lu+aḥuno, omar, ‘Lázəmyo nḥatu li+Mărank̇e! U+Fərmanaṯxu mi+dawla qām, laybi mḥaménanxu! Nḥatu li+Mărank̇e!’ An+nošayḏan kə́pwalle ʕəṣro+bote harke, naḥiti li+Mărank̇e, ŭ be Laḥdək̇ste aṯən! Kə́twayle ḥḏaḥṣar+abne. Mtarasle ann+abne ŭ ab+brazìn ŭ ann+aḥunone aʕmayye, maḥtile bu+quṣro d̥ Ḥaḥ. Maḥtile bu+quṣro d̥ Ḥaḥ, Azzé li+naqabe d Bequsyone. (Azzúx l Bequsyone? I+naqabe dʕawwə́l kobəlqat aʕla.) Omar, ‘Brawo qusnoye qām u+Fərmanaṯxu mi+dawla! Laybi mḥamenalxu, qumu l Ḥaḥ!” Laq+qusnòyeste maṭʕanne azzehən l Ḥāḥ.
contents.versio: 223. And he came and said to us as well, to my father in-law and the brother, he says, ‘You must go down to Mărank̇e! Your Firman has come from the government; I am unable to defend you. Go down to Mărank̇e!’ Our people numbered ten houses here, they went down to Mărank̇e, and the Laḥdək̇ family also came. He had eleven sons. He sent the sons, nephews, and brothers with them, he put them in the castle of Ḥāḥ. He put them in the castle of Ḥāḥ. He went to the Bequsyone mountain pass (Did you go to Bequsyone? The mountain pass where you first view it). He says, ‘Oh brother! Beqŭsyonians, your Firman has come from the government, I am unable to defend you, go up to Ḥāḥ!’ The Beqŭsyonians also packed up and went to Ḥāḥ.

contents.textus: 224. Kəmmi, ‘I+teno d Haró...,’ hul uʕdo lo+kuḏʕono ‘i+teno d Haró’ áyna-o. Kalayo bu+dyarawo d̥qəm Ḥaḥ, bdav d Bequsyone ... ŭ ha ánnaqqa komaḥkən, yani, komaḥkəllan, lo+ḥzelan aḥna d̥komaḥkəllan.
contents.versio: 224. They say, ‘Haro’s fig tree…’ Until now, I do not know which one is ‘Haro’s fig tree’. It’s right there, on that hill that is in front of Ḥāḥ, towards Bequsyone … And nowadays, they tell a story, like, they tell us a story, we have not seen what they tell us.

contents.textus: 225. Əmmi aq+qamoye, mə́rralle, mərre lmore du+quṣro, ‘Hak̇a g̊ḥowútəllan, maru: Šfaʕu l ʕíwardo! ŭ hak̇a lo+g̊ḥowùtəllan, maru: Ftaḥu u+tarʕo du+quṣro! Saliqi. (28: 02) ‘Qusnoye, šfaʕu l ʕíwardo, darbo layt bu+quṣro!” Ftīḥ u+tarʕo du+quṣro šanayye, žboy dloṯənne. Aṯən, əmmi, aq+qamoye čiki bu+quṣro, aḥ+ḥaroye fayiši si+teno d Haró.
contents.versio: 225. The first ones say, they told him, they told the lord of the castle, ‘If you accept us, say, ‘Keep going to ʕIwardo!’ If you do not accept us, say, ‘Open the castle gate!’ They went up. ‘Beqŭsyonians, keep going to ʕIwardo, there is no room in the castle!’ The castle gate opened for them, lest they enter. They came, they say, the first ones sneaked into the castle, the last ones stayed beside Haro’s fig tree.

contents.textus: 226. Aṯyo i+kawmo, mṣafela Zāz, aṯyo laḥ+Ḥarbe d Gawro kəmmina, kīt qriṯo, hawxa ḥarbe bayn l Bequsyone ŭ l Ḥāḥ, b̥qarʕe d̥ṭuro manək. Aṯən ltamo, kətwa gubo tamo, mašəġġe iḏayye ŭ foṯayye, štalle, ḥərre ga aq+qŭsnoye azzə́n l Ḥaḥ. Mḥalle kmo+tfəngat mənne, áḥnaste, ar+rezanayḏan―Šaʕe d be-Yaḥqo, Asmar d be-Masʕəd, Murad d be Laʕgo, Gawriye d be Mŭqsi, ar+rezánatwayne, bətfə́ngatwayne―madʕarre aʕlayye. Ḥaǧo omar ‘Ṣabbavno! Male Ḥanuno ŭ Qanuno... kalé b Bequsyone, zoxu lu+māl di+arʕo, lo+quṭlutu aq+qusnoye!’
contents.versio: 226. The mob came, it cleansed Zāz, it came to what we call the Ruins of Gawro, there is a village, like so, some ruins between Bequsyone and Ḥāḥ, on top of one of those mountains. They came there, there was a cistern there, they washed their hands and faces, they drank, they looked and hey, Beqŭsyonians had gone to Ḥāḥ. They shot several rifles at them, and we too, our leaders―Šaʕe Yaḥqo, Asmar Masʕəd, Murad Laʕgo and Gawriye Muqsi were the leaders, they had guns―they responded to them. Haǧo says, ‘Sons of bitches! The property of Hanuno and Qanuno … Here it is in Bequsyone, go for the riches of the land, do not kill the Bequsyonians!’

contents.textus: 227. Edi šridi lu+māl di+arʕo, ʕeze ŭ qanyone, lḥefat ŭ ṣəfər, u+māl di+arʕo. Naḥiti l Bequsyone. Qusnoye lə+qṭīl! Kulle čiki bu+quṣro. Fayiši arbʕi+yawme bu+quṣro. Ánnaqqa ḥăšă (gŭle qəm nḥirayxu) towalā́t latwa, ŭ bi+də̀rtowa, ŭ ḥemo, ŭ qáyṭowa. Mu+həlm+ŭ+gəlm dəḥḏoḏe, ŭ mu+reḥo, nafəl eš baynaṯṯe. H̱moṯi əmmo, ‘Tleṯi+nafšoṯo b̥ḥa yawmo qwəḷḷan bi+dərto du+quṣro.’
contents.versio: 227. Then they went after the riches of the land, goats and cattle, quilts and copperware, the riches of the land. They went down to Bequsyone. The Beqŭsyonians were not killed! All of them sneaked into the castle. They stayed forty days in the castle. Now then, excuse me (a rose for your noses!), there was no toilet, and it was in the courtyard, and it was hot and summer. From each other’s breath-shmeath and from the smell, a plague spread among them. My mother-in-law says, ‘One day, we buried thirty people in the courtyard of the castle’.

contents.textus: 228. Edi kəmmallux. Edi azzehən, nafiqi. Aṯi Šex Fatḥalla d be ..., me ʕƏntáb, ŭ aṯi be Čalabine ŭ i+ḥkume aṯyo. Lawən ʕal baxt di+ḥkume hul dlaṯi u+Šex, ŭ edi ftəḥḥe u+tarʕo du+quṣro. Ftəḥḥe u+tarʕo du+quṣro.
contents.versio: 228. Then, I’ll tell you. Then they went away, they headed out. Sheikh Fatḥullah of the … family, from ʕƏntab, came, and it was the Čelebi family who came, and the government came. They did not trust the government as long as the sheikh hadn’t come, and then they opened the door of the castle. They opened the door of the castle.

contents.textus: 229. Mede latwa. Disa bizi ʕal aṭ+ṭaye. Disa hawən greʕe laṭ+ṭaye, ruʕye ŭ baqore ŭ dawore, azzə́n disa bayn aṭ+ṭaye. Azzə́n bayn aṭ+ṭaye bәkmo+šnaye, hul dʔaṯən edi li+qriṯo. E hawxa.
contents.versio: 229. There was not anything left. Once again, they scattered among the Muslims. Once again, the Muslims had them as servants, shepherds, cowherds, and farmers, once again they went among the Muslims. They went among the Muslims for several years until they then came back to the village. Yes, like so.

contents.textus: 230. I. Hat koṯe lbolax dínaqqa Bequsyone ... kmo+bote kətwa eba, bu+zabnawo?
contents.versio: 230. I. Do you remember when Bequsyone … how many houses were there in it, at that time?

contents.textus: 231. N. Kə̀pwayla mo+ŭ+ḥamši, tartemo+bote, ġắlăbewayne. Mo+ŭ+ḥamši+bòtewayne, tartemo+bòtewayne.
contents.versio: 231. N. It contained one hundred and fifty, two hundred houses, they were many. There were one hundred and fifty houses, there were two hundred houses.

contents.textus: 232. I. Mu+zabno d̥koṯe lbolax...
contents.versio: 232. From the time that you remember …

contents.textus: 233. N. E, i+qriṯo ʕamə́rtowa. Yani, u+qamoyo dnafəq me Bequsyone, əəə... Amsiḥ əmmíwaynale, u+abro d̥ Ṣawme Mírək̇e, u+aḥuno d̥qašo Usəv. Balki šamiʕat bəšme. Kowe yani u+mərhovaṯxu, u+abro du+ʕammo, u+ḥaṯnaṯxu Brahim, u+ḥaṯnaṯxu da+kfarzòyeyo, hawxa. Edi mə‿ftīḥ u+darbano, məqmi+ṭayuṯo, band ŭ barbăriye, məqəm ḥḏoḏe, hə́nnəkste...
contents.versio: 233. Yes, the village was established (lit. ‘built’). Like, the first one who left Bequsyone…. We called him Amsiḥ, the son of Ṣawme Mirəke and the brother of Fr Usəv. Maybe you have heard his name. He is your conjugal kin, his cousin, your in-law Brahim, he is your Kfarzean in-law (lit. ‘your in-law of the Kfarzeans’), like so. Then, when this way opened, away from Islam, sectarianism, and partisanship, away from each other, they too…

contents.textus: 234. I. Howewa barbăriye b Bequsyóneste?
contents.versio: 234. I. Was there partisanship in Bequsyone as well?

contents.textus: 235. N. Hul úʕdoste barbăríyeyo!
contents.versio: 235. N. Until now even there is partisanship!

contents.textus: 236. I. E ʕal mən? Yani, Dakšuriye ŭ Haverk̇iye?
contents.versio: 236. I. Because of what? Like, the Dakshori and the Havarki?

contents.textus: 237. N. Lo, lo, Haverk̇iye lo+fāš!
contents.versio: 237. No, no, the Havarki did not survive.

contents.textus: 238. I. Mənwa i+măsale?
contents.versio: 238. What was the problem?

contents.textus: 239. N. Haverk̇iye lo+fāš. Mašraṭ, e, məḷḷi aḥna Havérk̇iwayna. Li+ḥkume maqə́mlalan, mašraṭ ġaman xila. ḥəngi aṭ+ṭaye mʕantiwa minan, əmmi d ... aq+qoruǧiye mʕantiwa minan, əmmi, ‘Dhowe qaṭlo ba+d̥koṯani, gəzzoxu eba! B Aloho, i+ḥkume əmmo gdobanxu ʕárabatste! Mede du+baxto! Daʔəm gabánwayne, uxliwa ŭ šotənwa. Dhowənwa emeklí ma+d̥koṯani, əmmiwa “Mšāl b̥kēf d̥ TtayzaT, konušqina iḏa, kəbʕina dəmfaḥlolan!
contents.versio: 239. N. The Havarki did not survive. Believe it or not, yes, I said we were Havarki. The government uprooted us, believe it or not, it worried about us. Because the Muslims hated us so much, they say that… the village guards hated us so much, they say, ‘If there is any killing in these places, you will be in the thick of it (lit. ‘you will go into it’)’. By God, the government says they will give you even cars! What an honour! They were always by our side, they would eat and drink. When they would become retired from these places, they would say, ‘Ask how auntie is doing (lit. ‘ask about the auntie’s well-being’), give her a kiss for us (lit. ‘we are kissing her hand’), we want her to forgive us’.

contents.textus: 240. Edi maqə́mmallan l Bequsyone, fayišina šwaʕ̥+šnaye xwiní b Bequsyone. Veǧa aq+qusnoye lo+mṫaḥmàllallan. Gah əmmiwa, ‘Haverk̇íyene’, gah əmmiwa, ‘ṭălắbane!’ Maqə́mmallan, maqə́mmallan. Tlaṯ+kore mḥállallan laq+qusnoye, hul d̥qayimina. Yani zəríyatwayna: ono ŭ u+qašo ŭ u+muxtā̀r. Emi ŭ i+emaṯṯe bnoṯo dʕammone ḥaq. ŭ dámṯiste i+ḥoṯo du+ḥàsyoyo ŭ i+barṯo du+ʕammo du+qašo ŭ du+muxtārwa.
contents.versio: 240. Then they uprooted us to Bequsyone, we stayed seven years like pariahs in Bequsyone. Now then, the Beqŭsyonians, they could not stand us. Sometimes they said, ‘They are Havarki’, sometimes they said, ‘They are insurgents!’ They uprooted us, they uprooted us. Three times the people of Bequsyone beat us until we left. Like, we were family: I, the priest, and the village headman. My mother and their mother, real cousins. And my sister in-law as well, she is the sister of a bishop and the cousin of the priest and the village headman.

contents.textus: 241. Mašraṭ tlaṯ+kore mḥállallan, mofáqqallan. Fayišina šwaʕ̥+šne mə‿ftīḥ u+darbo daq+qəryawoṯe. Mraǧaʕlan, huwwe daṣṭə́r diḏan, edi aṯina. ʕOmar baytux ŭ dəṯṯe tavda. Ann+avayani, lḥa me ... u+qašawo d̥koḥṓr b Mār Gawriye...
contents.versio: 241. Believe it or not, three times they beat us, they drove us away. We had stayed for seven years when the way to the villages was opened. We applied, they gave us permission, then we came. Thanks to you and them together! These buildings, someone from… that priest that looks after Mor Gabriel…

contents.textus: 242. I. Hans?
contents.versio: 242. Hans?

contents.textus: 243. N. Mdagele əšti+alfo aʕman!
contents.versio: 243. He swindled us sixty thousand (i.e., liras)!

contents.textus: 244. I. Hans Hollerweger...
contents.versio: 244. Hans Hollerweger…

contents.textus: 245. N. E, e. Ánnaqqa mṭəlle. B Mār Gawriye kəmmi, mərre, ‘Aq+qəryawoṯe kulle daʕiri...” Húlelan arbʕi, ŭ aʕ+ʕəsri+ḥrene lúwallanne. Edi ʕomar baytux ŭ dəṯṯe, hən lan+naʕimayḏan, hən lar+roḥumayḏan. Dost xŭdani, an+naʕime, ax+xwarzinaṯxu da+ kfarzoye, d Həndo ŭ hanək...
contents.versio: 245. Then he brought it. In Mor Gabriel, they say, they said, ‘All the villages have returned…’ He gave us forty, but they did not give us the other twenty. Then thanks to you and them, our children (gave) some, our friends (gave) some. Pals like these ones, the children, your Kfarzean nephews (lit. ‘your nephews of the Kfarzeans’), Həndo’s and the like …

contents.textus: 246. I. Koḏaʕna...
contents.versio: 246. I know her…

contents.textus: 247. N. Hən marke ŭ hən marke, l Aloho maqəḏyole. Ann+avayani, yani dəmmat, bele, balki muklo ŭ maštyo hawi əšmo, elo ann+avayani, dawla d ăḷo driše du+ʕamo, lu+ʕamo maʕmáḷḷelanne, ŭ hawxa. Ha maṭina luʕdo, ṫəžmərra sāġ! Əhə...
contents.versio: 247. Some from here and some from there, God made it happen. These buildings, like, you say, yes, probably food and drink were in short supply (lit. ‘became little’), but the buildings, thanks to the people, the people built them for us, and so forth. Here we have come to now, be well for my sake! Heh.

contents.textus: 248. I. Ṫəžmərra sāġṫə́r!
contents.versio: 248. Be even better for my sake!

contents.textus: 1. Kətwa latwa rab̰‿m Ăḷo latwa. Ḥaq, ḥaq, ḥaq!
contents.versio: 1. It was, it wasn’t, greater than God there wasn’t. Truth! Truth! Truth!

contents.textus: 2. Kətwa keze. Malaxla bu+darbo, malaxla bu+darbo, maṭyo lu+baqoro.
contents.versio: 2. There was a beetle. She went along a road, she went along a road, she met a cowherd.

contents.textus: 3. Omar, ‘Keze qwərto, lay gəzzáx?’ Əmmo, K‘K̇úla+bávē+kḗzē’.K
contents.versio: 3. He says, ‘You silly beetle, where are you going?’ She says, K‘To hell with “you beetle”!’ K

contents.textus: 4. Omar, ‘Məd‿domaṇṇax?’—‘Mar, “Naze, názeliya, du+čarčaf yaroqo, du+ṣʕuno semoqo, lay gəzzáx?”’
contents.versio: 4. He says, ‘What shall I call you?’ —‘Say, “Darling, delightful one! She of the green veil, she of the red shoes, where are you going?”’

contents.textus: 5. Əmmo, ‘Naze, názeliya, du+čarčaf yaroqo, du+ṣʕuno semoqo, lay gəzzáx?’
contents.versio: 5. She (i.e., he) says, ‘Darling, delightful one, she of the green veil, she of the red shoes, where are you going?’

contents.textus: 6. Əmmo, ‘Gəzzí saymalli ḥa’. Omar, ‘Tax! Ono ŭ hat saymina ḥḏoḏe!’
contents.versio: 6. She says, ‘I am going to marry a man’. He says, ‘Come! You and I should marry each other’.
